description: SLW Hub Round 1: 1.3 GHz, 433.59 MHz and 2.45 GHz sphere experiments with rod attenuators, a microwave oven experiment, a To-Do list, a range finder and a Joule-loss analysis.
text: Round 1 · SLW Hub · draft v0.1 Round 1: three sphere experiments and a microwave oven Each experiment uses a transmitting sphere, a receiving sphere and a rod attenuator between them, with brass and W1 tool-steel rods cut to λ/2 for each band. The oven replaces the transmitting sphere at 2.45 GHz. We are testing hypotheses, not reporting detections. Tests of hypotheses, not results. Mainstream electrodynamics treats free-space radio as transverse (TEM). A longitudinal or scalar component is a hypothesis we are testing, and nothing on these pages claims that scalar or longitudinal waves have been detected. Values marked proposal are our suggestions and are not measured or sourced. Draft v0.1, 4 Oct 2026, written by Grok Bot for Dan Britton. The four benches 1.3 GHz sphere experiment (Experiment A) Frequency: 1296.000 MHz (λ = 231.3 mm) 3/4 in sphere TX and RX (K-Mac KB-1820) Rods: 115.66 mm (λ/2), 1/8 in, brass and W1 tool steel Plate: 6.00 x 6.00 x 0.50 in cast acrylic (152.4 x 152.4 x 12.7 mm) Open the page · To-do · Joule loss · Range finder 433.59 MHz sphere experiment (Experiment B) Frequency: 433.59 MHz (λ = 691.4 mm) 2.50 in ball TX and RX (K-Mac KB-2016), no balun; the Monstein and Wesley replication Rods: 346.00 mm (λ/2), 1/8 in, brass and W1 tool steel Plate: 15.00 x 15.00 x 0.50 in cast acrylic (381.0 x 381.0 x 12.7 mm) Open the page · To-do · Joule loss · Range finder 2.45 GHz sphere experiment (new) Frequency: 2450.0 MHz (λ = 122.4 mm) 3/4 in sphere TX and RX, same sphere as Experiment A Rods: 61.18 mm (λ/2), 1/8 in, brass and W1 tool steel Plate: 4.00 x 4.00 x 0.25 in cast acrylic (101.6 x 101.6 x 6.35 mm) proposal stubs 12.2 / 30.6 mm; nothing built yet Open the page · To-do · Joule loss · Range finder Microwave oven experiment The oven is its own 2.45 GHz transmitter A 3/4 in sphere is the detector Same controls as Experiment B, including the rod fixture Receive only, from outside; safety rules first Open the page · To-do · Power balance · Safety What every bench shares Baselines first: VNA S11 and S21 with the rods out, then the rods in, using the VNA how-to; spectrum-analyzer noise floor with the transmitter off. Rod scan: turn the rod array through φ and fit T = exp(-κ cos²φ) (Monstein and Wesley form), for brass and then W1. Range: tape-measure r, then compare with the range finder estimates (a tape is the truth, the estimates are hypotheses). Joule loss: compare κ between materials and bands, and read the limits on the Joule-loss page. Fixture position (proposal): repeat the rod scan with the fixture near the transmitter, midway and near the receiver, logging TX S11 as a loading check, and compare κ by station. Monstein and Wesley do not say where their array sat. See the Joule-loss page. Log everything: grounding state of the cage, instrument settings and raw files in every row. Tools and checklists To-Do list Checkboxes saved in your browser, grouped by experiment Rod delivery from Newport, fixtures, baselines, builds, oven Automatic range finder Phase slope, time domain, two-frequency, null counting Dipole direction finding for each band Calculator, CSV paste and plot Joule loss and power balance What the rod data can and cannot show Brass versus W1, skin depth, dissipated fraction VNA how-to VNA6000-A manual, calibration, S11 and S21 steps Rod jigs Acrylic plates and drilling patterns for the three bands Everything else All the earlier pages (Experiments C to G, the briefing, setup and shop pages, the Simulation Lab, papers) are kept exactly where they were. They are folded away so the focus stays on Round 1. description: Archive of other C×nuclei experiment channels (A–D, F–I). Main focus is Channel E on c-nuclei.html.
text: Archive · other C×nuclei candidates · 2026-09-06 Other candidate ideas (C × nuclei archive) Background sketches parked off the main Channel E page — wider-net candidates and theory extras kept for later retrieval. Educational only — no claim of measured nuclear effects. Front door: c-nuclei.html = Channel E focus (Hively chemical/EC lean, kit, buy list). This archive holds Channels A–D, F–I, Rentzber detail, wider-net citations, and the multi-channel experiment menu. ← Back to Channel E focus Theory upgrade · Rentzber (2026) Natan Rentzber, Scalar-Longitudinal Radiation in Extended Electrodynamics with Multipole Theory and a Compensated Source Model, arXiv:2608.19405 (2026). Conditional EED predictions — does not claim charge nonconservation in nature. Key takeaways for experiment design: Source: the scalar channel is sourced only by Λ = ∂ρ/∂t + ∇·J (continuity anomaly). Bound polarization / magnetization sources do not source C. Far-zone SLW: EL, B=0, C co-propagating; cos²θ dipole pattern vs Maxwell’s sin²θ. Detector corollary (critical design constraint): a conserved test current extracts no cycle-averaged energy from a pure incident SLW under the adopted field-only balance. Nuclear detectors therefore need either (a) coupling to residual EL / potentials, (b) an anomalous detector Λd, or (c) a non-adopted-current observable — phase, EFG, or electron density at the nucleus (EC). Ordinary ohmic pickup alone is the wrong primary meter for a pure SLW claim. Lineage (cite lightly as adjacent theory): van Vlaenderen & Waser; Minotti & Modanese detector papers. Why nuclei (the publishable hook) Nuclei carry charge multipoles, magnetic moments, and (for quadrupole nuclei) couple to electric field gradients (EFG). If C is a real scalar EM degree of freedom with energy density ∼ C²/(2μ), the open question is whether it couples to nuclear charge/current multipoles beyond ordinary E/B. That coupling — bounded, falsifiable, honestly framed — is what would make a paper. A null bound is publishable too. Rentzber’s energy-null for conserved currents pushes the menu toward EC density, EFG/NQR, PAC, Mössbauer, and phase / sideband observables rather than “just count betas near the launcher.” Proposed interaction channels (archive) Channel E lives on the main page. Everything else is below for retrieval. Channel A · charge / continuity Back-action of C onto nuclear charge EED’s source for C is (∂ρ/∂t + ∇·J). Nuclear transitions rearrange charge; a back-action of C onto nuclear charge density would appear as a phase or rate shift. Effective sketches (to be bounded experimentally): δHC ∼ gC · Qnuc · C or ∫ ρnuc C dV with gC a dimensionless coupling. For quadrupole nuclei, prefer δH ∼ (κ/2) Qij ∂i∂j χC where χC is a potential whose Laplacian relates to C. Keep honest: the microscopic operator is not settled — the experiment bounds effective couplings, it does not invent them. Channel B · EFG bridge (Hubler) · library · collaboration PAC / EFG as a nuclear readout Hubler (2023), J. Condensed Matter Nucl. Sci. 38, 78–88, uses perturbed angular correlation (PAC; 181Hf→181Ta) to measure EFG at the nucleus in PdH/D. That paper is AHE / phonon · LENR-adjacent — not a bifilar or Faraday-cage protocol (see Library). EFG is an ordinary electric-field-gradient observable at nuclear sites. An SLW-class longitudinal E (or a C-correlated gradient) that modulates the local EFG would be a legitimate, measurable nuclear readout — even if AHE/phonon claims stay adjacent and unlabeled as proven on this hub. Hubler 2023 PDF Channel C · spin / DNP · adjacent, not C proof Ventura–Sokol / Falcon / Alzofon as a parallel program Mainstream DNP/DNO (Jeffries, Dynamic Nuclear Orientation, 1963): microwave-driven transfer of electron polarization to nuclei near EPR — an accepted NMR-enhancement method. That is ordinary condensed-matter physics. Falcon Space / Mark Sokol (APEC coverage by Tim Ventura; public Falcon materials) test Alzofon’s hypothesis that nuclear orientation might affect apparent mass / inertia. Framing on this hub: Public sources only (e.g. Falcon DNO–mass PDF; Alzofon 1981 AIAA; Ventura/APEC interviews as journalism). S/X-band DNP inside a Faraday cage is a nuclear-spin control channel — useful as “nuclei as sensors/actuators.” Alzofon–Sokol inertia/gravity claims are speculative hypotheses, not accepted physics, and are not Hively C proof. Mapping: DNP is a parallel “nuclei as sensors/actuators” program this hub refuses to exclude; it is not evidence that dynamical C couples to nuclei. Keep as parallel adjacent — not primary. Channel D · decay rates · contested vs accepted (reframe) Contested solar / Fischbach claims vs accepted EC chemistry Contested (do not elevate): environmental / solar-modulation claims of decay-rate variation (Fischbach, Jenkins, and others). Metrology reviews (Pommé et al.; Norman/Cooper-style nulls) attribute many reported signals to systematics. Frame carefully: somewhat discussed / contested, not “well established.” Generic β Geiger counting alone is a weak primary channel. Accepted (elevate as the serious decay family): electron-capture (EC) rates that track electron density at the nucleus — especially 7Be chemical-host shifts (~0.1–1%). See Channel E. Proposal for any decay side channel near an SLW-class source: temperature / humidity / background locks — the same caution already on SW vs SLW. This is not evidence already in hand on this bench. Channel F · 14N NQR · tabletop EFG sensor Nuclear quadrupole resonance without CERN PAC 14N NQR (MHz) reads the EFG at nitrogen sites without a PAC collaboration. Homemade spectrometers exist (e.g. Hiblot / Canet-class fully homemade 14N NQR; modern SoC-FPGA compact NQR). Sensitivity is the hard part (cryo, averaging, sample mass). Experiment: NQR sample (e.g. NaNO2 / pharma 14N) co-located with an SLW bifilar/sleeve; look for line shift / broadening vs RF-off / TEM stub / Faraday wrap. Direct EFG bridge complementary to Hubler PAC (Channel B). Channel G · scalar Aharonov–Bohm / time-varying Φ · mainstream QM · SW-leaning Energy / phase shifts from potentials in (ideally) field-free regions Scalar AB: phase or energy from a time-varying scalar potential in regions where E and B are (ideally) zero. Neutron interferometry: Allman et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 68, 2409 (1992); Phys. Rev. A 48, 1799 (1993). Atom interferometry and related work. Energy-level sidebands from time-varying V(t) with E=0: Chiao et al., Phys. Rev. A 107, 042209 (2023). PDF now local in the Library (arXiv:2212.03437v2 preprint matching the published PRA). Mapping: closer to Hively SW (E=B=0, potentials/C) than to SLW. Experiment path: Faraday-cage / shielded volume with modulated Φ (or C-proxy) and NMR / atomic clock / Ramsey probe for sidebands — distinct from cage-attenuation SLW tests. Label carefully: scalar AB is accepted QM for known Φ; whether Hively C equals that Φ coupling is the open EED claim. Not an SW detector unless the triad is logged. Channel H · Mössbauer / nuclear resonance γ · collaboration High-Q nuclear γ readout RF / magnetic fields create Mössbauer sidebands (classic Heiman / Pfeiffer / Walker work). Modern coherent X-ray control of 57Fe nuclear excitons: Heeg et al., Nature 590, 401–404 (2021); doi:10.1038/s41586-021-03276-x — educational pointer to γ spectroscopy as a high-Q nuclear sensor near an SLW source if collaboration access exists. Garage rank: low without a Mössbauer lab. Channel I · distinguish EED’s C from beyond-SM scalar bosons HCI / g-factor exclusion-plot culture — not the same object Precision HCI / bound-electron g-factor / “nuclide shift” papers constrain hypothetical light scalar mediators coupled to electrons/nucleons (e.g. arXiv:2508.00685; arXiv:2608.23703, 2025–2026 class). Note: EED’s C is an EM 4-potential divergence field, not the same object as a Yukawa scalar boson — but the experimental culture of bounding new scalar couplings to nuclei (exclusion plots) is the publishable template for reporting |gC| or |δλ/λ| bounds from Channels E–G. Atomic adjacent · Hively patent hint · not nuclear proof mS→nS / 1S→2S electronic transitions US 9,306,527 mentions facilitating mS→nS (1S→2S) atomic transitions. Keep as an atomic (electronic) adjacent channel — optional optical / atomic probe near SLW — not nuclear proof. Experiment menu (falsifiable sketch) Educational design. Part 97 / licensed RF where applicable. Success = a published bound (or a clean null) on |δλ/λ|, NQR/EFG shift, or sideband amplitude vs a C-proxy amplitude. Rank for garage/HAM lab vs collaboration: 7Be (or other EC) counting with locks — best “accepted physics → EED bound” path (Channel E). 14N NQR shift hunt near 1296 / 433 MHz SLW launcher (Channel F). NMR / Ramsey / clock sideband hunt in a shielded Φ/C volume — SW-leaning (Channel G). PAC/EFG or Mössbauer if collaboration (Channels B, H). Keep DNP / Alzofon as parallel adjacent, not primary (Channel C). Primary launcher: SLW-class — 1296 MHz sleeve + bifilar or 433 MHz balls; keep the two feeds electrically separate (A/B benches separate; same rule as the lab pages). Controls (unchanged): RF off, TEM stub, Faraday wrap, distance scan, T / humidity / background locks. Rentzber constraint: prefer observables that are not pure conserved-current energy extraction (EC density, EFG/NQR, phase/sidebands). Explicit: this is not an SW detector unless the triad is logged (SW vs SLW). PMT / decay side channels are optional SLW effects, not SW proof. Library sources used Hively & Land 2021 JPCS — EED and SHP Hively 2026-09-05 — decay-rate variability by chemical compound (literature note) Hively & Land IARD 2020 slides Hively US 9,306,527 B1 — SLW patent (atomic mS→nS hint: electronic adjacent, not nuclear proof) Hubler 2023 JCMNS 38 — AHE/phonon · PAC/EFG · not SLW hardware Zhvirblis 1995 The Bagel Game (tr. Bob W. Greenyer) — educational-historical only; not a lab protocol NASA/CR-2005-213749 Alexander Vol. II — survey context, not endorsement Open web: Falcon Sokol DNO/mass PDF; Alzofon 1981 AIAA; Jeffries Dynamic Nuclear Orientation (1963); Ventura/APEC interviews (journalism) Reed & Hively, Symmetry 12, 2110 (2020) — EED companion when useful Greenyer / starfire.tech: related tools only — not this bench’s simulator Optional sibling map (keep SW/SLW discipline): Meyl theory detailed… (Meyl→LENR toroidal-moment adjacency; not SW evidence) Wider-net open-web citations (added 2026-09-05) Rentzber, arXiv:2608.19405 — SLW multipole theory; Λ-only sourcing; conserved-current energy-null; conditional EED Johlige et al., Phys. Rev. C 2, 1616 (1970) — 7Be EC chemical-environment shifts Segrè & Wiegand, Phys. Rev. 75, 39 (1949) — early 7Be atomic-electron effect Ohtsuki et al., PRL 93, 112501 (2004); 98, 252501 (2007) — 7Be@C60 Allman et al., PRL 68, 2409 (1992); PRA 48, 1799 (1993) — scalar Aharonov–Bohm (neutrons) Chiao et al., Phys. Rev. A 107, 042209 (2023) — energy-level sidebands from time-varying V(t), E=0; Library PDF Hiblot / Canet et al., C. R. Chimie (2008) — fully homemade 14N NQR spectrometer; NaNO2 / pharma 14N practice Heeg et al., Nature 590, 401–404 (2021); doi:10.1038/s41586-021-03276-x — coherent X-ray control of 57Fe nuclear excitons Classic RF Mössbauer sidebands: Heiman, Pfeiffer & Walker (1968–1972) HCI / scalar-mediator bounds (template, not identity): arXiv:2508.00685; arXiv:2608.23703 Adjacent theory (light cite): van Vlaenderen & Waser; Minotti & Modanese detector papers ← Back to Channel E focus What this is not: free energy, over-unity, medical advice, Meyl kits as SW evidence, a private Hively email dump, or a street address. Contested decay-rate (solar/Fischbach) and Alzofon–Sokol claims are not strengthened here. Inclusion of adjacent literature is not endorsement. description: Hively-steered Channel E: C-modulation of EC/chemical decay rates — Lady Lake garage kit, buy list, library. Educational; not a claim of measured decay shifts.
text: Lab note · 2026-09-06 · Channel E focus · Hively EED · Lady Lake garage C × nuclei — Channel E (EC / charge density) first article Educational design note focused on the experiment path Lee Hively steered toward: C-wave modulation of radioactive decay is allowed by EED; chemical / S-orbital charge-density effects on electron-capture rates; an experiment is the only way to validate. Not a claim that decay-rate shifts were measured on this bench. Hively reply · 2026-09-05/06 (paraphrase, not a private-email dump): Lee’s read is that C-wave modulation of radioactive decay is allowed by EED, and that an experiment is the only way to validate the effect. He points to peer-reviewed chemical-compound / S-orbital charge-density decay-rate variability (Channel E lean — not Channel G as first). Later checks found smaller shifts than early reports, but nonzero. EED hook he names: ρ c² C in the energy balance or J·C in the momentum balance; he does not yet have a clear theoretical model. Literature table: Hively decay-rate variability note (PDF). Do not strengthen contested solar/Fischbach claims from this banner. Public summary (do not strengthen): This page proposes falsifiable coupling sketches between Hively’s dynamical scalar field C and nuclear degrees of freedom. It is a theory/experiment design note. It does not claim anomalous heat, decay-rate shifts, or mass change were observed here. Scope lock: This is not an SW detector (see SW vs SLW). Nuclear / decay / EFG / interferometry side channels remain optional SLW effects (or SW-leaning Φ probes when triad-logged), not SW proof. Adjacent LENR / AHE / Alzofon–Sokol threads are labeled adjacent — not Hively C proof. Do not strengthen Alzofon, contested solar/Fischbach decay, or mass-change claims. Other candidate ideas (archive) Garage kit inventory Library SW vs SLW What Lee said (paraphrase · Sep 5–6, 2026) Joule / SW thread: his read of the Grok note is that C-wave modulation of radioactive decay is allowed by EED; “An experiment is the only way to validate the effect.” Earlier: SLW has Joule loss; SW/C does not (but 1/r²); a solid C×nuclei model would be publishable. Contested solar/Fischbach framing is his conversation context — this page does not elevate it. Channel-G vote reply + Word note: peer-reviewed chemical-compound / charge-density decay-rate variability (S-orbital near the nuclide). Examples he named (early literature magnitudes; later checks often smaller but nonzero): Tc compounds ~0.27%; BeF₂ vs Be metal ~0.08%; Nb⁹⁰ᵐ metal vs NbF₅ ~3.6%; I-131 solution vs crystals ~0.5%. EED hook: ρ c² C in energy balance or J·C in momentum; he does not yet have a clear theoretical model. Literature table (hub mirror): Hively 2026-09-05 Decay-rate variability by chemical compound (PDF) · .docx · Emery / Hahn / Norman / Tossell lineage. Not a private-email dump. Dan’s reading: prioritize Channel E (EC / chemical environment / density-at-nucleus) for a first garage bound next to the 1296 / 433 MHz SLW benches. Channel G and other sketches live in the archive. What Hively’s C is From Hively & Land, J. Phys.: Conf. Ser. 1956 012011 (2021), and the hub’s SW vs SLW note: EED promotes the Lorenz leftover to a physical dynamical field C ≡ ∇·A + (1/c²) ∂Φ/∂t with wave equation ∇²C − (1/c²)∂²C/∂t² = −μ (∂ρ/∂t + ∇·J) and energy density ∼ C²/(2μ). Split used on this hub: SLW: B=0, C≠0, longitudinal EL ∥ ∇C SW: E=B=0, C≠0 Hively’s short-time charge-fluctuation reading of the RHS (Heisenberg-style continuity mismatch) is his interpretation; it needs independent tests. Reed & Hively, Symmetry 12, 2110 (2020), is a related EED companion when a deeper math tip is useful — not required for this nuclear sketch. Why EC fits the publishable hook: if C (or EL) modulates electron density at the nucleus, electron capture is the decay family that already shows accepted chemical sensitivity. Rentzber’s conserved-current energy-null (detail in archive) also pushes away from “just count betas” toward EC / EFG / phase observables. A null bound is publishable. The experiment (Channel E) Channel E · 7Be EC · density-at-nucleus meter · mainstream Electron capture as the right decay family The 7Be EC rate depends on electron density at the nucleus. Chemical hosts change λ by ~0.1–1% — a known, small, accepted effect class (classic Johlige / Segrè; modern implant / host papers; Be@C60). Unlike contested solar-modulation claims, this is textbook nuclear / atomic physics. Johlige, Aumann & Born, Phys. Rev. C 2, 1616 (1970) — chemical-combination EC half-life shifts. Segrè & Wiegand, Phys. Rev. 75, 39 (1949) — early atomic-electron effect on 7Be. Ohtsuki et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 93, 112501 (2004); 98, 252501 (2007) — 7Be@C60 vs Be metal (~0.8–1.5%). Implant/host precision campaigns, e.g. Phys. Rev. C 75, 012801 (2007) — host-material systematics. Experiment: place a calibrated 7Be source (or other EC nuclide) near an SLW launcher with environmental locks; look for RF-on vs RF-off bound on |δλ/λ| beyond the chemical baseline. A publishable null is OK. Framing: if C or EL modulates local electron density / continuum at the nucleus, EC is the right decay family — not generic β Geiger counting alone. description: Side-by-side SLW comparison table and illustrative SNR model.
text: Compare · illustrative Side-by-side table and an educational SNR toy Numbers move so you can see which assumption matters. They are not a validated link budget. The top model is the briefing-deck scaling. The lower strip shows the paper/patent formulas used on the original simulators. Illustrative educational model. Noise floors, radiation resistance, 50% coil efficiency, and plasma responsivity are literature-inspired parameters, not calibrated lab values. Do not use for engineering or regulatory decisions. Comparison at a glance Aspect Nikolova–Zimmerman Hively (EED) Primary emphasis Vector potential A + momentum waves Longitudinal E + scalar C (SLW) Tx hardware Waveguide / TM01 (1296 MHz stovepipe) or folded dipole Monopole + skirt balun; bifilar pancake; original tests ~8 GHz Rx hardware Biased plasma / fluorescent U-tube Bifilar pancake (face-on) or matching monopole Scaling used in toys |A| ∝ I/r ; Idet ∝ I/r P ∝ I², S ∝ 1/r² ; briefing uses a slightly slower field falloff Demonstrated / claimed range ~1.5 km experimental (1296 MHz) Table-top copper penetration at ~8 GHz (IARD 2020); long range is theoretical in the toys Core references US 8,165,531; QEX 2011; CEM-R-46 US 9,306,527; Physics Essays 2019; IARD 2020 Interactive briefing model Adapted from the Educational Briefing slide 07 and the Combined SNR page. Presets include the N–Z 2 A @ 1.5 km anecdote. Transmit current Itx 5.00 A Distance r 50.0 km 2 A @ 1.5 km (N–Z exp.) 5 A @ 50 km 8 A @ 250 km 5 A @ 400 km Emerald = N–Z briefing SNR. Amber = Hively briefing SNR. Vertical dashed line = current r. N–Z · vector potential Tx power (illust.) — |A| amplitude — Detector I — SNR — Hively · longitudinal E Tx power (illust.) — |Elong| — Detector I — SNR — Paper / patent strip (same I and r) These use the Combined-SNR and Hively-simulator formulas, still educational: N–Z: Am = μ₀ Im / (2π k₀ r) at 1.3 GHz, R ≈ 264030 m/H, IRMS = R Am/√2 Hively (Eq. 38/B5 as corrected by the Erratum, FACT; I = peak, ASSUMPTION): POUT(r) = S = I² Z₀ / [2 (4π r)²] W/m²; Ptotal = 4π r² POUT = I² Z₀ / (8π) W (DERIVED / ASSUMPTION: spherical integral), Aeff = 78.5 cm², η = 50%, Iout = √(S Aeff η / 50 Ω) N–Z |Am| — N–Z IRMS — Hively Ptotal (derived) — Hively POUT(r) = S (W/m²) — Ptotal (derived) at 5 A is ~375 W with Z₀ ≈ 376.73 Ω (it was ~749 W with the pre-erratum I² Z₀/(4π) form used until 2026-09-29; the erratum halves it, −3.01 dB. See P_OUT erratum audit) — a large current for a stub, which is why the toys look optimistic. Real 23 cm amateur power is far lower; see the Lab legal box. Mix-and-match antennas (from the original page) Purity factor ≈ fraction of power in the irrotational / longitudinal-potential mode. Hively bifilar aims near 1; a conventional dipole is much lower. Plasma detectors primarily sense time-varying A; bifilar coils convert longitudinal E into gradient current. Path loss in that simulator was a generalized 1/rn (default n=2) plus optional medium dB/km — again a cartoon.

title: 1.3 GHz sphere experiment (Experiment A)
headings: 4. What results would and would not mean
description: Round 1: 1296 MHz sphere transmitter and receiver with a rod attenuator (brass and W1), VNA baselines, range estimate and Joule-loss analysis.
text: Round 1 · 1.3 GHz · sphere transmitter, sphere receiver, rod attenuator for the longitudinal E-field Experiment A · 1.3 GHz The bench is two 3/4 in aluminium spheres (one transmitting, one receiving) on a non-metallic rail, with a 3 x 3 array of half-wave rods between them that can be turned through an angle φ. Round 1 adds the rod attenuator to Experiment A (older hub text says rods are Experiment B only; Dan's 4 Oct 2026 plan supersedes that), VNA S21 baselines, an automatic range estimate, and a Joule-loss analysis of the rod data. Tests of hypotheses, not results. Mainstream electrodynamics treats free-space radio as transverse (TEM). A longitudinal or scalar component is a hypothesis we are testing, and nothing on these pages claims that scalar or longitudinal waves have been detected. Values marked proposal are our suggestions and are not measured or sourced. Draft v0.1, 4 Oct 2026, written by Grok Bot for Dan Britton. Bench numbers Run order Controls What results would mean Three-position fixture scan Tools To-Do for this band 1. Bench numbers Labels: fact from a cited source or plain arithmetic, hypothesis an extension we are testing, proposal our suggestion, not built or measured. Item Value Source or status Frequency 1296.000 MHz FACT for B (Monstein and Wesley); the band choice for A and 2.45 GHz is Dan's extension Wavelength λ = c/f 231.32 mm arithmetic, c = 299 792 458 m/s λ/2 (standing-wave and null spacing) 115.66 mm arithmetic; see range-finder.html λ/(2π) (reactive near-field boundary of a small source) 36.8 mm arithmetic; ordinary near fields have a radial E component inside this distance Spheres K-Mac KB-1820, 0.750 in (19.05 mm) 3003 aluminium hollow ball, ships with no hole; fed by the RG-405U centre conductor soldered into a #76 pin hole, shield kept off the ball (see Exp A feed dimensions) hub setup.html, sphere.html Rods: material, diameter Brass (C36000 expected), then W1 tool steel; 1/8 in = 3.175 mm rod-jig page; shop order pending Rods: length (λ/2 free space) 115.66 mm ± 0.3 mm hypothesis scaled from Monstein and Wesley Array 3 x 3, pitch λ/4 = 57.83 mm, span λ/2 rod-jig numbers.json (two arrays: one rotates, one fixed) Plate 6.00 x 6.00 x 0.50 in cast acrylic (152.4 x 152.4 x 12.7 mm) rod-jig page (draft, not yet built) Expected mass per rod brass 7.8 g, W1 7.2 g density 8.5 and 7.85 g/cm³; use as a mix-up check Keep steel away from rods by ≥ 36.8 mm (λ/2π) rod-jig page design choice Dipole Detector DD-1296 tip-to-tip 109.6 mm design, 115.7 mm cut long and trimmed; 1.5 mm feed gap sim-lab/dipole-detector/ (first-pass numbers; trim and re-check) VNA calibration slot 1, sweep 1100 to 1500 MHz vna-howto.html section 4 Exp A feed dimensions (corrected 5 Oct 2026) Why the shield must not touch the sphere: the sphere is the driven element, fed by the centre conductor. If the RG-405U outer conductor is bonded to the ball, the ball becomes a closed shield cap and a pin inside only excites a shorted cavity. This design is proposal derived for this hub, not taken from Monstein and Wesley (their Experiment B feed is different). Mounting background: mount-ideas.html#expt-a. Item mm in Source or status Sphere 19.05 OD 0.750 OD fact K-Mac KB-1820, listed as 3003 aluminium. Wall thickness not stated on the hub: measure it and confirm the material on a spare ball RG-405U centre 0.51, PTFE 1.68, outer 2.20 centre 0.020, PTFE 0.066, outer 0.086 fact tools.html Pin hole in the sphere wall #76 drill (0.51), or #75 (0.53) for a snug fit; 2.5 deep (2 to 3) #76 (0.020), or #75 (0.021); 0.10 deep (0.08 to 0.12) proposal derived Pin joint Centre conductor soldered into the hole. On aluminium use aluminium solder with aluminium flux (tin-lead will not wet it), or silver conductive epoxy proposal derived PTFE exposed past the shield cut 1.5 (1 to 2) 0.06 (0.04 to 0.08) proposal derived Bare centre conductor past the PTFE end 4.0 = 1.5 in air + 2.5 in the hole 0.16 = 0.06 in air + 0.10 in the hole proposal derived Shield cut end to sphere surface 3.0 (1.5 PTFE + 1.5 bare wire) 0.12 (0.06 + 0.06) proposal derived. The shield never touches the sphere Total past the shield cut 5.5 (3.0 outside the ball + 2.5 in the hole) 0.22 arithmetic: about 0.024 λ at 231.3 mm, so the feed adds no significant radiating length Sleeve balun (λ/4) 57.8 in air 2.28 in air fact setup.html#sleeve. With a dielectric filler of relative permittivity εr, multiply by 1/√εr. Tube over the jacket and shield; far end soldered to the shield; open end toward the sphere, level with the shield cut (about 3.0 mm from the ball), never touching it. It chokes common-mode current on the outside of the shield Connector SMA on the generator end of the RG-405U only; no bulkhead on the ball proposal derived If the measured wall is thinner than 2.5 mm, the pin hole goes through: insert the pin by the wall thickness only (bare wire = 1.5 mm plus the wall), solder at the outside surface, and log it. proposal Band rules. 23 cm amateur band, licensed operation, milliwatt levels (see setup.html). 2. Run order Inspect the rods (length, diameter, magnet and mass test) on the To-Do page. Do not start until the bags are labelled brass or W1. Calibrate the VNA in slot 1 (1100 to 1500 MHz); full SOLT with the TX and RX cables, then check that a THRU reads 0 dB (vna-howto.html). Noise floor: terminate both ports and record S21 with the settings you will use. Anything within 10 dB of that floor is not usable. S11 of each sphere at the SMA reference plane. Record the lowest dip and the value at 1296.000 MHz. Do not tune to chase a number; log it and compare after any change. S21 baseline with no rods at a tape-measured reference range r0 (sphere centre to sphere centre). The hub's Experiment A guidance is to keep the receiver at 1 to 2 λ or more (about 0.25 to 0.5 m) on a non-metallic rail with a laser or scale and ±1 mm fine adjust (setup.html#ranging-a). Candidate ranges: 2λ = 0.46 m, 3λ = 0.69 m, 4λ = 0.93 m, 6λ = 1.39 m, 8λ = 1.85 m (proposal). Save frequency, dB and phase as CSV. Plates only (acrylic plates and bases, no rods): repeat the S21 baseline. This isolates the plate. Range check: paste the S21 sweep into the range finder and compare its estimate with the tape. Brass rods, angle scan: rotate the H array through φ = 0 to 180° in 10° steps (then once over 0 to 360° as an artefact check), logging S21 magnitude at the carrier each time. The V array stays fixed. Run this first with the fixture MIDWAY; the three-station version is in section 5. Settle after each step: after every 10° turn, hands off and wait about 3 s (or until the live trace is flat) before reading, so the rods stop ringing. Log it as settle_s. Estimates and reasons: rod-jig page, section 7. Fit the scan to T = T0 exp(-κ cos²(φ - φ0)) on the Joule-loss page. Keep κ, φ0, T0 and the residual. W1 rods: same plates, same positions, same range, same VNA settings. Fit again and compare κ with the brass value. Independent cross-check with a TinySA Ultra as receiver (peak hold) for one brass and one W1 scan. Dipole Detector DD-1296 in place of the receiving sphere: rotate it through 360°, fit the figure-eight on the range-finder page. Repeat on a second day. Save every raw file; edit nothing. Ranges are centre to centre. Keep cables taped down after calibration; a moved cable is a phase error. Never exceed +10 dBm or 5 V DC on a VNA port. 3. Controls Control Why TX off (VNA port 1 terminated or TinySA generator off) Anything left is pickup, drift or the receiver itself. 50 Ω load in place of the TX sphere A signal that survives a dummy load is not coming from the sphere. RX terminated with 50 Ω Receiver and cable leakage floor. Rods removed, plates in; then plates removed Separates the rods from their holder. TX sphere, with its SMA bulkhead and feed, rotated 90° about the TX to RX axis A transverse (TEM) signal from a sphere and feed has a polarisation set by the feed axis, so T(φ) should move with it. A hypothetical longitudinal component would not care. This is a proposal for a discriminating test. TX and RX swapped Checks reciprocity and symmetry of the fixture. Three ranges, not one Distance dependence separates near-field terms from radiating terms. Cage open and closed (if a cage is used) Record grounded or floating in every log row. No cable through a cage wall. 4. What results would and would not mean Observation Ordinary reading Would support the hypothesis only if The receiver sphere sees the transmitter Expected. Two small antennas couple at short range through ordinary near and far fields. Not evidence by itself. Detection is the instrument check, not the result. T(φ) follows exp(-κ cos²φ) A wire array attenuates the field component along its wires. Transverse waves do this too (a wire-grid polariser). The curve does not move when the TX sphere and feed are rotated 90°, and κ behaves as the Joule-loss page predicts when brass is swapped for W1. W1 and brass give the same κ Loss is dominated by scattering from good conductors, independent of conductivity. Disfavours κ proportional to σ (literal Joule). Nothing more. W1 κ is about σW1/σbrass times the brass value Possible with real absorption in the rods. Repeats on another day, in another place, at a second frequency. Figure-eight peaks end-on from a known source Inside about λ/2π (and still somewhat beyond) an ordinary source has a radial E component. It persists at several λ and falls off as 1/r, not as the near-field terms. 5. Three-position fixture scan (proposal) Added 4 Oct 2026. Analysis calculators: Joule-loss page, section 8. Checklist: To-Do group. hypothesis Dan's early-attenuation idea. A rotating rod fixture placed close to the transmitter should give a more measurable change in the detected amplitude than one placed midway or near the receiver, because paths that would otherwise reflect off objects between TX and RX are attenuated before they can reflect. To keep the fixture out of the source's reactive near field, the closest point of approach of any rod during the rotation must stay at least λ/(2π) from the TX sphere centre: 110.0 mm at 433.59 MHz, 36.8 mm at 1296 MHz, 19.5 mm at 2450 MHz. This is a hypothesis test and a proposal. Nothing here is a measured result. Where does the fixture go? The sources do not say. Monstein and Wesley (2002) report testing the wave by "intervening a cubic array of 9 half-wavelength wires" (abstract) and call it a polarizer-analyzer. They give no distance from either ball. Butterworth et al. (2013), describing that apparatus, write "Between Tx and Rx are positioned a pair of rotatable polarizer-analyzer arrays", which is where the word "between" comes from. Neither source fixes a position along the line, so this test treats the position as a variable to measure. Station geometry at 1296 MHz Item Value Status λ/(2π) standoff 36.8 mm fact arithmetic; Dan's rule is a closest approach to the TX sphere centre of at least this value Array envelope radius R = √2 λ/4 81.8 mm arithmetic; farthest rod tip from the turntable axis, assuming the axis passes through the centre of the 3 x 3 array Smallest pivot distance (standoff + R) 118.6 mm arithmetic; about one rod length (115.66 mm) Proposed NEAR pivot (1.2 rod lengths) 138.8 mm; closest rod approach 57.0 mm proposal Reference separation r = 4λ 925.3 mm (0.925 m) proposal; use your tape-measured r and do not change it between stations Pivot distance from the TX sphere centre: NEAR TX / MIDWAY / NEAR RX 138.8 / 462.6 / 786.5 mm proposal; NEAR RX mirrors NEAR TX (r minus the NEAR pivot), so the closest approach to the RX sphere is also 57.0 mm Pivot means the turntable axis. The V array (rods vertical, fixed) travels with the rotating array as one fixture; give it the same clearance and log the H to V spacing. If your turntable axis is not through the array centre, recompute with calculator G. Protocol Fix the geometry. Choose r once (4λ above, or your own) and keep heights, cables, TX power, VNA settings and cage state fixed. Only the fixture moves, along the non-metallic rail. Mark the three pivot positions and hand-rotate the fixture through 360° at each near station with a tape: no rod point may come closer than 36.8 mm to the nearer sphere centre. Reference runs at every station: rods out, plates only (no rods), and an ambient baseline with the TX off. Angle scan at every station: φ = 0 to 180° in 10° steps, then once over 0 to 360°. At each angle log the detected amplitude, the TX S11 at the carrier (VNA port 1 at the SMA reference plane, to catch near-field loading or detuning), the optional RX S11 (the port 2 reflection on a two-port VNA) and the ambient baseline. Order: NEAR TX, MIDWAY, NEAR RX, then the reverse, so slow drift cancels. Repeat with W1 rods in the same holes and stations, then on a second day (and, if time allows, at r + λ/4 to move the standing-wave phase). Fit each station with calculator F and compare κ across stations and between brass and W1. Log columns: date_time, pass (A = 0 to 180, B = 0 to 360), station (NEAR_TX, MIDWAY, NEAR_RX), material (brass, W1, none), band_MHz, r_m, pivot_mm (TX sphere centre to turntable axis), closest_approach_mm, angle_deg, rx_level_dB, tx_s11_dB, rx_s11_dB, ambient_dB, cage_state, fixture_cage, turn_method, settle_s, notes. Download the CSV template or use the blank sheet on the Joule-loss page. How to read it Observation Ordinary reading and caveats Reading under this test κ deepest at NEAR TX and the TX S11 stays stable across the scan The array subtends a larger angle seen from near the source, so plain shadowing also predicts this. Absorption and scattering are not separated. Supports the early-attenuation idea as a pattern. Needs repeats, W1, and the 90° TX rotation control before it means more. TX S11 moves with the rod angle at NEAR TX The rods load or detune the source: a near-field coupling artefact. Do not read κ at that station as attenuation. Move the fixture out and repeat. κ about equal at all three stations Loss does not depend on where the fixture sits. No support for early attenuation; position-independent. κ deepest MIDWAY or NEAR RX, or the rods-crossed level L0 shifts with station Reflection nulls and multipath can mimic any of these: moving the fixture changes which paths cross the array and the standing-wave phase. Check the plates-only runs, shift r by λ/4 and repeat before believing a station effect. 6. Tools for this band Range finder, preset to 1296.000 MHz: phase slope, time-domain peak, null spacing, two-ray nulls, dipole direction finding. Joule-loss calculator, preset to 1296.000 MHz: rod-scan fit, brass versus W1, power-balance bookkeeping. Three-station calculator F and station planner G (proposal): kappa per station, TX S11 loading flag. title: 2.45 GHz sphere experiment
headings: 4. What results would and would not mean
description: Round 1: can a 3/4 in sphere launch and detect 2.45 GHz, and does the rod attenuator behave like the lower bands? The instrument check before the microwave oven test.
text: Round 1 · 2.45 GHz · sphere transmitter, sphere receiver, rod attenuator for the longitudinal E-field 2.45 GHz sphere experiment · 2.45 GHz A new third band for the same sphere-to-sphere bench. We reuse the 3/4 in sphere from Experiment A at 2.45 GHz and ask two things: (1) can the sphere launch a 2.45 GHz signal that a second sphere detects, and (2) does the rod attenuator give a similar T(φ) curve to the lower bands? This is the instrument check that the microwave oven experiment then reuses with the oven as the transmitter. Tests of hypotheses, not results. The ordinary wave dominates; this is the Monstein and Wesley style scan (Run 1 above). 2 Caged, each sphere in its own enclosure Open In The ordinary wave is mostly removed, but leakage reaching the rods (seams, the feed hole, the RX chain) is still possible. 3 Caged Caged In The strongest version. A rod-angle pattern that survives this, and repeats, is the interesting one. 4 Caged (as in run 2 and run 3) As in that run Out (plates in, material = none) Each caged run repeated with the rods removed. Separates rod effects from cage and turntable effects. Build notes Numbers marked derived are plain arithmetic from λ = 691.42 mm at 433.59 MHz and the station table in section 5. They are guidelines, not measured shielding. Turn the turntable without opening a gap. Best: a non-metallic shaft (acrylic, PTFE or Delrin) through a short metal tube bonded all round to the cage wall, with the angle dial on the outside end. The shaft must not be metal: a metal shaft through the tube turns it into a coaxial line, which passes RF at any frequency. Alternative: a hand crank on the same kind of shaft, Dan's string and drill method with the string through the same kind of small tube, or open the cage to turn and close it again before each reading (slower, and the closed state must be checked every time). derived Size of the shaft hole. A round hole only passes waves above its TE11 cutoff, fc = 1.841 c / (π D). The cutoff diameter is about 405 mm at 433.59 MHz (and about 72 mm at 2.45 GHz, if the cage is ever reused on that bench). Use a hole far smaller: about 10 mm bore. Well below cutoff, a tube attenuates about 30 dB for each diameter of length in ideal theory, so a 10 mm bore tube at least 30 mm long gives roughly 90 dB on paper at either frequency. A plastic shaft filling the tube lowers the cutoff a little (by the square root of its permittivity), which changes nothing at these sizes. Real seams leak more than theory, which is why the cage is measured (below). derived Keep the cage walls away from the rods. Use at least λ/(2π) = 110 mm between the walls and the swept rod envelope, the same rule the page uses for steel near the rods, and more where room allows (λ/2 = 346 mm is a comfortable target). With the array envelope radius of 244.5 mm (section 5), that means an inside width of at least about 0.71 m in the turning plane (about 1.18 m for λ/2 clearance), and the rod stack height (345.7 mm) plus 2 × 110 mm vertically, more if the fixed V array shares the cage. derived Station fit. At r = 4λ, the NEAR TX and NEAR RX pivots (415.2 mm from a sphere centre) leave only about 60 mm between a 0.71 m wide fixture cage and the sphere centre, so they cannot be used with a caged fixture and caged spheres. Use MIDWAY (1382.8 mm), or lengthen r and recompute with calculator G. derived The closed cage is a resonant box. A cube about 0.71 m inside has its lowest resonance near 300 MHz, so at 433.59 MHz the closed fixture cage supports standing waves. Any ordinary leakage that does get in can bounce around and depend on rod angle. Run 4 (rods out) and the cage shielding check are there to catch that. Bond the seams. Overlap every mesh seam and the door or lid seam, and bond them continuously (conductive tape, clamped overlap or stitched seam). No cables through the fixture cage wall: nothing inside it needs power or signal. Instruments in the caged runs. Section 3 rules out cables through a cage wall, so with each sphere in its own cage the source and receiver sit inside the sphere cages on battery, for example two TinySA units recording to microSD, as in section 8b. Check each cage before the runs. Put a TinySA generator inside the cage on battery (MODE → SIGNAL GENERATOR, 433.59 MHz, -19 dBm) driving a small antenna, and a second TinySA with an antenna outside at a fixed distance. Read the level with the cage open, then closed. The difference is the shielding in dB. If the closed reading is at the noise floor, log it as "at least" that many dB. Repeat after any change to seams, the door or the shaft. Settle step. The rod settle step still applies: after each 10° step wait about 3 s, or turn the shaft smoothly. Log cage state in every row: cage_state for the sphere cages (open, or closed with layout), the new fixture_cage column (open, caged), material (brass, W1, none for rods out), and the latest shielding check in the notes. 7. Rod jolts and settle time A bumped rod rings briefly, like a plucked ruler. Each rod is held at mid-length in the acrylic plate, so it behaves as two cantilevers. estimate The lowest bending mode is about 51 to 55 Hz for the 346 mm brass rods and about 76 to 82 Hz for W1. The shorter rods on the 1.3 and 2.45 GHz benches ring at a few hundred Hz to a few kHz. With an assumed Q of about 100, the long brass rods take about 2 s to settle. Working and assumptions: rod-jig page, section 7. A possible small effect, not a proven problem. A rod that is still swinging moves slightly in the field, which could wobble the S21 or TinySA reading. Nobody has seen this on this bench yet. The one-minute flick test below tells you whether it matters on yours. It is the jolts that matter, not turning versus stopping. Two methods are fine: (a) Step and settle (recommended default): turn to each angle, take your hands off, wait about 3 s, then read. Log the wait as settle_s. (b) Continuous: also fine if the motion is smooth, for example a slow motor drive or Dan's string and drill method. A reading or sweep that lasts longer than about 1 s averages out any small leftover ringing. Avoid jerky hand turns, or a turntable with detent clicks, while a reading is being taken. The same settle step applies in the caged rod fixture configuration. One-minute check. Watch the live S21 trace on the VNA (or the TinySA trace), lightly flick one rod, and see whether the trace wobbles. If it does not, rod jiggle is a non-issue and the settle time is just cheap insurance. Step-by-step: run the flick test Turning the lazy Susan smoothly: string and drill method Dan's idea, 8 Oct 2026. A proposal, not yet tried on this bench. Tie a string to the edge of the lazy Susan and let a cordless (battery) drill at low speed wind the string onto its chuck. The turntable then turns slowly, smoothly and continuously, which is method (b) above. Why it is gentle. The string only pulls, so little drill vibration reaches the rods. Wrap, do not just tie. For a full 360° scan, wrap the string a few turns around the rim (or a drum on the turntable) so it leaves the rim tangentially. A string tied at one point pulls at a changing angle, so the rate varies and it cannot pull past about half a turn. Start and stop are the jolts. Start the drill before you start logging, and stop logging before you release the trigger. The start and stop are when the rods get kicked. Stick-slip is the real jiggle risk. A cheap turntable bearing can stick and jump. Oil the bearing and add a slight constant drag, for example a felt pad rubbing on the underside, so the string stays taut and the motion stays even. Drill noise. A brushed drill motor gives off broadband RF noise from its brushes. Keep the drill outside any cage, on battery, a few feet from the receiver. In the caged configuration, pass the string through a small bonded tube like the shaft tube (about 10 mm bore, at least 30 mm long). Plain nylon or cotton string carries no RF; do not use a string with a metal core or tinsel. Angle against time. Log the time as each 30° mark on the dial passes (a phone video of the dial and the screen together works), then read the level against angle afterwards. Log turn_method = drill (or hand-step for the step and settle method). derived Turn rate, formula only. Turntable speed (rev/min) = d × N / (2R), where d is the winding diameter on the chuck, N the drill speed in rev/min and R the radius where the string leaves the turntable. In degrees per second that is 3 × d × N / R. The winding diameter grows as string builds up on the chuck, so the rate creeps up during a scan; that is another reason to log the dial marks rather than assume a steady rate. Two checks before using it for data, with the flick-test setup: Drill running, transmitter off. Always take this trace first, with the drill where it will be during the scan. Anything above the transmitter-off floor at 433.59 MHz is drill noise; move the drill farther away until it is gone. Drill running, no flick. Transmitter on, turntable turning, nobody touching anything. Run it first with the rods out (plates only), where nothing should change with angle, then with the rods in. If the trace is as flat as at rest (apart from the slow change with angle when the rods are in), the method is clean. Why not simulate it? A full model of the 346 mm rod in Bob Greenyer's Standing Wave Project is too slender for the tool's in-browser grid (about 40 × 40 × 40 cells), so the live trace is the better check. 8. Flick test, step by step Back to Rod jolts and settle time Two ways to run it. Use whichever instrument you will use for the scan, or both. The rods, plates, spheres, range r and fixture station stay exactly as they will be for the real scan (MIDWAY is a good first station). Flick tool: a wooden dowel or pencil about 30 cm long, so your hand and body stay out of the TX to RX path. Your body near the path changes S21 by itself, which is why the steps include a no-touch control. 8a. With the VNA6000-A (S21) Menu paths below are the ones on the hub's VNA how-to, quoted from the NanoRFE VNA6000 user manual (2022/11). Firmware on your unit may differ. Calibrate. Recall the Exp B calibration (slot 0, 380 to 490 MHz): CAL → RECALL → RECALL 0. If there is none, do the SOLT calibration with cables, including THRU, as in VNA how-to, section 5. Check that a THRU reads about 0 dB, and that a C-number shows on the left of the screen. Connect port 1 to the TX ball and port 2 to the RX ball, with the same cables used for calibration. Tape the cables down. Single frequency. STIMULUS → CW FREQ, enter 433.59 MHz. This is the manual's zero span: one frequency sent continuously, so the trace shows S21 over time. (If you prefer to stay swept, use STIMULUS → CENTER 433.59 MHz and a narrow STIMULUS → SPAN, for example 1 MHz, and watch the marker.) Changing the range interpolates the calibration, which is fine here: this test looks at changes, not absolute values. Traces. DISPLAY → TRACE → TRACE 0, then DISPLAY → CHANNEL → CH1 THROUGH and DISPLAY → FORMAT → LOGMAG. Then DISPLAY → TRACE → TRACE 1, DISPLAY → CHANNEL → CH1 THROUGH and DISPLAY → FORMAT → PHASE. Zoom in. Use DISPLAY → SCALE to make the vertical scale fine (for example about 0.5 dB and about 5 degrees per division), and DISPLAY → SCALE → REFERENCE POSITION to bring both traces to mid-screen. Keep it sweeping. Make sure PAUSE SWEEP is not active, so the trace keeps updating. Baseline. Hands off and step back for 30 s. Note the normal jitter of the trace, peak to peak, in dB and in degrees. Take a screenshot (or a phone photo with the C-number and axis visible). Control: no touch. Bring the dowel up to a rod, hold it there for 2 s without touching, then withdraw it. Note any change. That is the stick and body effect alone. Flick. Lightly flick the free tip of one rod with the dowel (start with the centre rod, H5), withdraw the dowel at once and stand still. Watch both traces. Read it. Note the wobble peak to peak in dB and degrees, and how many seconds it takes to go flat again. A phone video of the screen makes the timing easy. The VNA probably refreshes too slowly to draw a 50 Hz ring as a clean wave (inference), so look for the trace turning ragged or jumping and then calming. Repeat three times, then with an outer rod, then with the W1 rods. Finally do one real 10° turntable step and watch the same way, since that is the jolt the scan actually makes. 8b. With TinySA Ultra+ ZS406 units (generator and receiver) Menu names are from the official tinySA Ultra / Ultra+ menu tree and its linked menu-tree chart. Use two of the three ZS406 units: one as the source, one as the receiver. Source (TinySA #1). MODE → SIGNAL GENERATOR. Set FREQ to 433.59 MHz (sine output works up to 900 MHz on the Ultra+) and LEVEL to -19 dBm. Turn the output on with the LOW OUTPUT button. Connect it to the TX ball. Receiver (TinySA #2) on the RX ball, in MODE → SPECTRUM ANALYZER. Find the carrier. FREQUENCY → CENTER 433.59 MHz and FREQUENCY → SPAN 200 kHz. Then MARKER → SEARCH MARKER → PEAK SEARCH and note the marker frequency. The two units' clocks differ slightly, so the carrier may sit a little off 433.59 MHz. Zero span. FREQUENCY → ZERO SPAN and enter the marker frequency from step 3. The screen now shows level against time at that one frequency. RBW. FREQUENCY → RBW → 30kHz. That is wide enough to tolerate the small clock offset between the two units. Use 10kHz if the carrier is steady and you want a lower noise floor. Level. MARKER → MARKER OPS → ->REF LEVEL puts the carrier near the top. Then LEVEL → SCALE/DIV 1 dB. Leave LEVEL → LNA off unless the carrier is within about 10 dB of the noise. Time axis. DISPLAY → SWEEP TIME 1 s. With the default 290 points that is about 3.4 ms per point, fine enough to draw a 50 to 80 Hz ring directly on the trace. Make sure TRACE → CALC is OFF (no averaging, no hold), or the wobble will be smoothed away. Baseline, control and flick: as VNA steps 7 to 9. Note the normal jitter (dB peak to peak), the no-touch change, then the flick wobble and how long it takes to go flat. Freeze and save. DISPLAY → PAUSE SWEEP freezes a trace that shows the wobble. STORAGE → SAVE CAPTURE saves a screenshot and STORAGE → SAVE TRACES saves the trace as CSV to the microSD card. Turn PAUSE SWEEP off again to continue. Repeat as VNA step 11, including one real 10° turntable step. What counts as "matters" Does not matter: the flick wobble is no bigger than the baseline jitter, or no bigger than the no-touch control. Keep the 3 s settle as insurance and move on. Handled by the settle time: the wobble is visible but has gone flat within 3 s. Keep 3 s (or the decay time you measured plus a margin). Matters: the wobble is still there after 3 s, or it is larger than the effect you are trying to measure, for example the smallest step-to-step change in the angle scan you care about, or the allowed 0° versus 360° return-to-start difference. Then lengthen the settle time, use a smooth drive, or damp the rods (for example firmer O-rings), and repeat the test. What to log (one row per flick): date_time, instrument (VNA with cal slot, or TinySA with RBW and sweep time), frequency, rod material and which rod, flick method, baseline jitter (dB and degrees, peak to peak), no-touch control change, flick wobble (dB and degrees, peak to peak), decay time to flat (s), the settle_s you chose, and the screenshot, CSV or video file name. Back to Rod jolts and settle time · Back to Run order Better ideas welcome. Steve Morris and any other reader: if you know a better way to turn the turntable smoothly, to reduce rod jiggle, or to cut cage leakage (seams, the shaft or string hole, the feed hole), please tell us. Email Dan Britton at BrittonSolutions@icloud.com, the address in the footer of every page. Better ideas win. 9. Tools for this band Range finder, preset to 433.59 MHz: phase slope, time-domain peak, null spacing, two-ray nulls, dipole direction finding. Joule-loss calculator, preset to 433.59 MHz: rod-scan fit, brass versus W1, power-balance bookkeeping. Three-station calculator F and station planner G (proposal): kappa per station, TX S11 loading flag. text: Experiment C · graphical SNR v1 · illustrative · not a measurement From SLW transmitter to PMT current — a picture you can tune Move the sliders and watch four windows update: whole signal chain, power density vs distance, Ohmic loss vs conductor path, and PMT anode current / recovered AM. Parent: Experiment C. Cart: parts + rough $. Illustrative only. Hively P_OUT (W/m²) + 1/r² are theory cartoons; αohm and ηatom are unknown until measured. SLW: E∥≠0 → σE² loss. SW: E=0 → α forced 0. 8 GHz is not a 10.2 eV photon. Main sliders TX Mode I_peak P_RF feed Use P_RF·η η_launch Range r Ohmic path L α_ohm (power Np/m) A_atom η_atom PMT / electronics sliders PMT channel Photocathode QE Optics transmission PMT gain M Dark current C9663 transimpedance AM depth m f_mod RBW SLW/SW P_total (W, derived)— At atom: S— PMT cathode current— PMT anode current— AM current swing— C9663 output— TinySA tone— Count SNR (1 s)— TX → P_total → 1/r² → Ohmic path → atom → photons → PMT cathode → gain → anode current → C9663 → attenuator → TinySA Graph windows 1 · Whole chain (dB budget) Bars show each stage’s power/current proxy on a common dB ladder. Use as a human picture, not calibration. 2 · Power density vs range Teal = geometric 1/r²; orange = after current Ohmic path factor. 3 · Ohmic survival vs path length SLW falls as exp(−αL) in this power-loss toy. SW stays flat (α=0). 4 · PMT anode current + recovered AM Current waveform at f_mod. Dashed line = PMT dark current. TinySA reads the AM tone after C9663. Detailed readout Equations P_total = η_launch · I_peak² Z0/(8π) (or η_launch · P_RF) # DERIVED / ASSUMPTION (spherical integral, total watts 4πr²·P_OUT); I-driven branch: P_OUT(r) = S_geom = I_peak² Z0/[2(4πr)²] W/m² (Hively & Loebl 2019 Eq. 38/B5 as corrected by the Erratum = FACT; I = peak = ASSUMPTION) S_geom = P_OUT(r) = P_total/(4πr²) ; S = S_geom exp(−α_ohm L) P_interact = S A_atom η_atom photon rate = P_interact/E_gap ; E_gap = 10.2 eV I_cathode = e · photon_rate · QE · T_optics I_anode = M · I_cathode + I_dark ΔI_AM = m · M · I_cathode V_C9663 = ΔI_AM · Z_transimpedance P_50Ω = V_rms²/50 ; TinySA tone = 10 log10(P/1mW) Author-confirmed, 2026-09-30 (FACT, author-confirmed). The charge-relaxation transient printed in Hively & Loebl 2019 Eq. (A5) and US 9,306,527 col. 5 has ε and σ swapped; Dr. Hively confirmed in a private email to Dan (2026-09-30) that E = E0 exp(−σt/ε), τ = ε/σ is correct. This page does not compute that transient; its Ohmic factor is the spatial exp(−αL). Loss term here: Joule σE∥² only, or none (Erratum toggle). See the Corrections log. Formula history (2026-09-29). The current-driven branch used the total-watts quantity (then labelled P_OUT) η_launch · I_peak² Z0/(4π) (patent US 9,306,527 Eq. 15; Eq. 38/B5 as first printed in 2019, without the ½). The erratum adds the ½, so the total and S from the I input are 3.01 dB lower. The P_RF (dBm) branch is a power-in input, not derived from I, and is unchanged. FACT the ½ (erratum); ASSUMPTION I is peak; HYP the launch efficiency and the SLW chain. Loss term: Hively’s Joule term σE∥² (Eq. 44) or none (erratum α = 0) only. See P_OUT erratum audit. Units (2026-09-30, label change only; no number changed). The paper's P_OUT is a power density in W/m² at range r; the total-watts quantity formerly labelled P_rad is now P_total = 4π r² · P_OUT (DERIVED / ASSUMPTION: spherical integral). I = peak is an ASSUMPTION (confirmed by Dan Britton 2026-09-30). Cross-reference (documented difference): patent US 9,306,527 Eq. 15, total I² Z₀/(4π) W, is twice the erratum-integrated total I² Z₀/(8π); the erratum does not correct the patent. PMT output-current model is a first-order average-current / sinusoidal-envelope picture. Real single-photon work uses pulse height, discriminator, dead time, and count statistics. Keep anode average below the tube’s rated current; never raw anode to TinySA. v1 · 9 Sep 2026.

description: Experiment C (v1 draft): Faraday-caged SLW/SW launcher, hydrogen or clock-atom 1S–2S readout, dual PMT bandpass at 243 nm and 121.6 nm, TEM-null monitors, quench-control discriminator. 8 GHz is not a 10.2 eV photon.
text: Experiment C · v1 draft · 9 Sep 2026 · educational / predicted channel · not a completed Hively spectroscopy result Experiment C — Faraday-caged SLW/SW source with atomic 1S–2S optical-UV readout New: VNA guide for Steve: VNA checks for the RF arm (sphere, stub, cables, filter). No cable crosses the cage wall. A third bench, separate from the 1296 MHz cage (A) and the 433 MHz balls+rods (B). Goal: ask whether a Faraday-caged scalar-longitudinal / scalar-wave source can move population on a dipole-forbidden S–S interval (hydrogen 1S–2S, or a documented clock-atom S–S), with ordinary TEM fields vetoed at the atom, while dual solar-blind PMTs count later TEM UV at 243 nm and 121.6 nm. Theory and patent context: Hively US 9,306,527, Hively/Reed EED, Navy US 12,525,711 B1 SLW antenna patent. Atomic optical readout is a predicted channel. TX and detector banks below list stub / sphere / bifilar / NZ-style plasma and PMT + side transducers; the SNR companion includes SLW Ohmic path loss. Do not treat 8 GHz as a 10.2 eV photon. An RF SLW launcher (GHz class) is not a single quantum that bridges the 1S–2S gap. See § Frequency plan. The PMT does not hear the C-wave; it hears later TEM UV after the atom returns by an allowed channel. Master page: index.html#expt-c. Field dictionary / SW vs SLW: sw-vs-slw.html. Cage hardware lineage: setup.html (Experiment A). Library: Hively patent & EED papers. Adjacent nuclei focus (different claim): c-nuclei.html. Exact claim under test Claim (v1): A Faraday-caged SLW/SW source transfers population on the 1S–2S interval of hydrogen (or a documented clock-atom S–S), or modulates that interval in a lock-in sense, while companion TEM-null sensors show E⊥ and B below a pre-registered TEM leakage budget at the atom location. Pass is not “we saw some UV.” Pass requires modulation transfer + TEM veto + quench discriminator (below). 243 nm alone is the known two-photon diagnostic — not proof of SLW. 121.6 nm with quench on is ordinary Lyman-α from 2S→2P mixing. The interesting channel is 121.6 nm that tracks the SLW/SW modulator with quench off (and TEM budget held). Field dictionary (do not mix) Mode Fields Energy / momentum Eddy / skin Ohmic (Joule) TEM E⊥, B yes / yes (E×B) yes yes SLW B=0, C≠0, E∥ ≠ 0 yes / yes (C E / μ) no yes (J=σE∥) SW B=0, E=0, C≠0 yes (C²/2μ) / no no no Do not say “SLW has no losses.” Say: no eddy / no classical skin barrier; SLW still has linear Ohmic loss; SW has neither. Hively: SLW from irrotational / gradient current J=∇κ; SW is the E=0 special case of C = ∇·A + εμ ∂Φ/∂t. Frequency plan (explicit) 1S–2S gap ≈ 10.2 eV two-photon diagnostic: 243 nm ≈ 1.23×10¹⁵ Hz = 1.23 PHz full gap as one quantum / Lyman-α λ: 121.6 nm ≈ 2.47×10¹⁵ Hz = 2.47 PHz RF cage lineage (this hub / Hively tests): ~1.3 GHz (Expt A) or ~8×10⁹ Hz class 8 GHz / 1.23 PHz ≈ 6.5×10⁻⁶ → not a direct pump v1 architecture (chosen): RF SLW/SW as modulator / gate, not as the 10.2 eV photon. Optical clock / calibration arm (TEM, known physics). A 243 nm two-photon source (or a commercial clock-laser stack for a chosen S–S atom) establishes the line, calibrates the PMTs, and provides a source-dark baseline. This arm is ordinary CED/QED. RF SLW/SW arm (contested). SLW Ohmic / propagation loss (do not forget) SLW is not lossless. No eddy / no classical skin pile-up (B=0), but longitudinal E still drives J=σE and local Joule density σE∥². Pure SW (E=0) has no σE² term. Do not say “SLW has no losses.” Local Ohmic density (CED + EED agree on the form): p_Joule = J·E = σ E∥². Hively US 9,306,527: with J=σE, the SLW E equation admits a transient E = E0 exp(−σ t / ε), with charge-relaxation time τ = ε / σ (E0 is the initial field, σ is the conductivity in S/m, ε is the permittivity in F/m, t is time; patent EQN. 12 family, exponent corrected, see the note below) and table item that E, C, and J exchange energy in conductive media (EQNs 11–17). Free-space radiated power cartoon is isotropic P_OUT (patent EQN. 15 / JPCS Eq. 22) falling as 1/r² — that is geometric spreading, not Ohmic. Note on the exponent (FACT): The standard EM derivation (Ohm’s law J = σE in the continuity equation, plus Gauss’s law) gives dρ/dt = −(σ/ε) ρ, which is the form above. The exponent must have no units: σ/ε has units of 1/s, while ε/σ has units of seconds. Hively & Land’s IARD 2020 slide 60 prints this same form. For copper, ε0/σ ≈ 1.5×10⁻¹⁹ s, which matches the ~10⁻¹⁹ s decay the 2019 paper itself states next to Eq. A5. The 2019 paper (Phys. Essays 32, 112, Eq. A5, p. 122) and US 9,306,527 B1 (col. 5) print the exponent inverted (ε and σ swapped); this is a typo, confirmed by the author (next bullet). The 2022 Erratum (Phys. Essays 35, 320) rewrote Appendix A and dropped this transient, so there is no current published form to match. This is a charge-relaxation transient in time, not a path loss over distance. Author-confirmed, 2026-09-30 (FACT, author-confirmed): Dr. Lee Hively confirmed the exponent in a private email to Dan on 2026-09-30: “The form, E = E0 e^(-sigma t/epsilon), is the correct one.” Eq. (A5), p. 122 of Hively & Loebl 2019, and the exponent before EQN. 12 in US 9,306,527 B1 (col. 5) therefore have ε and σ swapped (typos as printed). The correct form is E = E0 exp(−σ t / ε) with τ = ε / σ, and IARD 2020 slide 60 is correct. See the Corrections log. JPCS 2021: SLW impedance Z uses JL=σEL and loss tangent tan δε = ε″/ε′ (their Eq. 21); still no eddy skin term. SNR implication: path through air ≈ geometric 1/r²; path through seawater / metal / lossy dielectric must include an extra Ohmic attenuation for SLW. headings: Experiment G — Undersea SLW link via hydrogen 2S tickled relaxation
Field reaching the atoms vs seawater range
description: Experiment G (expt-g-v0.1, desk model G0): can a ~1 GHz scalar-longitudinal wave (HYP) cross seawater, a steel hull and a Faraday cage and tickle metastable hydrogen 2S atoms into Lyman-alpha? Default: Hively's Joule-loss term included (SLW 1/e length about 1.45 cm in seawater, so centimetres); Erratum no-loss case as a toggle. Meissner-Wentz seawater, Lamb-Retherford quench physics, 2E1 background, link budget, detector options, gates G0-G3. Educational, contested, illustrative.
text: expt-g-v0.1 · gate G0 (desk model) · illustrative, not a measurement · Cloud twin pending sync (expt-g-v0.1) Experiment G — Undersea SLW link via hydrogen 2S tickled relaxation Dan controls both ends of an undersea link. A transmitter sends a radio-frequency field at about 1057.8 MHz through seawater, a steel hull and a metal box. Inside the box, hydrogen atoms parked in a long-lived state (called 2S) are nudged by that field into a short-lived state (2P). Each nudged atom then gives off one ultraviolet photon (Lyman-α, 121.567 nm), which a detector counts. Switching the transmitter on and off switches the photon count up and down, and that carries the data. The transmitted wave is assumed to be a scalar-longitudinal wave (SLW), the hypothetical wave in Hively's extended electrodynamics. That is a HYPothesis, not established physics. The key question, answered first Using Hively's own Joule-loss term, how far does a ~1 GHz SLW get through seawater? With the Joule-loss term, a ~1 GHz SLW falls by a factor e every 1.45 cm of seawater (599 dB/m at 1057.8 MHz, 15 °C, salinity 35), so the range is centimetres. Ordinary radio (TEM), the classical comparison, falls by e every 1.10 cm (788 dB/m). Default on this page (hub rule, 25 Sep 2026): Hively's Joule-loss term is included for SLW in conductive media. This matches Experiment C's field dictionary, which lists SLW as “Eddy / skin: no; Ohmic (Joule): yes (J=σE∥)” and SW as “no” for both, and says: “Do not say ‘SLW has no losses.’ Say: no eddy / no classical skin barrier; SLW still has linear Ohmic loss; SW has neither.” Experiment C's Ohmic section adds that longitudinal E “still drives J=σE and local Joule density σE∥². Pure SW (E=0) has no σE² term.” So on this page SLW has no eddy-current or skin-effect loss, but it does have Joule loss σE∥². SW has neither. Longest range (1 s, SNR 5) SLW with Joule loss default TEM-equal (classical comparison) Erratum α = 0 toggle, not default Best lab receiver today, 1 W 5.72 cm 4.59 cm 2.96 m Best lab receiver today, 1 kW 9.93 cm 7.81 cm 93.5 m Best possible receiver, 1 W 11.9 cm 9.31 cm 435 m Best possible receiver, 1 kW 16.4 cm 12.8 cm 13.8 km Default: Hively's Joule term J·E counted as a real loss (ASSUMPTION for the algebra, hub rule for the choice). The Joule term is J·E in the energy balance, Eq. (44) of Hively & Loebl 2019, with Ohm's law J = σE. We charge the Joule heat σE∥² against the SLW power flow CE/μ from Eq. (44), using Hively's SLW impedance, Eq. (37), and his definition σ = ε0ε″ω. The field then falls by e every 1.45 cm (599 dB/m). Even 1 kW reaches only 9.93 cm with today's best lab receiver and 16.4 cm with the best possible one. TEM-equal (classical comparison). If the SLW loses energy exactly like ordinary radio (1.10 cm), 1 W reaches 4.59 cm and 1 kW reaches 7.81 cm. Erratum α = 0: a non-default toggle (HYP). Hively & Loebl's 2022 Erratum argues that the Joule term cancels. What it says, in context (Phys. Essays 35, 320, 2022, doi:10.4006/0836-1398-35.3.320): “This Erratum corrects errors in Appendix A of our paper for derivation of the no-skin-effect constraint. The scalar longitudinal wave (SLW) has only irrotational fields and no magnetic field from Eq. (27), B = 0 … Substituting the expressions for E and C from Eqs. (18) and (20) into Eq. (A.5) gives the longitudinal component of the A-wave equation: … (A6). Physically, Eq. (A6) means that the SLW is not subject to resistive loss in conductive media. The same no-loss result occurs from the energy balance equation, Eq. (44), by substituting for (ρ/ε) from Eq. (22) and by substituting for JL from Eq. (21) with B = 0; then cancelling terms. Consequently, the SLW is unconstrained by the skin effect and power loss in resistive media.” With that toggle on, seawater absorbs nothing, and only spreading and the receiver limit range: 1 W reaches 2.96 m (lab) or 435 m (best possible). Choose it with control 3 below or in “All controls”. ⚠ Open conflict, flagged and not resolved here. The Erratum's “not subject to resistive loss” contradicts Experiment C's dictionary and Ohmic section (“SLW still has linear Ohmic loss”, “Do not say ‘SLW has no losses’”). This page follows the hub rule and uses Joule loss by default. It keeps the Erratum only as a labelled toggle. experiment-c.html is left unchanged. Only the G2 pool mockup (control e: vary salinity and range) can settle it. The unknown parameter is αSLW, the SLW field attenuation in seawater in nepers per metre. It is not an extra constant in Hively's formulas; it encodes which reading is right. Presets: Joule-loss value (default), TEM value, 0 (Erratum toggle), or a custom slider. Distances here are for a 1 s count with a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 5, a lossless hull and cage (Thull = Tcage = 1), and SLW coupling η = 1. Distances under about one wavelength in water (2.99 cm) are near-field, where our far-field formula is only indicative. Details: Hively term · link budget. How the receiver is shielded (FACT for ordinary radio, HYP for SLW). The detector sits in its own Faraday cage, a closed metal box that strips out ordinary radio (TEM) waves. The steel hull is not that cage, because crew Wi-Fi and other radios live inside the hull. The SLW is assumed (HYP) to pass through the cage wall. No cable crosses the cage wall: a battery sits inside, and data leave by optical fibre. So any count change that follows the transmitter must come through the wall, and control (a) below tests whether ordinary radio can explain it. Gate sequence (do not skip) G0 · desk modelThis page: chain model, link budget, detector comparison, Mathematica twin. Paper result only. Status: in progress. G1 · TEM bench baselineReproduce standard RF quenching of 2S at 1058 MHz with an ordinary antenna. This proves the receiver works before any SLW claim. G2 · POOL MOCKUPDetector in its own cage, inside a steel hull mockup, in water of known salinity, with the transmitter outside. Controls (a)–(e) are all required. details G3 · comms demoOnly if G2 is positive: bit error rate against range. Try it Four controls. Everything else sits in the tabs further down. Coloured labels: FACT textbook or measured physics · HYP Hively hypothesis, untested · ASSUMPTION a modelling choice we made. 1 · Seawater path length (range) Range = 5 cm (default: inside the Joule-loss range). The slider goes from 1 cm to 1 km. 2 · Transmitter power PTX = 1 W (1 mW to 10 kW). Assumes the antenna sends power equally in all directions. 3 · How much does seawater absorb the SLW? Joule loss (default) Same as radio (TEM) Erratum: none (toggle) This is αSLW, the make-or-break unknown (HYP). The default includes Hively's Joule loss σE∥². The Erratum button is Hively's 2022 no-loss claim, kept for comparison only. 4 · Which 2S receiver? The thick line is the one currently selected. Dashed line: the field this receiver needs (SNR 5 in 1 s). Where a line is above the dashed line, the link works. Grey band: under one wavelength in water, where the formula is only indicative. Words and symbols used on this page (plain English) SLW, scalar-longitudinal wave A wave predicted by Hively's “extended electrodynamics” (EED). It has an electric field pointing along its direction of travel and no magnetic field. It has never been independently confirmed. HYP On this hub (Experiment C dictionary): no eddy-current or skin loss, but Joule loss σE∥² in conducting water. SW, scalar wave The E = 0 special case (only the scalar field C). Per the same dictionary it has neither skin loss nor Joule loss. HYP TEM, ordinary radio The normal radio wave of textbook physics (Maxwell). A closed metal box blocks it, and seawater absorbs it within centimetres at 1 GHz. FACT 2S and 2P Two excited states of hydrogen. 2S lives 0.1215 s on its own, so it is “metastable”. 2P lives only 1.60 ns before emitting a Lyman-α photon. Lamb shift, L The tiny energy gap between 2S and 2P. As a radio frequency it is 1057.8 MHz (NIST ASD). A field at this frequency “tickles” 2S into 2P. Lyman-α The ultraviolet photon (121.567 nm) emitted when 2P falls to the ground state 1S. 2E1 background A lone 2S atom eventually decays by giving off two photons that share 10.2 eV. Their energies are spread over a broad range, and a few land inside the Lyman-α filter. Stray-field quench Small leftover electric fields in the apparatus also knock 2S atoms down, giving real Lyman-α photons that look exactly like signal. With today's best field control this is the largest background. E (V/m) Electric field strength in volts per metre. We quote the peak value. The rms value is 0.707 × peak. α (Np/m, dB/m) Attenuation: how fast a field dies away in water. The field falls by a factor e (2.718) every 1/α metres. 1 Np/m = 8.686 dB/m. N2S Number of hydrogen atoms held in 2S at the receiver. εdet Overall detection efficiency: the fraction of emitted Lyman-α photons that are actually counted. SEcage (dB) Shielding effectiveness of the detector's cage against ordinary radio. 80 dB means the field inside is 10,000 times weaker than outside. Thull, Tcage The fraction of SLW field that gets through the hull and through the cage. Both are unknown (HYP) and are swept from 10−12 to 1 and 10−6 to 1. η How strongly an SLW field tickles 2S compared with an ordinary field of the same size. η = 1 means “the same”. Unknown (HYP), swept from 10−12 to 1. SNR Signal-to-noise ratio: how far the transmitter-on count rises above the random scatter of the background counts. See also Experiment C and Experiment F (Hydrogen SW).
