description: Archived possible future experiment. A speculative strip transmitter and detector (PVDF film or BST beam) driven and read by TinySA Ultras inside a Faraday cage, with a toroid A-source, sphere receivers, Simulation Lab feasibility numbers, Bob Greenyer's Standing Wave Project and O-Animator visuals, the Zeenko amplifiers and a distance test.
text: Archive · Possible future experiment Experiment H: scalar-wave strip transmitter and detector (TinySA Ultra) Archived: possible future experiment. Speculative; any scalar coupling of the strip is a hypothesis with no predicted size. A thin electroded strip (PVDF film or a BST beam) is driven by one TinySA Ultra and an identical strip inside a closed Faraday cage is read by another. Ordinary electric, magnetic, acoustic and vibration coupling must be measured and ruled out first. The default expectation is a null result. This page is not on the Round 1 schedule. Tests of hypotheses, not results. Nothing here is an established effect. Mainstream electrodynamics has no scalar wave of this kind; the extended electrodynamics papers cited below propose one. No published source gives a coupling size for a strip, a sphere or a toroid, so this page predicts only the ordinary background that a reading would have to beat. Labels: fact quoted from a cited source or tool output, derived our own calculation from stated assumptions, assumption an input value we chose, hyp a hypothesis we would be testing. Draft prepared by Grok Bot for Dan Britton, 7 Oct 2026. Numbers come from our own estimates and the Simulation Lab feasibility model (Python, published sources only). 1 Idea 2 Scalar wave idea 3 TinySA Ultra specs 4 Driving the strip 5 Configurations 1 to 3 6 Receiver 7 Layout and controls 8 Mobius strip 9 Config 4 (dropped) 10 Config 5 toroid 10b Config 6 electret 11 Simulation results 12 Standing Wave Project 13 Range and amplifiers 14 Modelling tools 15 Connections and soldering 16 Parts list 17 References 18 Derived values Acknowledgements 1. Idea in one paragraph hyp Use a thin insulating strip with electrodes on both faces as the transmitter. Drive it electrically so it flexes or vibrates; the strain gradient (flexoelectric) or strain (piezoelectric) moves bound charge back and forth inside the insulator. A second, identical strip in a closed Faraday cage is the detector (reciprocity: the element that turns charge motion into strain should also turn the reverse process into a voltage). Ordinary E and B coupling should be blocked by the cage and checked with probes. Any residual signal that survives all controls would be a candidate for a non-classical channel. The default expectation is a null result. 2. The scalar wave idea, from the published papers fact In the published extended electrodynamics papers (Hively and Loebl 2019 [4]; Hively and Land 2021 [5]) the Lorenz condition is not imposed. That leaves a dynamical scalar field, written in the 2019 paper as C = div A + (1/c²) ∂Φ/∂t (A is the vector potential, Φ the scalar potential). Its wave equation is driven by the charge-balance term ∂ρ/∂t + div J (Hively and Loebl 2019, Eq. 25). The same paper (Section VII) describes a scalar-longitudinal wave (SLW) and a separate scalar wave with E = 0. This experiment uses only that generic picture. It does not depend on any equation beyond it, and it does not assume the theory is right. hyp Why a strip: bending or straining an insulator moves bound charge inside it with no conduction current loop. Our hypothesis, not a claim in the published papers, is that such bound-charge motion could act as a source of C. If it does, a strip is a compact, electrically simple source and, by reciprocity, also a sensor. 3. TinySA Ultra: the specs that matter fact Quoted from the official tinysa.org wiki: Specification [1], Menu Tree [2], Limitations [3]. The original Ultra is HW V0.4.5.x; the Ultra+ is ZS406 (HW V0.4.6) and ZS407 (HW V0.5.3). The kit units are all ZS406, so the ZS407-only limits quoted below (6 GHz square wave, 7.3 GHz analyzer) do not apply here; for the ZS406 the generator square wave goes to 4.4 GHz and the analyzer to 6 GHz in ULTRA mode. Every frequency used in this experiment (109 kHz, 39 MHz, 1296 MHz) is well inside those limits. Signal generator Item Official value Source Clean sine output "Sine wave output with harmonics below -40dB of fundamental from 100kHz to 800MHz (900MHz for Ultra+)" [1] Above 800 MHz "Cleanest signal mode: square wave, up to 4.4GHz (6 GHz for ZS407)"; "Highest accuracy mode ... up to 5.4GHz (7.3 GHz for ZS407)" [1] Output level "selectable in 1dB steps between -115dBm and -19dBm" [1], [2] Level accuracy "+/- 2dB up to 800Mhz between -72dBm and -19dBm, less accuracy below -72dBm" [1] Frequency resolution "Output frequency resolution 57.2Hz" [1] Modulation "AM or FM modulation frequencies between 50Hz and 5kHz (AM) or 1kHz (FM)" [1], [2] AM depth "between 10% and 100%" [1], [2] FM deviation "between 1kHz and 300kHz" [1], [2] Sweep frequency sweep "over selectable frequency span"; "output level sweep over maximum the entire output level range"; menu has SPAN, LEVEL CHANGE, SWEEP TIME, SWEEP POINTS [1], [2] Battery "at least 2 hours (3 hours for Ultra+)" [1] Spectrum analyzer Item Official value Source Input range "from 100kHz to 800MHz (900 MHz for Ultra+) in normal mode and up to 6GHz (7.3GHz for ZS407) with ULTRA mode" [1] Below 100 kHz "Below 0.1MHz the sensitivity starts to reduce." [3] RBW "Resolution filters with a width of 0.2, 1, 3, 10, 30, 100, 300, 600 and 850 kHz"; "The minimum resolution bandwidth of 200Hz" [1], [3] Sensitivity "Lowest discernible signal with LNA at 30MHz using a resolution bandwidth of 200Hz of -145dBm" [1] Input "Input impedance 50 ohm when input attenuation set to 10dB or more"; "Maximum +/-5V DC input" [1] Audio "Headphone output for listening to the demodulated audio (AM only)" [1] Zero span ZERO SPAN mode exists (span 0 Hz at a set center) [2] What this means (our reading): The generator cannot make audio or low kHz directly. Its lowest clean sine is 100 kHz. AM and FM only exist as modulation on a carrier (AM rate 50 Hz to 5 kHz). derived The maximum sine level is -19 dBm: about 25 mV rms into 50 ohm (about 50 mV open-circuit EMF). That is small, so a passive voltage step-up or an amplifier helps (section 13). The analyzer does not see audio-rate tones directly. An audio-rate modulation shows up as AM sidebands around the carrier, as a level variation in zero span, or by ear on the headphone output (AM only). 4. Can a TinySA Ultra drive the strip? (a) Directly at a mechanical resonance: yes, if the resonance is at 100 kHz or above. That rules out the low bending modes of a long film strip (Hz to a few kHz) but allows several useful modes. Element (example) Mode First guess derived Assumptions PVDF film 28 µm, 20 x 100 mm length extensional about 6 kHz (too low) bar speed about 1185 m/s (Y 2.5 GPa, density 1780 kg/m³) assumption PVDF film cut 5 mm wide width extensional about 120 kHz same PVDF film 28 µm thickness mode about 39 MHz thickness sound speed about 2200 m/s assumption PVDF film 52 µm thickness mode about 21 MHz same SrTiO3 or BST beam, 0.5 mm thick, 2 mm free length, clamped first bending mode about 100 to 145 kHz f1 = 0.1615 t v / L², v about 5000 to 7200 m/s assumption These are starting points only. The real resonance must be found by sweeping. (b) As a GHz carrier AM-modulated at the resonance: not useful by itself. A strip cannot follow a GHz field mechanically, and a linear dielectric does not demodulate. The strip would only feel the envelope if something nonlinear in the path rectifies it (a diode junction, a contact, electrostriction, heating). That adds a classical demodulation path you would then have to rule out, and the AM rate tops out at 5 kHz, below most useful resonances. Keep it only as a deliberate control. Strip capacitance derived (parallel plate, εr = 12, C = ε0 εr A / t): Strip Thickness C X at 120 kHz at 300 kHz at 1 MHz at 39 MHz 20 x 100 mm 28 µm 7.6 nF 175 ohm 70 ohm 21 ohm 0.5 ohm 20 x 100 mm 52 µm 4.1 nF 325 ohm 130 ohm 39 ohm 1.0 ohm 20 x 5 mm 28 µm 0.38 nF 3.5 kohm 1.4 kohm 420 ohm 11 ohm 5 x 5 mm electrode 28 µm 95 pF 14 kohm 5.6 kohm 1.7 kohm 43 ohm A full 20 x 100 mm PVDF strip is not a high-impedance load at a few hundred kHz; it is close to 50 ohm there. It only becomes high impedance at low frequency or when the electrode is small. 5. Configurations 1 to 3 Configuration 1 (start here): PVDF thickness mode, direct 50 ohm drive Strip: metallized PVDF, 28 µm (or 52 µm), with the active electrode trimmed to about 5 x 5 mm. For the leaded TE DT1-028K/L element, see section 11. Drive frequency: the measured thickness resonance, first guess about 39 MHz for 28 µm or about 21 MHz for 52 µm derived. Why: a 5 x 5 mm electrode is about 43 ohm reactive at 39 MHz, so the TinySA can drive it straight from the SMA port. The receiver works where the TinySA is most sensitive (its spec is quoted at 30 MHz). A copper mesh cage shields much better at tens of MHz than at 100 kHz. The thickness mode also has a large strain gradient across the film. Caveat: PVDF is piezoelectric, so most of its charge motion is piezo, not flexo. It is not a pure flexo test. Configuration 2 (flexo-focused): stiff beam bending mode, about 110 kHz Strip: a centrosymmetric insulator with a known flexoelectric response: BST (Ma and Cross 2002 [7]) or a SrTiO3 single crystal (Zubko et al. 2007 [8]). Recommended form (section 11): a free-free 5 x 2 x 0.5 mm beam at about 109 kHz, held at its bending nodes, electrodes on both faces. Note that commercial 70/30 BST (Tc 33 °C) is ferroelectric, not paraelectric, at room temperature. Matching: a BST beam is 0.7 to 1.8 nF, so the 5 x 2 x 0.5 mm beam is about 820 ohm at 109 kHz and needs a 1.19 mH series tuning coil. Only SrTiO3 is down at a few hundred pF. A step-up transformer on a ferrite toroid rated for 100 kHz (1:3 or 1:4 turns) is an optional addition. derived The tuning coil can be built from the Glarks toroid kit already on hand: five 220 µH units plus one 100 µH in series give about 1.2 mH (toroids barely couple to each other, so the values add). Measure the series string and its Q on the VNA first; the seller gives no Q figure. Drive level: the Zeenko amplifiers in the kit give only about 5 dB at 100 kHz (section 13), so they do not help here. Finding the resonance: use the generator SWEEP (SPAN plus SWEEP TIME) across the expected band with the receive strip, or the drive strip's own current through a small sense resistor, on the second TinySA, and pick the peak. Re-check inside the cage, since clamping and temperature move it. Configuration 3 (not recommended) GHz carrier with AM at the strip resonance. Keep only as a control that should show nothing unless a nonlinear element is present. 6. Receiver Second TinySA Ultra in spectrum analyzer mode, LNA on, on an identical strip (same material, size, clamp). Front end: for Configuration 1 a 5 x 5 mm strip is near 50 ohm at resonance, so a direct connection or a low-noise 50 ohm amplifier is fine (a Zeenko ZK06-UM ahead of the TinySA helps here, section 13). For Configuration 2 the strip is kohms, so put a high-impedance buffer at the strip: an ADA4817 FET-input op-amp follower (as modelled), a BF862 or J310 JFET source follower, or a charge amplifier, then a 50 ohm driver. Battery power, inside a small shielded box at the strip. Settings: center on the drive frequency, narrow span or zero span, RBW 200 Hz (the minimum), averaging on. Keying: switch the generator OUTPUT on and off on a fixed schedule (for example 30 s on, 30 s off, 20 cycles). A real coupling shows as an on/off difference that tracks the schedule. Log traces to SD. Averaging: compare the mean on level against the mean off level and its scatter. The rated floor is about -145 dBm with LNA at 30 MHz and 200 Hz RBW [1]. Optional: slow AM (1 kHz, 100 % depth) on the drive, and look for sidebands at ±1 kHz. A sideband pair is a second fingerprint that the signal came from the generator. 7. Layout and controls Layout: RX strip, buffer and RX TinySA on battery inside the closed Faraday cage. TX strip and TX TinySA outside at a fixed distance (or inside their own small shielded box, which is better). Nothing conductive through the cage wall. Read the RX display through the mesh or from the SD log afterward. Strips on separate tables with soft mounts. Controls (each run logged): H10 magnetic probe at the RX strip position: must read nothing above floor with TX on. E-field probe at the RX strip position: must read nothing above floor with TX on. Dummy strip: replace the RX strip with a capacitor of the same value and lead layout (no mechanical response). Any signal that remains is electrical pickup. Source off and detuned: TX off; then TX on but well off the mechanical resonance. A strip mechanism should drop sharply off resonance; a leakage path will not. Strip swap: swap TX and RX strips (reciprocity), then swap in a non-active strip (unpoled PVDF, plain PTFE film with the same electrodes, or the uncut Mobius film below). Signal should follow the active material. Clamped strip: same RX strip glued rigidly to a block so it cannot flex. Vibration: run TX into a dummy load on the same table, and tap or shake test with a contact pickup. Separate tables and soft mounts. Acoustic: ultrasound in air at 100 kHz travels centimeters to meters. Test with an acoustic barrier (closed foam box) around TX and an ultrasonic microphone or spare strip as a monitor. Thermal: step the drive level and duty cycle; a thermal path responds slowly (seconds) and follows power, not frequency. No cage: repeat the run on the open bench at the same distance. With the caged run this measures the cage's attenuation. A caged signal only counts if it is far above what that attenuation predicts. Cage leakage calibration: in place of the strips, use a small loop and a small dipole at the same frequency to measure the cage shielding directly. hyp What would count as interesting: a keyed on/off signal inside the closed cage that is above leakage predictions, disappears with the dummy, clamped and non-active strips, follows the mechanical resonance, survives the vibration, acoustic and thermal checks, and falls off with distance like a radiated wave (section 13). 8. Mobius strip: honest evaluation Idea Physical mechanism? Verdict Mobius-wound loop or Mobius resistor (non-inductive) Yes. Currents run in opposite directions in two closely spaced conductors, so the loop area and magnetic response cancel, like a bifilar coil or twisted pair. Useful but ordinary. Good for B-rejecting leads or a pickup with very low loop area. A tight twisted pair does the same job. Mobius metallized film strip The two faces become one continuous surface, so the two electrodes become one. There is no voltage between faces to read. Kills the normal flexo or piezo readout. Only useful as a "should read zero" control strip. Built-in twist strain gradient Partly. A twisted strip has a static strain gradient, which gives a static polarization, not a signal at the drive frequency. May slightly bias the material. Does not replace the AC drive. Bottom line: the only physically useful Mobius element is non-inductive wiring for B rejection, and that is conventional. An uncut Mobius metallized strip is worth building as a control. Nothing in Mobius topology by itself predicts a scalar wave source. 9. Configuration 4: sphere collector driving the strip (evaluated and dropped) Status: evaluated and dropped (Simulation Lab, 7 Oct 2026). derived The sphere-to-strip path, read optically or acoustically, is 62 to 95 dB worse than wiring the same sphere straight into a high-impedance buffer and TinySA #2 (62 to 92 dB with the 2.5 in sphere). The reason: the strip's large capacitance soaks up the sphere's charge and leaves a tiny voltage, and the strip's mechanical resonance gives no rejection of leakage at the same frequency (leakage at the drive frequency drives the electrode just as a hypothetical signal would). Use the direct sphere-to-buffer path instead. The idea is kept below for the record. Idea: a metal sphere as the collector and the strip as a mechanical filter, read without wires. Collector: one of the two spheres on hand, inside the closed cage on an insulating stand: (a) the 3/4 in (19.05 mm) sphere with no hole, or (b) the 2.5 in (63.5 mm) hollow sphere with a 1/4 in hole in the bottom. hyp Proposed mechanism: a scalar wave arriving at the sphere would move charge on it at the wave frequency. No published source gives a sphere charge or current per unit of C, so this step has no number. Coupling: a short lead from the sphere to the active electrode of the receive strip; the strip's other electrode returns to the cage floor or a small counterpoise plate. Charge on the electrode would drive the strip by the converse flexoelectric or piezo effect. derived Self capacitance is about 1.06 pF (3/4 in) and 3.53 pF (2.5 in), much smaller than the strip (95 pF for a 5 x 5 mm PVDF electrode, 0.7 to 1.8 nF for the BST beam). That mismatch is why the chain loses. Readout (non-galvanic): optical lever with a split photodiode (beam mode), fibre or Michelson interferometer (PVDF thickness mode), or an ultrasonic pickup, all battery powered in their own shielded box. Baseline it was compared against: sphere into an ADA4817 or BF862 buffer into TinySA #2, same position, same TX settings. That direct path won by 62 to 95 dB in minimum detectable charge. 10. Configuration 5: toroid A-source, Aharonov-Bohm geometry Idea: a small toroidal coil gives a vector potential A outside its core with almost no B outside, the geometry of the Aharonov-Bohm experiments [9], [10]. Use it as a known-A test source for the probes. Source: a small toroidal coil inside the closed cage, driven by TinySA #1. TinySA #1 must run inside the cage on battery, or be fed over an RF-over-fibre link, because no cable may cross the wall. A 50 ohm series resistor at the coil keeps the load near 50 ohm. derived At -19 dBm the coil current is at most about 0.5 mA rms. Toroids on hand: a Glarks 30-piece toroid inductor kit (5 each of 10, 22, 33, 47, 100 and 220 µH, about 12 to 13 mm outside diameter, 0.4 to 0.6 mm wire). The core material is not stated by the seller; the yellow-white paint usually marks an iron-powder mix meant for the kHz range, so treat these as 109 kHz parts only. derived At 109 kHz the 100 µH unit is about 68 ohm and the 220 µH unit about 151 ohm; with the 50 ohm series resistor the drive current is about 0.4 mA and 0.3 mA rms. A factory winding that steps once around the core also acts as a one-turn loop, so add a return wire laid back around the core under the winding to cancel most of that stray B. With 5 identical units of each value, the reversed, shielded and spare toroids for the controls can all be the same part. At 39 MHz and up these cores are lossy and the larger values are likely past their self-resonance, so use proper RF toroid cores and your own winding there. Before use, sweep one 220 µH unit on the VNA to find its self-resonant frequency and Q at 109 kHz. derived Consequence: with source and receiver in the same enclosure, the cage gives no isolation. At 10 cm, ordinary pickup is +3 to +90 dB above the TinySA floor for the spheres and the bifilar coil (and -17 to +57 dB for the strip), over 0.1 to 800 MHz and all toroids modelled. It falls as the inverse cube of distance in the near field. Probes: either sphere, the bifilar coil and the PVDF strip, each near the toroid but not threading its hole, plus the H10 and E-field probes to map leakage. The 2.5 in sphere picks up about 5 to 7 dB more ordinary leakage than the 3/4 in sphere. Use 10 cm or more. fact Conventional EM, important: outside an ideal toroid B is zero but A is not, and at RF that A changes in time. Conventional theory then gives a real E field outside, E = -∂A/∂t, with no B (the Maxwell-Lodge effect [11]). Any loop that threads the hole is simply a transformer secondary. So this is a known-A source, but at RF it is also a known-E source, and that E is a calculable, classical signal. Null baseline (leakage): winding pitch and gaps leak B near the core; a helical winding acts as one extra turn around the major circumference (bring the return lead back along the core, or add a counter-wound layer); winding voltages make a small electric dipole near the hot end (a slotted copper foil shield reduces it). Controls: rotate the toroid about each axis; reverse it (a pure A coupling only changes sign, the hot-end E leakage moves); swap in a non-inductive 50 ohm dummy of the same lead layout; source off, then TinySA #1 into a 50 ohm load; shielded toroid (copper can); change distance (5 to 50 cm) and check the inverse-cube law; a calibration loop threading the core to confirm the drive. hyp Expected outcome: conventionally, the probes respond only to leakage plus the classical E = -∂A/∂t field, both calculable. For a toroid fed with ordinary charge-conserving current, the published Hively papers give no non-zero source term and no coupling coefficient, so the framework as published gives no number for this configuration. Anything reproducible beyond the classical prediction that survives the controls would be an unexplained observation, not a tested prediction. O-Animator, same view: A only (left) reaches beyond the torus, B only (right) stays in the tube. An illustration from Bob Greenyer's fractal model, not a calculation. Rendered with Bob Greenyer's O-Animator (starfire.tech). The O-Animator renders a fractal set of tori (31 even at the lowest depth), the colours are its own shading, and the background particle cloud could not be turned off. Treat the picture as a qualitative illustration of A without B, not as a field map of a real coil. 10b. Configuration 6: electret element (idea under evaluation, Oct 8 2026) Status: idea under evaluation. Nothing bought or built. Configurations 1 to 3 with the 5 PVDF strips stay the baseline. Numbered "10b" so the later section numbers and links stay as they were. The open questions for Dan are at the end of this section. Idea (Dan Britton): use an electret as the source and receiver element. An electret is a dielectric that holds a quasi-permanent trapped charge or frozen polarization. The proposed source is that stored charge, moved mechanically (flexed or squeezed) at the drive frequency, with an identical element as the receiver. How it relates to the PVDF strip fact Poled PVDF is already electret-like: poling freezes in its polarization. The TE (Measurement Specialties) piezo film manual gives d31 = 23 pC/N, d33 = -33 pC/N and relative permittivity 12 [18]. The electret adds one of two things: more charge moved per unit strain, or a charge that can be removed or reversed for a control. So PVDF stays the baseline and the electret is an addition, not a replacement. fact Ferroelectrets (charged cellular polypropylene, the EMFi or Emfit film) hold charge on the walls of flat air voids. Published d33 values: about 250 pC/N quasi-static and 140 pC/N at 600 kHz [20]; up to about 1200 pC/N quasi-static after pressure expansion, about 350 pC/N just below the thickness resonance, with the resonance at 150 to 400 kHz [21]; about 200 pC/N after corona charging, in an air-coupled ultrasonic receiver [24]. A review puts ferroelectret d33 at up to about 20 times that of the best conventional piezoelectric polymers [19]. fact Off-the-shelf sensor film is much lower: the Emfit L-series sheet is specified at 25 pC/N ±20 % (normal force), 0.4 mm thick, relative permittivity about 1.1, 22 pF/cm², operating range -20 to +70 °C [26]. That is about the same as PVDF's |d33|, so any gain depends on which film is bought. fact It is a squeeze effect, not a bend effect. Emfit states that the film responds to thickness change rather than strain, and that flexing gives only low signal levels [26]. For a flexing drive, PVDF (d31 = 23 pC/N) stays the better material. Ferroelectret film needs to be pressed, for example by a piezo stack or by sound pressure. fact Stability: Cellular PP d33 is roughly independent of humidity near and below room temperature, but heating above about 60 °C reduces it [22]. Annealing at 70 °C and above causes decay [21]. One study measured about 600 to 700 pC/N fresh after corona charging, decaying to near 200 pC/N after several months, and about 150 pC/N for samples at 25,000 h. It also measured a film resonance at 97.25 kHz by laser interferometry [23]. Same soldering rule as PVDF: leads only, never heat the film. Strongest advantage: a clean control Discharged twin: an identical element with its charge removed has the same outline, capacitance, lead dress and mechanics, but no stored charge. With DIY film (below), the cleanest twin is an uncharged piece cut from the same sheet. Flip test: turn the film over between the same electrodes and leads. The stored polarization then points the other way, so any response that comes through the stored charge should flip sign (180°). Direct electrical pickup on the leads does not flip. Bias null (optional, needs HV): a DC bias equal and opposite to the film's internal voltage makes a cellular PP receiver insensitive. That internal voltage was 473 ± 16 V for one layer [24]. Be honest about what these controls separate. On the TX side, a charged and a discharged element on the same shaker give almost the same sound, so the pair separates charge motion from acoustics. On the RX side, an electret's acoustic sensitivity also comes from its charge. Discharging or flipping the receiver therefore separates charge-coupled pickup from plain electrical pickup, but not from sound. Reading a sign flip needs phase. The TinySA reads amplitude only. Use a phase-capable instrument on the open bench (for example a two-channel scope with a reference from the generator). Biggest risk: an electret is a microphone fact An electret condenser microphone is a charged membrane plus a JFET [27]. Cellular PP films are used as air-coupled ultrasonic transmitters and receivers at 100 to 200 kHz [24], [25]. So the element senses sound and vibration by design, and acoustic and vibration leakage is expected to dominate. Isolation at least as strict as for the PVDF strip: all the controls in section 7, and the roughly 133 dB of mechanical isolation estimated in section 11. Added controls for this configuration: Charged element, no drive: the RX element in place with TX off, to log the ambient sound and vibration floor. Discharged detector: swap in the discharged twin at the RX position. Discharged source: the discharged twin on the same shaker at the TX position. Flipped film at TX and at RX, one at a time. Acoustic monitor: the ultrasonic microphone (parts list) beside the RX element, logged in every run. Drive A mechanical drive limits this to acoustic and ultrasonic frequencies: 109 kHz at best, not 39 MHz or 1296 MHz. A shaker brings its own fields. A voice coil makes a B field at the drive frequency; a piezo stack makes an E field from its drive voltage. Options: Piezo shaker in a shielded box (die-cast), with the electret outside on a short insulating pushrod. Run the shaker into the discharged twin as a control. Electrical drive: electret transducers are reciprocal [26], so TinySA #1 plus a step-up transformer can drive the film directly. derived With the 1:4 step-up from section 5, about 50 mV EMF becomes about 0.2 V unloaded. Thickness change = d33 x V: about 0.04 nm at 200 pC/N, against about 0.007 nm for PVDF at 33 pC/N. Published ferroelectret ultrasonic transmitters are pulsed at 1.8 kV [25], about 79 dB more voltage. Electrical drive also puts the drive voltage straight onto the element, which is the same E leakage problem as the PVDF strip. Low-frequency crank (hand or motor flexing a film): a sanity demo only. It sits below the TinySA's 100 kHz bottom end, so read it with a scope or a sound card. Cheapest first test: a pair of electret mic capsules fact Example part: Same Sky (formerly CUI) CMA-4544PF-W, rated 20 Hz to 20 kHz, -44 ±2 dB re 1 V/Pa at 1 kHz, 3 V typical (10 V maximum), 2.2 kΩ output impedance. It has an internal FET, so it needs DC bias and a blocking capacitor [27]. Purpose: measure acoustic and vibration leakage through the cage, not the scalar question. Source outside the cage: a small speaker, or a capsule. Receiver inside on battery bias: a second capsule, logged by a battery recorder or phone inside the cage. Compare cage open and closed, foam box on and off, and soft mounts on and off. Limits: Audio band only. The TinySA starts at 100 kHz and cannot read these capsules, and leakage at 109 kHz still needs the ultrasonic microphone. A capsule cannot easily be discharged, so capsules give no clean charge control. Order of buying: capsules first. If audio-band leakage through the closed cage is already large, fix the isolation before buying anything else. Buy ferroelectret film only after that. DIY option: corona-charged PTFE or FEP fact Published setups: Point-to-plane corona on PTFE: needle at ±12 kV, 4 cm gap, 5 min. Non-porous PTFE held about 1500 V more initial surface potential than porous PTFE [30]. Corona triode on 25 to 125 µm films (PP, PET, PMMA, PC, FEP): 12 kV needle, 2 kV grid [29]. A constant-current triode charged FEP foils to surface potentials up to ±6 kV [28]. Advantage: charge one piece and keep an uncharged twin from the same sheet. This gives the cleanest discharged control. assumption Safety (general HV practice, not from the sources above): kV supplies can injure. Use a current-limited supply, a grounded sample plate and a grounding stick. Keep one hand away, and ventilate (corona makes ozone). Keep flammables away. Do this only if Dan has or wants an HV supply. Standing Wave Project cross-check Bob Greenyer's Standing Wave Project could find the modes and clamp or node points of a carrier plate: a metal shim of 0.5 mm or more with the film laminated on (a bender), free or clamped, with the plate at least 20 mm across. Limits, honestly: Electret films (tens of µm to 0.4 mm) are below its 0.5 mm minimum thickness. It has no PP, PTFE, FEP or PVDF material. A tensioned mic diaphragm is outside what it models. It cannot check the film itself, only a stiff carrier. Expected outcome hyp Conventionally, moving bound charge conserves charge. It gives an ordinary near-field E that falls off fast with distance, plus acoustic and vibration pickup, both calculable. The published Hively papers give no source term or coupling coefficient for an electret, so the framework as published gives no number for this configuration. Anything reproducible that survives the controls would be an unexplained observation, not a confirmed prediction. Open questions for Dan Which electret: ferroelectret film (Emfit cellular PP), DIY corona-charged PTFE or FEP, or electret mic capsules? Mechanical or electrical drive, and what target frequency? (109 kHz is the realistic ceiling for a mechanical drive.) Keep the 5 PVDF strips on order? Recommended: yes, they stay the baseline. Do you have, or want, a high-voltage supply for corona charging? It is a shock and ozone hazard. Should Simulation Lab model electret film modes and charge motion against PVDF? What budget for this configuration? 11. Simulation results (Simulation Lab, 7 Oct 2026) Python model, published sources only. It predicts no scalar-wave signal size, because no published source gives one. What it predicts is the ordinary background that a null or positive reading has to beat. Configuration 1 (PVDF thickness mode) derived Works only with a small electrode, about 5 x 5 mm. Thickness resonance 38.97 MHz (28 µm) or 20.99 MHz (52 µm). The 5 x 5 mm electrode is about 42 ohm there (94.9 pF) and gets about 29.5 mV at -19 dBm straight from the TinySA. The full 20 x 100 mm strip is about 0.5 ohm, effectively a short. Optional series match: about 180 nH at 39 MHz. Config 1 with the TE DT1-028K/L leaded element fact The part (TE data sheet): film 16 x 41 mm, electrode 12 x 30 mm, 28 µm PVDF, about 1.38 nF, d31 23 pC/N, riveted lugs and 300 mm 28 AWG leads, rated 0 to 70 °C. derived Find the resonance first: the silver ink and protective coating may pull the thickness resonance down to about 23 to 30 MHz, so sweep 10 to 50 MHz on the VNA before anything else. derived The full electrode is a near short: about 2.9 ohm at resonance, so only about 5 % of the TinySA's power gets in (about 2.9 mV across the film). derived Leads: the supplied 300 mm leads are 47 to 102 ohm reactive at 39 MHz. Cut them to 2 to 5 cm and twist them. RX: use the element as bought. TX, option 1: trim the electrode to about 5 x 5 mm. Ink removal is untested and there is a risk of shorting the faces, so try it on a sacrificial element first. derived TX, option 2: an L-match, about 708 pF shunt and about 35 nH series (the series value includes the lead), gives about 11 mV and 74 % of the power. Tune it on the VNA at the measured resonance. Plan for 5 elements: #1 RX, #2 TX, #3 trim trial, #4 spare, #5 shorted control. Dummy: copper tape electrodes on polyester film plus a C0G capacitor to match the capacitance (no mechanical response). derived Film modes: length 12.9 to 18.3 kHz, width 33 to 47 kHz. Both are below the TinySA's 100 kHz bottom end. derived Untrimmed TX leakage at 0.3 m: +37 dB above the TinySA floor with no cage, and -23 / -43 / -63 dB relative to the floor at 60 / 80 / 100 dB shielding (before any TX amplifier, section 13). Configuration 2 (BST beam) derived Best as a free-free 5 x 2 x 0.5 mm beam at about 109 kHz (109.4 kHz first bending mode), held at the mode-1 nodes, 0.224 and 0.776 of the length (1.12 mm and 3.88 mm from one end), on the centreline. Leads attach on the same node lines, on the centreline. Series tuning coil 1.19 mH (wind it after measuring the beam's capacitance on the VNA). That gives about 0.5 V across the beam. The original 2 mm cantilever is too stubby (L/t = 4) for beam theory and cannot be checked in the Standing Wave Project. derived Twist mode: an independent torsion calculation (Saint-Venant bar, ν 0.35) puts the beam's (1,1) twist mode at about 144 kHz. Scaling the Standing Wave Project result gives about 170 kHz (section 12). We use 144 kHz as the conservative value; the real value is probably between the two. The 109.4 kHz drive is well clear: the 1.19 mH tuned circuit is 15 dB down at 144 kHz (19 dB at 170 kHz), and symmetric full-width electrodes cannot drive twist. Twist only couples in through asymmetry (off-centre leads, supports or epoxy dots, misregistered electrodes, a chipped edge). After mounting, sweep 100 to 200 kHz once: a strong second peak near 145 to 170 kHz means the mount or a lead is asymmetric. Leakage and risks (Configurations 1 and 2) derived With the cage at 80 dB shielding or better, ordinary leakage is below the TinySA floor at 0.3 to 3 m. At only 60 dB, the BST setup at 0.3 m sits right at the floor. The main risks are not radio leakage: 110 kHz sound through the mesh (upper bound +27 dB above the floor at 0.3 m; a solid 0.5 mm steel wall would cut it to -39 dB). Table vibration (about 133 dB of mechanical isolation needed: separate stands, soft mounts, node supports). Cage seams and the real shielding number at the test frequency. RX fully inside the cage on battery, with no cable through the wall. Configurations 4 and 5 Configuration 4: dropped. 62 to 95 dB worse than the direct sphere-to-buffer path (section 9). Configuration 5: TinySA #1 must be inside on battery or fed by fibre, so the cage gives no isolation. Ordinary pickup at 10 cm is +3 to +90 dB above the floor (section 10). Spheres derived Self capacitance: 1.06 pF (3/4 in) and 3.53 pF (2.5 in). Hollow or solid makes no difference; the 1/4 in hole changes it by only 0.0053 %. derived Wired straight to the buffer, the small sphere is better for a charge-like source (0.019 vs 0.029 aC/√Hz) and the big sphere is about 7 dB better for a voltage-like source (18.1 vs 8.16 nV/√Hz). Which one matters is hypothetical. derived The 3/4 in shell's breathing mode is about 113 kHz (assuming a 1 mm brass shell assumption), only about 4 kHz above the 109 kHz beam drive. The 2.5 in shell has low modes at 13 to 33 kHz and a dense set near 100 kHz. Tap-test each sphere and soft-mount it before choosing the drive frequency. Wall thickness and material still need measuring. Update: vendor data gives both spheres as 3003 aluminium; FEM shell modes from imported meshes, and an aluminium breathing-mode estimate of about 146 kHz for the 3/4 in shell, are in section 12 (Hollow sphere modes). Corrections to earlier estimates BST beam capacitance is 0.7 to 1.8 nF (εr about 104 near Tc), not "a few hundred pF". The smaller figure only holds for SrTiO3. Commercial BST (70/30, Tc 33 °C) is ferroelectric at room temperature, so it can carry a piezo response. Ma and Cross's 67/33 ceramic has Tc 21 °C. Keep the beam above Tc, or note the risk. 12. Standing Wave Project cross-check Input: a free 50 x 20 x 5 mm steel plate in Bob Greenyer's Standing Wave Project. This is the 5 x 2 x 0.5 mm BST beam scaled up x10, because the app's minimum plate size is 20 mm. Steel was chosen because its bar sound speed is close to BST's (5170 vs 5323 m/s). Mode SWP tool fact Simulation Lab derived Difference Scaled to the BST beam (2,0) first lengthwise bending 10.75 kHz 10.63 kHz (Euler-Bernoulli) +1.1 % tool x 10.291 = about 111 kHz; beam theory 109.4 kHz (1,1) twisting 16.51 kHz 14.34 kHz (Saint-Venant torsion) +15 % tool scaled about 170 kHz; torsion calculation about 144 kHz (conservative) (3,0) second lengthwise bending 29.85 kHz 29.31 kHz (Euler-Bernoulli) +1.8 % tool x 10.291 = about 307 kHz; beam theory 301.6 kHz Result: Bob Greenyer's Standing Wave Project independently confirmed the strip's (BST beam's) bending modes to within 2 % of the beam-theory values, and it located the clamp points: its mode-1 node lines, about 22 % of the length from each end, are where the beam is held and where the leads attach (1.12 mm and 3.88 mm on the real beam). The two bending modes agree with beam theory within 2 % (+1.1 % and +1.8 %), and the mode-1 node lines sit at about 22 % of the length from each end, matching the 0.224 / 0.776 support points. The twist mode differs by about 15 %. Simulation Lab's reading (not confirmed against the tool's code) is that a thin-plate twisting stiffness reads high for a bar only 4 times wider than it is thick. Torsion also scales with shear modulus, which moves the tool-scaled value to about 166 kHz for BST's Poisson ratio. The real value is probably 144 to 166 kHz. On the real beam: the drive mode is about 109 to 111 kHz, the twisting mode is 144 to 170 kHz (keep clear), and the next bending mode is about 302 to 307 kHz. Figure 1. Standing Wave Project, steel 50 x 20 x 5 mm free plate, (2,0) first bending mode at 10.75 kHz. Black bands are the node lines, about 22 % from each end. Scaled: about 111 kHz on the BST beam. Computed with Bob Greenyer's Standing Wave Project (starfire.tech). Figure 2. Same plate, (1,1) twisting mode at 16.51 kHz. Scaled: about 170 kHz on the BST beam; an independent torsion calculation gives about 144 kHz. Keep the drive clear of it. Computed with Bob Greenyer's Standing Wave Project (starfire.tech). Figure 3. Same plate, (3,0) second bending mode at 29.85 kHz. Scaled: about 307 kHz on the BST beam. Computed with Bob Greenyer's Standing Wave Project (starfire.tech). Hollow sphere modes (imported STL, FEM) Bob Greenyer's Standing Wave Project imports user meshes (STL, OBJ or GLTF), needs no login, and solves true elastic eigenmodes of the imported geometry with its FEM engine. Both spheres were imported as hollow shells. Method. STL meshes were built from vendor data: K-Mac KB-1820, 3/4 in (19.05 mm) 3003 aluminium hollow ball, closed. Wall 1.0 mm assumption, because the vendor does not list it. Download: kb1820-0.75in-closed-shell-1mm.stl K-Mac KB-2016, 2.5 in (63.5 mm) 3003 aluminium, wall 0.132 in (3.35 mm), 1/4 in bottom hole. Download: kb2016-2.5in-shell-3.35mm-quarter-inch-hole.stl The tool rescales every import to a 180 mm bounding box. For a uniformly scaled solid of the same material, frequency …

text: Archive page. This is the previous home page, kept unchanged so existing links and bookmarks still work. The current focus is Round 1: the 1.3 GHz, 433.59 MHz and 2.45 GHz sphere experiments and the microwave oven. All archived pages. Educational briefing hub · Experiments A–F Scalar longitudinal waves — three benches, one shared field kit Study aid for patents, papers, and electrically separate benches: a 1296 MHz Faraday-cage with a ¾″ aluminum hollow sphere + SMA bulkhead (A; Cricut/bifilar/sleeve archived at setup.html#archive-bifilar), a 433.59 MHz ball + polarizer-rod test with no balun (B), and a Faraday-caged SLW/SW → atomic 1S–2S optical readout draft (C). Not a claim that SLW is established physics. A · 1296 MHz B · 433 MHz C · atomic 1S–2S D · hypersonic plasma E · Exodus capacitors F · hydrogen SW G · undersea 2S link Shared kit Briefing Library Author Dan Britton Contact BrittonSolutions@icloud.com Source repos 9wzg44nz44-glitch A 1296.000 MHz · 23 cm · ¾″ KB-1820 sphere B 433.59 MHz · 70 cm · balls + rods · no balun C Caged SLW/SW · 1S–2S optical UV · v1 draft G Undersea SLW · H 2S tickle at 1057.8 MHz · desk study Tone Academic, warm, skeptical Educational only. Experiments A and B do not share an RF feed; C–F are separate proposed tracks. Licensed amateur-radio experimenters and students mapping the “missing-term” literature. Not for medical devices, “free energy,” or unlicensed transmitters. Briefing, comparison table, and paper library stay in the site nav: Learn · Compare · Library. Mainstream classical electrodynamics (CED) is TEM. SLW / extended electrodynamics is not settled physics. Not a measurement. Square-wave drive is full of harmonics and mixer spurs — not a clean sine. Sealed mesh is quoted 50–60 dB RadioScreen, not Hively’s copper-pipe 25,000 dB. Licensed milliwatts on 23 cm only. No magnetron. Ptx TinySA generator (dBm; default −19 dBm) r stub-tip → pancake (m) Cage (both tents) Show SMA-end leak on Detector LNA (~20 dB, NF ≈ 5 dB) Default sealed = 55 dB per tent, two tents so power is down 110 dB if you apply both. That is still a mesh screen, not 2885 copper skin depths. Near-field: lab r is often inside 2D²/λ for a small stub — Friis is a far-field estimate, labeled as such. Illustrative SNR at the TinySA detector TEM (Friis, far-field caveat) SLW / Hively (Eq. 38/B5 as corrected by the erratum) Assumptions stated in the equations section: 50 Ω, RBW B = 100 kHz (log the real RBW), thermal floor N0 = −174 dBm/Hz at 290 K, Hively NF = 3 dB unless LNA on (NF ≈ 5 dB, +20 dB gain on Psig only — still illustrative). TinySA input is 50 Ω when internal atten ≥ 10 dB. Equations on this page (as coded) Physics version tem-slw-1296-v0.1.2 (page, js/fields.js and SLW-TEM-fields-1296MHz.wl). The “SMA-end leak on” checkbox changes the drawing only, not any number. f = 1.296×109 Hz, c = 299792458 m/s, μ0 = 4π×10−7, Z0 = 376.73031346177 Ω, RL = 50 Ω. TinySA → current P = 10^((P_tx,dBm − 30)/10) W into 50 Ω I_rms = sqrt(P / 50) I_peak = I_rms * sqrt(2) TEM received (Friis, far-field; honest near-field caveat) G_tx ≈ 1.5 (short monopole, linear, not dBi marketing) A_eff,TEM = 3λ² / (8π) (same short-monopole estimate) P_rx,TEM = P_tx * G_tx * A_eff,TEM / (4 π r²) [far field] P_rx,mesh = P_rx * 10^(−Att_dB / 10) per tent; two tents when sealed SNR_TEM,dB = P_rx,dBm − (−174 + 10 log10(B) + NF) B = 100 kHz NF = 3 dB (5 dB if LNA box checked) Near-field flags when r < 2 D²/λ with D ≈ λ/4 stub, or r < λ/(2π). Hively SLW (Hively & Loebl 2019 Eq. 38/B5 as corrected by the Erratum) P_OUT(r) = S(r) = I_peak² Z_0 / [2 (4π r)²] W/m² (Hively & Loebl 2019, Eq. 38/B5 as corrected by the Erratum, Phys. Essays 32(3) 417; Z_0 = √(μ/ε) = η ≈ 376.73 Ω) FACT P_total = 4π r² · P_OUT = I_peak² Z_0 / (8π) W (DERIVED / ASSUMPTION: spherical integral of P_OUT, isotropic; not the paper's P_OUT; the toy total-power readout) A_eff = π (0.05)² = 7.854×10⁻³ m² (10 cm palm coil, η = 0.50) P_load = S A_eff η * 10^(−Att_dB/10) per tent SNR_Hively,dB = P_load,dBm − (−174 + 10 log10(B) + NF) FACT the ½ and the (4πr)² grouping are from the erratum. ASSUMPTION I is the peak amplitude of the drive current (the erratum does not say peak or rms). HYP applying this to the TinySA output current and to the palm-coil pickup is the hypothesis under test; the isotropic SLW cartoon is unchanged otherwise. Loss term: none (erratum α = 0 toggle) or Hively’s Joule term σE∥² (Eq. 44) only. Formula history. Before 2026-09-29 this page used the total-watts quantity P_rad = I_peak² Z_0 / (4π) (patent US 9,306,527 Eq. 15), i.e. S = I_peak² Z_0 / (4π r)². That is the form of Eq. 38/B5 as first printed in 2019, without the factor ½. The erratum adds the ½, so S, P_total, P_load and SNRHively are each 3.01 dB lower than before. Am and Az (NZ / Zimmerman) are unchanged. Details: P_OUT erratum audit. Units (2026-09-30, label change only; no number changed). The paper's P_OUT is a power density in W/m² at range r; this page's former “P_rad” in watts is now labelled P_total (DERIVED). I = peak is an ASSUMPTION (confirmed by Dan Britton 2026-09-30). Cross-reference (documented difference): patent US 9,306,527 Eq. 15, total I² Z₀/(4π) W, is twice the erratum-integrated total I² Z₀/(8π); the erratum does not correct the patent. Old HTML sliders used I ≈ 5 A (P_total ≈ 375 W with the erratum; ≈ 749 W with the old form). This page uses TinySA milliwatts, so P_total is tiny. The shape of S∝1/r² is the toy; do not treat 5 A as a TinySA number. description: Chiao et al. 2023 scalar electric Aharonov–Bohm proposal (PRA 107, 042209): summary, the 2025 Gao Comment and Reply, Dan Britton’s notes with evaluation, and an EED (Hively–Loebl) reading that predicts a longitudinal E inside the cage.
text: Library · Future experiments Scalar electric Aharonov–Bohm inside a Faraday sphere Chiao, Hart, Scheibner, Sharping, Inan, Singleton & Tobar (2023), Phys. Rev. A 107, 042209, plus the 2025 Comment and Reply. Summary, Dan’s reading notes with an evaluation, and an EED (Hively–Loebl) interpretation. Labels: FACT = what the papers say; HYP = our interpretation or derivation, not published and not settled physics. Educational. The EED section is our own derivation from the Hively–Loebl equations, not a statement by Dr. Hively, Chiao et al., or Gao. Sign conventions still need checking against Hively & Loebl 2019. Download PDF (arXiv v2) arXiv:2212.03437 PRA 107, 042209 Gao Comment, PRA 111, 066203 Gao preprint Chiao et al. Reply, PRA 111, 066204 Summary of the paper (FACT) Setup. A closed conducting (Faraday) shell has an oscillating voltage V(t) = V0 cos Ωt applied to its surface. The drive is a voltage on the shell itself, not an incident electromagnetic wave. Inside, the electric field is zero and the potential is spatially uniform, apart from very small fields that any time variation produces. Claim. A quantum system inside picks up a time-dependent Aharonov–Bohm phase φ(t) = α sin Ωt with α = eV0/(ħΩ). Expanding with Bessel functions (Jacobi–Anger) splits each level Ei into sidebands Ei ± nħΩ weighted by Jn(α). For large α the strongest sidebands sit near Ei ± eV0. Relation to known physics. The math is the same as the AC Stark / Autler–Townes effect without the polarizability term, because E = 0. The authors argue the sidebands survive a gauge change because the wavefunction phase changes along with the potential. Proposed test. Rubidium vapor inside the cage with Ω = 10⁸ s⁻¹ (about 15.9 MHz) and V0 = 0.5 mV. That gives α ≈ 7.6×10³ and sidebands about eV0/h ≈ 121 GHz away, easily resolved against the Rb D1 line. The readout is electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) in a Λ scheme using 5S1/2, 5P1/2, and the ground state’s upper sideband. Charged quantum dots are offered as an alternative probe. The S→S point. The sideband is an image of the ground state, so it has S character. The electric-dipole selection rule forbids a direct S→S transition. The paper uses that rule to predict a transparency hole from destructive two-path interference in energy space, which it calls the energy-space analog of AB interference in coordinate space. The 2025 published debate (FACT) Gao, Comment, PRA 111, 066203 (13 Jun 2025). Inside the cage the uniform potential can be removed with λ(t) = (V0/Ω) sin Ωt, which leaves V′ = 0, A′ = 0 and H′ = H0. The gauge-invariant energy −(∂tS + eV) stays Ei, so transition energies do not move and the sidebands are artifacts of the gauge. Gao contrasts this with the magnetic AB ring, where the phase ∮A·dl is topological and cannot be removed. Gao also suggests a “true gauge” picture in which something physical does change inside the cage but cannot be measured. Chiao et al., Reply, PRA 111, 066204 (same issue). The authors say Gao’s gauging procedure is inconsistent and would give wrong answers if applied the same way to the magnetic AB effect. They reaffirm that the energy shifts are physical. Status. As of this page, no experiment has been reported that settles it. Dan’s reading notes, with evaluation Dan · forbidden S-to-S “This paper speaks to the forbidden S to S transitions.” Correct, with one refinement. The paper invokes the S→S dipole selection rule. It does not claim the transition becomes allowed. The rule forbids jumping from the ground state to its own S-type sideband, and that is what shapes the predicted EIT transparency hole. The forbidden transition is part of the readout mechanism, not the effect being discovered. Dan · Faraday sphere with sinusoidal modulation “A time-varying scalar potential … inside a Faraday spherical cage which itself is subject to a sinusoidal exterior electromagnetic modulation, leaving only the scalar field modulation inside.” Essentially right; one correction. The modulation is a voltage driven onto the shell, not an exterior electromagnetic wave. That matters: a wave would be screened, while a shell voltage moves the potential inside by the same amount everywhere. The spelling is Aharonov–Bohm. Our added critique (HYP, not in Gao). The paper’s Hamiltonian H0 + eV(t) is written for one charge. For a neutral rubidium atom, the electron and the nucleus-plus-core sit in the same uniform potential with opposite charges, so their coupling terms cancel. Any shift that did exist would also be common to all levels of the same system, so optical transition frequencies would not change. A convincing test probably needs a net-charged probe (quantum dot, trapped ion) or a charge path referenced to something outside the cage. Dan · longitudinal E inside the cage “The paper is silent on a longitudinal electric field also possibly being present inside the Faraday cage, as I think Dr. Hively declares physically possible.” Right: the paper is silent, because it assumes standard electrodynamics. For a perfectly symmetric shell, standard electrodynamics gives exactly zero E inside at any frequency, since a spherically symmetric charge oscillation produces no interior or radiated field. Under Hively’s extended electrodynamics the answer changes (next section). EED reading of the same cage (HYP) Using the SI equations from our Hively–Loebl ledger: E = −∇Φ − ∂t A B = ∇×A C = ∇·A + (1/c²) ∂t Φ ∇·E + ∂t C = ρ/ε0 ∇×B − (1/c²) ∂t E − ∇C = μ0 J Modes: TEM (C = 0) · SLW (B = 0, E ∥ k, C ≠ 0) · SW (E = B = 0, C ≠ 0) C is not zero inside. With the paper’s interior potentials (A = 0, Φ = V0 cos Ωt), C = (1/c²) ∂tΦ = −(V0 Ω/c²) sin Ωt, uniform in space and oscillating in time. Gao’s gauge change is not allowed in EED. EED only permits gauge functions with □λ = 0, because other choices change the physical field C. Gao’s λ = (V0/Ω) sin Ωt has □λ = −(V0 Ω/c²) sin Ωt ≠ 0. In EED terms Chiao et al. are right that something physical changes inside. Note that the same objection applies to the gauge argument inside Chiao et al.’s own paper. E cannot be zero. With no charge inside, the EED Gauss law demands ∇·E = −∂tC ≠ 0, which is equivalent to □Φ = 0. Solving for a sphere of radius R with Φ(R) = V0 cos Ωt and k = Ω/c: Φ(r) = V0 cos Ωt · R sin(kr) / (r sin kR) E_r(r) = V0 cos Ωt · R [sin(kr) − kr cos(kr)] / (r² sin kR) ≈ (r/3)(Ω²/c²) V0 cos Ωt for kR ≪ 1. The field is radial (longitudinal), zero at the center, and has B = 0. That is an SLW, not a pure SW. A pure SW cannot oscillate in a charge-free, field-free region. If E = B = 0 and ρ = J = 0, the two equations above force ∂tC = 0 and ∇C = 0. Under these equations, a time-varying C inside the cage always brings a longitudinal E with it. Resonance. The solution blows up at kR = π (shell diameter = one wavelength). That would be a spherically symmetric interior resonance that standard electrodynamics does not have. Case (HYP numbers) Drive V0 f Shell radius kR E_r at the wall Chiao et al. Rb proposal (R assumed 0.1 m) 0.5 mV 15.9 MHz 100 mm 0.033 1.9×10⁻⁶ V/m Exp B 2.5″ sphere, TinySA −19 dBm 35 mV pk 433.59 MHz 31.75 mm 0.289 3.1×10⁻² V/m Exp A ¾″ sphere, TinySA −19 dBm 35 mV pk 1296 MHz 9.525 mm 0.259 8.2×10⁻² V/m ¾″ sphere, 2.45 GHz 35 mV pk 2450 MHz 9.525 mm 0.489 3.0×10⁻¹ V/m First kR = π resonance: 4.72 GHz for the 2.5″ sphere, 15.7 GHz for the ¾″ sphere, 1.50 GHz for a 0.1 m radius shell. Role in pure scalar-wave detection Concept (FACT). The paper is a proposal for sensing a time-varying scalar potential in a region where E and B are zero. That is the regime scalar-wave detection is aimed at, and it comes from mainstream physicists (Chiao, Tobar) in Phys. Rev. A. Three competing predictions (HYP framing). Gao and standard textbook gauge reasoning predict no effect inside. Chiao et al. predict energy sidebands. EED predicts a small radial longitudinal E growing toward the wall, and a scalar resonance at kR = π. A driven Faraday sphere with a probe inside could in principle tell these apart. Candidate future experiment (worked out as a home bench test as home experiment FX-1 below). Drive an Exp A or Exp B aluminum sphere’s potential directly from the TinySA, place a small radial E-probe inside off center, and read it out without a conducting path to the outside reference (battery-powered recorder or fiber, in the spirit of Tomilin’s sealed box). Controls: probe rotated tangential, probe at the center (EED predicts zero there), and frequency swept toward kR = π. The main false-positive risks are feed-point asymmetry, holes or seams in the shell, and cable pickup, all of which also give small interior fields in standard electrodynamics. Proposed home experiment · FX-1 driven Faraday sphere (draft, HYP) What this can and cannot test. This bench test looks for the EED prediction (a radial longitudinal E inside a driven metal sphere). Standard electrodynamics predicts zero apart from leakage. It cannot test Chiao et al.’s energy sidebands, which need atoms and lasers. All predicted numbers below come from our own EED derivation and assume the shell pins the potential at its surface. That assumption is standard for conductors but untested in EED, and Hively’s claim that SLW passes through conductors could mean different boundary conditions apply. Treat the numbers as a target, not a promise. Simulator: FX-1 SNR simulator (physics fx1-snr-v0.2.1). It predicts the Tekbox E5/H10/H20/H5 probe reading on a TinySA Ultra, inside and outside the sphere. Standard physics uses openEMS FDTD fields of the actual geometry and seam-leak options (FACT); the EED interior field is the hypothesis (HYP). Wolfram Cloud twin: pending sync. 1 · Making the spherical cage Best shielding: two metal bowls. Two identical deep stainless-steel mixing bowls, as close to hemispherical as you can find (about 11″ across gives R ≈ 0.14 m), clamped rim to rim. Overlap the rim seam with copper foil tape and hold it with binder clips. Solid metal shields far better than mesh, and the TinySA fits inside. The drawback is that you can’t see the screen, so use the timed on/off method in step 4. See-through: RadioScreen over a form. Use two plastic salad bowls, a beach ball, or two wire hanging-basket frames as the form. Press RadioScreen over each half and trim the pleats, or cut 8–12 orange-peel gores. Join every seam with at least 1 cm of overlap under conductive fabric tape or copper tape, and join the two halves with an overlapping flange and clips. You can read the TinySA through the mesh, as with the kit tents. The trade-off is shielding: about 60 dB on the catalog below 1 GHz and about 50 dB at 1.3 GHz. Either way: keep the shape as round as you can, since the formulas assume a sphere. Keep all openings small. Sit the sphere on your white HDPE blocks, at least 20 cm above a metal counterpoise (aluminum sheet or a large baking sheet) on the table. 2 · Gear (all from the kit unless noted) TinySA Ultra #1 (generator, outside) at 433.59 MHz, then one Zeenko ZK06-UM 21 dB amp. About +2 dBm out gives roughly 0.4 V peak on the shell. Center conductor to the shell exterior with a short clip lead; coax shield to the counterpoise. The shell becomes the “hot” electrode. This is milliwatt-level operation inside the 70 cm amateur band, under your license. TinySA Ultra #2 (receiver, inside, on battery) with the Tekbox E5 on its short SMB cable. Bond the TinySA case to the inside of the shell with a short strap of copper tape so the whole receiver rides at shell potential, which is the Chiao et al. idea of everything inside sharing one potential. Add a second Zeenko amp in front of it if readings sit near the floor, and log it. Second radial sensor: a 2–3 cm stub (bare center conductor of an RG-405 / SMA pigtail) on the receiver input, pointing toward the center while the TinySA sits against the wall. This measures E between the wall and the stub tip, which is radial by construction. Tekbox H20 for the inside B-null (EED says B = 0 by symmetry; ordinary leakage carries B). TinySA Ultra #3 (outside monitor) with the telescopic monopole at a fixed spot, to confirm the drive level each run. To buy: the bowls or mesh form, copper foil tape, binder clips, a clip lead. Everything else is on hand. 3 · What each theory predicts Setup (EED HYP numbers) kR Er at r = 0.25R Er at r = 0.7R E5 reading (≈ −60 dBm at 1 V/m, 433 MHz) Bowl sphere R 0.14 m · 433.59 MHz · 35 mV (TinySA only) 1.27 0.044 V/m 0.12 V/m about −87 / −79 dBm Bowl sphere R 0.14 m · 433.59 MHz · 0.4 V (with Zeenko) 1.27 0.51 V/m 1.3 V/m about −66 / −58 dBm Bowl sphere R 0.14 m · 100 MHz · 0.4 V 0.29 0.021 V/m 0.058 V/m about −94 / −85 dBm (E5 calibration differs at 100 MHz) EED: field is radial only, near zero at the center, larger toward the wall, B at the noise floor, scales linearly with drive voltage, and rises steeply with frequency toward a resonance at kR = π (about 1.07 GHz for R 0.14 m). At 433 MHz with 0.4 V the predicted interior field is within a factor of about 2–3 of the ordinary field just outside the shell (V0/R ≈ 2.9 V/m). That is a large, unambiguous target. Standard electrodynamics: only leakage. It should sit 50–60 dB or more below the outside field (more with solid bowls), point in no consistent radial direction, carry B, depend on where the seams and feed are, and peak near ordinary cavity modes (lowest near 0.94 GHz for R 0.14 m) rather than 1.07 GHz. Chiao et al.: no E either way; this test says nothing about their sidebands. 4 · Procedure Floor. Close the sphere with the generator off. Record the receiver floor at 433.59 MHz (narrow RBW, waterfall on). Timed drive with microSD logging. Drive the shell 60 s on, 60 s off, three or more cycles (phone stopwatch, log the times). Record on the inside receiver’s microSD card (full details in 5 · Data recording), since the waterfall itself cannot be saved as data: Timestamped CSVs (preferred): set the TinySA clock, turn on STORAGE › AUTO NAME, set a trigger level a few dB above the generator-off floor, and enable TRIGGER › AUTO SAVE. Each crossing writes a trace CSV (at most one per 30 s, hence 60 s cycles). File times should match the on periods. The generator-off run should write no files. Waterfall screenshot: large waterfall shows the last 80 sweeps; set SWEEP TIME so 80 sweeps span the run (3 s per sweep gives 4 min). After opening the sphere, press PAUSE, then STORAGE › SAVE CAPTURE. Expect on/off stripes; the lid opening marks the end. Use a narrow span (about 1 MHz) around 433.59 MHz. Menu names follow the tinySA wiki and can shift between firmware versions, so do a two-minute dry run with the sphere open to confirm files land on the card. Outside reference. With the E5 just outside the shell (same distance from the wall), record the reading at the same drive. The inside/outside ratio is the key number: about −7 dB for EED, −50 dB or lower for ordinary leakage. Position. Probe near the center, then at about 0.7R. EED predicts an 8.3 dB rise toward the wall at 433 MHz. Orientation. Repeat at 0.7R with the E5 radial, then tangential. EED predicts the tangential reading drops to the floor. B-null. Swap to the H20 inside at the same spot. EED predicts B at the floor; ordinary leakage shows B. Linearity. Drop the drive by 10 dB. The interior reading should drop 10 dB under both theories; if not, suspect receiver overload or pickup. Frequency sweep. Step 100, 250, 433.59, 700, 900, 1000, 1070, 1200 MHz (amateur-band points where you transmit; otherwise keep to milliwatts and brief). Look for a rise toward 1.07 GHz (EED) versus peaks near 0.94 GHz (ordinary cavity mode). Leakage controls. Move the feed point to a different spot on the shell and rotate the seam; a real EED signal should not care, leakage will. Then ground the shell to the counterpoise and drive the telescopic monopole beside it at the same power; that reading is your ordinary-leakage floor. Log sphere type and size, seam treatment, feed point, frequency, drive dBm, amp on/off, probe type, position, orientation, RBW, and the inside/outside ratio. 5 · Data recording (TinySA Ultra microSD) The sphere is closed during a run, so the inside receiver must record by itself. The TinySA Ultra saves three kinds of files to its microSD card: trace data as CSV (SAVE TRACES), screen images as BMP (SAVE CAPTURE), and instrument settings (SAVE SETTINGS). It cannot export the waterfall as numbers, only as part of a screen image. Menu names below follow the tinySA wiki and can shift slightly between firmware versions. Once, before the first session. Insert a microSD card in each TinySA you will use. Set the clock so file names carry the right date and time. Turn on STORAGE › AUTO NAME (files are named like SA_YYMMDD_HHMMSS). Lock the settings. On the inside receiver set center 433.59 MHz, span about 1 MHz, a narrow RBW, and the amp on or off as planned. Save them with STORAGE › SAVE SETTINGS and name the file (for example FX1-433). Reload it with LOAD SETTINGS at the start of every run, so all runs are comparable. Do the same on the outside monitor. Hands-off CSV logging. Measure the floor with the generator off. Set the trigger level a few dB above that floor and enable TRIGGER › AUTO SAVE. Each time the signal crosses the level, the receiver writes a trace CSV, at most once every 30 s. That is why the drive runs 60 s on and 60 s off. Waterfall image. The large waterfall holds the last 80 sweeps (small holds 40). Set SWEEP TIME so 80 sweeps cover the run; 3 s per sweep covers 4 minutes. After opening the sphere, press PAUSE at once, then SAVE CAPTURE. End of each run. With the sweep paused, also do SAVE TRACES (the final trace as CSV). If you ran a max-hold trace, it is saved too. Controls get recorded the same way. The generator-off run should produce no AUTO SAVE files. Record the outside-reference, tangential, center, H20, and leakage-control runs with the same settings file. After the session. Copy each card to a laptop folder such as FX1/2026-MM-DD/run01, keeping the inside receiver’s and the outside monitor’s files in separate subfolders. Do not rename the auto-named files, since the name is the timestamp. Dry run first. With the sphere open, run two minutes of the on/off pattern and confirm that CSVs and the capture actually appear on the card. Run-log columns (one row per run, on paper or a spreadsheet): date · run # · sphere (bowls / mesh, diameter) · seam treatment · feed-point location · frequency · generator dBm · drive amp on/off · receiver amp on/off · probe (E5 / stub / H20) · probe position (center / 0.7R / outside) · orientation (radial / tangential) · RBW · settings file · on/off start times · CSV file names · capture file name · peak on-level dBm · off-level dBm · inside/outside ratio dB · notes. Reading the result. A radial-only interior field near the EED size, zero-ish at the center, with no B and indifferent to feed and seam placement, would be strong support for the EED reading and worth sending to Dr. Hively. A field that is small, carries B, and moves around with the seams is ordinary leakage, which is the standard-physics expectation. Anything in between needs better shielding before drawing a conclusion. Open checks. (1) Confirm signs and the allowed-gauge condition against Hively–Loebl 2019. (2) Decide whether to ask Dr. Hively directly (Dan’s call). (3) Read the Chiao et al. Reply in full before building on the gauge argument. Back to the library

description: FX-1 SNR simulator (fx1-snr-v0.2.1): expected Tekbox probe reading on a TinySA inside and outside a driven metal sphere at 433.59 MHz. openEMS FDTD fields (FACT) vs the EED hypothesis (HYP). Novice-friendly front view; details in tabs. Educational, not a measurement.
text: fx1-snr-v0.2.1 · FX-1 home experiment · illustrative, not a measurement · Cloud twin pending sync (fx1-snr-v0.2.1) FX-1: what should the probe read? A metal sphere (two 11″ stainless bowls) is driven with a 433.59 MHz radio signal. A small probe connected to a TinySA spectrum analyser sits either inside the sphere or outside it. This page predicts the reading two ways. Standard physics uses Maxwell's equations and an openEMS computer simulation. The EED hypothesis is the unproven "scalar wave" idea being tested. Loading… Standard physics (FACT)— EED hypothesis (HYP, unproven)— 1 · Where is the probe? Inside the sphere Outside the sphere Inside, TinySA #2 is sealed in with the probe. Outside, TinySA #3 is on the bench. 2 · How far from the centre? 3 · How well is the seam sealed? The seam is where the two bowls meet under the copper tape. Any gap lets a little ordinary signal leak in. Only matters when the probe is inside. 4 · How strong is the drive? TinySA alone (−19 dBm) TinySA + 21 dB amp (+2 dBm) dBm is signal power in decibels relative to 1 milliwatt. Every 10 dB is a factor of 10 in power: 0 dBm = 1 mW, −30 dBm = 1 µW. description: What can be measured about Joule loss with the rod attenuator at 433.59, 1296 and 2450 MHz: insertion loss, brass versus W1 tests, power balance limits and calculators.
text: Round 1 · analysis · draft v0.1 Joule loss and power balance Can we measure how much of the transmitted wave is lost as Joule heating, using the rod attenuator at each frequency? Short answer: we can measure the insertion loss and its dependence on rod angle, material and frequency very well. We cannot, with a VNA and a spectrum analyzer alone, separate rod heating from rod scattering. This page says exactly what is and is not measurable, gives a test that can separate the main loss readings, and offers calculators. Tests of hypotheses, not results. Mainstream electrodynamics treats free-space radio as transverse (TEM). A longitudinal or scalar component is a hypothesis we are testing, and nothing on these pages claims that scalar or longitudinal waves have been detected. Values marked proposal are our suggestions and are not measured or sourced. Draft v0.1, 4 Oct 2026, written by Grok Bot for Dan Britton. Framing rule carried over from the hub. Under the SLW hypothesis the hub does not use skin-depth, permeability or ferromagnetic arguments to rank or dismiss SLW or SW (see loss-modes). Section 5 computes those quantities anyway, but only as the ordinary-physics (TEM) control: the number a transverse-wave explanation predicts, so that data can be compared with it. Those lines are tagged "transverse-EM reasoning, not applicable under the SLW hypothesis". What "Joule loss" can mean What is measurable Rod attenuator model Predictions TEM control Power balance Calculators Three-station scan Oven Limits and falsifiers Sources 1. Three things people mean by "Joule loss" Insertion loss of the rod array: how many dB the received signal drops when the rods are in. measurable directly from S21 or from the spectrum analyzer. Power actually turned into heat in the rods. not directly measurable here. At milliwatt drive the heating is of order micro-kelvin (rod-thermal), far below any thermometer we have. It has to be inferred. The Joule term σE∥² in the theory. In Monstein and Wesley (2002) it is the whole explanation of the rod curve (Eq. 7 to 9). Hively and Loebl's later papers disagree with each other about whether an SLW has resistive loss at all (joule-loss-positions). model The experiment can measure (1) and use materials and frequencies to test which version of (3) is consistent. It cannot, on its own, give (2). 2. What is measurable, and what each number does and does not tell you Quantity How Tells you Does not tell you S21(φ) magnitude, rods in, angle φ VNA, CW at the carrier or a narrow sweep; or TinySA peak hold Insertion loss versus rod angle; κ and the aligned-angle loss Whether the lost power was absorbed or scattered S21 with rods out, plates only Same, same cal Reference level T0; plate effect S11 of the TX sphere, rods in versus out VNA port 1 Whether the rods change the TX match (reflection) enough to matter Anything about the RX side κ for brass versus W1, same geometry Two scans Whether loss depends on conductivity The mechanism, if it does not κ versus band Three benches How loss scales with rod length and frequency Geometry effects are mixed in: rod diameter is fixed at 1/8 in, so L/D changes by 109, 36 and 19 1 - |S11|² - |S21|² VNA Power not returned to either port For two antennas in open air it includes all radiation to elsewhere; see section 6 Heat in a rod Thermocouple or IR camera Real absorbed power Not feasible at milliwatts; would need watts, and the oven is the only watt-level source (never with rods inside it) 3. The rod attenuator model fact (as published) Monstein and Wesley, p. 516 to 517: only the E component along a wire, E0 cos φ, produces Ohmic loss. Eq. (7): δP = -σA E0² cos²φ δL. Eq. (8): δ⟨S⟩ = -(σ/c) cos²φ ⟨S⟩ δL. Eq. (9): T = exp[-κ cos²φ], with κ "a constant proportional to the length L of the wire". Their fit used κ = 4.4 for brass at 433.59 MHz; κ was fitted, not computed from σ. T(φ) = T0 exp[-κ cos²(φ - φ0)] ⇔ level(dB) = L0 - 4.343 κ cos²(φ - φ0) For κ = 4.4 the loss with the rods aligned (φ = φ0) is 19.1 dB (T = 0.012). The calculator below fits this form by least squares (the angle φ0 is scanned, L0 and κ are linear) and reports a standard error. fact A wire array attenuates the field component along its wires for an ordinary transverse wave too (it is a wire-grid polariser). So a good fit to this form does not distinguish an SLW from a TEM wave. What can be compared is how κ behaves. 4. Predictions that can be tested (and would fail) The hub's rod-thermal page gives three readings of rod loss under the SLW framing; the table adds the ordinary scattering reading as a control. The ratio and scaling columns are what the two brass-versus-W1 scans and the three bands can measure. Reading κ(W1) / κ(brass) κ versus band (same material, λ/2 rods) Basis Joule-literal (M&W Eq. 7 to 9, κ ∝ σ L) σW1/σbrass = 0.36 (annealed), 0.27 (hardened) ∝ L ∝ 1/f: 1 : 0.334 : 0.177 for 433.59 : 1296 : 2450 MHz hypothesis M&W equations taken literally with σ from the table in section 5 Energy-capped Joule (hub S1-capped) 1.0 Set by the intercepted area, not predicted here hypothesis (rod-thermal) Charge relaxation only (hub S2) No prediction for the received signal None hypothesis; effect on heating negligible (rod-thermal) Ordinary scattering by good conductors (control) about 1.0 About constant if the geometry were scaled exactly; drifts here because rod diameter is fixed fact for the wire-grid picture; transverse-EM reasoning, not applicable under the SLW hypothesis The test. Run the identical scan with brass and then W1 rods (same plates, same positions). If κ(W1)/κ(brass) is near 0.36 or 0.27 with a small error, the literal Joule reading is favoured and scattering is not the whole story. If it is near 1, the literal reading is disfavoured. If it matches neither, something else (fixture repeatability, W1 magnetism, rod length error) is at work. Then check the band scaling with the same material. proposal Decide the acceptance thresholds before taking data. 5. Ordinary-physics control: skin depth and rod resistance fact (transverse-EM reasoning, not applicable under the SLW hypothesis) The skin depth is δ = 1/√(π f μ0μr σ) and the surface resistance is Rs = 1/(σδ). Conductivities and sources: Brass C36000: 26% IACS, resistivity 6.63 µΩ·cm, σ = 1.508 × 107 S/m (Aviva Metals data sheet; MakeItFrom C36000). W1 annealed: resistivity 0.185 µΩ·m (EngMats C80W1; a steel-mill datasheet gives 0.20 Ω·mm²/m = 5.0 × 106 S/m; the hub's rod-thermal page uses 5.0 × 106 from MetalZenith 0.18 to 0.22 µΩ·m), σ = 5.4 × 106 S/m used here. W1 hardened: 7.1% IACS (MakeItFrom, hardened W1), σ = 4.1 × 106 S/m. The hub's rod-thermal page uses 3.3 × 106 S/m (MatWeb, 30 µΩ·cm). The spread is real; measure your rods' resistance if it matters. Copper: 5.8 × 107 S/m (IACS definition). W1 relative permeability: not sourced. W1 is a plain carbon steel and ferromagnetic, but we found no value at GHz. The last row uses μr = 100 purely as an assumption to show the sensitivity; the effective permeability of steel at hundreds of MHz is usually far lower than the low-frequency value, and it needs measuring. The calculator estimates, for a resonant half-wave rod, the fraction of intercepted power that becomes heat: about 0.1 to 0.5% for brass and W1 with μr = 1, up to a few percent if W1 behaved with μr = 100. If the measured insertion loss is 10 to 20 dB while a TEM estimate of heating is well under 1% of intercepted power, nearly all of the TEM loss is scattering. That is why S21 alone cannot give Joule heating. 6. Power balance, and the limit of what S-parameters can tell you For power incident from the TX port, conservation gives: Pin = Preflected + Preceived + Pabsorbed in rods + Pscattered elsewhere + Pother losses The VNA gives Preflected = |S11|²Pin and Preceived = |S21|²Pin. Two cases: A true two-port fixture (everything the RX does not get goes into the fixture): dissipated fraction = 1 - |S11|² - |S21|². Valid if nothing radiates away. It does not hold for two antennas in open air. Two antennas in air (our case): use the difference between rods in and rods out with an identical setup. The fraction of received power the rods remove is 1 - Tin/Tout. The part of that which shows up as extra input reflection is small unless the rods detune the TX. The rest is absorbed or scattered away from the RX, and S-parameters cannot split those. What can split them. Material swap (section 4): scattering by a good conductor is nearly the same for brass and W1, absorption is not (if the absorption model holds). A change in loss between materials is an absorption difference. Closed-box power balance proposal: put the rod array inside a small shielded enclosure fed by two ports through the walls, measure S11 and S21 with and without rods. Then 1 - |S11|² - |S21|² is wall plus rod dissipation, and the empty-box value removes the walls. This does not reproduce free-space propagation, so it tests the rods as absorbers, not the free-space claim. Anechoic or reverberation chamber: integrates all scattered power. Not available to us. Calorimetry: needs watts. Only the oven is that strong (see section 9, and never with rods inside). 7. Calculators All run in your browser. Level can be dB or dBm because only differences are used. A control number only. 8. Three-station fixture scan: where along the line should the rods sit? (proposal) Added 4 Oct 2026. Proposal and hypothesis test. No result is claimed. Band pages: 1.3 GHz · 433.59 MHz · 2.45 GHz · oven · checklist. hypothesis Dan's early-attenuation idea. A rotating rod fixture placed close to the transmitter should give a more measurable change in the detected amplitude than one placed midway or near the receiver, because paths that would otherwise reflect off objects between TX and RX are attenuated before they can reflect. To keep the fixture out of the source's reactive near field, the closest point of approach of any rod during the rotation must stay at least λ/(2π) from the TX sphere centre: 110.0 mm at 433.59 MHz, 36.8 mm at 1296 MHz, 19.5 mm at 2450 MHz. This is a hypothesis test and a proposal. Nothing here is a measured result. Where does the fixture go? The sources do not say. Monstein and Wesley (2002) report testing the wave by "intervening a cubic array of 9 half-wavelength wires" (abstract) and call it a polarizer-analyzer. They give no distance from either ball. Butterworth et al. (2013), describing that apparatus, write "Between Tx and Rx are positioned a pair of rotatable polarizer-analyzer arrays", which is where the word "between" comes from. Neither source fixes a position along the line, so this test treats the position as a variable to measure. Geometry rule Assume the turntable axis passes through the centre of the 3 x 3 array (centre rod H5 on the TX to RX line, mid-length). In plan view the farthest point of the array from the axis is a corner rod tip at R = √2 λ/4 (rod half-length λ/4, outer column offset λ/4). So the closest approach of any rod to the nearer sphere centre is (pivot distance) minus R, and the rule is (pivot distance) ≥ λ/(2π) + R. For this test it replaces the looser earlier wording "rod cube at least λ/(2π) from either ball", which did not say which point of the cube it meant. The V array needs the same clearance. At 433.59 MHz this puts the NEAR pivot at about 0.41 m, inside the 0.3 to 0.5 m range suggested for the first trial. Rod lengths used: 346.00, 115.66 and 61.18 mm. Protocol Fix r, heights, cables, power, VNA settings and cage state. Only the fixture moves, along a non-metallic rail, to NEAR TX, MIDWAY and NEAR RX (the mirror of NEAR TX). At each station: rods out, plates only, and an ambient baseline (TX off); then the φ scan. At 433.59 MHz (Experiment B) that is the full 0 to 360° in 10° steps (37 readings, the 360° reading being the return-to-start check), for brass and W1 tool steel (annealed), open bench first and then in a closed Faraday cage (Dr. Hively's requested change, per Dan's 5 Oct 2026 email to Steve; exp-433). At 1296 and 2450 MHz the pages still use 0 to 180° in 10° steps, then once over 0 to 360°. At each angle log the detected amplitude, the TX S11 (VNA port 1, to detect near-field loading or detuning), the optional RX S11 (port 2 reflection) and the ambient level. Run the stations NEAR TX, MIDWAY, NEAR RX and then the reverse to cancel drift. Repeat with W1 rods, and on a second day. If possible repeat at r + λ/4. Fit κ per station in calculator F below, for brass and for W1. The oven version, with no VNA on the oven, is on the oven page.
