description: Grok Bot initial ideas, subject to better ideas from anyone: ways to mount an RG-405 stub antenna so its tip sits at the geometric center of the Experiment A KB-1820 (0.750 in) and Experiment B KB-2016 (2.50 in) aluminum spheres, with the sleeve balun outside.
text: Experiments A & B · stub antenna inside the sphere · mounting concepts Mounting ideas: putting the stub tip at the center of the A and B spheres GROK BOT INITIAL IDEAS — SUBJECT TO BETTER IDEAS FROM ANYONE These are starting points, not final designs. Nothing here has been built or tested. Steve Morris and anyone else with shop or RF experience: please improve, replace or reject any of them. Better ideas win. Dan wants a short stub antenna (the bare center wire at the end of a coax cable) to poke into each hollow aluminum sphere so that the tip sits exactly at the sphere’s geometric center, with the connector and the sleeve balun kept outside. This page lists ways to hold the stub there, for the tiny Experiment A ball and the roomier Experiment B ball. CORRECTED 5 Oct 2026 Experiment A: the centre-tip idea does not work on the ¾″ ball. The RG-405U shield must not touch the sphere, and the centre conductor is soldered into a #76 pin hole so that the sphere is the driven element. See A1 and exp-1296.html#feed. The Experiment B section is unchanged. The short version Experiment A (¾″ ball, 1296 MHz): CORRECTED 5 Oct 2026 the centre conductor is soldered into a #76 (0.020″) pin hole 2.5 mm deep, with 1.5 mm of PTFE exposed and the shield cut end 3.0 mm off the ball. The shield never touches the ball (A1, exp-1296.html#feed). Experiment B (2.50″ ball, 433.59 MHz): the ball already has a ¼″ hole. A plastic “top-hat” bushing in that hole can center the coax with no metalwork on the ball. A plastic guide rod that spans the inside of the ball can put the tip at the center automatically. Experiment B (A no longer uses a centre tip): the tip depth, measured from the outside surface at the hole, is the sphere radius: 31.75 mm for B (9.525 mm would be the A value). The wall thickness decides how much bare wire is inside. The radius, not λ/10, sets the stub length inside the ball. Materials: non-ferrous only. Nylon, PTFE (Teflon) or Delrin (acetal) plastics; brass or nylon screws; no steel in the RF path. Words used on this page (tap to hide) Stub: the short length of bare center conductor left when the outer conductor and dielectric of a coax cable are stripped back. It is the antenna. On this hub it is cut from RG-405/U semi-rigid coax (tools.html, sleeve-balun.html). Sleeve balun (also called a bazooka choke): a close-fitting metal tube over the coax, soldered to the coax outer conductor at one end (the “cold” end) and open at the other end, which faces the stub tip. It is about λ/4 long and reduces current on the outside of the coax. How-to: setup.html#sleeve. λ (lambda): free-space wavelength, c/f, where c is the speed of light and f the frequency. Bulkhead: a connector made to mount through a hole in a panel or wall, held by a nut or thread. The hub’s is the Amphenol 901-9875 SMA-female bulkhead. Standoff: a non-conductive spacer that holds a part at a fixed distance or position. R, t: sphere outer radius (half the outside diameter) and wall thickness. Geometric center: the point inside the ball that is R from every point on its outside surface. Labels: FACT from a datasheet, the patent or another hub page (linked). IDEA an untested suggestion. ASSUMPTION something we assume and still need to check. CONFLICT two hub sources disagree. Key numbers Item Experiment A Experiment B Source Sphere K-Mac KB-1820, 3003 Al hollow, 0.750″ (19.05 mm) OD K-Mac KB-2016, 3003 Al hollow, 2.50″ (63.5 mm) OD FACT Sheet A, Sheet B Radius R (tip depth from outside surface) 9.525 mm 31.75 mm FACT half the OD Wall thickness t Not stated on the hub. Must be measured (method below) ≈ 0.132″ (3.35 mm) FACT sphere.html, Sheet B Bare wire inside, if the dielectric stops at the inner wall (R − t) Not used for A after the 5 Oct 2026 correction 31.75 − 3.35 ≈ 28.4 mm FACT geometry Exp A feed (corrected 5 Oct 2026) #76 pin hole 2.5 mm (0.10″) deep; PTFE 1.5 mm (0.06″); bare wire 4.0 mm (0.16″); shield 3.0 mm (0.12″) off the ball Unchanged IDEA derived, exp-1296.html#feed Hole as received None; one must be drilled ¼″ (0.250″), stock FACT shop-drawing.html Frequency · λ 1296 MHz · 231.3 mm 433.59 MHz · 691.4 mm FACT sleeve-balun.html λ/4 sleeve (air) 57.8 mm 172.9 mm FACT sleeve-balun.html λ/10 “first-article” stub 23.1 mm (does not fit: longer than R) 69.1 mm (does not fit: longer than R) FACT sleeve-balun.html, setup#sleeve RG-405/U coax outer OD 0.086″ (≈2.2 mm); PTFE dielectric OD ≈ 0.066″ (1.68 mm); center conductor 0.020″ (0.51 mm), silver-plated copper-clad steel FACT tools.html, sleeve-balun.html SMA bulkhead Amphenol 901-9875, 1/4-36 UNEF thread (major ≈ 0.250″ / 6.35 mm); hub’s preferred clearance hole 6.5 mm; do not tap thin ball walls. Not used on the Experiment A ball after the 5 Oct 2026 correction FACT setup#sphere-a, sphere#sma-install FACT The hub’s RG-405 center conductor is copper-clad steel. That comes with the cable. The “no steel” rule on this page is about screws, clamps and fixtures you add. How small can the hole be? CORRECTED 5 Oct 2026 Experiment A: only the 0.51 mm centre conductor enters the wall, so the hole is a #76 (0.020″) or #75 (0.021″) pin hole. The larger holes below are kept for Experiment B and for reference. FACT Only the PTFE dielectric and center wire go through the wall (the outer conductor stops at the outside surface): the hole must clear 1.68 mm. A #50 drill (0.070″, 1.78 mm) is the next common size up. FACT The whole RG-405 goes through (outer conductor inside the wall): the hole must clear ≈2.2 mm. A #43 drill (0.089″, 2.26 mm) is the next common size up. FACT The 901-9875 bulkhead goes through the wall: 6.5 mm clearance (hub). On the ¾″ ball that hole is about one-third of the ball’s diameter. IDEA Smaller holes keep the shell closer to a closed sphere and leave more metal around the hole. Try the drill on a spare ball first; the KB-1820 comes in a 10-pack (setup#sphere-a). Before any design: measure the wall and plan the depth IDEA With the hole drilled (A) or using the stock hole (B), and nothing installed, put a caliper depth rod through the hole until it touches the far inside wall. Call the reading d. FACT (geometry) d = OD − t for the far wall. If the wall is uniform, t ≈ OD − d. Repeat at a few angles and on a spare ball. FACT (geometry) The tip belongs at depth R from the outside surface at the hole: 9.525 mm (A) or 31.75 mm (B). That holds whatever the wall thickness. (For Experiment A after the correction, use the wall reading to check that a 2.5 mm deep pin hole fits; see A1.) IDEA Put a fixed depth stop on the coax (a collar, a PTFE sleeve cut to length, or a paint mark read under magnification) so the insertion is repeatable. IDEA A flat caliper base rests on the hole rim, which is slightly below the top of the curve. From the sphere geometry that error is about 0.04 mm for a 1.8 mm hole in A, 0.16 mm for B’s ¼″ hole, but 0.57 mm for a 6.5 mm hole in A. For big holes, measure from a thin straightedge laid across the rim. Experiment A — ¾″ KB-1820 at 1296 MHz FACT No hole yet. The inside diameter is less than 19 mm, and the hub already says an interior locknut will not fit (“¾″ ID is too tight”, Sheet A). CORRECTED 5 Oct 2026 The Experiment A feed is now A1: shield off the ball, centre conductor soldered into a pin hole. A3 and A4 below are superseded; A2 is revised as an option with dimensions for all three frequencies (the sphere connection is still open, waiting on Steve’s RF design). IDEA Every Experiment A concept holds the coax from the outside. Internal standoffs, internal 3D-printed cradles and internal nuts are judged not practical here: there is no way to get them in through a 2–6.5 mm hole, or to adjust them once they are inside. A1 · Pin-hole feed (corrected 5 Oct 2026): centre conductor soldered into a #76 pin hole; shield kept off the ball CORRECTED 5 Oct 2026 The earlier A1 text put the PTFE and wire through a #50 hole with the tip free at the center, and offered bonding the outer conductor to the ball. That was wrong for Experiment A: a shield bonded to the ball makes it a closed shield cap, and a free pin inside only excites a shorted cavity. The sphere is the driven element. IDEA Derived for this hub, not from Monstein and Wesley. Build values (full table: exp-1296.html#feed): Pin hole: #76 drill (0.020″, 0.51 mm), or #75 (0.021″, 0.53 mm) for a snug fit, 2.5 mm (0.10″) deep (2 to 3 mm). Centre conductor soldered in the hole: aluminum solder with aluminum flux, or silver conductive epoxy. ASSUMPTION the ball is 3003 aluminum as listed; confirm on a spare ball. PTFE exposed past the shield cut: 1.5 mm (0.06″). Bare centre conductor past the PTFE end: 4.0 mm (0.16″), of which 2.5 mm (0.10″) is in the hole and 1.5 mm (0.06″) in air. Shield cut end to sphere surface: 3.0 mm (0.12″). The shield never touches the ball. If the wall is thinner than 2.5 mm, the hole goes through: insert the pin by the wall thickness only and log it. Pros Smallest possible hole; shell stays almost closed; no connector or extra hardware on the ball; the feed is about 0.024 λ long. Cons The one small joint carries all the mechanical load; ordinary tin-lead solder does not wet aluminum (FACT needs aluminum flux or conductive epoxy); the wall thickness is still unknown. Sleeve: λ/4 = 57.8 mm (2.28″) in air, over the jacket and shield, far end soldered to the shield, open end toward the ball, level with the shield cut and never touching the ball. Pair it with A5 for strain relief. A2 · External collar with a set screw (revised 5 Oct 2026): a non-metallic collar that holds the sleeve and shield off the ball, dimensioned for 1296, 2450 and 433.59 MHz OPEN QUESTION How the coax connects to the sphere is still open. Neither Monstein and Wesley nor US 12,525,711 B1 clearly says. Per Dan’s 5 Oct 2026, 6:45 PM email, we are waiting on Steve’s RF design and his VNA (S11) check before anything is drilled. The dimensions below follow the current Experiment A feed (exp-1296.html#feed: centre conductor soldered into a pin hole, shield never touching the ball) and will change if Steve picks a different feed. IDEA Status: an option again, not superseded. The old A2 used a brass or aluminum collar bonded over a #43 hole, which put the shield on the ball. The revised A2 uses a Delrin or nylon collar with a saddle face bonded to the ball with epoxy. Its bore is a slip fit on the sleeve’s outside diameter (measure the tube you use), and a nylon set screw locks the sleeve. The collar is longer than the gap G, so the sleeve’s open end, and the shield cut level with it, sit inside the collar and cannot touch the ball. The centre conductor still goes into a #76 (0.020″, 0.51 mm) or #75 (0.021″, 0.53 mm) pin hole, as in A1. What the collar adds: it sets and holds G while the pin joint is soldered or the epoxy cures, it sets the angle, and it takes the strain off the small pin joint. Pros G can be set and checked before the pin is bonded; the collar takes the mechanical load off the pin joint; no metal is added to the ball; the same drawing works at all three frequencies. Cons Epoxy and plastic sit right at the feed (compare S11 with and without the collar on the VNA6000-A); once the pin is soldered, G can no longer be adjusted; PTFE is hard to glue, so use Delrin or nylon for the collar. A2 sketch, not to scale, concept only. Ls is the sleeve, P the shield cut back (PTFE exposed), W the bare wire in air, H the pin depth in the sphere wall, G the gap from the shield cut to the ball and T the centre conductor protruding past the sleeve’s open end. A2 dimensions, RG-405U (centre 0.51 mm / 0.020″, PTFE 1.68 mm / 0.066″, outer 2.20 mm / 0.086″): Frequency, λ Sphere Ls, λ/4 sleeve in air Ls if PTFE-filled (εr 2.1) P: shield cut back (PTFE exposed) W: bare wire in air H: pin in hole G: shield cut to ball T: protrusion past sleeve open end T / λ 1296 MHz, 231.32 mm KB-1820, 19.05 mm 57.83 mm (2.28″) 39.91 mm (1.57″) 1.5 mm (0.06″) 1.5 mm (0.06″) 2.5 mm (0.10″) 3.0 mm (0.12″) 5.5 mm (0.22″) 0.024 2450 MHz, 122.36 mm KB-1820, 19.05 mm 30.59 mm (1.20″) 21.11 mm (0.83″) 1.0 mm (0.04″) 1.0 mm (0.04″) 1.5 mm (0.06″) 2.0 mm (0.08″) 3.5 mm (0.14″) 0.029 433.59 MHz, 691.42 mm KB-2016, 63.5 mm, wall 3.35 mm 172.85 mm (6.81″) 119.28 mm (4.70″) 1.5 mm (0.06″) 1.5 mm (0.06″) 2.5 mm (0.10″) 3.0 mm (0.12″) 5.5 mm (0.22″) 0.008 Which values are derived, and the assumptions: FACT (arithmetic) λ = c/f with c = 299 792 458 m/s, and Ls = λ/4 in air. The PTFE-filled value is λ/4 × 1/√2.1 = λ/4 × 0.690. It applies only if the whole space between the sleeve and the shield is PTFE; with tape or a partial filler the right length falls in between, so cut long and trim on the VNA. IDEA (derived) The sleeve’s open end is level with the shield cut, as on exp-1296.html#feed, so the protrusion past the sleeve’s open end is T = P + W + H, and G = P + W. IDEA (derived) 1296 MHz: the current Experiment A feed values, unchanged. IDEA (derived) 2450 MHz: scaled down so the feed stays under 0.03 λ (3.5 mm = 0.029 λ). Keeping the 1296 values would give 0.045 λ. The pin depth is 1.5 mm; the KB-1820 wall is still unknown. IDEA (derived) 433.59 MHz: kept at the 1296 values, not scaled up. A longer exposed feed would only add radiating length, and 5.5 mm is already 0.008 λ. The KB-2016 wall is ≈3.35 mm (sphere.html), so a 2.5 mm blind pin hole leaves about 0.85 mm of wall. The hub’s Experiment B feed is still the Monstein and Wesley one (sphere#sma-install); this row only applies if A2 is used on B. ASSUMPTION The balls are 3003 aluminum as listed, so the pin needs aluminum solder with aluminum flux, or silver conductive epoxy. The KB-1820 wall must be measured; if it is thinner than H, the pin hole goes through and H becomes the wall thickness. A3 · The hub’s SMA bulkhead path plus an internal extension wire CORRECTED 5 Oct 2026 Superseded for Experiment A. The bulkhead body is bonded to the ball, so the shield is on the ball. Use A1 and exp-1296.html#feed. Kept for the record. FACT The hub already has a shop plan for the ¾″ ball: an exterior flange or boss, a 6.5 mm clearance hole, and the 901-9875 body bonded to the shell (Sheet A). IDEA For a stub at the center, solder a short straight wire to the bulkhead’s center contact so its tip ends R = 9.525 mm below the outside surface. The sleeve goes on the external cable. Pros Matches the existing Sheet A; the ball can be unplugged; the thread is held by the flange, not the thin wall. Cons The 6.5 mm hole is large for a 19 mm ball; the bulkhead’s rear body may take up much of the space inside (ASSUMPTION: check the 901-9875 drawing); the extension adds a solder joint inside that you cannot see. Tip at center: measure from the flange face and subtract the flange thickness. Sleeve: on the feed cable, open end toward the connector. A4 · Potted plastic guide tube CORRECTED 5 Oct 2026 Superseded for Experiment A. It puts a free tip inside the ball instead of driving the sphere. Use A1 and exp-1296.html#feed. Kept for the record. IDEA Push a short Delrin or nylon tube (OD a slip fit in a #43 or slightly larger hole, bore a slip fit on the RG-405 or on its 1.68 mm dielectric) a millimetre or so through the wall. Hold it square in a jig and pot it from the outside with a small epoxy fillet. The coax then slides in to its depth stop and gets a drop of adhesive or a nylon set screw. Pros Sets the angle as well as the depth; spreads the load; no metal bonding to aluminum. Cons Permanent; epoxy and plastic sit right at the feed; FACT PTFE is hard to glue unless etched, so Delrin or nylon is easier here. A5 · External non-metallic saddle (combine with A1, A2 or A4) IDEA A 3D-printed (PETG or nylon) or machined Delrin saddle clamps the ball on one side and the coax (or sleeve) on the other, on one straight axis, and screws to the non-metallic TX sled with nylon screws. The small joint at the ball then carries no load when the cable is handled. Pros Protects the tiny joint; keeps the coax on the radial axis so the tip stays on the center; easy to print. Cons More parts; plastic near the ball (keep it thin and away from the hole if possible). Experiment B — 2.50″ KB-2016 at 433.59 MHz FACT The ball has a stock ¼″ (0.250″) hole, the wall is ≈3.35 mm, and the hub says not to tap that hole: 0.250″ is the thread’s major diameter, not a tap drill (sphere#sma-install). IDEA There is room inside, but anything that goes inside must pass through a hole about 6.35 mm wide. B1 · Top-hat plastic bushing in the stock ¼″ hole: no metalwork on the ball IDEA Turn a PTFE, Delrin or nylon bushing with a shank that is a snug fit in the 0.250″ hole (≈ wall length, 3.35 mm) and a flange outside. The center bore is a slip fit on the RG-405 (≈2.2 mm) or on its dielectric (1.68 mm). Hold it with a thin nylon nut or a split ring on the inside if you can reach it, or a small epoxy bead outside. A nylon set screw in the flange locks the coax at depth R = 31.75 mm. Pros Uses the hole as is; reversible; centers the coax on the hole axis; cheap. Cons The coax outer conductor is insulated from the shell unless you add a bond, which differs from the hub’s “outer as shield” default; PTFE creeps under set-screw pressure (Delrin is stiffer); the stock hole must point at the center (ASSUMPTION: check that the hole is radial). B1 sketch, not to scale, concept only. The bushing fills the stock hole and centers the coax; the sleeve stays outside. B2 · Full-diameter plastic guide rod: the tip lands on the center by construction IDEA Measure the inside diameter through the hole (method above: ID ≈ 63.5 − 2 × 3.35 ≈ 56.8 mm if the wall is uniform). Make a Delrin or PTFE rod just under 6.3 mm OD, as long as the measured ID, with a 0.55 mm blind bore drilled along its axis from one end to exactly half its length. Slide it in until it touches the far wall. The bare stub then goes into the bore, and the tip bottoms out at the midpoint of the rod, which is the geometric center. Hold the rod’s outer end with B1’s bushing. Pros Self-locating and easy to check: if the rod touches the far wall, the tip is at the center; the stub is supported along its length and cannot bend. Cons Puts a plastic rod across the whole diameter, so the stub is embedded in dielectric (IDEA: compare S11 with and without it on the VNA6000); a long 0.55 mm bore is hard to drill straight; the rod is hard to remove. B2 sketch, not to scale, concept only. B3 · The hub’s SMA bulkhead path plus an internal extension wire FACT Hub plan for B: keep or ream the stock hole to 6.5 mm clearance and clamp the 901-9875 with a locknut and washer through the wall. Do not tap (Sheet B). There is room for the inside nut on this ball. IDEA Solder a straight wire to the bulkhead’s center contact so its tip ends 31.75 mm below the outside surface. Pros Matches Sheet B; the ball can be unplugged; the thread is held by a nut, not the wall. Cons Reaming changes the stock hole; the extension joint is hidden inside; a long bare extension can sag unless supported (combine with B2’s rod). B4 · External clamp collar (B-sized version of A2) IDEA A brass collar with a curved saddle face is bonded over the stock hole, with a bore for the RG-405 and a brass or nylon set screw. Alternatively, a split brass clamp ring around a PTFE sleeve on the coax, screwed to an external saddle. Pros Adjustable depth; bonds the outer conductor to the shell if you want that; no work inside the ball. Cons Bonding brass to aluminum (use conductive epoxy or a mechanical clamp); the collar must be square to the hole axis. B5 · Potted Delrin tube and B6 · machined boss (heavier options) IDEA B5: as in A4, a Delrin or nylon tube in the ¼″ hole, potted from outside. B6: a machined aluminum boss bonded over the hole, thick enough for ≥2–3 full thread pitches (FACT hub rule; 1/4-36 pitch = 1/36″ ≈ 0.71 mm, so ≥1.4–2.1 mm of boss), then tapped 1/4-36 UNEF 2B in the boss only. FACT Monstein & Wesley’s Fig. 1 ball used a machined 18 mm shaft and 34 mm base at the feed (sphere.html). A boss is the catalog-ball version of that. Pros Strong and permanent; a boss gives a real thread. Cons Needs a machine shop; permanent; more metal at the feed. IDEA Internal 3D-printed cradle for B: a full cradle cannot pass through the ¼″ hole, so it would mean cutting and re-joining the ball. Not recommended; B2’s rod is the “internal support” that fits through the hole. Checking that the tip really is at the center IDEA Depth stop plus measurement: the stop is set to R from the tip (9.525 mm A, 31.75 mm B), measured under magnification with calipers before assembly. IDEA Sacrificial ball (A): the KB-1820 is sold in a 10-pack. Drill one exactly like the real ones, then saw it in half to see where the tip ends up. It also serves as a drilling practice piece. IDEA Printed see-through mockup (B): print a clear 63.5 mm half-shell with a ¼″ hole in the same place, and set the depth stop against it before touching the real ball (only two KB-2016 were bought, sphere.html). IDEA X-ray: a dental or industrial X-ray shows the copper-clad wire against the thin aluminum shell; a quick way to confirm on the finished part. IDEA Borescope or phone light (B only, before the coax goes in): a small inspection camera through the ¼″ hole can check for swarf and burrs inside. It is not precise enough to locate the tip. IDEA S11 repeatability: log S11 for each assembly on the VNA6000-A. It does not tell you where the tip is, but a TX/RX pair that differs a lot suggests the two builds are not the same. Practical build notes IDEA Holding a 19 mm ball for drilling: a V-block or soft (aluminum or wood) vise jaws with a matching cup, so the drill axis passes through the center and the thin wall is not crushed. Line up the drill with the V-block centerline. IDEA Starting the hole: a light spot with a sharp center drill or a very light center punch (a heavy punch can dent a thin stamped wall). Then a small pilot, then the final size or a step drill. Low speed and light feed. IDEA Deburr inside and out; no swarf left inside. Blow out, rinse with isopropyl alcohol, shake and listen: a rattle means a chip is still inside. Drilling with the hole facing down helps chips fall out. FACT Thread engagement: the hub says do not tap a thin ball wall; tap 1/4-36 only in a boss at least 2–3 pitches (≈1.4–2.1 mm) thick (setup#sphere-a, shop drawing). ASSUMPTION The KB-1820 wall is probably thinner than that; measure it. If it is, use a nut (only B has room), a boss (A2, A3, B6) or epoxy (A4, B5). FACT Connector and sleeve stay outside the ball in every concept here, as Dan asked. FACT Non-ferrous only: 3003 aluminum, brass, copper, PTFE, Delrin and nylon are all non-ferrous. No steel screws, washers or clamps in the RF path. How each concept fits the sleeve balun FACT Hub sleeve rule (Keyport-style): a close-fitting tube over the RG-405 jacket, soldered to the outer conductor at the cold end (away from the tip), open end toward the stub tip; λ/4 in air = 57.8 mm (A) or 172.9 mm (B); trim shorter if the gap has tape or PTFE (sleeve-balun.html, setup#sleeve). With the stub inside the ball, the sleeve’s open end faces the ball. CORRECTED 5 Oct 2026 Experiment A: the sleeve’s open end is level with the shield cut, about 3.0 mm from the ball, and never touches it (exp-1296.html#feed). IDEA Open questions for Dan, Steve or anyone else: How big a gap should there be between the sleeve’s open end and the ball surface? Should the sleeve touch the ball, or be kept off it with a thin PTFE washer? For Experiment A it is settled: the coax outer conductor must not touch the ball (A1). For Experiment B, should the outer conductor be bonded to the shell (the hub’s “outer as shield” default, from Monstein and Wesley Fig. 1) or insulated from it? These choices change the electrical setup, so pick one, log it, and keep the TX and RX identical. What the references actually say US 12,525,711 B1 (Paulus & Gentile, US Navy / NUWC Keyport, issued 13 Jan 2026): local PDF FACT Col. 6, lines 27–47 (FIGS. 7A–7B): the monopole antenna “may further comprise a spherical transmitter 80 enclosing the antenna portion 21 and the shielded portion 23 of the center conductor 20.” The sphere “may be made of conductive materials such as various metallic elements and alloys that may include copper,” “may be substantially solid, and molded or adapted to connect to the balun 60,” “may comprise an antenna cavity 81,” and “may be connected to a cable jacket 26.” The sphere “may have a radius 80′, and a balun length 60″ equivalent to the radius 80′,” and “the radius 80′ may be equivalent to a fourth of a wavelength.” “The spherical transmitter 80 may comprise the antenna tube 29.” FACT Claims 10–17 repeat this: the spherical transmitter encloses the antenna portion and the shielded portion (claim 10), a metallic sphere (11), substantially solid and adapted to connect to the balun (12), an antenna cavity (13), connected to the cable jacket (14), balun length equal to the sphere radius (16), radius equal to λ/4 (17). FACT The balun attaches to the shield: “a balun 60 may be connected to the shield 40 at a contact location 61 on the shield 40 … located on an exterior surface 62 of the shield,” with a closed end at the contact and an open end facing the tip (claims 1 and 6). FACT In FIG. 7A the balun (60), shield (40) and antenna tube (29) are drawn inside the sphere’s cavity (81), and the cable jacket (26) enters through the sphere wall. FIG. 7B shows a solid, hatched sphere with the balun embedded in it. The patent says its drawings are “not necessarily to scale.” DIFFERENCE Dan’s layout is not the patent’s FIG. 7. The patent puts the balun inside a sphere whose radius is λ/4, which would be 57.8 mm at 1296 MHz or 172.9 mm at 433.59 MHz. Our balls have radii of 9.525 mm and 31.75 mm, so the sleeve cannot fit inside and stays outside. IDEA In FIG. 7A the radius line 80′ appears to start at the end of the shield, with the antenna tube continuing past it. The patent does not say the tip is at the center; putting the tip at the center is Dan’s choice. FACT The patent gives no mounting hardware for the sphere: no fasteners, potting or standoffs. Nothing on this page comes from the patent except the idea that a sphere encloses the antenna and the balun attaches to the shield. Tomilin, Lukin & Gulkov 2021 (Russian marine channel, ball and rod): library card · kit gap list FACT (hub library card) A 60 mm copper sphere is joined by a metal rod to the center of a Tesla flat spiral at 27.4 MHz, and the whole antenna is insulated from seawater by a dielectric layer. The rod meets the sphere from the outside; it is not a stub inside the sphere. It is a useful example of holding a sphere on a rod, not a template for a stub at the center. The physics claims are contested (see the card). Hub pages this page relies on shop-drawing.html Sheet A and Sheet B: bulkhead mounting, 6.5 mm clearance, flange/boss, “do not tap”. setup.html#sphere-a, #sleeve: A sphere facts; sleeve how-to (λ/10 = 23.1 mm stub, 57.8 mm sleeve). sleeve-balun.html: cut table for 1296 and 433.59 MHz; RG-405 data. tools.html: RG-405 dielectric OD, live calculator. sphere.html: B sphere facts, wall 0.132″, SMA install; MW Fig. 1. kit.html: VNA, cargo. Hub conflicts noticed while writing this page CONFLICT Balun on Experiment B. index.html#expt-b and sphere.html say “No balun of any type” on the 433.59 MHz ball (“coax into the ball, outer as shield”). sleeve-balun.html says the shop order “adds Keyport-style sleeves for A and B” and lists 172.9 mm for 433.59 MHz. Dan’s brief for this page also puts a sleeve on B. Not resolved here. CONFLICT Sleeve on Experiment A. index.html and setup.html call the sleeve-stub an archived or optional control, with the ¾″ sphere plus bulkhead as the first article. This page describes a new combination (stub inside the sphere, sleeve outside) that the other pages do not yet mention. CONFLICT Stub length. The hub’s first-article stub is λ/10 (23.1 mm at 1296, 69.1 mm at 433.59). A stub whose tip is at the center can only have R − t of bare wire inside the ball (under 9.5 mm for A, ≈28.4 mm for B). tools.html also defaults to a 0.25λ stub. CONFLICT Sleeve orientation wording. tools.html describes the sleeve as “shorted at the antenna end, open at the far end”. sleeve-balun.html and setup.html#sleeve say it is soldered at the cold end away from the tip, open end toward the tip. This page follows sleeve-balun.html and setup.html. MISSING KB-1820 wall thickness is not stated anywhere on the hub. It must be measured. Pages-only planning note, no simulator and no Cloud twin. Grok Bot initial ideas, 26 Sep 2026, subject to better ideas from anyone. No physics equations are introduced here; the numbers are hub facts or simple geometry (radius = half the diameter). This page © 2026 Dan Britton, educational use.

description: Round 1 microwave oven experiment: a 2.45 GHz oven as transmitter and a 3/4 inch sphere as detector, with the Experiment B rod controls and safety rules.
text: Round 1 · microwave oven experiment · draft v0.1 Microwave oven experiment Use the 3/4 in sphere from Experiment A as a detector next to a 2.45 GHz microwave oven, and subject the oven's leakage to the same controls as Experiment B, including the rod fixture. The oven is its own transmitter; the sphere only listens. Tests of hypotheses, not results. Mainstream electrodynamics treats free-space radio as transverse (TEM). A longitudinal or scalar component is a hypothesis we are testing, and nothing on these pages claims that scalar or longitudinal waves have been detected. Values marked proposal are our suggestions and are not measured or sourced. Draft v0.1, 4 Oct 2026, written by Grok Bot for Dan Britton. Safety rules (read before any bench work). Rods, spheres, probes, TinySA, cables and every other piece of metal stay outside the oven. Loose metal in a running oven can arc and damage the magnetron and the oven. Never run the oven empty. Use a water load (a microwave-safe container with about 1 kg of water). Do not defeat or bypass the door interlocks and do not open or modify the oven. Never connect the VNA, or any instrument input, to the oven antenna, waveguide or cavity. Receive only, from outside, through an attenuator. The federal limit for new ovens is 5 mW/cm² at 5 cm (21 CFR 1030.10). Do not try to raise leakage. Keep people out of the line between the oven and the receiver and use timed runs. Stay clear of anyone with a pacemaker or similar device. Protect the analyzer input: start with at least 20 dB of attenuation and a spectrum-analyzer maximum-input check against its manual. Increase sensitivity only after seeing the level. Why Two stages Geometry Controls Measurement states Three-position fixture scan Power balance Range finding Falsifiers Prep list 1. Why an oven, and what a detection would mean A household oven is a few hundred watts to over a kilowatt of 2.45 GHz power. Dan's hypothesis is that anything that makes a transverse wave also makes some longitudinal (SLW) component. The oven is the only source we have with enough power for effects that are not microwatts. The honest framing: fact An oven leaks ordinary transverse 2.45 GHz radiation. A sphere, a dipole or any other antenna will receive it. Seeing a signal says nothing about SLW. fact Within about λ/2π = 19.5 mm of a small source, and in the reactive region of a large aperture like a door seam, ordinary fields have a component along the line to the source. That is why the hub's near-field plan says the receiver must be well outside it. hypothesis If an SLW component exists, the rod fixture, the TX-sphere rotation and the brass versus W1 swap would respond differently from a TEM wave (see Joule-loss predictions). The oven experiment asks whether the oven's leakage follows the same T(φ) behaviour as the sphere transmitters, and in what way it differs. Questions: Q1 can the 3/4 in sphere launch and detect 2.45 GHz at all (Stage 1, exp-2450)? Q2 what does the oven's received signal look like with a sphere detector, and how does it vary with state, distance and angle (Stage 2)? Q3 does the oven, put through the Experiment B controls, behave like the sphere transmitter or differently? 2. Two stages Stage 1: sphere to sphere at 2.45 GHz Page: exp-2450.html TX: 3/4 in sphere on the VNA, CW at 2450 MHz, about -10 dBm RX: second 3/4 in sphere Aim: shows the sphere is a working antenna at 2.45 GHz, gives the clean reference for the rod curve Stage 2: oven as TX, sphere as RX This page Oven leakage out of the door, receive-only Same RX sphere, same cables, same rod fixture, same angle scan Aim: Experiment B controls applied to the oven proposal Do Stage 1 first. It tells us what a clean 2.45 GHz sphere link looks like, which the oven data are compared against. 3. Geometry Schematic, not to scale. The oven door faces the receiver; the rod fixture stands on a non-metallic support between them; r is measured with a tape from the door plane to the sphere centre. Notation. r = oven door to RX sphere centre distance. λ = 122.4 mm at 2450 MHz, λ/2 = 61.18 mm. Stage 2a, near survey proposal: r from about 0.5 to 2 m with at least 20 dB of attenuation, to find where the signal is and how strong. In this zone the ordinary near field of the door seam is still mixed in, so these data are about signal strength and polarisation, not an SLW test. Stage 2b, far test proposal following the hub's near-field plan: at least 4 m (one 2D²/λ for a 0.5 m door), with 10 to 12 m recommended, receiver inside Dan's Faraday cage. That is a long run in a house, so check the room layout and expect multipath from walls and floor (see range-finder). Rod fixture. The 2.45 GHz fixture is the 4 x 4 x 1/4 in plate with a 3 x 3 array of 61.18 mm rods at 30.6 mm pitch (exp-2450). Place it between the oven and the sphere, with its centre on the line, at least λ/2π = 19.5 mm from the sphere and well away from the door seam. It has to sit on a non-metallic stand outside the closed door. Its position along the line is a variable: see section 6. 4. The same controls as Experiment B, applied to the oven Experiment B control In the sphere experiment At the oven Rod angle scan, T = exp(-κ cos²φ) Rotate the 3 x 3 array, log level Same array, same angle zero, same fit (calculator C); level from the analyzer Brass versus W1 rods Swap the arrays Swap the arrays, oven at the same power and load Rods out, plate only Reference level T0 Same, repeated each session TX orientation Rotate the TX sphere 90° Rotate the oven 90° on the bench (or the receiver about the line) Distance and null search Move the RX along the rail, S21 amplitude and phase Move the RX in steps of λ/4 (30.6 mm) or less, amplitude only (no coherent reference) TEM control Wire-grid and stub-length controls Same wire-grid control (rods across the line) Faraday cage RX inside versus outside RX inside versus outside (grounding state recorded on every row) Background Rods in, TX off Oven off, then oven on with a water load The hub has a recorded observation about the oven and a cage coil (see rod-thermal); it is unverified and is not used as evidence here. Steve Morris's baseline recipe (TinySA in spectrum-analyzer mode, 1.7 to 3.0 GHz, peak hold, a generator tone at 1.9 GHz, runs outside the cage and then inside with oven off and on) is the template for every state below. 5. Measurement states and settings Baseline, oven off: room noise, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, the generator reference tone if used. Peak hold for 60 s. Oven on, 100% power, water load: timed runs of 30 s or less, with rests. Peak hold plus channel power across 2.40 to 2.50 GHz. The magnetron frequency moves with load and temperature, so a single bin is not reliable. Duty cycling (lower power settings): the magnetron turns on and off over a cycle of seconds, so use a time-domain (zero-span) trace if the analyzer supports it. proposal For each state record: date and time, oven make and model, power setting, water mass and temperature, r, rod material, angle, cage state (open or closed, grounded or not), attenuator, analyzer settings (RBW, detector, sweep) and the file name. The lab protocol and CSV log has a table format. 6. Three-position fixture scan at the oven (proposal) Added 4 Oct 2026. Adapted from the sphere benches (exp-2450). Analysis: Joule-loss page, section 8. Checklist: To-Do group. hypothesis Dan's early-attenuation idea, at the oven. The rotating fixture sits between the oven door and the receiving sphere. Placed close to the oven it should change the detected amplitude more than when it is midway or near the sphere, because paths that would reflect off objects between the two are attenuated before they can reflect. The closest point of approach of any rod during the rotation stays at least λ/(2π) = 19.5 mm from the door plane (and well away from the door seam). This is a hypothesis test and a proposal, not a result. Where does the fixture go? The sources do not say. Monstein and Wesley (2002) report testing the wave by "intervening a cubic array of 9 half-wavelength wires" (abstract) and call it a polarizer-analyzer. They give no distance from either ball. Butterworth et al. (2013), describing that apparatus, write "Between Tx and Rx are positioned a pair of rotatable polarizer-analyzer arrays", which is where the word "between" comes from. Neither source fixes a position along the line, so this test treats the position as a variable to measure. Station geometry at 2.45 GHz Item Value Status λ/(2π) standoff 19.5 mm fact arithmetic. A door is an extended aperture, so its near-field region is larger than a small sphere's; treat 19.5 mm as a floor. Array envelope radius R = √2 λ/4 43.3 mm arithmetic; turntable axis assumed through the array centre Proposed pivot distance from the door plane, NEAR OVEN 150.0 mm; closest rod approach 106.7 mm proposal; larger than the sphere-bench value (73.4 mm) because the door is an aperture Reference separation r (door plane to sphere centre) 1000.0 mm proposal; the top of the Stage 2a range. Use the tape-measured r. Pivot distance from the door: NEAR OVEN / MIDWAY / NEAR SPHERE 150.0 / 500.0 / 850.0 mm proposal; NEAR SPHERE mirrors NEAR OVEN, so the closest approach to the sphere is also 106.7 mm Protocol, with the oven safety rules kept Rods, stand and fixture stay outside the closed door on a non-metallic stand. Never put rods, the sphere, probes or any metal inside the oven. Use a water load (about 1 kg), 100% power, timed runs of 30 s or less with rests, and at least 20 dB of attenuation ahead of the analyzer. Fix the geometry: oven position and orientation, r, sphere height, cables, analyzer settings. Only the fixture moves, between NEAR OVEN, MIDWAY and NEAR SPHERE. Reference states at every station: oven off (ambient), oven on with the fixture removed, oven on with plates only. Angle scan at every station: φ = 0 to 180° in 10° steps, then once over 0 to 360°. Each angle needs its own timed run with a rest, so one scan is 19 runs; use a fresh or cooled water load per station and consider a 20° step for the first pass (proposal). Log the sphere-side level (peak hold and channel power across 2.40 to 2.50 GHz) for each run. Source loading check. There is no TX S11 here, and the VNA or any instrument input must never be connected to the oven. Use a fixed off-axis monitor (a second sphere or dipole that never moves, behind at least 20 dB of attenuation) and log its level and the magnetron peak frequency for every run. If either moves with the rod angle at NEAR OVEN, the fixture is loading the oven or pulling the magnetron. Optional: RX sphere S11 with the VNA, oven off only, to check the fixture is not detuning the sphere. Order and repeats: NEAR OVEN, MIDWAY, NEAR SPHERE, then reverse; brass, then W1 in the same holes; repeat on a second day. Fit each station with calculator F, pasting the monitor level into the third column. The oven is not coherent with the instrument, so amplitude only. The magnetron frequency and output drift with load and temperature, which is why the fixed monitor matters: compare the sphere level to the monitor level, not to a fixed number. Log columns are those of the CSV template, with the monitor level in the tx_s11_dB column (rename it in your file). After each 10° rod step, wait about 3 s (or until the trace is flat) so the rods stop ringing, and log it as settle_s (rod-jig page, section 7). How to read it Observation Ordinary reading and caveats Reading under this test κ deepest at NEAR OVEN and the monitor level and magnetron frequency stay stable across the scan The array subtends a larger angle seen from near the oven door, so plain shadowing also predicts this. Absorption and scattering are not separated. Supports the early-attenuation idea as a pattern. Needs repeats, W1, and the 90° TX rotation control before it means more. Monitor level or magnetron frequency moves with the rod angle at NEAR OVEN The fixture loads the oven or pulls the magnetron: a near-field coupling artefact. Do not read κ at that station as attenuation. Move the fixture out and repeat. κ about equal at all three stations Loss does not depend on where the fixture sits. No support for early attenuation; position-independent. κ deepest MIDWAY or NEAR SPHERE, or the rods-crossed level L0 shifts with station Reflection nulls and multipath can mimic any of these: moving the fixture changes which paths cross the array and the standing-wave phase. Check the plates-only runs, shift r by λ/4 and repeat before believing a station effect. 7. Power balance, safely The full write-up is on the Joule-loss page. In short: the oven's output is estimated by water calorimetry (P = m c ΔT / t); the leaked signal is measured only as a relative level through a fixed attenuator; the rod effect is the change in that level with angle and material. The leaked fraction of the magnetron output cannot be derived from these alone because the sphere is not a calibrated antenna. 8. Range finding at the oven The oven is not coherent with the instrument, so the VNA-phase methods on the range-finder page do not apply. What remains: amplitude nulls versus position from ground and wall reflections (the "Two-ray nulls" tab of the calculator), dipole direction finding from two positions (direction-finding section), and the tape measure. As an assumed example with both antennas 1 m above a flat floor, the two-ray model puts the first nulls at 2.45 GHz near 32.7, 10.8, 6.4 and 4.5 m (Monstein and Wesley convention) or 16.3, 8.0, 5.3 and 3.8 m (ideal ground). The two conventions disagree, indoor floors and walls add more reflections, and so null positions are a cross-check to compare against the tape, not a stand-alone measurement. All range estimates here are hypotheses to test. 9. What would count against the idea The oven's received level tracks the ordinary-wave picture: it falls with r roughly as 1/r in the far field, follows the TX orientation (rotating the oven or the TX sphere by 90° changes the curve) and is the same for brass and W1. The rod curve is explained fully by the wire-grid control. No difference between inside and outside the Faraday cage beyond ordinary shielding. Results not repeatable between sessions beyond the quoted uncertainty. Repeat each scan at least twice, with the fixture re-seated. A result that differs from these would be interesting, and would then need independent checks (a second oven, a second analyzer, a different room) before being believed. 10. Prep list The checkable list is on the To-Do page (oven group), and the range and Joule groups there cover the analysis tools. Items that block the oven work: Stage 1 data from exp-2450 (sphere link works at 2.45 GHz). 2.45 GHz rods (brass and W1) and the 4 x 4 in plate, delivered and inspected. 20 dB attenuators and a suitable stand (non-metallic) for the rod fixture. An agreed water-load and timing procedure, and a bystander-free room.

description: Automatic range finder and dipole direction finder for the Round 1 experiments: phase slope, time domain, two-ray nulls, null spacing, figure-eight fit and triangulation, with a tape-measure calibration table.
text: Round 1 · tool · draft v0.1 Range finder and direction-finding dipoles How far apart are the transmitter and the receiver, and in which direction is the transmitter? This page defines the notation, says which parts are ordinary validated physics and which are hypotheses, and gives an in-browser calculator that turns VNA sweeps, null positions and dipole rotations into a range with an uncertainty. It works for the three sphere benches and, with limits, for the microwave oven. Tests of hypotheses, not results. Mainstream electrodynamics treats free-space radio as transverse (TEM). A longitudinal or scalar component is a hypothesis we are testing, and nothing on these pages claims that scalar or longitudinal waves have been detected. Values marked proposal are our suggestions and are not measured or sourced. Draft v0.1, 4 Oct 2026, written by Grok Bot for Dan Britton. Notation The idea, read honestly Validated or hypothesis? Numbers Calculator Dipole direction finders Calibrate and falsify Sources 1. Notation r: straight-line distance from the TX sphere centre to the RX sphere centre (the "range"). This is the hub's usual meaning (setup.html "range r is sphere-to-sphere"). x: horizontal ground distance between TX and RX, used only in the two-ray (ground-reflection) model, as in Monstein and Wesley (2002). With heights h1, h2: r = √(x² + (h2 - h1)²). λ = c/f in free space, c = 299 792 458 m/s. The S21 phase is simply called "phase" here, in degrees; φ is reserved for the rod angle on the Joule-loss page. 2. The idea, read honestly Monstein and Wesley saw signal minima at several distances along a street (39 m and 23 m confirmed, others "probably exist"). Their own model explains them as two-path interference: the direct wave plus a wave reflected from the ground. Null positions depend only on λ and the two antenna heights (see the ranging page; for their geometry the model gives 119.2, 39.3, 23.0, 15.8 m). That is ordinary multipath, and it is useful: it means a TX and RX pair over a reflecting surface carries distance information with no extra hardware. So Dan's reading, that an "automatic range finder" is built into the Experiment B setup, is reasonable as an engineering idea, with one correction: the nulls are not SLW-specific, so seeing them says nothing about longitudinal waves. What we can test is whether the information can be read out automatically and reliably at 433.59 MHz, 1296 MHz and 2450 MHz, on the sphere benches and at the oven. The same VNA sweep we need anyway for the rod baselines also holds phase slope and ripple, so the readout can be a button. Improvements on the first idea. Do not walk the receiver; sweep frequency. The null pattern moves with frequency, so the ripple in |S21| versus f gives the path difference without moving anything. Phase slope. Over a clean single path, S21 phase falls by 360° every c/r in frequency, so r = -(d phase/df) c/360. Two frequencies resolve it coarsely; one frequency refines it to a fraction of λ. Time-domain gating. A Hann-windowed inverse transform of the complex S21 shows the direct path and the ground bounce as separate peaks when they are farther apart than about c/B. Self-consistency test for null series. A real two-ray series has 1/xn equally spaced; the calculator reports whether it is. Triangulation. Two dipole bearings give r with no multipath assumption (and work on the oven, which has no coherent reference). Tape-measure calibration table with a plot of estimate versus tape, so the claim "it works" is a number. 3. What is validated and what is hypothesis Method Status Needs How it fails (falsifier) Phase slope, S21 phase vs f validated physics (stepped-frequency ranging; vna-howto.html section 8) Clean line of sight, r above a few λ, same cables for cal and run Estimate versus tape has slope not equal to 1, or scatter above the quoted error Two-frequency and coarse-fine validated Phase stable to a few degrees, no cable movement Candidate list never contains the tape value Time-domain peak validated (VNA time-domain mode) Bandwidth B; resolution c/B (1.5 m at 200 MHz) Earliest peak disagrees with the tape after a cable-delay correction Two-ray nulls and ripple period validated for the model; Monstein and Wesley saw 2 of 4 predicted minima Heights known to a few cm; open ground Ripple period does not change as the model predicts when a height is changed Null spacing λ/2 along a line validated for a standing wave between two reflecting objects Receiver moved in steps well below λ/4 Spacing is not λ/2 (the nulls come from something else) Dipole figure-eight, bearing validated for the pattern of a dipole Known polarisation, calibration on a known source Peak direction wanders with turntable zero or cable position "The peak is end-on, so the wave is longitudinal" hypothesis Several ranges, several wavelengths out, TX rotated 90° End-on part dies as the ordinary near-field terms do, or follows the TX orientation "Built-in range finder" works automatically on 1.3 and 2.45 GHz and on the oven hypothesis (an engineering claim to be tested) Tape-calibrated table of at least 5 ranges per band Errors above the thresholds you set before looking at the data 4. Example, 2.45 GHz, both antennas 1.00 m above ground (effective heights 1.00 m + λ/2, the Monstein and Wesley convention; proposal geometry). Indoors, walls and the oven itself will add many more paths and this clean series will not appear. 5. Calculator Everything runs in your browser; nothing is uploaded. Paste numbers separated by commas, spaces or tabs; lines starting with # are ignored. The "Load synthetic example" buttons make clearly labelled fake data so you can see what the output looks like. Dipole direction-finding antennas, one per band The Dipole Detector is a centre-fed brass-rod receiving dipole (1/8 in, 1.5 mm feed gap, SMA edge-mount jack, quarter-wave sleeve balun, non-conductive plate), described on the build sheet page. It is a receiving antenna, not one of the polarising rods; keep it separate from the rod arrays. First-pass lengths (cut long and trim): Unit Band Design tip to tip (mm) Cut tip to tip (mm) Cut each half (mm) Sleeve length at velocity factor 1.0 (mm) DD-433 433.59 MHz 332.2 345.7 172.8 172.9 DD-1296 1.3 GHz 109.6 115.7 57.9 57.8 DD-2450 2.45 GHz 57.2 61.2 30.6 30.6 How it finds direction. A dipole's received power follows cos² of the angle between its axis and the E-field direction. Rotate it on a turntable, fit the figure-eight, and the maximum (or the null) gives an axis direction. fact For a transverse wave with E along the dipole, the maximum is broadside to the source and the null is end-on. A null is sharper than a peak, so it makes the better pointer. hypothesis For a wave with an E component along the propagation direction (the SLW claim), the maximum would be end-on instead. So the same rotation is also a polarisation test: compare the fitted peak with the known source bearing. caution Close to any small antenna (inside roughly λ/(2π) and not far beyond) an ordinary field also has a radial E component, so an end-on peak near the TX proves nothing. The hub's near-field plan advises keeping detectors several wavelengths out. Look at how the end-on part changes with range. Bearing has a 180° ambiguity; resolve it by moving the antenna or by a second station. Calibrate on a source at a known bearing first, with the TX feed axis set so the E direction is known. Check that the sleeve works (slide test in vna-howto.html section 7). Coax carrying common-mode current bends the pattern and fakes bearings. Procedure (proposal). Dipole horizontal on a turntable with a 1° scale; TX feed axis horizontal and perpendicular to the line; rotate in 15° steps over 360° (the second half is a free symmetry check), log the level at each step with the VNA at one CW frequency or the TinySA in peak hold; fit; repeat at three ranges; rotate the TX sphere 90° and repeat. 7. Calibrate against a tape, and how to falsify Before looking at data, write down thresholds (for example a maximum allowed error as a fraction of λ or as centimetres) in the To-Do list. These are yours to choose; this page does not set them. For each band, measure at least five ranges with a tape or laser, centre to centre, and run the estimate each time. Fit estimate = slope × tape + offset. A constant offset is a phase-centre or cable correction. A slope that is not 1, or scatter above the quoted error, fails the method on that band. Repeat with the rods in and out. If the rods move the range estimate, the rods are changing the propagation path, which is itself interesting. Repeat on another day and in another place. Two-ray results should move when you change a height; if they do not, the ripple is not from the ground. The oven. The oven gives no coherent reference, so VNA phase methods do not apply (and the VNA must never be connected to the oven antenna or cavity). Use amplitude nulls along a line, the dipole bearings with triangulation, and the tape. The magnetron's frequency drifts, so ripple-in-frequency is not available from the oven alone. 8. Sources C. Monstein and J. P. Wesley, "Observation of scalar longitudinal electrodynamic waves", Europhys. Lett. 59(4), 514 (2002), doi:10.1209/epl/i2002-00136-9: two-ray nulls, Eq. 11 to 17. Hub summaries: ranging page, monstein.html. NanoRFE VNA6000 user manual (2022/11) and the hub's VNA how-to: S21 phase and time-domain use. C. A. Balanis, Antenna Theory: Analysis and Design: dipole pattern and field regions. M. I. Skolnik, Introduction to Radar Systems: stepped-frequency ranging. Hub near-field plan for the oven: magnetron-nearfield. Dipole numbers: dipole-detector. The calculator's functions were checked with node against synthetic data (phase slope, two-frequency, coarse-fine, time domain, null spacing, two-ray nulls reproducing 119.2, 39.3, 23.0 and 15.8 m for the 2002 geometry, figure-eight fit, triangulation). Real data will be messier than the examples.

title: Ranging a Scalar-Longitudinal Transmitter
headings: Worked example (verified in JavaScript and Python)
Two-detector ratio calculator HYPOTHESIS: p = 4, G = 1
What does not depend on SLW theory
Falsifiers: results that would sink the idea
description: Analysis page: how far away is a scalar-longitudinal-wave (SLW) transmitter? Ground-image null checkpoints (Monstein & Wesley 2002), wavefront-curvature fill-in with two detectors, and a hypothetical two-detector (SLW + Josephson) ratio. Every claim labeled FACT, HYPOTHESIS or ASSUMPTION.
text: Analysis page · distance estimation · not one of Experiments A–G Ranging a Scalar-Longitudinal Transmitter Goal: estimate how far away a scalar-longitudinal-wave (SLW) transmitter is, using what a receiver can measure as it moves. We build up in three layers: fixed checkpoints from ground-reflection nulls, a two-detector trick to fill in between them, and a more speculative two-detector ratio. Educational only. Mainstream classical electrodynamics treats free-space radio as transverse (TEM); scalar-longitudinal waves are disputed. Sections 1 and 2 use plain two-path geometry that works for any wave. Section 3 depends on unverified extended-electrodynamics assumptions. FACT published measurement, standard geometry or arithmetic HYPOTHESIS unproven physics we are testing ASSUMPTION taken as true to make the numbers work; check at your site 1 · Null checkpoints FACT FACT The ground acts like a mirror. The receiver gets the direct wave from the transmitter plus a reflected wave that seems to come from an “image” transmitter below the ground. The reflected path is a little longer. Wherever that extra length is an odd number of half-wavelengths, the two waves partly cancel and the signal dips. These dips (nulls) sit at fixed distances that depend only on the wavelength and the two antenna heights. The result holds for any kind of wave, so it does not depend on any SLW theory. The published case: Monstein & Wesley (2002) FACT Frequency 433.59 MHz, so λ = c/f = 0.6914 m. Transmitter ball 4.0 m above ground; receiver ball 4.4 m above ground. FACT To agree with their observations, M&W put the effective reflecting plane λ/2 = 34.6 cm below the ground surface (the ground conducts poorly, about 10⁻³ S/m). That gives effective heights y = 4.346 m and y′ = 4.746 m. ASSUMPTION The same λ/2 offset applies to your ground; it depends on soil conductivity. FACT Distances: direct path R = √(x² + (y′ − y)²); image path R′ = √(x² + (y′ + y)²), where x is the horizontal distance. FACT Their large-distance signal (eq. 15): S(x) ≈ (ωk / 2x²) · [A² + B² + 2AB·cos k(R′ − R)], k = 2π/λ Here A and B are the direct and image amplitudes. From their data B²/A² = 0.482, so B/A = 0.694. FACT Minima occur when R′ − R = (2n + 1)·λ/2, for n = 0, 1, 2, … (eq. 17). Larger n gives a null closer to the transmitter. FACT M&W’s Table I predicts minima at 119, 39, 23 and 16 m (n = 0…3). They report that their observations agree at 39 m and 23 m. For the other two they say the minima “probably exist” but noise and roughly ±5 m of GPS error made them indefinite. FACT Our own calculation from their effective heights gives 119.2, 39.3, 23.0 and 15.8 m (plus 11.7 m and closer). Each dip reaches (1 − B/A)², which is 10.3 dB below the direct-wave-only level. The calculator below reproduces these numbers. FACT Measured fall-off: in the range 20–100 m, M&W’s data fit (1/x²)·[1 + 0.945·cos k(R′ − R)]. Beyond about 100 m the signal dropped faster than 1/x²: an extra exponential loss of 1/e per 145 m, which they attribute to ground losses. Which null am I on? Every null looks alike, so a single dip does not tell you which one it is. Two practical ways to find out: FACT Count from a known position. Start close to the transmitter at a distance you have measured, then walk or drive outward and count the dips. Going outward, n decreases by 1 at each dip; the last dip (n = 0) is the farthest. FACT Switch frequency. Null positions scale with frequency: for far nulls, x grows roughly in proportion to f. Change f by a known amount (for example +10%) and see which dip moves by the amount the calculator predicts for each n. The matching prediction identifies n. At 1.1 × 433.59 MHz the 39.3 m null moves to about 42.7 m and the 119.2 m null to about 129.3 m. Null calculator FACT Change any box; results update instantly. The defaults are Monstein & Wesley’s setup. Frequency f (MHz) Tx height, physical (m) Rx height, physical (m) B/A (image ÷ direct amplitude) Round the λ/2 offset to the nearest millimetre, as M&W publish it (0.346 m). Effective height = physical height + λ/2. Untick to use the exact λ/2. At the defaults the exact value 0.3457 m gives 39.2 and 119.1 m instead of 39.3 and 119.2 m. n null at x (m) R (m) R′ (m) R′ − R (m) Plot: multipath factor F(x) = 1 + (B/A)² + 2(B/A)·cos k(R′ − R), in dB relative to the direct wave alone (0 dB), against distance x on a log scale from 10 to 300 m. The 1/x² spreading is not included, so only the ground-reflection ripple shows. Dashed lines mark the nulls. 2 · Wavefront-curvature fill-in (between nulls) Nulls act as mile-markers, but you are usually somewhere between two of them. To fill the gap, place two identical SLW detectors a known distance d apart on the line pointing at the transmitter. The nearer detector sits at r₁ and the farther one at r₂ = r₁ + d. Because the wave spreads out, the nearer detector reads slightly stronger. FACT M&W measured power falling as 1/x² (amplitude ∝ 1/x) from 20 to 100 m, with extra loss beyond 100 m. ASSUMPTION Amplitude falls as 1/r at your site over the baseline. FACT (arithmetic, given that assumption) A₁/A₂ = r₂/r₁ = (r₁ + d)/r₁, so r₁ = d / (A₁/A₂ − 1) No Josephson junction or exotic detector is needed, just two matched SLW detectors. FACT Divide out the ground ripple first. Each reading includes the multipath factor F from Section 1, and F differs between the two positions. Divide each amplitude by √F at its own position before taking the ratio. This needs B/A to have been measured, for example from null depth. FACT Sensitivity is the hard part. At 80 m with d = 2 m the amplitude ratio is only 1.025 (0.21 dB). An error of just ±0.02 dB moves the answer to about 73–88 m. You need detectors and electronics stable to about 0.02 dB. A longer baseline helps: the ratio grows roughly in proportion to d. FACT If M&W’s extra loss (1/e per 145 m in power) is present and not removed, it adds about 0.06 dB across a 2 m baseline. That makes the 80 m example read about 62 m. ASSUMPTION M&W saw this extra loss beyond 100 m; whether it also acts at shorter range at your site is unknown. Two-detector curvature calculator ASSUMPTION: 1/r amplitude Baseline d (m) Measured ratio, near ÷ far, after F correction (dB) A ratio in dB is the same number whether you read power or amplitude, because dB = 20·log₁₀(amplitude ratio) = 10·log₁₀(power ratio). 3 · Two-detector ratio HYPOTHESIS This idea uses two different detectors: an SLW power detector and a Josephson-junction (JJ) phase detector. Both see the same transmitter current I₀. If their readings depend on I₀ in different ways, dividing one by the other could cancel the unknown transmitter strength. This section works through when that also leaves range information and when it does not. HYPOTHESIS SLW detector power: PL = CL·I₀²·r−p·F(r), where F is the Section 1 ground factor and p is the power fall-off exponent. HYPOTHESIS JJ phase: φ = CJ·I₀·r−1·G(r). This assumes the junction responds linearly to the vector potential A, per Hively & Loebl’s extended electrodynamics as relayed by Dan; it has not yet been checked against the paper’s equation numbers. ASSUMPTION G = 1 (no ground-reflection effect in the JJ channel). FACT (algebra, given those models) PL/φ² = (CL/CJ²)·r2−p·F(r). The transmitter current I₀ cancels. FACT (algebra) If p = 2 (both channels effectively 1/r in amplitude), range cancels too. Any combination PLm·φn carries I₀ and r with the same exponent (2m + n), so removing I₀ always removes r. HYPOTHESIS The method therefore works only if the SLW field falls as 1/r² (power p = 4). You also need one calibration shot at a known distance rcal. Then: r = rcal · √[ (φ²/PL) ÷ (φcal²/Pcal) · F(r)/F(rcal) ] Because F(r) depends on the unknown r, the equation has to be solved numerically. Worked example (verified in JavaScript and Python) ASSUMPTION p = 4, G = 1, and M&W geometry and B/A (Section 1 defaults). Calibration at rcal = 20 m; the true target is at 80 m. FACT F(20 m) = 2.246 (R′ − R = 1.966 m); F(80 m) = 1.424 (R′ − R = 0.514 m). FACT PL ratio = (20/80)⁴ × 1.424/2.246 = 0.00248, i.e. −26.1 dB. That splits into −24.1 dB from distance and −2.0 dB from the ground path. φ ratio = 20/80 = 0.250. FACT Quantity (φ ratio)² ÷ PL ratio = 0.0625 / 0.00248 = 25.24. FACT Without the F correction: r = 20·√25.24 = 100.5 m, which is 26% too far. With F(80)/F(20) = 0.634: r = 80.0 m. FACT Watch out: more than one answer. Because F ripples, the equation has several solutions between 10 and 300 m. For this example they are 22.7, 23.3, 37.0, 42.4 and 80.0 m. Simple repeated substitution starting from F ratio = 1 jumps around (100.5 → 38.0 → 26.3 → 91.3 → 55.3 …) and does not settle reliably. The calculator therefore scans the whole range and lists every solution. FACT Picking the right answer: use the null bracket from Section 1. Here both 42.4 and 80.0 m lie between the 39.3 m and 119.2 m nulls, so the bracket alone is not enough; add the Section 2 curvature estimate. ASSUMPTION A repeat at a second frequency also works if the model holds at both frequencies: the true distance stays put while the false solutions move. Two-detector ratio calculator HYPOTHESIS: p = 4, G = 1 Uses the frequency, heights and B/A from the Section 1 calculator for F(r). Ratios are target ÷ calibration. Calibration distance rcal (m) PL ratio, target ÷ cal (dB) φ ratio, target ÷ cal (linear) 4 · Caveats, unknowns and falsifiers What does not depend on SLW theory FACT Null positions depend only on wavelength and the two (effective) heights. FACT The F correction is plain geometry once B/A has been measured at your site. What depends on extended electrodynamics (EED) HYPOTHESIS A pure scalar wave exists with E = 0 and B = 0. HYPOTHESIS Its 1/r fall-off, which Section 2 and the JJ channel in Section 3 rely on. HYPOTHESIS A linear Josephson-junction response to it. HYPOTHESIS The power exponent p (range information needs p = 4). Unknowns ASSUMPTION G = 1: the reflection coefficient for the JJ channel is unknown. ASSUMPTION The ratio of source strengths for SW (scalar wave) and SLW is fixed; nobody has checked that it is. Falsifiers: results that would sink the idea (a) PL/φ² stays flat as distance changes. That means p = 2, so the ratio carries no range information. (b) The JJ nulls fall at different distances from the SLW nulls. Then the two detectors are not seeing the same wave. (c) The JJ reading does not respond when the transmitter is keyed on and off, or does not fall as 1/r. (d) Either reading survives the controls: transmitter off, a dummy load in place of the antenna, and the detector sealed in a Faraday cage. FACT A sealed cage strips ordinary TEM radio. HYPOTHESIS SLW passes through the cage wall. FACT Practical point: Josephson junctions need cryogenic cooling and magnetic shielding. This is not a backyard detector. No Wolfram Cloud twin planned (analysis page); numbers cross-checked in Python. The Python script reproduces the calculator outputs: null distances, F values, the Section 2 example, the worked example and its full root list. Sources Monstein, C. & Wesley, J.P., “Observation of scalar longitudinal electrodynamic waves”, Europhysics Letters 59(4), 514 (2002). Hub summary: Monstein page. Hively, L.M. & Loebl, A.S., “Classical and extended electrodynamics”, Physics Essays 32 (2019), plus the 2022 Erratum. Dan’s reviewed note, 2026-09-27. Analysis page, 27 Sep 2026. The JJ-channel model is relayed from Dan’s reading of Hively & Loebl and has not been checked against the paper’s equation numbers. This page © 2026 Dan Britton.
