text: Simulation Lab report · Joule loss / conductive media · faithful HTML conversion Joule-loss positions: Monstein & Wesley (2002) vs Hively (2016–2022) What Monstein & Wesley (2002) and Hively (2016–2022) actually say about Joule (Ohmic) loss of scalar-longitudinal waves, quoted from rendered page images with page/eq/slide citations, and where the positions agree or differ. MIXED ← Simulation Lab catalogue Provenance /workspace/sim-lab/sub-sources/JOULE_LOSS_POSITIONS.md (last modified 2026-09-26 16:05 EDT) Updated 2026-09-30: author-confirmed note and TYPO labels on the printed exponent (no other change). Converted to HTML 2026-09-28 (EDT) as a faithful conversion: text, numbers, equations and labels are the source's own. No new equations were added; only the TEM tags described below and the edits listed here were made. Three local-file references were neutralised: a path inside a private draft folder, and the file name of an internal comparison note (not published; its file name misspelled Joule). No physics text changed. Status lines inside the source (for example "nothing published", "HELD", "draft") describe the state when it was written. This page is its GitHub Pages twin, published 2026-09-28. No Wolfram Cloud twin planned (analysis/report page, not one of Experiments A–G). Numbers are Python-computed; WL compare OWED where the source says so. Framing rules on this page (Dan). Under the SLW hypothesis no skin-depth, permeability, ferromagnetic or cage shielding-effectiveness argument is used to rank or dismiss SLW/SW. The Faraday cage strips TEM noise (FACT); an SLW passing the cage wall is HYP. Every passage that uses transverse-EM (TEM / classical / cage-SE) reasoning is tagged transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis. FACT / HYP / ASSUMPTION labels are kept exactly as in the source. FACT, author-confirmed Author-confirmed, 2026-09-30. In a private email from Dr. Hively to Dan (2026-09-30), Dr. Lee Hively confirmed the charge-relaxation exponent: "The form, E = E0 e^(-sigma t/epsilon), is the correct one." So Eq. (A5), p. 122 of Hively & Loebl 2019, and the exponent before EQN. 12 in US 9,306,527 B1 (col. 5), which print e^(−εt/σ), have ε and σ swapped (typos as printed). The correct form is E = E0 exp(−σt/ε) with relaxation time τ = ε/σ, and IARD 2020 slide 60 is correct. See the Corrections log. Where this page quotes the printed form below, the quote is kept as printed and labelled TYPO as printed. Read-only research for Dan, 2026-09-26 (~16:30 ET). No hub page, SYNC_LEDGER or draft file was edited. Nobody was contacted and nothing was bought. Labels FACT: taken directly from a source, with page/eq/slide and the words quoted. HYP: our inference or our algebra. "Not stated in source" means exactly that. Method. Every equation below was read from a rendered page image (pdftoppm, 170–300 dpi), not from extracted text, which garbles σ, ε and □. □ = d'Alembertian. The IARD slide font drops it; the patent prints only "²". "∈" is the patent's glyph for ε. Sources used (all local) M&W: C. Monstein & J. P. Wesley, "Observation of scalar longitudinal electrodynamic waves", Europhys. Lett. 59(4), 514–520 (2002). Hub copy: /workspace/hub-efield-repo/papers/Monstein-Wesley-2002-EPL-Scalar-Longitudinal-Waves.pdf. 7 pages; the full text was readable. Provenance of the hub copy (PDF "Creator: Preview", 2016) is not stated. I did not check whether EPL offers it open-access. HL2019: L. M. Hively & A. S. Loebl, "Classical and extended electrodynamics", Phys. Essays 32, 112–126 (2019). Hub copy papers/Hively-Loebl-2019-…pdf. IARD 2020: Hively & Land, "Extended Electrodynamics and SHP Theory", IARD 2020 slides. Hub copy papers/Hively-Land-IARD-2020-EED-and-SHP-slides.pdf (72 slides). Erratum 2022: Hively & Loebl, Erratum, Phys. Essays 35, 320 (2022). One page; local PDF copy. Patent: L. M. Hively, US 9,306,527 B1 (Apr. 5, 2016). Hub copy papers/Hively-US9306527B1-…pdf. Not read: Erratum Phys. Essays 32(3), 417 (Sept 2019). It is paywalled; see Blockers. Update 2026-09-29: the 2019 erratum has since been read. It corrects Eq. (38)/(B5) to P_OUT = I² r̂ / [2 (4πr)²] · √(μ/ε) and Eq. (44) to energy density B²/2μ + C²/2μ + εE²/2 (FACT). It does not touch the Joule term J·E. See P_OUT erratum audit. 1. Monstein & Wesley 2002: loss or attenuation of the longitudinal E field 1.1 Their field theory has no loss term FACT, p. 514, Eq. (1): "∇²Φ − ∂²Φ²/∂t²c² = −4πρ, (1)" (printed exactly so, including the "Φ²"). FACT, p. 514, Eq. (2): "S⃗ = −∇Φ ∂Φ/∂t, D = (∇Φ)²/2 + (∂Φ/∂tc)²/2. (2)" FACT, p. 515, Eq. (5): "E⃗ = ∇Φ = [k q cos(kr − ωt)/r − q sin(kr − ωt)/r²]e⃗_r, (5)" FACT, p. 515, Eq. (6): "⟨S⃗⟩_t = k ω q/(2r²)e⃗_r, (6)" FACT: Eqs. (1)–(6) contain no conductivity σ, no Ohm's law and no damping term. The only source term is −4πρ. HYP: the −4πρ and "∂Φ/∂tc" forms suggest Gaussian units. Not stated in source. 1.2 Joule (Ohmic) loss that they DO derive: the wire polarizer (pp. 516–517) FACT, p. 516: "…only the E⃗ field component E₀ cos(φ) in the direction of a wire produces Ohmic losses. The Ohmic loss δP per unit time in an element δL of the wire is then equal to δP = −(δV)²/δR, where δV = E₀ cos(φ)δL is the potential across the element δL and where δR = δL/σA is the resistance of the wire element of length δL, and A is the cross-sectional area and σ the conductivity of the brass wires; thus," Eq. (7), p. 516: "δP = −[σAE₀² cos²(φ)] δL. (7)" FACT, pp. 516–517: "It may be readily shown from the first of eqs. (2) that the time average energy flux in the wire equals the time average electric field E₀ squared times c, ⟨P/A⟩_t = ⟨S⟩_t = cE₀². Thus, from eq. (7) for the rate of energy flow loss δ⟨S⟩_t in the wire per unit length δL is given by" Eq. (8), p. 517: "δ⟨S⟩_t = −(σ/c) cos²(φ)⟨S⟩_t δL. (8)" FACT, p. 517: "Integrating eq. (8), the fractional energy transmitted through the wire of length L is" Eq. (9), p. 517: "T = exp[−κ cos²(φ)], (9)" The text continues: "where κ is a constant proportional to the length L of the wire. … the theoretical result eq. (9) can be chosen to fit the observations when κ = 4.4, as shown in fig. 3." Fig. 3 caption, p. 516: "The solid curve presents the theory, eq. (9), T = exp[−4.4 cos²(φ)] for the best-fit value of κ." Derived or assumed? FACT: they derive Eq. (7) from Ohm's law (δR = δL/σA) and Eqs. (8)–(9) from it. FACT: κ is fitted (4.4), not computed from σ. No numerical σ for brass is given (not stated in source). Type of attenuation. FACT: it is in distance: per unit wire length δL, exponential in L. It concerns energy flux (power), and it is a Joule term: δP ∝ σE∥²·(A δL), with E∥ = E₀cos φ. Medium and frequency. FACT: a 3×3 array of "9 wires of length λ/2 (34.6 cm)" (p. 516), brass, at 433.59 MHz (Fig. 3 caption). HYP: Eq. (8) taken literally, with a metallic σ, would give a far larger κ than 4.4 for 34.6 cm wires. The fitted κ is therefore not a quantitative check of Eq. (8). This depends on the unit system (see 1.1) and is not computed in the source. 1.3 The excess loss over distance above ground (p. 520): measured, attributed, no equation FACT, p. 520: "Exponential loss of the signal with distance. – It is apparent from fig. 5 that the observed signal beyond 100 m decreases more rapidly with distance than the inverse square of the distance. This loss corresponds to an additional exponential loss with distance corresponding to 1/eth decrease in the signal for a distance of 145 m. This loss is probably due to the Ohmic losses produced by the currents induced in the Earth by the longitudinal E⃗ field, which is parallel to the Earth's surface. No such loss would be expected for transverse wave, where the electric E⃗ field is normal to the Earth's surface. This exponential decay of the signal with distance, thus, further indicates the fact that longitudinal electrodynamic waves are involved." FACT: there is no equation number, no formula and no conductivity value attached to this loss. It is an empirical extra exponential in distance, read off Fig. 5. It is attributed ("probably") to Ohmic loss in the Earth, not derived. FACT, p. 517: "The signal observed equals the time average energy flux S⃗, as given by the first of eqs. (2)." So "signal" means power flux. HYP (our arithmetic): 1/e in power at 145 m gives α_P ≈ 1/145 ≈ 6.9×10⁻³ m⁻¹ ≈ 0.030 dB/m. The field coefficient would be ≈ 3.4×10⁻³ m⁻¹. Neither number is in the source. FACT, p. 517 (the only Earth-conductivity number): "Since the conductivity of the Earth is only about 10⁻³ ℧/m [4], the effective reflecting surface of the Earth is a little below the actual surface. To agree with observations, the effective surface is chosen as half wavelength, λ/2 = 34.6 cm, below the actual surface." This σ is used for the image/reflection geometry, not for the loss (not stated in source). Medium, frequency, geometry and other numbers FACT: propagation in air above ground on the bank of the river Rhein near Sennwald, Switzerland (p. 518), at 433.59 MHz (Abstract). FACT: source 4.0 m and receiver 4.4 m above ground (Abstract); effective heights "y = 4.346 m and y′ = 4.746 m. (12)" (p. 517). FACT: Fig. 5 spans 10–1000 m; acknowledgments mention "distance of 1 kilometer". FACT: agreement with Eq. (14) is "quite satisfactory for x < 100 m" (p. 519). FACT: minima observed at 39 m and 23 m (Table I, p. 518; p. 519). Earth reflection coefficient "ℜ = B²/A² = 0.482. (24)" (p. 519). Asymptotic fit "⟨S_x⟩_t = (1/x²)[1 + 0.945 cos k(R′ − R)], (23)" (p. 519). 1.4 Answer to Q1 in one line FACT: M&W give one derived Joule loss law, Eqs. (7)–(9): Ohmic loss σE∥² in brass wires, exponential in wire length, fitted with κ = 4.4. FACT: for the ground loss over distance they give no equation. They give a measured extra 1/e per 145 m (power) beyond 100 m at 433.59 MHz over ground, which they say is "probably" Earth Ohmic loss. FACT: their scalar field equations (1)–(6) contain no conductivity. Both losses are added from Ohm's law or from the data, outside the field theory. 2. Hively's position on a Joule loss term for the SLW E field 2(a). Hively & Loebl, Phys. Essays 32, 112 (2019) FACT, p. 114, Eqs. (21)–(22): "∇ × B − (1/c²) ∂E/∂t − ∇C = μJ; (21)" "∇•E + ∂C/∂t = ρ/ε. (22)" FACT, p. 116 (the no-skin-effect argument): "The resultant electric field is Eᴸ = Jᴸ/σ = ∇κ/σ for media with a linear conductivity, σ. Eᴸ and Jᴸ for the SLW are curl-free. Faraday's law becomes ∇ × Eᴸ = −Ḃ = ∇ × ∇κ/σ = 0. … Thus, no eddy currents occur, so the SLW is unimpeded by the skin effect for propagation through linearly conductive media. See also Graham et al.⁵³ and Appendix A." Then: "C, Eᴸ, and Jᴸ are all related by Eq. (32b) with⁵⁴ σ = ε_o ε″ ω and ε = ε_o(ε′ − jε″) for a SLW impedance, Z," FACT, p. 116, Eq. (37): "Z = |E_r|/|C/μ_oμ′| = √(μ_o/ε_o) √(μ′/ε′) (1 − 1/(jkr))/(1 − j tan(δ_ε)). (37)" Text: "Equation (37) assumes spherical waves in linear conductive media: Eᴸ = E_r r̂ exp[j(kr − ωt)]/r, together with C = C_o exp[j(kr − ωt)]/r." FACT, p. 117, Eq. (44) as printed: "∂/∂t (B²/2μ + C²/2μ + εE²) + ∇•(E × B/μ + CE/μ) + J•E = ρC/(εμ). (44)" How it is built (p. 117): "EED predicts a revised energy balance, Eq. (44), from the sum of: (C/μ) times Eq. (22); (B/μ)• applied to Faraday's law; and application of −(E/μ)• applied to Eq. (21)." After it: "Equation (44) has new energy density terms: scalar field energy (C²/2μ), SLW energy (CE/μ), and a power source (ρC/εμ)." Note: Eq. 44 prints "εE²" without /2, while the patent's EQN. 14 prints "εE²/2" (see 2(d)). FACT, p. 117: "Revised energy balance, Eq. (44), shows that the scalar-wave energy is C²/2μ ∼ 1/r². Thus, the total scalar-wave energy, 4πr²(C²/2μ), is constant through a spherical boundary around a source and C(r → ∞) → 0, as expected." FACT: HL2019 does not call J·E in Eq. 44 a loss or a gain for the SLW, and gives no attenuation constant. Not stated in source. FACT, p. 122, Appendix A, Eqs. (A4)–(A7): "(A4) □²(Ė + J/ε) = □²(Ė + σE/ε)." "One solution to Eq. (A4) sets the terms inside the parentheses to zero, as a transient solution⁴ that typically decays in ∼10⁻¹⁹ s" "E = E_o e^(−εt/σ). (A5)" TYPO as printed (ε and σ swapped; author-confirmed 2026-09-30, correct form E = E_o e^(−σt/ε)) (A6) "E = E_o(r)e^(−jωt)"; then (A7) □²E = 0. "The lack of a source term on the RHS of Eq. (A7) means that the SLW propagates without loss in isotropic, homogeneous conductive media (σ = constant). That is, the SLW is unconstrained by the skin effect." This is a time transient, not a distance attenuation. The units issue (τ = ε/σ favours e^(−σt/ε)) is in the internal Joule-term comparison note (not published). Resolved 2026-09-30: author-confirmed, see the note at the top of this page. FACT, pp. 119–120: "…resonance-cavity effects that are not included in the present theory. SLW attenuation in conductive media is the subject of future work. The combined solid-copper thickness (2 × 1.02 mm) is 2914 skin depths in the result of Fig. 4, which should produce a classical attenuation of ∼10⁻¹²⁶⁵ in TEM waves. The test measurement yielded an attenuation between −115 dB at r = 2 cm separation and −137 dB at r = 30 cm. Extrapolating the straight-line fit to a separation of 2 mm (where the enclosed antennas are barely separated) gives −79 dB and −86 dB, for an attenuation of ∼10⁻⁴." transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis FACT, p. 121: "Wave penetration of the two 1-mm thick Faraday enclosures (2-mm total) demonstrates the low-loss nature of the SLW in conductive media. A more accurate and compelling result clearly requires a much better experimental design, which is the subject of future work." Summary, 2019. FACT: "without loss" in (A7) text, but "low-loss" on p. 121, and attenuation in conductive media is "future work" on p. 120. HYP: the 2019 position is no skin effect plus no loss in linear media in theory, while the measured loss is not claimed to be zero. 2(b). IARD 2020 slides (Hively & Land) FACT, slide 10 "2. What is EED? (5)": item "7. No skin-effect dissipation in linear, conductive media". FACT, slide 23: "•No constraint by skin effect in linearly conductive media". FACT, slide 60 "SLW Attenuation in Conductive Media": "J = σE ⇒ □²(Ė + J/ε) = □²(Ė + σE/ε) = 0" "Ė + σE/ε = 0 ⇒ E = E_o e^(−σt/ε)" "E = E_o(r)e^(−jωt) ⇒ □²E = 0 ⇒ lossless propagation in linear conductive media" FACT, slide 61 "No SLW Attenuation in Conductive Media": "□²(Ė + σE/ε) = 0, with σ=σ(E) ≡ σ(|E|) ⇒ □²(−jω + σ/ε)E + (E/ε)(∂σ/∂E)□²E = 0" "One solution for: □²E = 0, as before (E=E_r)" "Second solution for: −jωε + σ + E ∂(−jωε+σ)/∂E = 0:" "… E₂/E₁ = −jε₁′(1 + jε₁″/ε₁′)/[−jε₂′(1 + jε₂″/ε₂′)] = (ε₁′/ε₂′)(1+jtanδ₁)/(1+jtanδ₂); tanδ = ε″/ε′ ⇒ loss in media with σ = σ(|E|)" HYP: Despite its title, slide 61 states a loss mechanism, but only for field-dependent (nonlinear) σ. It is expressed as an amplitude ratio between two media states, not as a per-metre exponential or a Joule σE² term. For linear σ the slides say "lossless". Slide 60's e^(−σt/ε) is a time transient. 2(c). Erratum, Phys. Essays 35, 320 (2022): single page, p. 320, render-checked FACT: "This Erratum corrects errors in Appendix A of our paper for derivation of the no-skin-effect constraint. The scalar longitudinal wave (SLW) has only irrotational fields and no magnetic field from Eq. (27), B = 0, yielding from Eq. (23)" (A1) "□²B = μ∇ × Jᴸ = 0 ⇒ ∇ × ∇ × Jᴸ = 0 ⇒ ∇(∇ · Jᴸ) − ∇²Jᴸ = 0 ⇒ ∇(∇ · Jᴸ) = ∇²Jᴸ" (A2) "□²C = −μ(ρ̇ + ∇·Jᴸ) ⇒ ∇□²C/ε = −μ[∇ρ̇/ε + ∇(∇·Jᴸ)/ε] ⇒ ∇□²C/ε = −μ[∇ρ̇/ε + ∇²Jᴸ/ε] ⇒ ∇ρ̇/ε = −□²∇C/(εμ) − ∇²Jᴸ/ε" (A3) "□²Eᴸ = ∇ρ/ε + μJ̇ᴸ ⇒ □²Ėᴸ = ∇ρ̇/ε + μJ̈ᴸ ⇒ □²Ėᴸ = −□²∇C/(εμ) − ∇²Jᴸ/ε + μJ̈ᴸ ⇒ □²Ėᴸ = −□²∇C/(εμ) − □²Jᴸ/ε" "Moving all the terms to the left-hand side gives: □²Ėᴸ + □²∇C/(εμ) + □²Jᴸ/ε = 0 ⇒ (□²/εμ)(εμĖᴸ + ∇C + μJᴸ) = 0 (A4)" "The expression inside the right-most parentheses of Eq. (A4) is Eq. (21) with only the irrotational terms on the left-hand side and ∇ × B = 0, because B = 0 for the irrotational fields from Eq. (27)" "εμĖᴸ + ∇C + μJᴸ = 0. (A5)" "Substituting the expressions for E and C from Eqs. (18) and (20) into Eq. (A.5) gives the longitudinal component of the A-wave equation: □²Aᴸ = μJᴸ. (A6)" Closing, verbatim: "Physically, Eq. (A6) means that the SLW is not subject to resistive loss in conductive media. The same no-loss result occurs from the energy balance equation, Eq. (44), by substituting for (ρ/ε) from Eq. (22) and by substituting for Jᴸ from Eq. (21) with B = 0, then cancelling terms. Consequently, the SLW is unconstrained by the skin effect and power loss in resistive media." FACT: not in the Erratum: no σ, no Ohm's law J = σE, no exponential and no transient; no displayed algebra for the Eq. (44) cancellation (it is described in words only); no statement that J·E = 0; no mention of heating. 2(d). US 9,306,527 B1 (2016) FACT, col. 5 ~l. 46–56 (the transient): "…Linear electrical conductivity (σ), J=σE, then may give ²(Ė+σE/∈)=0. A very rapidly decaying, transient solution may arise by setting the terms inside the parentheses to zero, giving E=E_o exp(−∈t/σ). TYPO as printed (∈ and σ swapped; author-confirmed 2026-09-30, correct form E=E_o exp(−σt/∈)) … A second solution may use the non-transient form, E=E_o(r) exp(−jωt), which yields: □²E=0. (12)" FACT, col. 6 ll. 1–13: "…Third, these equations may have zero on the RHS for propagation in conductive media. This last result may arise from B=0 for the SLW, implying no back-electromagnetic field from Ḃ in Faraday's law that in turn may give no (circulating) eddy currents. Consequently, the SLW may not be subject to the skin effect in media with linear electrical conductivity." FACT, col. 6 ll. 13–15: "C, E, and J may interact via EQN. 6, which can be rewritten using J=σE, and identifying the electrical conductivity with the imaginary part of the complex permittivity ∈″= σ/∈_oω:" followed by EQN. (13) "C/E_r = (ε′/c)((1 + jα)/(1 + j/kr)) (13)". FACT, col. 6 ~l. 35–43, EQN. 14 and the key sentence: "∂/∂t(B²/2μ + C²/2μ + εE²/2) + ∇·(E×B/μ + CE/μ) + J·E − ρC/(εμ) = 0. (14)" "Use of the spherical wave forms for E and C in EQN. 14 with B=0 and the ratio of (C/E_r) from EQN. 13 may yield an identity, 0=0; the same result may arise for plane waves, thus explicitly verifying the no-skin-effect prediction." FACT, col. 6 Table 1: "3) SLW propagates in conductive media without the skin effect. EQNS. 8-12"; "6) C, E, and J exchange energy in conductive media. EQNS. 11-17". FACT, col. 9 ll. ~5–25 (FIG. 3): "The thickness of the two spherical caps corresponds to 2885 skin depths, which should produce a classical attenuation of −25,064 db (down by a factor of 10⁻¹²⁵³). The test measurement yielded an attenuation between −115 db at r=2 cm separation to −137 db at r=30 cm. … gives −79 db and −86 db (down by a factor of 10⁻⁴). The difference … corresponds to >1249 orders of magnitude between attenuation for classical waves and the measured attenuation for the SLW." FACT, claim 1 (col. 19): "…wherein scalar-longitudinal waves transmitted by the first conductor propagate through a conductive medium with substantially lower attenuation relative to a classical skin-depth attenuation." Claim 9 (coil) and the system claim use the same wording. HYP: the patent claims reduced attenuation ("substantially lower"), not zero. It also frames J·E as energy exchange among C, E and J (Table 1, item 6), not dissipation. Its "0=0" sentence is the same cancellation the Erratum later invokes. 2(e). What the Erratum's conclusion means for a Joule term σE∥² FACT: J·E appears explicitly in Eq. (44) (HL2019 p. 117) and in EQN. 14 (patent). With J = σE it would be σE² (HYP: the substitution J = σE is the patent's col. 6 wording, not Eq. 44's). FACT: Hively does not say J·E = 0, and does not say σE² disappears. He says the "no-loss result occurs from … Eq. (44), by substituting for (ρ/ε) from Eq. (22) and … Jᴸ from Eq. (21) with B = 0, then cancelling terms" (Erratum, p. 320). The patent says "may yield an identity, 0=0" (col. 6). FACT: Eq. (44) itself was built from Eqs. (21), (22) and Faraday's law (p. 117 quote above). So how far does the source show the cancellation? Only in words: "substituting … then cancelling terms". No algebra is shown in the Erratum or the patent. HYP (our algebra, not in any source). This carries out exactly the substitution the Erratum names, using only printed equations. Assumptions: B = 0. μ is constant. 1/c² = εμ. This is implied by the Erratum calling "εμĖᴸ + ∇C + μJᴸ = 0" "Eq. (21) … with ∇ × B = 0". Eq. (21) with B = 0 gives μJ = −εμĖ − ∇C, so J·E = −(ε/2)∂(E²)/∂t − E·∇C/μ. Eq. (22) gives ρC/(εμ) = C(∇·E + ∂C/∂t)/μ. Also, ∇·(CE/μ) = (E·∇C + C∇·E)/μ. Inserting these into Eq. (44): With the energy density written εE²/2 (as in patent EQN. 14 and HL2019 p. 116 text "4πr²(εE²/2)"), every term cancels and Eq. (44) reduces to 0 = 0. This matches the patent's "identity, 0=0". With Eq. (44) exactly as printed (εE²), a residual (ε/2)∂(E²)/∂t = 0 is left over. This is one more sign the printed "εE²" is a typo (also flagged in REDO_SLW.md as ASSUMPTION). Interpretation (HYP). The Joule term is not shown to vanish. It is re-expressed through Eq. (21) as field-energy change −∂(εE²/2)/∂t plus a C-coupling term −E·∇C/μ, which then cancel against the other terms. That is Hively's "C, E, and J exchange energy" picture: conduction work is traded with the E and C fields rather than lost. Caveat (HYP). Eq. (44) was built from Eqs. (21)–(22). Substituting them back must give an identity for any fields that satisfy them. The same happens with the classical Poynting theorem, yet classical TEM waves in conductors do attenuate. So the cancellation alone does not show that σE² heating is absent or replenished. It shows the balance is self-consistent. Where the replenishing energy comes from (the ρC/(εμ) "power source", or the C field) is not quantified in any Hively source. transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis HYP (side note, relevant to the σ/ε typo). Putting Ohm's law Jᴸ = σEᴸ into the Erratum's (A5) gives εμĖ + μσE = −∇C. Its homogeneous part decays as e^(−σt/ε), the slide-60 form. The Erratum itself does not make this substitution. Our α_J is not Hively's. FACT (REDO_SLW.md §1.2, lines 22, 61–77, 112): "Our per-metre Joule attenuation α_J = σ_H|Z|/2 is not in any Hively text. It is our construction …" It needs a magnitude-only impedance substitution, a choice of E∥ and σ, and "deletion of the ρC/(εμ) source term. That source term is the one Hively's Erratum uses to cancel J·E." HYP: α_J is therefore a reading Hively explicitly rejects. It is sensitive to our conventions (186 km ↔ 1.06 cm at 60 Hz under one convention change, REDO_SLW §1.2d). 3. Reconciling Monstein & Wesley with Hively ⚠ Rows/columns in this table that refer to TEM / classical / cage SE: transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis # Point Label 1 M&W attribute a measured extra exponential loss (1/e in power per 145 m, beyond 100 m, 433.59 MHz) to "Ohmic losses produced by the currents induced in the Earth by the longitudinal E⃗ field" (p. 520). Hively says the SLW "is not subject to resistive loss in conductive media" (Erratum p. 320) and gives "lossless propagation in linear conductive media" (IARD slide 60). FACT (both quotes) 2 Taken at face value these conflict, if M&W's wave is Hively's SLW and the Earth is a linear conductive medium in Hively's sense. HYP 3 The clearest direct conflict is the wire polarizer. M&W derive and use a Joule term δP = −[σAE₀²cos²(φ)]δL (Eq. 7) as real dissipation, fitted as T = exp[−4.4cos²φ]. Hively's framework says J·E cancels in the energy balance. FACT (equations); HYP (that the two are in conflict) 4 Hively's own account of the same polarizer result (HL2019 App. D, p. 124): "The signal was strongly attenuated for the dipole-array parallel to the transmitter-receiver direction. No attenuation occurred for an array orientation perpendicular…". He does not say whether he accepts M&W's Ohmic mechanism. FACT; mechanism not stated in source 5 Different geometry. M&W's wave travels through air above the ground (antennas 4.0/4.4 m high). The loss is attributed to currents induced in the Earth, a grazing/near-surface mechanism. Hively's claims concern propagation through conductors (copper Faraday enclosures, 2914 skin depths). FACT (setups); HYP (that they are different mechanisms) 6 Different theories. M&W: a pure scalar-potential Φ wave, E = ∇Φ, energy flux S = −∇Φ ∂Φ/∂t (Eqs. 1–2), with "∇ · J⃗ = 0" inside the ball (p. 515) and no C field. Hively: EED with a dynamical C, B = 0, a gradient-driven Jᴸ = ∇κ (HL2019 p. 116) and SLW energy flux CE/μ (Eq. 44). FACT 7 Because of point 6, M&W's "scalar wave" and Hively's "SLW" may not be the same object. M&W's divergenceless source current contrasts with Hively's gradient-driven current. So a loss claim for one does not automatically transfer to the other. HYP 8 Measured vs derived. M&W's ground loss is empirical and "probably" Ohmic, with no formula and no σ used. Hively's "no loss" is derived (A6 plus the Eq. 44 cancellation), while his own measurements say "low-loss" (p. 121) and "substantially lower attenuation" (patent claim 1), and call conductive-media attenuation "future work" (p. 120). FACT 9 Neither source gives a validated per-metre SLW Joule attenuation formula. M&W's Eq. (8) rate σ/c is for wires and was not used quantitatively (κ was fitted). Hively gives none. FACT (absence); HYP (that Eq. 8 was not a quantitative check) 10 Hively's critique of the M&W setup (HL2019 App. D, p. 124): "The outer conductor of the coaxial cable was grounded, inducing unquantified electrical ground currents. … These tests were poorly controlled, and not reproducible." Also: "TMW and the Butterworth omitted the image current, leading to poor agreement between the test results and the models." FACT 11 Classical return or ground currents (point 10) and TEM ground-wave loss could explain some or all of M&W's excess loss beyond 100 m without any SLW Joule loss. Hively does not make this argument explicitly. HYP; not stated in source 12 Hively's only stated loss mechanism is nonlinear σ = σ(|E|) (IARD slide 61). M&W do not discuss nonlinear σ. Whether moist ground at 433 MHz is "nonlinear" in Hively's sense is not addressed by either. FACT (slide 61; M&W silence); HYP (relevance) 13 For our modelling: M&W's 1/e-per-145 m is an over-ground, 433.59 MHz, single-site empirical number, not a σE∥² law. It cannot be transferred to seawater, hull steel or other frequencies without an assumed mechanism. Converting it to α_P ≈ 6.9×10⁻³ m⁻¹ (≈ 0.030 dB/m) is our arithmetic. HYP Blockers and what would clear them Erratum Phys. Essays 32(3), 417 (30 Sep 2019) (DOI 10.4006/0836-1398-32.3.417; the one the hub library links) is unread. text: Simulation Lab · loss-mode comparison · loss-modes-v0.1 · 2026-09-30 Three readings of SLW loss: Joule-literal, Erratum α = 0, and charge relaxation Dan asked whether the Joule term is being used properly. Some Hively texts say a scalar-longitudinal wave (SLW) has no loss in conducting media. Monstein & Wesley (2002) report an ohmic-like loss with distance. This page puts three clearly labelled readings side by side, using the hub's existing model code, and says what Monstein & Wesley's numbers can and cannot tell apart. MIXED FACT = from a paper, patent or erratum (equation and page given). HYP = Hively's SLW hypothesis or our inference. ASSUMPTION = a modelling choice made on this page. ← Simulation Lab catalogue · Equation source and meaning map · Joule-loss positions · Corrections log Framing rules on this page (Dan). Under the SLW hypothesis there is no skin-depth, permeability or ferromagnetic argument anywhere below. Allowed loss terms: Hively's Joule term σE∥² (Hively & Loebl 2019 Eq. 44 as corrected by the 2019 erratum), or none (the 2022 Erratum's "not subject to resistive loss"). Any classical transverse-EM reasoning is tagged transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis. Nobody has been contacted about any of this. The 2019 erratum PDF is private: its equations are cited, the PDF is not embedded or linked. 1. The three modes, defined Mode What it says about the wave Where it comes from Status A: Joule-literal The field loses energy through the Joule term σE∥². The field falls as exp(−αJ r) and the power as exp(−2 αJ r), on top of the 1/r² spreading. αJ = σH|Z|/2, with σH = ε₀ε″ω and |Z| the far-field SLW impedance. The J·E term is in Hively & Loebl 2019 Eq. 44 (p. 117) and patent EQN. 14. σ = ε₀ε″ω is in the text after Eq. 36 (p. 116) and |Z| is Eq. 37 (p. 116). The per-metre αJ is not in any Hively text: it is the hub's construction, copied unchanged from alphaJ() in the /slw-rcs/ page (same as Experiment G and sleeve-balun-snr v0.3). FACT for Eq. 44, Eq. 36 text and Eq. 37 as printed. ASSUMPTION (ours) for αJ: a magnitude-only |Z|, a choice of E∥, and dropping the source term ρC/(εμ) that the Erratum uses to cancel J·E. B: Erratum α = 0 No propagation loss at all: α = 0, so only 1/r² spreading. Hively & Loebl, Erratum, Phys. Essays 35(3) 320 (2022), p. 320: "the SLW is not subject to resistive loss in conductive media". The same conclusion is in 2019 App. A (A7), p. 122 ("propagates without loss"), and IARD 2020 slide 60 ("lossless propagation in linear conductive media"). FACT that the sources say this. HYP that it is physically right. C: charge relaxation only The wave itself is not attenuated (its curve equals Mode B). Free charge in the medium relaxes as E = E₀ exp(−σt/ε), with relaxation time τ = ε/σ. Dr. Hively's private confirmation to Dan, 2026-09-30: "The form, E = E0 e^(-sigma t/epsilon), is the correct one." Printed forms in 2019 Eq. (A5), p. 122, and patent US 9,306,527 col. 5 have ε and σ swapped (typo). IARD 2020 slide 60 is correct. See the corrections log. FACT for the exponent and τ (author-confirmed). HYP for how it maps onto a received signal: undetermined (section 4). 2. Predicted signal versus distance under each mode Pick a medium, a frequency and a distance range. Every curve includes the same 1/x² spreading of a spherical wave (power, dB relative to 1 m). ASSUMPTION (ours) The spreading law and the use of one α for the whole path are conventions of the hub's model, not results from a source. The 1/r² fall-off itself is Hively & Loebl 2019 p. 117 (energy 4πr²·C²/2μ constant) and Monstein & Wesley Eq. 6. Medium Frequency σ (S/m) ε′ (relative, real part) Plot from (m) Plot to (m) Table distances (m) Mode A Joule-literal Mode B Erratum α = 0 Mode C (HYP) wave curve = B, dashed What each mode predicts at the table distances distance (m) spreading only (dB re 1 m) Mode A (dB re 1 m) Mode B (dB re 1 m) Mode C wave (dB re 1 m) crossing time t = d/v (s) ASSUMPTION t ÷ τ Power in dB relative to the value at 1 m, received power ∝ 1/d² × exp(−2αJd) for Mode A. The crossing time uses v = c/√ε′, a plane-wave speed in the medium that we assume only to give the last two columns a scale; it is not a prediction of the SLW speed. "t ÷ τ" is the exponent that exp(−σt/ε) would have at that t. It is shown because it follows directly from τ = ε/σ, not because Mode C applies it to the wave (section 4). Seawater and fresh-water ε and σ come from the Meissner & Wentz 2004 code the hub already uses; the ground and custom values are editable ASSUMPTIONS (section 6). Load the Rhine case: air, 433.59 MHz, 10 to 1000 m In air all three modes coincide (σ ≈ 0), which is the point of section 5. 3. What follows directly: τ = ε/σ for each medium FACT (author-confirmed exponent) E = E₀ exp(−σt/ε), τ = ε/σ, with ε = ε₀εr. τ/period = τ·f tells you how many relaxation times fit in one wave cycle: if it is much less than 1, free charge relaxes many times per cycle; if it is much greater than 1, charge hardly moves during a cycle. "Distance in τ" is how far the assumed plane-wave speed v = c/√ε′ would carry a signal in one τ (ASSUMPTION). εr here is the static value (MW2004 εs for the water rows), evaluated at 433.59 MHz for seawater and fresh water. Medium σ (S/m) εr τ = ε/σ (s) τ ÷ period at 433.59 MHz at 1296 MHz at 2450 MHz v·τ (m) The 2019 paper states a copper transient of ∼10⁻¹⁹ s beside Eq. (A5) (p. 122); the copper row agrees in order of magnitude. The water and ground σ and εr are representative values, not from any SLW source (section 6). Brass ε is taken as ε₀ (ASSUMPTION). Air has σ ≈ 0, so τ is unbounded and the transient does nothing. 4. How Mode C enters a received-signal prediction: it cannot be made without inventing physics Mode C, stated minimally FACT Hively & Loebl 2019 (A4)–(A7), p. 122: the transient solution Ė + σE/ε = 0 decays as exp(−σt/ε) (correct form per the author). The same appendix then sets the transient aside and takes the non-transient solution E = E₀(r) e^(−jωt), □²E = 0, for which "the SLW propagates without loss" (A7). IARD 2020 slide 60 says the same in the same order. The 2022 Erratum drops the transient altogether. HYP Mode C keeps that split: the propagating wave is not attenuated (curve identical to Mode B), and the transient describes what free charge does in time. ASSUMPTION Nothing in any source we have turns the transient into a factor on the received signal. The exponent is in time t after a disturbance of the free charge. A received signal at distance d involves a travel time, not a waiting time after a step, and no source says that t = d/v, or any other t, belongs in that exponent. FACT (arithmetic) If one did put t = d/v into exp(−σt/ε), the exponent would be the "t ÷ τ" column of the table in section 2. It would be huge in seawater at any distance beyond a few millimetres (v·τ ≈ 5.3 mm in the table) and would equal an attenuation constant σ/(ε₀ c √ε′). That would be a propagation loss, which is what Mode C says is absent, so we do not do it. What is undetermined Which time t, if any, enters the received signal (source-side, travel time, detector integration time). Whether the relaxation acts on the amplitude of E, on C, or only on stored free charge. Whether the receiver sees the relaxing charge at all (M&W and Hively both use a ball or monopole receiver that responds to induced charge, but no source gives the transfer function). Whether "linear" σ (Hively slide 60) still holds in a real medium at these frequencies (slide 61 gives a loss mechanism only for nonlinear σ(|E|)). So in this page Mode C's predicted signal is the Mode B curve, and what differs is only the τ table above. This is deliberate. A number that came from a guessed mapping would look like a prediction and would not be one. 5. The Monstein & Wesley Rhine geometry Everything in this section is read from M&W, Europhys. Lett. 59(4) 514 (2002), pp. 517–520, and agrees with the hub /ranging/ page. FACT 433.59 MHz (λ = 0.6914 m). Source ball at 4.0 m, receiver ball at 4.4 m physical height. Effective heights y = 4.346 m and y′ = 4.746 m (Eq. 12; the effective reflecting plane is λ/2 = 34.6 cm below the ground). The path is through air along a street on the bank of the Rhine near Sennwald, Switzerland (p. 518). They give the Earth's conductivity as "only about 10⁻³ S/m" and use it only to place that reflecting plane (p. 517). FACT Signal model Eq. (14) with direct and image amplitudes A and B, R² = (y′−y)² + x², R′² = (y′+y)² + x² (Eq. 11). Nulls at R′ − R = (2n+1)λ/2 (Eq. 17). Table I: predicted minima at 119, 39, 23 and 16 m; observed at 39 m and 23 m; the other two "probably exist" but are not definite (noise and ±5 m GPS uncertainty), p. 519. FACT Fitted: √(ωk/2)·A = 0.825 and √(ωk/2)·B = 0.573 (Eq. 22); ℜ = B²/A² = 0.482 (Eq. 24). Agreement with Eq. (14) is "quite satisfactory for x < 100 m". FACT p. 520: beyond about 100 m the signal falls faster than 1/x². "This loss corresponds to an additional exponential loss with distance corresponding to 1/eth decrease in the signal for a distance of 145 m. This loss is probably due to the Ohmic losses produced by the currents induced in the Earth by the longitudinal E field, which is parallel to the Earth's surface." No equation and no σ is given for this loss, and the "signal" is the energy flux (p. 517). FACT Fig. 5 (received power in dB versus distance, 10–1000 m) is a graph: one of six runs (V1) as dots, plus the Eq. (14) line. No numeric data points from Fig. 5 are recorded in the hub or in our notes, so none are plotted here. Rhine plot: M&W's own model, in air Gold: Eq. (14) with the Eq. (22) amplitudes, relative to x = 10 m. ASSUMPTION M&W state that Eqs. 20–21 are relative to the value at x = 10 m; we read the same normalisation for Eq. 14. Salmon: the same with their reported extra 1/e-in-power per 145 m applied beyond 100 m (our arithmetic: −10·log₁₀(e)·(x−100)/145 dB; the onset at exactly 100 m is our reading of "beyond 100 m"). Grey dotted: 1/x² only. Green vertical lines: the two nulls M&W observed (39 m, 23 m). Optional orange dotted: a Mode A ground what-if (HYP, below). Ground σ for the what-if (S/m) Ground ε′ for the what-if show the Mode A ground what-if on the plot gold M&W Eq. 14 (Eq. 22 A, B)salmon Eq. 14 + reported 145 m e-fold beyond 100 mgrey dotted 1/x² onlygreen observed nulls 39 m, 23 morange dotted Mode A ground what-if (optional) What each mode predicts at the Rhine distances (path in air, σ ≈ 0) x (m) M&W Eq. 14 (dB re 10 m) 1/x² only (dB re 10 m) image/multipath term (dB) M&W reported extra loss (dB) Mode A / B / C extra loss in air (dB) Mode A ground what-if (dB) "Mode A / B / C extra loss in air" is 0 for all three: with σ ≈ 0 the Joule term σE∥² is zero, Mode B has no loss, and Mode C has no relaxation (τ unbounded). The last column applies Mode A's αJ for the ground values you set above, over the path from 10 m to x, to the wave itself. M&W's wave is in air, so this is not what the Joule-literal reading says about their path; it is shown only to size the mismatch. Eq. 18 nulls recomputed from y and y′ with this page's code (m): (M&W Table I: 119, 39, 23, 16). Can M&W's data tell these readings apart? Short answer: no. The numbers say why. The Rhine path is through air, where σ ≈ 0. With σ ≈ 0 the Joule term is zero (Mode A), Mode B has no loss, and Mode C has no relaxation. All three give the same curve at every Rhine distance (0.00 dB apart in the table above). No quality of data could separate them on that path. FACT (path and medium from M&W p. 518) plus arithmetic. Do the path length and 1/x² spreading alone reproduce the observed distance dependence? Not beyond about 100 m, by M&W's own account. Their model (Eq. 14, the image-source term plus spreading) matches "quite satisfactorily" for x < 100 m, including nulls at 39 m and 23 m. Past 100 m they needed an extra factor of 1/e in power per 145 m. With our arithmetic that extra factor is only −0.57 dB at 119 m, but −5.99 dB at 300 m and −26.96 dB at 1000 m. FACT (their statements) HYP (our dB arithmetic). Butterworth et al. 2013 (J. Sci. Explor. 27(1) 13) describe M&W's data as "a long tail-off that roughly approximates an inverse-square relation until about 200 m which then falls off more rapidly", so even the onset distance is reported as 100 m by one source and 200 m by another. Is that extra loss a Mode A Joule loss? Not determinable. M&W give no σ and no equation for it (they say it is "probably" Ohmic loss from currents induced in the Earth). Taking the hub's Joule-literal construction and our representative ground (σ = 10⁻³ S/m, ε′ = 15, an ASSUMPTION, using M&W's own σ ≈ 10⁻³ S/m) gives a power e-fold length of about 10.28 m, about 14.1 times stronger than the reported 145 m. To get 145 m the construction needs an effective σ of about 7.09×10⁻⁵ S/m. That is a free parameter: one adjustable σ can be made to fit one number, so a fit would not be a test. ASSUMPTION (ground values, and applying αJ to a ground path at all) and the construction αJ is ours, not Hively's (section 1). Mode C has no received-signal prediction to compare (section 4). Other explanations are open. Hively & Loebl 2019 App. D, p. 124, say M&W's outer coaxial conductor was grounded ("inducing unquantified electrical ground currents"), that the tests were "poorly controlled, and not reproducible", and that M&W omitted the image current. Whether the excess loss is SLW Joule loss, classical ground loss, or set-up effects cannot be separated from what is recorded. What is missing for any real discrimination: (a) the raw Fig. 5 data points (the paper shows a graph only); (b) an effective ground σ and ε and a path geometry for the current induced in the ground, from any source; (c) a stated mapping from Mode C's relaxation to a received signal; (d) runs in a medium with large σ at a known distance, where Modes A, B and C actually differ (for seawater Mode A predicts about 313 dB/m of power loss at 433.59 MHz; B and C predict none). The wire-polarizer result (M&W Eqs. 7–9, κ = 4.4 fitted) is a separate Joule-type loss in brass and is not used here. What this page does NOT show It does not show that the SLW exists, that any of the three modes is true, or that Hively's or M&W's claims are right or wrong. It does not show what Dr. Hively thinks about Mode A or Mode C. Nobody has been contacted. The only author statement used is the single sentence quoted for the relaxation exponent. Mode A's αJ is the hub's construction, not a formula from any Hively text, and it depends on conventions (magnitude-only |Z|, choice of E∥, the dropped ρC/(εμ) source). The hub's own notes show another reasonable convention changes it by orders of magnitude at low frequency (Joule-loss positions; REDO_SLW §1.2). Mode C's curve is Mode B's. The page does not claim charge relaxation has no effect on a received signal, only that no source gives how it would enter. No measured Rhine data points are plotted, because none are recorded. The gold and salmon curves are M&W's own model, not their data. Ground and fresh-water σ and ε are representative values (section 6), not measurements of the Rhine bank. It does not use any skin-depth, permeability or ferromagnetic argument. The reasoning stays inside Hively's own Eq. 37, Eq. 44 and the Erratum. Classical transverse-EM numbers are not computed here. If you compare with them elsewhere, label them transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis. 6. Sources, values and provenance Mode A code. alphaJ(ep, epp, f) is copied unchanged from /slw-rcs/ (and from Experiment G, sleeve-balun-snr v0.3): αJ = ε₀ε″ω·|Z|/2 with |Z| = η₀/√ε′/√(1+tan²δ). Constants: c = 299 792 458 m/s, ε₀ = 8.8541878128×10⁻¹² F/m, μ₀ = 1.25663706212×10⁻⁶ H/m, η₀ = μ₀c. For the ground and custom media ε″ = σ/(ωε₀) (so σH = σ, dc conduction only); for seawater and fresh water the MW2004 dipolar part is added, as on /slw-rcs/. Seawater. Meissner & Wentz, IEEE TGRS 42(9) 1836 (2004), Eqs. 6–8, 11–17, 15 °C and 35 ppt, the same code the hub already uses. The user's rule of thumb "εr ≈ 80, σ ≈ 4 S/m" is close; the model gives σ = 4.291353 S/m and ε′ = 73.27 at 433.59 MHz. Fresh water, wet ground, dry ground. No hub values existed. Representative values (ASSUMPTION, editable): fresh water σ = 0.003 S/m with the MW2004 pure-water permittivity; wet ground ε′ = 30, σ = 0.01 S/m; medium-dry ground ε′ = 15, σ = 0.001 S/m. These follow the typical-values figure of ITU-R P.527-6 (Fig. 24) and P.527-3, which are given for ground-wave work below 30 MHz and vary at UHF (P.527-3 §2: "approximate range of values"). They are not from an SLW source. Brass and copper. Brass σ = 1.5080260×10⁷ S/m (hub rod-thermal numbers.json, from copper.org), copper 5.8×10⁷ S/m. Verification. Every number on this page was recomputed in independent Python and compared with this page's JavaScript to 6 significant figures (/workspace/sim-lab/loss-modes/xcheck_loss_modes.py; result in the ledger). Publication status. Analysis page, version loss-modes-v0.1. GitHub-only: No Wolfram Cloud twin planned (Wolfram blocked by Dan's decision). Equation sources, symbol meanings and their status are listed in the equation source and meaning map. Paper library: library.

Plan only; no SLW source strength is known. Under the SLW hypothesis no skin-depth, permeability, ferromagnetic or cage shielding-effectiveness argument is used to rank or dismiss SLW/SW. The Faraday cage strips TEM noise (FACT); an SLW passing the cage wall is HYP. Every passage that uses transverse-EM (TEM / classical / cage-SE) reasoning is tagged transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis. FACT / HYP / ASSUMPTION labels are kept exactly as in the source. Downloads nearfield_numbers.json openems_compare.json Workstream: Simulation Lab (Dan Britton) · Written: 2026-09-27 (ET) · Status: PLAN ONLY. No web page has been built, no Cloud twin exists, and nothing has been published or sent. Numbers: all come from nearfield_numbers.py → nearfield_numbers.json and openems_dipole_ratio.py → openems_compare.json, in this folder. They were computed in Python only; the Wolfram Language (WL) compare is OWED. How to read the labels Label Meaning FACT Established result with a citation. Textbook electromagnetics is FACT for transverse (TEM) and classical fields only; it is not established for SLW/SW. HYP A hypothesis being tested (Hively's SLW/SW framework, Dan's HYP). ASSUMPTION A value we chose or guessed, which Dan should check on the real oven. transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis This tag marks classical reasoning wherever it touches on SLW behaviour. 0. The question, and where it came from Source (verbal only): Hively, personal communication to D. Britton, verbal, reported by Dan, 2026-09. There is no written record. What was reported: the near field of any TEM source inherently contains longitudinal components, so SLW/SW detectors must sit well outside the near field. Otherwise a near-field longitudinal component could be mistaken for a distant SLW/SW. transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis HYP (Dan): anything that generates a transverse wave also generates an SLW, and possibly an SW. The two questions this plan answers: Does the near field of a 2.45 GHz oven magnetron (and of the oven's leakage points) contain a measurable longitudinal E alongside the transverse E? How far away must the SLW/SW detectors be so they can't confuse that ordinary near-field longitudinal E with a distant SLW/SW? Short answers FACT (classical): yes, very close to any source. Inside the oven it is everywhere. Outside it, the longitudinal share dies off quickly with distance. Recommendation: put the receiver at least 3 × 2D²/λ ≈ 10–12 m (≈ 100 λ) from the oven door, sealed inside Dan's Faraday cage. The absolute minimum is ≈ 4 m (1 × 2D²/λ for a 0.5 m door, ≈ 32 λ). 1. (a) Near-field boundaries at 2.45 GHz 1.1 Basic numbers FACT: λ = c/f = 0.1224 m (12.24 cm) at 2.45 GHz. The LG 2M246 magnetron datasheet gives 2460 MHz into a matched load. That makes a < 0.5 % difference, so it's ignored here. FACT (Balanis, Antenna Theory, 3rd ed., §4.2; Wheeler's "radian sphere"): for an electrically small source, the reactive near field is dominant inside r ≈ λ/2π = 1.95 cm (kr = 1). FACT (Balanis 3e §2.2.4; IEEE Std 145-2013, definitions of field regions): for a radiator of largest dimension D, where D is comparable to or larger than λ: the reactive near field extends to R1 = 0.62 √(D³/λ); the radiating near field (Fresnel region) runs from R1 to R2 = 2D²/λ; beyond R2 is the far field (Fraunhofer region). FACT (Balanis §2.2.4): for D ≪ λ, these D-based formulas give distances shorter than λ, and so they don't apply. The far field then requires r ≫ λ (in practice several λ). 1.2 Boundary table Source D (m) Label on D λ/2π R1 = 0.62√(D³/λ) R2 = 2D²/λ What governs (i) Magnetron antenna cap, inside the waveguide launcher 0.02 ASSUMPTION (cap ≈ 1.5–2 cm) 1.95 cm (0.5 cm) (0.65 cm) Electrically small (0.16 λ): λ/2π. But it sits inside a metal waveguide, so free-space regions do not apply at all (FACT). (ii) Oven cavity — — — — — FACT: a closed metal resonant cavity is entirely a standing-wave / "near-field" region. No far field exists inside it (Pozar 4e §6.3; Harrington 1961 §6-9, cavity modes). (iii-a) Door seam / choke gap, D = door diagonal 0.40 ASSUMPTION — 0.45 m 2.62 m Balanis §2.2.4 (D = 3.3 λ) (iii-a) Door seam / choke gap 0.45 ASSUMPTION — 0.54 m 3.31 m Balanis §2.2.4 (iii-a) Door seam / choke gap 0.50 ASSUMPTION — 0.63 m 4.09 m Balanis §2.2.4 (iii-b) Vent / mesh patch 0.05 ASSUMPTION 1.95 cm 2.0 cm 4.1 cm Electrically small: λ/2π; far field needs r ≫ λ (iii-b) Vent / mesh patch 0.10 ASSUMPTION 1.95 cm 5.6 cm 16.3 cm Borderline (0.8 λ); treat the far field as r ≳ several λ ASSUMPTION: treating the whole door diagonal as "the antenna" is the conservative worst case. Leakage comes from along the seam, so the largest possible D is the full seam extent. Action: Dan should measure his oven's door diagonal and re-run nearfield_numbers.py with the real value. ASSUMPTION: the vent is a perforated patch. Its holes are far below cutoff, so any leakage acts like a small source. 1.3 Classical longitudinal fields that exist for sure (FACT, and distinct from SLW) These are ordinary, textbook longitudinal (along-the-propagation-direction) field components. They are not Hively's SLW. The SLW is a HYP. The point of this plan is to keep the two from being confused. TE10 launcher waveguide (FACT, Pozar 4e §3.3): the TE10 mode has transverse E_y only. It has no longitudinal E, but it does have a longitudinal magnetic field H_z, alongside H_x. Computed for WR-340 (ASSUMPTION: oven launchers are close to, but not always exactly, WR-340, a = 86.36 mm): TE10 cutoff = 1.736 GHz; guide wavelength λg = 17.3 cm; peak |H_z| / |H_x| = 1.004 (≈ 0 dB). The longitudinal H is as large as the transverse H. FACT (Pozar 4e §4.7, probe excitation): longitudinal E appears only in the evanescent higher-order modes right around the magnetron's antenna probe. These decay within a fraction of a guide width. Cavity (FACT, Pozar 4e §6.3; Harrington 1961 §6-9): TM modes have a nonzero E_z, and TE modes have a nonzero H_z. A multimode oven cavity has field components along every axis. "Longitudinal" has no single meaning inside it. Small radiators, i.e. leaks near seams, slots and vents (FACT, Balanis 3e Eqs. 4-10a, 4-10b; Jackson 3e §9.2): the Hertzian (infinitesimal) dipole has a radial (longitudinal) E_r, which contains only the 1/r² and 1/r³ terms. The transverse E_θ also has a 1/r term, and that term is the one that radiates. So far from the source, E_r / E_θ → 0 (it falls as 2/kr, from the ratio of Eqs. 4-10a/4-10b). Close in, E_r dominates. 1.4 How big is the classical longitudinal E vs distance? (Balanis Eqs. 4-10a/b, computed) The ratio shown is the peak-to-peak magnitude ratio, |E_r| on the axis (θ = 0) divided by |E_θ| broadside (θ = 90°). The same ratio holds at θ = 45°. kr r r/λ |E_r|/|E_θ| dB 0.1 0.19 cm 0.016 2.02 +6.1 1 1.95 cm 0.16 2.83 +9.0 2 3.9 cm 0.32 1.24 +1.9 3 5.8 cm 0.48 0.74 −2.6 5 9.7 cm 0.80 0.42 −7.6 10 19.5 cm 1.6 0.20 −13.9 20 39 cm 3.2 0.100 −20.0 50 97 cm 8.0 0.040 −28.0 100 1.95 m 15.9 0.020 −34.0 300 5.84 m 47.7 0.0067 −43.5 1000 19.5 m 159 0.0020 −54.0 FACT (computed from the cited equations): the classical longitudinal share is −20 dB at 0.39 m (3.2 λ), −30 dB at 1.23 m (10 λ), −40 dB at 3.9 m (32 λ), about −50 dB at ≈ 12 m. Caveat (ASSUMPTION): a door seam 3–4 λ long is not a Hertzian dipole. For it, the Balanis §2.2.4 region distances (1.2) are the governing limits. The dipole table describes each small local leak point. Answer to question 1: FACT (classical): yes. A measurable longitudinal E exists within a few centimetres of any leak point (E_r ≥ E_θ for r ≲ 4 cm), and inside the launcher and cavity. Whether it is measurable outside the oven depends on the leak level. A legal oven leaks ≤ 5 mW/cm² at 5 cm (21 CFR 1030.10(c)(1)), and usually far less. That is easily detectable with a small probe at 5–20 cm (see Phase 1). 2. (b) Simulation approach (Wolfram Mathematica / Wolfram Cloud) Status: SPEC ONLY. Cloud publishing is BLOCKED (WOLFRAM_SAK unset; Dan's Mac is in storage; there is no wolframscript on the shared computer). The WL notebook is to be written and run when Mathematica is available. 2.1 WL-1: analytic Hertzian-dipole decomposition (textbook closed form) Inputs: f = 2.45 GHz and kr from 0.1 to 1000 (log-spaced). Fields: use Balanis 3e Eq. 4-10a (E_r) and Eq. 4-10b (E_θ) exactly as printed. Drop the common factor ηI₀l/(4π), which cancels in the ratio. Plot 1: 20·log10(|E_r(θ=0)| / |E_θ(θ=90°)|) vs r (log axis, in cm and in λ). Mark vertical lines at λ/2π, λ, R1 and R2 for D = 0.40/0.45/0.50 m, 3 × R2, and the −20/−30/−40 dB crossings. Plot 2: the same ratio at θ = 45° (it is identical, as a check). Pass criterion for the WL vs Python compare: every row of the table in §1.4 agrees to ≤ 0.01 dB, and the boundary table in §1.2 agrees to ≤ 1 mm. 2.2 WL-2: NDSolve / NDEigensystem FEM options (classical checks) Cavity eigenmodes: Use a rectangular box. ASSUMPTION: typical interior ≈ 0.33 × 0.33 × 0.22 m; Dan should measure his. Solve the scalar Helmholtz problem for TM modes (E_z with Dirichlet walls) with NDEigensystem on a 2D cross-section. Compare the eigenfrequencies with the closed-form rectangular-cavity resonances (Pozar 4e §6.3). Plot |E_z| for the modes nearest 2.45 GHz. This shows (FACT) that the cavity field is a standing wave with a longitudinal E. TE10 launcher (WR-340 cross-section): Plot the analytic TE10 field components from Pozar §3.3: E_y, H_x, H_z. Optionally, use NDEigensystem on the 2D cross-section to confirm the cut-off of 1.736 GHz. Readout: peak |H_z|/|H_x| = 1.004 (0.03 dB) at 2.45 GHz. Optional (only if a full-wave solver is available in WL, heavy): Model a slot in a conducting plane at 2.45 GHz and extract E along a line normal to the slot. Otherwise, use openEMS (§4). It already covers this job on the shared computer. What to plot, overall: the longitudinal-to-transverse ratio in dB vs distance, with the region boundaries overlaid. Each plot carries a FACT (classical TEM) label. transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis 2.3 GitHub Pages JS twin: specification only (do NOT build or publish now) Title: "Magnetron near-field: longitudinal vs transverse (classical) — test-plan companion". Controls: distance slider r, 0.5 cm → 30 m (log); source-size slider D, 1 cm → 0.6 m, defaulting to 0.45 m; frequency fixed at 2.45 GHz (with an optional 2.46 GHz toggle). Readouts: λ, λ/2π, R1, R2 and 3 × R2 for the chosen D; which region r is in (reactive near / radiating near / far; "inside a waveguide or cavity: not applicable" for the cap and cavity presets); the Hertzian ratio |E_r|/|E_θ|, as a number and in dB; r in units of λ and of R2. Plot: the ratio (dB) vs r with the boundary lines, plus a marker at the current slider value and the recommended detector zone shaded. Labels: every readout is tagged FACT (classical TEM; Balanis Eqs. 4-10a/b, §2.2.4), ASSUMPTION (D presets) or HYP. transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis Banner: "Cloud twin pending sync. Wolfram Cloud publishing is blocked; numbers are from Python (nearfield_numbers.json) and are not yet cross-checked against WL." HYP toggle: "Show SLW component (Hively framework)". When it is switched on, it shows this exact text and draws no curve: HYP — not computed. Hively's framework (Hively & Loebl 2019; US 9,306,527) predicts a scalar longitudinal wave, but no cited source gives a near-field SLW source strength (or near-field SLW field law) for a magnetron, an oven cavity or a door seam. Therefore this page computes no SLW value. The curves shown are classical TEM near-field components only; they are not SLW. transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis Compares owed once it is built: JS vs WL and JS vs Python (same pass criteria as §2.1). 3. (c) Test procedure and detector placement 3.0 Safety (all phases) FACT: 21 CFR 1030.10(c)(1) limits oven leakage to ≤ 1 mW/cm² at ≥ 5 cm before purchase and ≤ 5 mW/cm² thereafter. §1030.10(c)(2) requires at least two operational interlocks. FACT: 47 CFR 1.1310 Table 1 sets MPE limits for 1.5–100 GHz of 1.0 mW/cm² (general population) and 5 mW/cm² (occupational). Rules: The magnetron stays inside the intact, interlocked, unmodified oven. Never remove it, never run it outside the oven, never defeat an interlock, and never open the case. FACT (LG service manual LSMC3089BD): the high-voltage circuit is "nearly 4000 volts". The LG 2M246 anode runs at 4.40 kVp. Always run with a water load (e.g. 1 L of water in a microwave-safe container). Running empty damages the magnetron. Keep each run short (≤ 2 min) and change the water when it gets hot. Check the oven with a leakage meter before Phase 1. If it reads above 1 mW/cm² at 5 cm, stop and don't use that oven. People stay ≥ 1 m from the oven during runs, except when placing the Phase 1 probe with the oven OFF. 3.1 Phase 1 (classical, outside the cage): show the near-field longitudinal E exists, and map how fast it dies Purpose: to measure the ordinary, classical longitudinal component that Hively warned about. This gives the "confusion zone" a real, measured size. Probe: a short electric probe or small dipole (e.g. Tekbox E-field probe, or a DD-2450 cut short) feeding a TinySA on battery. This phase is outside the cage, so a coax is allowed. Pointing (at each distance): (A) radial: probe axis pointing at the leak point, which senses the longitudinal E; (B) transverse, horizontal; (C) transverse, vertical. Distances from the hottest seam point (found with the leakage meter): 5, 7, 10, 14, 20, 28, 40, 56, 80 cm and 1.1 m (steps of √2). Stop wherever the signal hits the TinySA floor. Expected (FACT, classical, Balanis Eqs. 4-10a/b, for a small leak): A/(B or C) ≈ 0 dB near 5 cm, falling to about −14 dB by 20 cm and −20 dB by 40 cm. The total level should drop about 12–18 dB per doubling inside ~λ, i.e. 1/r²–1/r³ behaviour, and about 6 dB per doubling beyond a few λ (1/r). ASSUMPTION: a real seam isn't a point dipole, so expect scatter. The trend is what matters. 3.2 Phase 2 (SLW/SW search): the receiver inside the sealed cage, far away Where the receiver goes Main position: ≥ 3 × 2D²/λ from the door face. Door diagonal D 3 × 2D²/λ In wavelengths 0.40 m 7.9 m 64 λ 0.45 m 9.9 m 81 λ 0.50 m (use as the default) 12.3 m 100 λ Recommendation: 10–12 m (≈ 100 λ). Here the classical longitudinal ratio of a small leak is ≈ −50 dB (FACT, from Eqs. 4-10a/b), and the door is 3 × deep into its far field (FACT, Balanis §2.2.4). Minimum (if space doesn't allow the main position): ≥ 4.1 m (1 × 2D²/λ for D = 0.5 m; ≈ 33 λ; classical ratio ≈ −40 dB). Report any result taken there as "minimum-distance". Oven orientation: the door faces the cage, because the door is the dominant external leak source. The cavity walls are solid metal, so leakage escapes mainly at the door seam and vents (ASSUMPTION: typical construction; Phase 1 leakage-meter survey confirms it for Dan's oven). Do a second set with the oven rotated 90° (see the controls). Detector and cage The receiver is a DD-2450 Dipole Detector plus a battery-powered receiver/logger (e.g. TinySA on battery), sealed inside Dan's Faraday cage. FACT (classical): the cage strips TEM. HYP: whether SLW passes the cage wall. transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis Do not use cage shielding numbers to predict or rank SLW/SW. Under the SLW hypothesis, the only material interaction is the Hively Joule term, J = σE (Hively & Loebl 2019, Eq. 44). transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis No cable crosses the cage wall. Power is a battery inside. Data comes out optically through a waveguide-below-cutoff tube, or is read after opening the cage. Detector orientation: measure three orientations: L: dipole axis along the line to the oven, i.e. longitudinal. HYP: this is where an SLW would couple, per Hively's longitudinal-E picture. T1 and T2: transverse. Measurement Frequency: 2.40–2.50 GHz; watch 2.45–2.46 GHz. ASSUMPTION: a transformer-type oven with a half-wave voltage doubler fires the magnetron in bursts at the mains rate (60 Hz). That on/off pattern is a signature the logger can look for. Inverter ovens differ; Dan should check which type his is. 3.3 Controls (each run is logged on a sheet) ⚠ Rows/columns in this table that refer to TEM / classical / cage SE: transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis # Control What it rules out Pass (for a candidate SLW/SW signal) C1 Oven OFF (plugged in, door shut) Background, receiver spurs, local Wi-Fi/Bluetooth at 2.4 GHz No 2.45 GHz signal. Record the floor. C2 Oven ON with a water load — (this is the test condition) Signal above the C1 floor, time-locked to oven on/off (and to the mains-rate burst pattern, if present) C3 Rotate the detector L → T1 → T2 Leaked TEM, which is transverse and polarization-dependent Record all three. HYP: an SLW favours L. A TEM leak favours T1/T2. C4 Distance sweep: e.g. 4.1, 5.8, 8.2, 11.6 m (steps of √2), cage moved each time Near-field contamination Fit the level vs r. 1/r (≈ 6 dB per doubling) = radiating; 1/r² (12 dB) or 1/r³ (18 dB) = near-field contamination → move farther. C5 Outside leakage monitor quiet: a second probe/receiver just outside the cage wall, plus a check at the oven Cage leaks; an oven fault The outside monitor near the cage stays at its floor, or its level is recorded. The oven stays ≤ 1 mW/cm² at 5 cm. C6 Dummy detector: DD-2450 replaced by a 50 Ω termination, cage sealed Pickup in the receiver itself, not the antenna No signal C7 Cage-open positive control (classical): cage door opened, oven ON Proves the receiver can see 2.45 GHz TEM at this distance Clear TEM signal (this calibrates the chain) C8 Oven rotated 90° / 180° Door-pattern (TEM) effects Record. HYP interpretation only. Important logic FACT (classical, Balanis Eqs. 4-10a/b): a radiating field falls as 1/r in amplitude. HYP (Hively & Loebl 2019, Table I item 11): the SLW is also claimed to fall as 1/r² in power, i.e. 1/r in field amplitude. So the distance sweep (C4) separates near-field from radiating. It does NOT separate SLW from TEM. That separation rests on the sealed cage (C5, C7), the controls (C1, C6) and orientation (C3). Even then, any "SLW" interpretation stays HYP. transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis Why the cage is expected to block TEM: that expectation is transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis. It is used only to remove TEM, never to predict SLW. 4. (d) openEMS cross-check (classical) Setup (FACT, run on the shared computer, 2026-09-27 ≈ 20:22 ET): see openems_dipole_ratio.py for the full script. Short centre-fed dipole: L = 12 mm (0.098 λ), wire radius 0.5 mm, 1 mm gap, 50 Ω lumped port. Domain ±245 mm, PML_8, mesh ≈ λ/25 far from the dipole, 1.25 M cells, 3 threads. Run time: 20 s, reaching −40 dB energy at 3330 timesteps. The frequency-domain E was dumped on the xz plane. Method: take E_r and E_θ at the same kr on the axis and on the broadside (the "peak" ratio), and at θ = 45°. Compare with the analytic ratio from Balanis Eqs. 4-10a/b. kr r (mm) openEMS peak ratio openEMS θ=45° analytic Δ peak (dB) Δ 45° (dB) 1 19.5 2.375 2.621 2.828 −1.52 −0.66 1.5 29.2 1.491 1.791 1.847 −1.86 −0.26 2 38.9 1.036 1.333 1.240 −1.57 +0.63 3 58.4 0.647 0.750 0.740 −1.17 +0.12 4 77.9 0.474 0.524 0.531 −0.99 −0.11 5 97.4 0.379 0.405 0.416 −0.81 −0.24 7 136.3 0.266 0.278 0.292 −0.79 −0.40 10 194.7 0.186 0.197 0.202 −0.70 −0.22 12 233.7 0.210 0.162 0.168 (+1.95) −0.31 Result (honest, relative): At θ = 45°, openEMS matches the textbook ratio within ±0.7 dB for kr = 1–12. The axis/broadside "peak" ratio reads 0.7–1.9 dB low for kr = 1–10. That is consistent with: a finite 12 mm dipole, rather than an infinitesimal one; grid-snapping of the sample points; our known systematic 7–9 % short offset on dipole length. The kr = 12 peak row is excluded: its broadside point (233.7 mm) sits inside or next to the PML (domain edge 245 mm). The trend (ratio falling as ≈ 2/kr) is reproduced. Treat this as a relative check only; the coarse mesh is not converged. Owed: a medium-mesh convergence run, and a slot-in-plane (seam-like) version. Keep to the same caps (timeout, nice, ≤ 3 threads) so the box doesn't hang, as it did on an earlier medium run; the WL comparison. 5. What this plan does NOT claim It computes no SLW or SW field. No cited source gives a near-field SLW source strength for a magnetron (HYP toggle, §2.3). It does not use skin depth, permeability or cage shielding effectiveness to rank or dismiss SLW/SW. Classical results are FACT for TEM/classical fields only. transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis 6. References Balanis, C. A., Antenna Theory: Analysis and Design, 3rd ed., Wiley 2005: §2.2.4 (field regions), §4.2 (infinitesimal dipole; Eqs. 4-10a, 4-10b; radian distance λ/2π). Britton, verbal, reported by Dan, 2026-09 (no written record). 21 CFR 1030.10 (microwave oven performance standard); 47 CFR 1.1310 (RF exposure limits); both read live 2026-09-27. description: Simulation Lab audit (2026-09-29): how every hub simulator, calculator and Mathematica/Python source computes P_OUT, the medium impedance, I squared and the factors 2 and (4 pi r)^2, against the Hively and Loebl 2019 erratum (Eq. 38, 44, B5). FACT / HYP / ASSUMPTION labelled.
text: Simulation Lab audit · P_OUT · Hively & Loebl 2019 erratum · 2026-09-29 P_OUT per the Hively & Loebl erratum: audit of every simulator The erratum (Phys. Essays 32(3), 417) corrects Eq. 38 and B5 to P_OUT = I² r̂ / [2 (4πr)²] · √(μ/ε) and Eq. 44 to εE²/2. This page records what each hub simulator used, whether it matches, and the numeric change at the preset distances. MIXED ← Simulation Lab catalogue Scope. This page audits every hub simulator, calculator and Mathematica/Python source for how P_OUT (radiated power), the medium impedance √(μ/ε), I² versus I, and the factors 2 and (4πr)² are computed. It is an analysis page: no Wolfram Cloud twin is planned. Citations: Hively & Loebl 2019 (Phys. Essays 32, 112) and the Erratum, Phys. Essays 32(3), 417 (2019). Labels: FACT = paper- or erratum-sourced, HYP = our inference or the SLW hypothesis itself, ASSUMPTION = a choice made here. Under the SLW hypothesis no skin-depth, permeability or ferromagnetic argument is used; the only loss term allowed is Hively’s Joule term σE∥² (2019 Eq. 44) or none (erratum α = 0 toggle). 1. What the erratum says (FACT) The erratum is one page: “Erratum: Classical and extended electrodynamics [Phys. Essays 32, 112 (2019)]”, Lee M. Hively and Andrew S. Loebl, published online 18 Sep 2019, DOI 10.4006/0836-1398-32.3.417, p. 417. The whole correction, quoted: “There were typographical errors in the recently published paper. The correct form of Eq. (38) is P_OUT = I² r̂ / [2 (4πr)²] · √(μ/ε) (38).” “The correct form of Eq. (44) is ∂/∂t ( B²/2μ + C²/2μ + εE²/2 ) + ∇·( E×B/μ + CE/μ ) + J·E = ρC/(εμ) (44).” “The correction to Eq. (38) results from correction of Eq. (B5) P_OUT = I² r̂ / [2 (4πr)²] · √(μ/ε) (B5).” P_OUT and r̂ are set in bold in the erratum. The relayed form (P_OUT = I² r̂ / (2 (4πr)²) · √(μ/ε)) matches the erratum exactly; there is no difference to flag. 2. What the erratum does not say, and what the 2019 paper supplies The erratum does not state the original printed form, and it does not define r̂ or I. (FACT: it is silent.) Original Eq. 38 and B5 (FACT, read from the 2019 paper, pp. 116 and 123): P_OUT = I² r̂ / (4πr)² · √(μ/ε), with no factor 2. The erratum therefore inserts the factor 2 in the denominator, i.e. a ½. Original Eq. 44 (FACT, same pages): the electric energy density was printed as εE², where the erratum has εE²/2. Every other term is the same. The 2019 text on pp. 116–117 already writes “4πr²(εE²/2)”, so the erratum confirms that the missing /2 was typographic. r̂ (FACT, 2019 p. 116, after Eq. 37): “the unit vector in the radial direction”. So P_OUT is a vector along +r̂ with the magnitude I²/[2(4πr)²]·√(μ/ε). I (FACT, 2019 Appendix B): “the current”, a phasor amplitude with e^{jωt} time dependence. The paper does not say peak or rms. Appendix B takes the outward flow from the time-averaged radial ⟨CE/μ⟩ of Eq. 44 and calls it isotropic, falling as r⁻². Hively & Land 2021 (J. Phys.: Conf. Ser., Eq. 22) already prints the corrected 2(4πr)² form and calls it the time-averaged SLW power. √(μ/ε) (FACT): the impedance of the medium. In free space it equals η = Z₀ ≈ 376.73 Ω. It is η, not 1/η. Not corrected by the erratum (FACT): US 9,306,527 Eq. 15, P_OUT = (I²/4π)√(μ/ε), in watts. Reed & Hively 2020 (Symmetry, Eq. 23) still prints the old form without the 2. 3. Units check of the erratum form as printed I² [A²] · √(μ/ε) [Ω] / (4πr)² [m²] = W / m² Integrated over a sphere of area 4πr²: ∮ P_OUT · dA = I² √(μ/ε) / (8π) [W] Patent Eq. 15 (older, in watts): I² √(μ/ε) / (4π) [W] So the erratum expression is dimensionally consistent as a power density (W/m², directed along r̂), even though the paper calls it “power output”. There is no dimensional error to repair. Two consequences follow. (a) The hub calls the total-watts quantity P_rad or P_OUT, and it derives S = P_rad/(4πr²); this is the same object as the erratum’s P_OUT once P_rad = I²Z₀/(8π). (b) The erratum total is half the total in patent Eq. 15. Both statements are algebra on FACT equations (HYP-free), but which of the two the paper means by I (peak or rms) is not settled by the erratum. ASSUMPTION used everywhere below: I is the peak amplitude of the drive current. This is what the hub code already used (I_pk = √2·I_rms from the 50 Ω identity), and the ½ then plays the role of the time average. If Dan reads I as rms, the ½ would be double-counted and the change would need revisiting. 4. What the simulations used before (from code and repo notes) Code: every I-driven page computed P_rad = I_pk² Z0 / (4π) (watts), then S = P_rad / (4π r²), which is S = I_pk² Z₀ / (4πr)². That is numerically the 2019 Eq. 38/B5 as first printed (no ½), and it is patent Eq. 15 spread over a sphere. Z₀ was used as η = 376.73 Ω (correct; never 1/η). Repo notes: expt-d/REPORT.md records B5 as “P_OUT = [I² r̂/(4πr)²]√(μ/ε)” (line 29) and flags the missing ½ as ±3 dB (line 164). PHYSICS_LOCK.md, physics-constants.json and sleeve-balun-snr/RESEARCH.md record the patent Eq. 15 chain. Earlier notes (the internal Joule-term comparison note, JOULE_LOSS_POSITIONS) listed the 2019 erratum as unread; it has now been read. Experiment D used the same as-printed form (Z0·I_pk²/(4πr)²), and in its modulation engine the factor 2 in 2·Z0·S_I/(4πr)² came from I_pk² = 2·I_rms². Under the erratum that 2 cancels against the ½. 5. Audit table Match column: yes / no / N/A (does not use P_OUT from I) / cannot tell. “No” always means the same thing: the as-printed form without the ½, i.e. S is 2× (3.0103 dB) too large. No page had the wrong impedance (η versus 1/η), a wrong r̂, or I versus I² errors. File / place Branch / PR Formula as coded Matches erratum?
