text: Simulation Lab report · rod / polarizer · faithful HTML conversion Contact current measurement on a polarizing rod: is an ammeter / Fluke worth it? Is an ammeter or Fluke worth it on a floating polarizing rod? Induced currents under S1 literal / S1 capped / S2 plus one CLASSICAL-TEM reference column, meter specs, contact loading, least-perturbing options and E5/H10 detectability. MIXED ← Simulation Lab catalogue Provenance /workspace/sim-lab/rod-thermal/contact/README.md (last modified 2026-09-27 18:51 EDT) /workspace/sim-lab/rod-thermal/contact/contact_tables.md (last modified 2026-09-27 18:51 EDT) Converted to HTML 2026-09-28 (EDT) as a faithful conversion: text, numbers, equations and labels are the source's own. No new equations were added; only the TEM tags described below and the edits listed here were made. Status lines inside the source (for example "nothing published", "HELD", "draft") describe the state when it was written. This page is its GitHub Pages twin, published 2026-09-28. No Wolfram Cloud twin planned (analysis/report page, not one of Experiments A–G). Numbers are Python-computed; WL compare OWED where the source says so. Framing rules on this page (Dan). Under the SLW hypothesis no skin-depth, permeability, ferromagnetic or cage shielding-effectiveness argument is used to rank or dismiss SLW/SW. The Faraday cage strips TEM noise (FACT); an SLW passing the cage wall is HYP. Every passage that uses transverse-EM (TEM / classical / cage-SE) reasoning is tagged transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis. FACT / HYP / ASSUMPTION labels are kept exactly as in the source. Downloads contact_numbers.json ← Rod thermal model 2026-09-27 (ET). Draft for Dan via the parent agent. Python only; WL compare OWED. Script: src/contact_current.py -> contact_numbers.json, contact_tables.md (full tables, both materials, 3 mm and 5 mm). Labels: FACT (cited), HYP, ASSUMPTION, CLASSICAL-TEM (textbook Maxwell result, kept apart from the SLW framework and never used to rank or dismiss SLW). SAFETY: rods, probes, meters and TinySAs stay outside the oven cavity. Loose metal in a running oven can arc and damage the magnetron. Short answer: no. A Fluke in current mode cannot read RF current at 433.59 MHz to 2.45 GHz at any amplitude: its AC current band stops at 2 kHz (87V) or 500 Hz (117) (FACT, Fluke specs). Wiring it across both rod ends also closes a loop and destroys the thing being measured (the floating half-wave rod). Use non-contact probes. If contact is pursued anyway, the least-perturbing option is a clamp-type RF current probe at 433.59 MHz only (Fischer F-65 class, which is not really contact); for true contact, a split rod with a small sense resistor and a fiber/resistive-lead detector, accepting that it becomes a dipole with a feed gap. 1. Induced current in one floating half-wave rod What the SLW sources give: US 9,306,527 has J = sigma E (col. 5 l. ~53, col. 6 l. ~14) and the no-skin-effect claim (col. 6 ll. ~6-12). HL2019 Eq. 44 (p. 117) has J.E. M&W Eq. 7 (EPL 59, 514, p. 516) gives Joule power per length, with the internal field taken equal to E0 cos phi. Keyport US 12,525,711 gives nothing for receiving rods. None of them gives a current formula or a current distribution for a floating rod (FACT: not found). So everything below is derived from the models' own quantities, plus labelled assumptions: S1 literal: I = sigma E A (uniform J = sigma E over the cross-section, internal = external field: HYP). A floating rod must have I = 0 at its ends (charge continuity, classical), so a uniform current is self-inconsistent at the ends. It also gives amperes to tens of kA, far more than the incident flux can supply: unphysical. S1 capped: P = S pi a^2 (1 - e^-4.4) (M&W <P/A> = <S>, Eq. 9 kappa, HYP), R = L/(sigma A) (no skin effect: Hively's claim, used as HYP). Current: I = sqrt(P/R) if uniform (ASSUMPTION), or peak I0 = sqrt(2P/R) for I0 cos(kz) (ASSUMPTION, classical half-wave shape). Because R is milliohms, even nanowatts give sub-mA to mA currents. S2 surface charge: I = omega eps0 E A (report Model S2, HYP). Material-independent. CLASSICAL-TEM reference (one column): short-circuited half-wave rod parallel to E (i.e. perpendicular to propagation): I0 = E (lambda/pi)/|73.1 + j42.5| (effective length lambda/pi and Z_in, Balanis, Antenna Theory 4e, Sec. 4.6, Eq. 4-93a). This is the M&W "no attenuation" orientation, not the SLW one. transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis E_rms = sqrt(Z0 S) (HYP map for SLW; identical for a classical plane wave). Scenarios: (a) and (b) are SLW flux at 2.45 GHz (HYP), and HYP flux only at 433.59 / 1296 MHz (the oven emits only 2.45 GHz). Hub drive: +2 dBm (TinySA + Zeenko, PHYSICS_LOCK.md:39; the HackRF power figure is still MISSING from the hub), at an assumed 1 m and 3 m. Brief table, peak current at rod centre (brass / W1 where they differ): ⚠ Rows/columns in this table that refer to TEM / classical / cage SE: transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis scenario freq S1 literal S1 capped, cos I0 S2 CLASSICAL-TEM broadside (a) 100 mW @ 30 ft 2450 22.6 A / 7.5 A 1.7 mA / 0.98 mA 204 nA 87 uA (a) 500 mW @ 30 ft 2450 50.6 A / 16.8 A 3.8 mA / 2.2 mA 457 nA 195 uA (b) FDA 5 mW/cm^2 2450 16 kA / 5.4 kA 1.24 A / 0.71 A 148 uA 63 mA (a) 100 mW, HYP flux 433.59 22.6 A / 7.5 A 0.72 mA / 0.41 mA 36 nA 493 uA (b) FDA, HYP flux 433.59 16 kA / 5.4 kA 519 mA / 299 mA 26 uA 357 mA hub +2 dBm @ 1 m 433.59 26 A / 8.6 A 825 uA / 475 uA 42 nA 567 uA hub +2 dBm @ 1 m 1296 26 A / 8.6 A 1.43 mA / 0.82 mA 124 nA 190 uA hub +2 dBm @ 3 m 433.59 8.7 A / 2.9 A 275 uA / 158 uA 14 nA 189 uA The spread across the SLW models is about 4-8 orders of magnitude (S2 nA to S1 capped mA), so the models do not predict the current. S1 capped: brass/W1 current = sqrt(3.02) = 1.74 at the same absorbed power. Fluke verdict (FACT, Fluke specs) Fluke 87V (Fluke 83V/87V detailed spec sheet): AC current 45 Hz to 2 kHz; 600.0 uA range, 0.1 uA resolution; burden 100 uV/uA (about 100 ohm in series); mA ranges 1.8 mV/mA; AC readings valid from 3 % of range (about 18 uA minimum on 600 uA); volts input 10 Mohm || < 100 pF; "in an RF field of 3 V/m total accuracy = specified accuracy" (EMC line). Fluke 117 (fluke.com spec page, 114-117 datasheet): AC amps 45 Hz to 500 Hz, 6.000 A range, 1 mA resolution; burden 2 mV/A; volts AC > 5 Mohm < 100 pF. 433.59 MHz is about 2e5 times above the 87V's top current frequency, and 2.45 GHz about 1e6 times. A DMM cannot read RF current at these frequencies regardless of amplitude (FACT from the spec). Any reading it shows is unspecified: rectification, pickup, or offset. Wiring the meter across both ends closes a loop (rod + two leads + shunt). The structure is no longer a floating half-wave rod; it becomes a loop/folded antenna with different resonances and current distribution (FACT, classical). 2. Contact loading (lumped numbers are illustrative only) freq lambda 1 m lead / lambda Xc of 100 pF XL of 1 m lead (1.51 uH) Xc of 0.8 pF (TAP2500) rod end impedance 433.59 MHz 0.691 m 1.45 3.7 ohm 4.1 kohm 459 ohm 2-5 kohm (HYP range) 1296 MHz 0.231 m 4.3 1.2 ohm 12 kohm 154 ohm 2-5 kohm 2450 MHz 0.122 m 8.2 0.65 ohm 23 kohm 81 ohm 2-5 kohm Lead inductance: Rosa/Grover straight-wire formula L = (mu0 l/2pi)[ln(2l/r) - 3/4] (classical; Grover, Inductance Calculations), giving 1.51 uH for 1 m of 0.5 mm-radius wire: matches the ~1 uH/m rule of thumb. Rod end impedance: classical half-wave end-feed values of about 2-5 kohm (AA5TB, "The End Fed Half Wave Antenna", practitioner source; depends on wire thickness). Treated here as a HYP range for our fat rods; no textbook value found for this geometry. Reading: the Fluke's < 100 pF input is 0.65-3.7 ohm against a kilohm end impedance, i.e. effectively a short at the rod end. The 1 m leads are 1.5-8 wavelengths long, so the lumped picture fails (lumped elements need dimensions << lambda; Pozar, Microwave Engineering, Ch. 2). The leads become resonant antennas themselves. In current mode the 87V adds about 100 ohm (uA range) in series: larger than the rod's classical R_rad of 73 ohm (Balanis Eq. 4-93). Least-perturbing contact options: (i) High-Z active probe: the Tektronix TAP2500 (FACT, Tek datasheet: >= 2.5 GHz, <= 0.8 pF, 40 kohm, TekVPI; needs a TekVPI scope such as DPO4000/7000). 0.8 pF is still 81-459 ohm, about 0.02-0.2 of the end impedance: heavy loading and detuning. It also needs a ground reference (a second conductor) and a multi-GHz scope. Price: not verified. (ii) Clamp-on RF current probe: the Tek CT6 does not fit (0.8 mm wire max, <= 2 GHz typical). Fischer F-65 (FACT, fischercc.com / Avalon listing): 10 kHz-1 GHz, 32 mm aperture (fits a 1/8 in rod), transfer impedance 1 ohm (1 MHz-1 GHz). 433.59 MHz only; no verified clamp probe covers 1296 or 2450 MHz with a 1/8 in window. Sensitivity at the TinySA floor: I_min ~ 0.56 uA (computed, ASSUMPTION floor). Caveat (HYP): a 71 mm OD ferrite/metal ring around the centre of a 346 mm resonant rod is itself a sizeable perturbation, even though Fischer describes "virtually no loading of the circuit". (iii) Split rod + series sense resistor at the centre (e.g. 1 ohm << 73 ohm R_rad, classical), read by a zero-bias Schottky detector with resistive (high-R) leads or a fiber-coupled readout. Power in 1 ohm: -90 dBm at 1 uA, -50 dBm at 100 uA, -30 dBm at 1 mA (computed). A diode detector needs roughly -50 dBm or more (ASSUMPTION, typical class, not verified): it would see S1-capped mA currents, but not S2 nA. Splitting the rod makes it a dipole with a feed gap, exactly what M&W's passive rods are not (HL2019 Appendix D, p. 124, describes M&W's array as "half-wavelength, linear, electric-dipole antennas"; M&W treat them as continuous wires, p. 516). (iv) RF thermocouple / thermal converter in series: needs a split rod too, and a heater drawing typically mA to tens of mA for a usable reading (ASSUMPTION, class, no product verified). It cannot see uA to nA. Least perturbing: for real galvanic contact, (iii) with a small resistor and fiber readout; at 433.59 MHz the F-65 clamp (ii) perturbs less and needs no cut. Overall, the non-contact near-field probe (Sec. 5) is least perturbing of all. 3. Comparison with the bifilar coil into 50 ohm The coil into the TinySA is a defined matched load: I = sqrt(P/50) (FACT identity). -40 dBm is 44.7 uA, -60 dBm 4.5 uA, -80 dBm 0.45 uA, -100 dBm 45 nA. Dan's actual coil readings (dBm) are not in the hub, so the coil current itself is unknown to us. A floating rod has no load; its current is set by the absorption model. Under the SLW models (HYP) the rod current ranges from nA (S2) to mA (S1 capped) for the same flux, so it could be anywhere from well below to well above a typical coil reading. Without an SLW coupling formula for either the coil or the rod, the comparison is undefined. It becomes defined only if Dan supplies the coil's dBm and we pick a rod model. CLASSICAL-TEM one line: at the FDA-limit door flux, a matched lambda/2 dipole delivers <= 98 mW (I ~ 37 mA into 73 ohm; A_e = 1.64 lambda^2/4pi, Balanis Sec. 2.15), while a shorted floating rod parallel to E carries I0 ~ 63 mA: the same ballpark classically. transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis 4. Recommendation Non-contact. A DMM is out on bandwidth alone (FACT). Contact methods all rebuild the object (loop, dipole-with-gap, or kilohm-end loading). Contact is worth doing only as a separate, labelled "modified-rod" experiment. The least-perturbing contact option is (iii) a split rod with a 1 ohm resistor and fiber/resistive-lead detector, or, at 433.59 MHz only, the F-65 clamp. Keep the unmodified rods for the M&W angle test. 5. Non-contact E5 / H10 near a rod (inside its own cage) Cage rule: the cage strips TEM noise (FACT, classical). That SLW passes the wall is HYP (patent col. 2 ll. 65-67). No cable crosses a wall; battery TinySA inside. Per Hively, a TEM-type probe does not pick up the SLW itself ("TEM antennas detect only waves that produce a circulating current", HL2019 p. 116), so inside the cage the E5/H10 should see only the rod's own local field (HYP inference from a FACT quote). transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis Classical near-field relations (CLASSICAL, quasi-static, valid for d << lambda/2pi): H beside the centre: H = I0/(2 pi rho), with rho = a + gap (Ampere; Jackson 3e Sec. 5.3). E off the end: end line-charge density |q| = I0/c for I0 cos(kz) (continuity). Field on axis at distance d from a semi-infinite uniform line charge: E = q/(4 pi eps0 d) = Z0 I0/(4 pi d) ~ 30 I0/d. This is an elementary Coulomb integral derived here, with an approximation (charge density taken as uniform near the end); not a formula quoted from a source. E5: -58.4 / -49.0 / -44.7 dBm at 433.59 / 1296 / 2450 MHz; H10: -7.1 / -4.5 / -9.8 dBm. If Dan's E5/H10 are not Tekbox TBPS01: unknown, must be calibrated. The factors are from uniform-field calibration; near a rod the field varies across the probe (ASSUMPTION, several dB error). Peak vs rms is not stated by Tekbox (ASSUMPTION, +/-3 dB). TinySA Ultra floor: -102 dBm at 30 kHz RBW (at 30 MHz, FACT spec). Scaled to 3 kHz RBW: -112 dBm (ASSUMPTION, thermal scaling). Sensitivity is about 10 dB lower above 2.5 GHz (FACT, tinysa.org Ultra-mode page), applied conservatively at 2.45 GHz: -102 dBm. SAFETY (read first) Rods, probes, TinySAs and cables stay OUTSIDE the oven cavity. Never put loose metal in a running microwave oven: it can arc and damage the magnetron (and the oven). The "near-door" scenario means rods on a non-metallic stand outside the closed door. Do not defeat interlocks or run the oven empty/modified. Oven leakage limits are a federal product standard (21 CFR 1030.10: 5 mW/cm^2 at 5 cm, FACT); do not try to increase leakage. 0. Sources: charge accumulation, and whether sigma*E_par^2 is a stated heating term US 9,306,527 B1 (Hively), FACT quotes: Col. 1 ll. 19-31: a classical linear monopole "driven by a sinusoidal current to put charge onto and remove charge from the linear conductor (antenna)" (charge-accumulator picture, transmitter). Col. 8 ll. ~44-55: "essentially all of the electrical current goes into charging and discharging the antenna." Col. 7 ll. ~21-23: reciprocity, transmitter geometry can act as receiver. Col. 5 l. ~53 and col. 6 l. ~14: "J=sigma E"; EQN. 14 (col. 6 l. ~36) contains the term J.E in the energy balance; col. 6 ll. ~39-44 says with B=0 it "may yield an identity, 0=0 ... verifying the no-skin-effect prediction". Table 1 item 6: "C, E, and J exchange energy in conductive media." Result: the patent never writes sigma*E^2 and never calls J.E heating/dissipation. No rod-absorption formula exists in the patent. Hively & Loebl, Phys. Essays 32, 112 (2019), FACT: Eq. (44), p. 117: d/dt(B^2/2mu + C^2/2mu + epsE^2) + div(ExB/mu + CE/mu) + J.E = rhoC/(eps mu). p. 116: "E^L = J^L/sigma ... no eddy currents occur". The paper does not call J.E a loss or give an attenuation constant. Keyport US 12,525,711 B1, FACT: silent on receiving rods, absorption, sigma*E^2, hysteresis, rod material (text search of Google full text: no "heat", "dissipat", "absorb", "hysteres", "ohmic", "joule", "resistiv", "attenuat"; only "conductive material" for antenna parts, col. 4 ll. 5-7). Monstein & Wesley, EPL 59, 514 (2002), FACT: p. 516: "only the E field component E0 cos(phi) in the direction of a wire produces Ohmic losses"; Eq. (7) dP = -[sigma A E0^2 cos^2 phi] dL. This is the only source-derived rod Joule formula (it assumes internal E = external E0 cos phi). Eq. (9) T = exp[-kappa cos^2 phi], kappa = 4.4 fitted. Verdict on sigma*E_par^2 as a heating term: from HL2019 Eq. 44 (J.E) + J = sigma E (paper and patent) and M&W Eq. 7 (paper). Not from the patent. Applying it to Dan's 1/8 in rods with internal E_par = external E_par is HYP (Dan's extrapolation). Geometry (L vs lambda/2) setting absorbed energy: no source formula; M&W kappa ~ L (FACT, Eq. 9 context) is the only length dependence stated. 2. Hysteresis question: W1 vs brass Conductivities (FACT): material source resistivity sigma (S/m) C36000 free-cutting brass copper.org C36000: 26 % IACS @ 68 F - 0.26 x 5.80e7 = 1.51e7 W1 (DIN 1.1545, C105W1), annealed htsteelmill datasheet: 0.20 ohm mm^2/m (avg) 20 uOhm cm 5.0e6 (MetalZenith 0.18-0.22 uOhm m -> 4.5-5.6e6) W1 hardened/tempered MatWeb 30 uOhm cm 30 uOhm cm 3.3e6 (The ~1e7 placeholder is not used.) Same E_par (Model S1, HYP internal = external): heating ratio brass/W1 = sigma ratio = 3.02 (range 2.71-3.32 annealed; 4.5 vs hardened W1). Brass wins, about 3x more Joule heating per unit volume at the same E_par. This contradicts the "high-hysteresis rods" advice under the sigma*E^2 picture. Reason: hysteresis loss needs a cycling H/B; SLW has B = 0 (Erratum 2022; patent col. 2 ll. 54-61 "no magnetic component", FACT), so mu_r and coercivity drop out of sigma*E^2 (HYP inference on FACT premises). Examples (tables.md): E_par = 0.1 V/m inside a 433.59 MHz rod -> brass 0.10 W, 3.0 K; W1 0.034 W, 1.1 K (painted). But see Sec. 3: those fields are not reachable from the scenario fluxes without violating energy conservation. Model S2, charge relaxation (HYP, first-principles continuity + Gauss): if the external E_par terminates on surface charge, E_in ~ (omega eps0/sigma) E_out, so p = (omega eps0 E_out)^2/sigma: ranking reverses, W1 > brass by 3x (via sigma, not hysteresis). Magnitude is ~1e-8 of S1-capped: negligible (<1e-8 K in every scenario). Model S1-capped (HYP, energy-conserving, M&W <P/A> = <S>): P = S * pi a^2 * (1 - exp(-kappa cos^2 phi)). Both metals absorb essentially everything through the cross-section -> material-independent (ratio 1.00). So: brass/W1 = 3.0 (S1 literal), 1.0 (S1 capped), 0.33 (S2). No model makes hysteresis matter. 2.1 Question for Dan: Dr. "Heidley/Hadley" (likely Dr. Hively, unconfirmed). We did NOT contact anyone. He specified HIGH-HYSTERESIS rods for the M&W 433.59 MHz replication and a full 360 deg Lazy Susan rotation. Possible justifications, all HYP: (i) Transverse-EM thinking: under ordinary TEM, magnetic loss in a ferromagnetic rod matters (TEM has B). Would test for TEM leakage, not SLW. transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis (ii) A transverse mode excited at the rod ends by the longitudinal field (end discontinuity), whose B could then cause hysteresis loss. No source equation found for this. (iii) Charge-relaxation difference. Quantitative, with assumption eps = eps0 for metals (stated): freq RF period tau brass = eps0/sigma tau W1 tau/T (brass, W1) 433.59 MHz 2.31 ns 5.9e-19 s 1.8e-18 s 2.6e-10, 7.7e-10 1296 MHz 0.772 ns 5.9e-19 s 1.8e-18 s 7.6e-10, 2.3e-9 2450 MHz 0.408 ns 5.9e-19 s 1.8e-18 s 1.4e-9, 4.3e-9 Arithmetic FACT: tau is 9-10 orders of magnitude shorter than the period for both; both relax essentially instantly. Interpretation HYP: (iii) cannot distinguish brass from W1 by relaxation speed. (Caveat: in real metals the response is limited by electron collision time ~1e-14 s, still << period, standard Drude picture; HYP-level remark.) This ties to the patent's own transient E = E0 exp(-...t) with exponent printed eps/sigma (col. 5 l. ~55, a typo for sigma/eps). 360 deg rotation, FACT + HYP: M&W Eq. 9 T = exp[-kappa cos^2 phi] is 180 deg periodic (FACT). Computed T(phi) at kappa = 4.4: 0.012 (0 deg), 0.037 (30), 0.333 (60), 1.000 (90), repeating identically 180-360. A full 360 deg sweep gives two repeats: a free consistency check; any 360 deg-periodic component points to asymmetry, a fixture/cable artifact, or a source off-axis (HYP on his intent). Also FACT: Hively himself rotated the receiving antenna 360 deg in 1 deg increments (HL2019 p. 121, Fig. 5), so a full 360 sweep matches his own practice. 3. Verdicts (HYP model, FACT arithmetic): (a) 30 ft leakage at any of 100/300/500 mW: sub-microkelvin (energy-capped); at most sub-millikelvin even with the unsourced L^2 collection area. Not IR-detectable. (b) Near-door at the FDA limit: ~55-85 mK per rod (capped), identical for brass and W1: below the 0.1-1 C IR-gun threshold, detectable only with a differential contact/fiber/camera-averaged setup (Sec. 4). Real ovens usually leak less than the limit (HYP; not measured). Only the unsourced L^2 area gives tens of K. 433.59 / 1296 MHz with the hub's +2 dBm drive: nanokelvin to sub-mK. Undetectable thermally. Even a hypothetical 1 W at 1 m gives <=0.1 mK capped (0.02-0.1 mK). The literal S1 formula (internal E = external) needs more power than the incident flux can supply in every case: it cannot be used without an energy cap. 3.4 One confound line (not the governing model) For ordinary TEM leakage at the door (not SLW), a lambda/2 2.45 GHz rod has a classical maximum available power of S * 1.64 lambda^2/(4 pi) = 50 W/m^2 x 1.95e-3 m^2 ~ 98 mW into a matched load (standard antenna effective aperture, FACT); an unloaded metal rod dissipates only a small fraction of that. This does not govern SLW, but it means any near-door rod heating is confounded by TEM leakage. transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis 4. Measurement protocol Emissivity (FACT, Optris table sourced to Bramson / Wolfe & Zissis): Brass, dull/tarnished: 0.22; oxidized: 0.61; polished: 0.03. Iron & steel, freshly worked with emery (dull bare bar): 0.24; rolled sheet 0.56; oxidized 0.74; rusty red 0.69. Black dull lacquer: 0.96-0.98 (Optris); black electrical tape 0.97 (ThermoWorks table); black plastic paint 0.95. Recommendation: put a flat black paint or black electrical-tape dot (eps ~0.96) on each rod at the same spot and set the IR instrument to 0.96. This removes the brass-vs-steel emissivity difference (0.22 vs 0.24 bare is too low and uncertain for IR). The paint/tape adds a thin lossy dielectric and a little mass; use identical dots on every rod, including the reference. (Aluminized-back Kapton is NOT high-eps: 0.24-0.86 depending on thickness, design1st table.) Irradiation time (computed): tau_th = m cp / (h A_s): painted 207-259 s (3.5-4.3 min); bare 313-405 s (5.2-6.8 min). Expose >= 5 tau_th: ~20 min painted, ~35 min bare before reading steady state, then an equal off period. Drift control: HVAC off, no people moving nearby, rods and HDPE plate equilibrated >= 1 h, room thermometer logged, identical dummy HDPE plate, repeated on/off cycles (oven on/off is the modulation; keep oven duty and water load identical each cycle). Differential measurement: worth doing (yes). Exposed rod vs an identical reference rod (same material, dot, mount) rotated to phi = 90 deg (M&W T = 1, predicted zero absorption) or placed far out of the beam. Caution: a metal "shield" is not a valid reference in Hively's framework because the SLW is claimed to pass Faraday enclosures (patent col. 2 ll. 65-67; col. 10 ll. 35-38); use rotation/distance. The difference cancels common room drift. Expected noise floor (typical-instrument values, not verified against Dan's instruments, HYP-level): IR spot thermometer: ~0.1 C resolution. Sees nothing predicted here. Thermal camera, both rods in one frame: NETD typically 30-70 mK per frame; averaging many frames and pixels along the rod: ~5-10 mK. Differential type-T thermocouple (junction on each rod): Seebeck ~40 uV/K (standard type-T tables); a 0.1 uV meter gives 2.5 mK resolution. Realistic air-current noise several mK, reduced by sqrt(N) over N on/off cycles -> ~1-5 mK floor after ~10 cycles (HYP). Caution: TC leads are metal conductors in the field; route them perpendicular to the propagation axis (phi = 90) and keep them identical on both rods; prefer fiber-optic (GaAs) probes, which have no metal leads, if available. Against predictions: only the near-door S1-capped case (~55-85 mK) is above this floor; everything else is below it. 5. NEW: Dan's Faraday-cage bifilar coil + E5 observation Observation (Dan's data, UNVERIFIED by us): inside a sealed Faraday cage with the oven on, the Hively bifilar coil + TinySA shows 2.45 GHz activity; an E5 E-probe on its own TinySA near the coil showed oven-correlated activity; with the E5 moved as far from the coil as possible it went quiet while the coil's TinySA kept showing activity. Dan's HYP: the coil, driven by the longitudinal field, carries oscillating charge/current and makes a local near field that the E5 picks up. 5.1 What the sources say (FACT quotes) about SLW producing transverse fields at conductors/receivers No source statement found that an SLW converts to, or produces, transverse/TEM fields at a receiving conductor. Checked US 9,306,527, HL2019, Keyport US 12,525,711. transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis US 9,306,527 col. 10 ll. 1-7 (bifilar coil): "There may be zero or approximately zero inductance associated with the coil as a result of magnetic-field cancellation by counter-going electrical currents in adjacent turns of the coil. There may be zero or approximately zero capacitance associated with the coil as a result of adjacent turns of the coil having the same or approximately the same electrical charge density." US 9,306,527 col. 10 ll. 35-38: a solid copper Faraday box enclosing the coil "may be configured to block most or all transverse electromagnetic waves impinging on the Faraday box." Col. 3 ll. 1-4: the result "may not be explainable by radiation of classical transverse waves because such waves are eliminated via Faraday cage(s)". US 9,306,527 col. 7 ll. ~21-23 and HL2019 p. 116: "a SLW transmitter can act as a receiver, and vice versa" (reciprocity). HL2019 p. 116: "The SLW has not been previously observed, because transverse electromagnetic (TEM) antennas detect only waves that produce a circulating current. A TEM transmitter produces only circulating currents, yielding C = 0 and E_L = 0 with no SLW power output or reception"; Appendix C, pp. 123-124: "This result explains the nondetection of the SLW by TEM antennas, which can detect waves that generate only a circulating current (no gradient-driven current)." transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis HL2019 p. 121 (Hively's own confounds): "One issue may be TEM signals being picked up by the coaxial cables, either inside or outside the Faraday cage... we did not use a TEM receiving antenna inside the Faraday cage to confirm the absence of such a signal." Also: "a longitudinal E-field component occurs in the near-field under classical (Maxwell) electrodynamics" within a few wavelengths (symbol garbled in extraction; ~3 lambda). transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis Keyport US 12,525,711 col. 7 l. ~62 to col. 8 l. 5: "Symmetric coil windings, such as a bifilar coil, may have SLW transmission advantages through cancelation of the E-Field [sic]. This may work similarly to a twisted pair ... and may cause the magnetic field of each wire to cancel with its opposing neighboring fields." Col. 7 ll. ~40-45: spark-fed antenna "capable of generating SLW and scalar waves, while reducing the transverse electromagnetic (TEM) wave 4." Col. 7 ll. ~46-52: one-wire capacitive coupling, "By sloshing electrons between two capacitive bodies, the sloshed current may be rectified on the receiving side." (Line numbers read from the rendered image, approximate.) transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis Consistency assessment: FACT (classical Maxwell): any time-varying charge/current distribution produces a reactive near field that falls off steeply. Reactive zone ~ lambda/(2 pi) (Wheeler radiansphere; kr = 1 in Jackson 3e Sec. 9.1): 110 mm @ 433.59 MHz, 36.8 mm @ 1296 MHz, 19.5 mm @ 2.45 GHz (computed). For a small neutral source the quasi-static E falls as 1/r^3 (electric-dipole near zone, Jackson 3e Sec. 9.2), vs 1/r far field. So IF the coil carries 2.45 GHz current, a local E near it is expected, and its steep fall-off fits "quiet when far." HYP: that the coil current is driven by an inbound SLW. Hively's framework says TEM-type receivers (a small E-probe is one) do not detect SLW directly (p. 116), so an E5 reading near the coil is, in that framework, most naturally a classical local field from the coil's current: consistent with Dan's HYP. But no source claims the coil re-emits classical fields, and Hively's own col. 10 says the bifilar coil cancels B and has ~zero capacitance, so by design its local fields should be small (HYP tension worth noting). transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis Important instrument FACT: tinySA Ultra covers 100 kHz-800 MHz in normal mode and up to 6 GHz only with ULTRA mode enabled (tinysa.org TinySA4 specification). It has a "spur suppression option for assessing if certain signals are internally generated" (same page). Use it. 5.2 Alternatives Dan should rule out (all HYP) (a) The coil's own TinySA/coax/USB/power path is the antenna, or a cage leak (seam, vent, cable) couples in and the coil (a conductor that concentrates whatever gets in) re-radiates it. Hively flagged exactly this cable pickup (HL2019 p. 121). (b) The two TinySAs couple to each other, or through a shared ground/battery/USB, when the E5 is near the coil (the instruments are closest then). (c) TinySA self-generated spurs/harmonics (LO, ULTRA-mode mixing products, firmware) near 2.45 GHz, possibly modulated by the oven's mains-synchronous magnetron switching via power lines or vibration. Cage rule check: no cable crosses the wall; battery power; data out only optically or after the run (stored traces). Were both TinySAs fully inside on battery, with USB unplugged? If not, that is a leak path and the result is not a Faraday test. 5.3 Discriminating controls (IDEA) Oven off vs on (same setup) and oven on with an empty-cage baseline (TinySA with 50 ohm terminator, no coil). E5 near a dummy: a non-resonant coil or a straight wire of the same wire length, in place of the Hively coil. Coil disconnected from its TinySA and terminated in 50 ohm, E5 kept near it. If E5 still sees the oven, the coil is not being driven via its TinySA path. Swap the TinySAs; move both instruments; enable spur suppression; repeat. Seal each TinySA in its own small shielded box (probe coax through a bulkhead), both inside the big cage. Distance sweep: E5 amplitude vs distance from the coil at fixed E5 orientation, log-log. Expected classical drops (computed): 5->50 mm: 20 dB for 1/r, 40 dB for 1/r^2, 60 dB for 1/r^3; 5->20 mm: 12 / 24 / 36 dB. A steep (~1/r^3 beyond the coil radius) fall-off centered on the coil supports a local source; a flat or 1/r curve, or one centered on a cable/instrument, points to (a)-(c). Keep within the TinySA's ~70 dB spur-free range (spec page). 5.4 Implication for the rods (HYP) If rods absorb by charge accumulation (sigma*E_par^2, HYP), they carry oscillating charge (max near the ends for a half-wave rod) and current (max at the center; classical half-wave distribution, FACT), so they should also show a local near field. IDEA: use a near-field probe sweep near a rod as an absorption proxy, with rotation phi as the key discriminator: a real rod-coupled signal should follow the M&W cos^2 phi dependence, 180 deg periodic, max at phi = 0/180 and minimum at 90/270, over a full 360 deg. Scale illustration (HYP arithmetic, nearfield.json): if the near-door S1-capped 0.39 mW were Joule loss with DC-uniform current (no skin effect per Hively), a 2.45 GHz rod would carry ~0.87 A rms (brass) / ~0.50 A (W1), i.e. classical H ~21 / 12 A/m at 5 mm: very easy to see with an H-probe. In Hively's framework the gradient-driven current has B = 0, so whether an H-probe sees an azimuthal field at the rod center is itself a discriminator between a classical current and Hively's irrotational current (HYP). Note this proxy is material-dependent (I ~ sqrt(sigma)) even when heating is not. 6. Instrumentation per frequency (rods floating, unperturbed; non-contact primary) Series ammeter / current probe: an ordinary ammeter cannot read RF current, and cutting the rod to insert one detunes it (FACT classical). Real example, verified: Tektronix CT6 (Tek datasheet): 250 kHz-2 GHz typical (1.5 GHz guaranteed), closed core that accepts bare wire up to 20 gauge (0.8 mm) only: it cannot fit a 1/8 in (3.175 mm) rod and does not reach 2.45 GHz. So clamp probes are a poor fit; treat as a "class of device." A thermocouple-type RF ammeter inside the rod is impractical. Non-contact current equivalent: a small shielded loop (H-probe, like H10) a few mm from the rod center (current maximum for a half-wave rod, FACT classical). Voltage: half-wave rod voltage maximum is at the ends (FACT classical). Any contact probe loads and detunes the rod; prefer a capacitive E-probe (like E5) a few mm from a rod end. TinySA + probes: H-probe near the center, E-probe near an end, spaced a few mm, either (1) fixed to the HDPE plate so they rotate with the rod (measures the rod's own response vs phi), or (2) fixed in space while the rod rotates (maps the field seen at one point; includes the probe-rod coupling). Both give different information; do both. The probe and its coax perturb the field and can themselves be the pickup (same caveat as the coil): repeat with the rod removed. Inside the cage: battery TinySA, no cable through the wall. 1296 and 2450 MHz need tinySA ULTRA mode (FACT, spec). Oscilloscope: Tek "5 Times Rule" (FACT, Tektronix XYZs of Oscilloscopes primer): bandwidth >= 5x signal for <2% amplitude error -> 2.2 GHz (433.59 MHz), 6.5 GHz (1296 MHz), 12.3 GHz (2.45 GHz). Prices not verified; say "multi-GHz real-time scope class, expensive." Not needed: the TinySA zero-span mode (min burst 50 us at 850 kHz RBW, spec page) or an SDR gives the envelope, which is enough for on/off and vs-phi work. SDR coverage (vendor specs, not re-fetched this session): HackRF One ~1 MHz-6 GHz; RTL-SDR (R820T2) up to ~1.7 GHz, so 433.59 and 1296 MHz only. Real-time brass vs W1: paired rods (one of each) at identical positions, differential IR camera or fiber-optic probes on painted dots, plus near-field probe amplitude vs phi for each material. Expect equal heating if S1-capped, brass 3x if S1 literal, W1 3x if S2; none predicts a hysteresis effect. 7. Open items / blockers HackRF power figure: not in hub (source missing). text: Simulation Lab report · radar / RCS · faithful HTML conversion Scalar-wave (SLW/SW) radar: research & design brief Feasibility, architecture, control plan, parts map, safety, phased plan and open questions for a bench SLW/SW radar. TEM-only Skolnik radar numbers are computed; no SLW echo can be computed because no source gives an SLW reflection law. MIXED ← Simulation Lab catalogue Provenance /workspace/sim-lab/scalar-wave-radar-design-brief.md (last modified 2026-09-27 19:59 EDT) Converted to HTML 2026-09-28 (EDT) as a faithful conversion: text, numbers, equations and labels are the source's own. No new equations were added; only the TEM tags described below and the edits listed here were made. Status lines inside the source (for example "nothing published", "HELD", "draft") describe the state when it was written. This page is its GitHub Pages twin, published 2026-09-28. No Wolfram Cloud twin planned (analysis/report page, not one of Experiments A–G). Numbers are Python-computed; WL compare OWED where the source says so. Framing rules on this page (Dan). Under the SLW hypothesis no skin-depth, permeability, ferromagnetic or cage shielding-effectiveness argument is used to rank or dismiss SLW/SW. The Faraday cage strips TEM noise (FACT); an SLW passing the cage wall is HYP. Every passage that uses transverse-EM (TEM / classical / cage-SE) reasoning is tagged transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis. FACT / HYP / ASSUMPTION labels are kept exactly as in the source. Downloads radar_numbers.json (Python output) radar_numbers.py (script) Simulation Lab · prepared by Grok Bot for Dan Britton · Sunday 2026-09-27, about 20:00 EDT · status: DRAFT, HELD (a markdown brief only; nothing published, sent, bought or built). Labels used on every claim: FACT: cited textbook, datasheet, regulation, or peer-reviewed mainstream result. HYP: the scalar-longitudinal-wave (SLW) / scalar-wave (SW) hypothesis as printed by Hively, Monstein & Wesley, Keyport, Zimmerman et al. Not independently replicated. ASSUMPTION: a choice or estimate made in this brief. TEM FACT: an established transverse-EM (ordinary radio) result. It is not established for SLW. transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis Where ordinary radio physics is used to reason about something, it is flagged: "transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis". House rules applied throughout: No new equations. Every equation has a source and equation number. Under the SLW hypothesis, material enters only through σ, via J = σE: Hively's Joule term J·E (Hively & Loebl 2019, Eq. 44), or α = 0 under the 2022 Erratum. No skin-depth, permeability or ferromagnetic arguments are used for SLW. TEM attenuation (cage shielding effectiveness, seawater, hull) is never used to rank or dismiss SLW/SW. The Faraday cage is there to strip TEM noise. SLW passing the cage wall is HYP. No cable ever crosses a cage wall. Electronics inside run on battery; data leaves by optical fibre through a waveguide-below-cutoff tube, or is read after opening. 0. The short version (read this first) An ordinary 2.45 GHz radar is doable with Dan's kit (TEM FACT). HackRF as a low-power continuous-wave (CW) or FM-CW transmitter, a TinySA or second SDR as receiver, and the brass DD-2450 dipoles or a simple can antenna would see a person walking at a few metres by Doppler. Skolnik's equations put the ideal reach at tens of metres (§2.6). This is the bench baseline, and it works whether or not SLW exists. transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis A true SLW radar cannot yet be specified. The existence of SLW propagation is HYP. Worse for "radar": no source (Hively, Monstein & Wesley, Keyport, Zimmerman) gives an SLW reflection or scattering law. There is no SLW "radar cross-section", so nobody can predict what an SLW echo from a target would be (§1.3). What can be built is an SLW radar experiment. It uses a bistatic, through-the-cage link with a moving or rotating target in the path. It is judged by a control plan that separates any SLW claim from ordinary TEM leakage (§2.5). Think of it as "does a moving object modulate what reaches the sealed-cage receiver?" rather than "echo ranging". transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis The microwave-oven magnetron is a poor radar source. Its spectrum is noisy and swept, it restarts 60 times a second, and at about 2460 MHz it runs above the 13 cm amateur band edge. Radiating it in free space is not legal and not safe. Keep it only as an optional high-power source inside a sealed, interlocked test cavity (the oven itself), e.g. as the "monopole into a closed cavity" SLW source already listed in sim-lab sub-sources/REDO_SLW.md. Safety dominates the oven parts. The transformer and HV capacitor are lethal: nearly 4000 V exists in the circuit, and the capacitor holds its charge after unplugging. The magnetron must never radiate outside a shielded cavity. The magnetron ceramics may be beryllium oxide: never break or grind them. 1. Feasibility 1.1 What any radar needs (TEM FACT, Skolnik) transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis A radar sends a known signal, catches the part that comes back from a target, and measures delay (range), frequency shift (Doppler / speed) and angle. The classical requirements, from Skolnik, Introduction to Radar Systems, 2nd ed., McGraw-Hill 1980: Detection range comes from the radar equation, Eq. (1.7) (TEM FACT, not established for SLW): R_max = [P_t · G · A_e · σ / ((4π)² · S_min)]^(1/4) where P_t is transmit power, G the transmit gain, A_e the receive effective area, σ the target's radar cross-section, and S_min the minimum detectable signal. Gain and aperture are linked by Eq. (1.8), G = 4πA_e/λ². transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis The 1/4 power is the famous R⁻⁴ (two-way spreading). It is a TEM result. transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis Hively claims SLW power falls as 1/r² one way (Hively & Loebl 2019, Table I item 11: "The SLW free-space attenuation goes like 1/r²"; HYP). A two-way SLW path would then also be 1/r⁴ only if SLW scattered like TEM. Nothing in the sources says so (§1.3). transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis Speed comes from the Doppler shift, Eq. (3.2a): f_d = 2v_r/λ (TEM FACT). transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis Range with a CW system comes from frequency modulation (FM-CW). For triangular modulation at rate f_m over deviation Δf, the beat frequency is Eq. (3.11): f_b = 4R·f_m·Δf/c (TEM FACT). transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis Coherence. Doppler and FM-CW both need a clean, stable transmit signal and a copy of it (a reference) at the receiver (Skolnik §3.1 and §3.2; TEM FACT). transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis 1.2 What the kit and the oven parts provide ⚠ Rows/columns in this table that refer to TEM / classical / cage SE: transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis Need What Dan has Verdict Clean, stable, low-power coherent transmitter HackRF One: typical max TX power 13–15 dBm at 2170–2740 MHz (Great Scott Gadgets, hackrf.readthedocs.io "HackRF One"; FACT). It is half-duplex: it transmits or receives, not both at once (same docs; FACT). TinySA Ultra generator: hub FACT max −19 dBm (physics-constants.json); whether it reaches 2.45 GHz depends on firmware (check the wiki; ASSUMPTION). Good for a TEM baseline. Needs a separate receiver, because HackRF is half-duplex. Receiver TinySA Ultra: floor −102 dBm at 30 kHz RBW (measured at 30 MHz), about 10 dB worse above 2.5 GHz, and ULTRA mode above 800 MHz leaks LO at up to −10 dBm from its RF input (TinySA wiki; FACT, from rod-thermal notes). RTL-SDR (R820T) stops near 1.7 GHz (sim-lab sub-sources/VERIFY.md; unverified spec), so it can't see 2.45 GHz but covers 433.59 and 1296 MHz. Adequate for Doppler of a person at a few metres (TEM). TinySA zero-span gives amplitude only, not phase; phase-coherent Doppler needs an SDR receiver (HackRF #2 or similar) or an external mixer. Antennas Brass dipoles DD-433 / DD-1296 / DD-2450 (/workspace/sim-lab/rod-thermal/dipole-detector/), KB-1820 and KB-2016 spheres, sleeve-balun monopoles (hub), bifilar coil. Good for TEM (a dipole is 2.15 dBi). For the SLW experiment, use the hub's claimed SLW transmit geometry (skirt/sleeve-balun monopole, Hively; Keyport) and the caged receivers. High power Oven magnetron: LG 2M246-class, 2460 MHz with a matched load, 1150 W average into a matched load, 1000 W in a typical oven, 4.40 kV peak anode, half-wave doubler supply (LG/Pactra 2M246 datasheet, local sim-lab/home-motors/src/2M246.pdf; FACT). Poor for radar (noisy, swept, restarts every mains cycle; §2.1). Dangerous and not legal to radiate (§4). Use only inside a sealed cavity. Waveguide, cavity The oven's own waveguide launcher and cavity (with the 21 CFR 1030.10 interlocks). Useful only as a closed test cavity for the magnetron. Not a radar antenna. HV transformer, capacitor, diode Microwave-oven transformer (MOT), HV capacitor, HV diode (the half-wave doubler). Not needed for any low-power radar. They are a lethal hazard (§4). Leave them in the oven or retire them. TEM-rejecting receiver (the SLW discriminator) Dipole Detector cage estimate (dipole-detector/CAGE_ESTIMATE.md: 60 cm cube, or 100×60×60 cm for all bands); FX-1 driven Faraday sphere; RadioScreen tents (hub Experiment A); battery TinySA inside. Good. This is the part of Dan's program that makes an SLW test possible at all. Signal processing Laptop + HackRF I/Q; TinySA SD logs; Python (numpy) in sim-lab. Good (standard FFT Doppler and FM-CW beat analysis). 1.3 The honest physics limits SLW existence is HYP. Hively's 8 GHz copper-shield tests (Hively & Loebl 2019, pp. 120–121, Fig. 4) and Monstein & Wesley's 433 MHz rod-polarizer measurements (EPL 59(4), 514, 2002) are single-lab and not independently replicated. Zimmerman's longitudinal-A work (Nikolova & Zimmerman 2007; Zimmerman QEX 2011, MPLB 2011, JAP 2013) and the Works & Works 2012 QEX confirmation are related claims. Works & Works also discuss a conventional EM interpretation (hub library.html). All HYP. No SLW scattering law = no SLW radar equation. Hively & Loebl 2019 give interface continuity (Eq. 26, normal ∇C/μ). They do not give a transmission or reflection coefficient (sim-lab sub-sources/REDO_SLW.md §5, open item 5). Hively's patent and papers discuss SLW sources and receivers, never an SLW echo from a passive target. So a monostatic "SLW echo" cannot be predicted from any source. HYP gap, not an engineering gap. The source-coupling constant is unknown. Hively's radiated power, US 9,306,527 EQN. 15, P = (I²/4π)√(μ/ε), and Hively & Loebl 2019 Eq. (B5), assume an ideal irrotational driver. The erratum (Phys. Essays 32(3) 417) corrects Eq. 38/B5 to P_OUT = I² r̂ / [2 (4πr)²] · √(μ/ε), a power density in W/m² at range r (FACT; I = peak is an ASSUMPTION, confirmed by Dan Britton 2026-09-30). Total watts 4πr²·P_OUT = I² Z₀/(8π) is a DERIVED / ASSUMPTION quantity (spherical integral); the patent Eq. 15 total I² Z₀/(4π) is twice that (documented difference; the patent text above is quoted as printed). See P_OUT erratum audit). Sim-lab Experiment D writes the unknown fraction as η (expt-d/REPORT.md §1). At UHF, Experiment D found Dan-class receivers not detectable for any η ≤ 1 at ≥ 10 km (expt-d/REPORT.md line 144). At bench range the hub's own HYP model is more hopeful: SleeveBalunSNR, −19 dBm drive, gives E∥ = 1.50 mV/m at 10 m and 0.12 V/m at one wavelength at 2.45 GHz with the erratum form of Eq. 38/B5 (img/efield/efield_summary.json; HYP). Before 2026-09-29 the hub used the 2019 as-printed form without the ½, which gave 2.13 mV/m and 0.17 V/m (3.01 dB higher). Those are one-way numbers. A radar echo would multiply in an unknown reflection factor. SLW range law gives no radar advantage. Hively & Loebl 2019 (Table I item 11; §VI) claim 1/r² one way, the same as TEM far-field power. The claimed advantages are only that SLW is unconstrained by the skin effect and passes conductive barriers (HYP). A through-wall or through-cage "radar" is therefore the only kind that would show something TEM can't. transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis Material dependence under SLW is via σ only. Joule term J·E with J = σE (Hively & Loebl 2019 Eq. 44), or no loss at all (Erratum 2022, α = 0; Hively & Land IARD 2020 slides 59–60, "No SLW Attenuation in Conductive Media"). Sim-lab's per-metre Joule attenuation α_J = σ_H|Z|/2 is our construction, not Hively's, and it is convention-sensitive (REDO_SLW.md §1.2). It must not carry weight in a radar design. Conventional 2.45 GHz radar is TEM FACT. transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis It is an ordinary Hertzian/transverse system. Seeing an echo with it proves nothing about SLW. A 2.45 GHz echo that appears only when the cage is open is TEM. transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis That is exactly why the TEM baseline is Phase 1: it calibrates the gear and defines what "ordinary leakage" looks like. transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis Feasibility verdict: TEM radar: YES (bench, metres to tens of metres; FACT). transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis SLW radar in the strict sense (echo ranging): NOT SPECIFIABLE with current theory. The scattering law is missing, the source coupling η is unknown, and SLW itself is HYP. SLW radar-style experiment: YES, as a controlled test. A bistatic, caged-receiver, moving-target modulation test with a strong TEM-rejection control plan. A positive result would be a significant anomaly needing replication. A null result bounds η, the product of source coupling and wall transmission. transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis 2. Architecture Everything below is a bench design (1–10 m, indoors or in a garage). Two chains share one layout. Chain T (TEM baseline): ordinary radar, to calibrate and to define leakage. transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis Chain S (SLW attempt): same transmitter family; the receiver sealed in a Faraday cage; discriminating controls. Chain T (TEM FACT) Chain S (SLW = HYP) HackRF TX ──BPF──> DD-2450 / can antenna HackRF or TinySA TX ──> Hively sleeve/skirt-balun monopole (coded CW or FM-CW, 2400-2450 MHz) (same code; also a closed-loop "C=0" control antenna) │ target (person, fan, plate) │ moving/rotating target, M&W rod polarizer ▼ ▼ RX antenna ──> HackRF #2 / TinySA (open air) ┌──────── sealed Faraday cage (no cable crosses) ────────┐ │ DD dipole / KB sphere / E5 probe → TinySA on battery │ │ data: SD card (read after) or fibre via WBC tube │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ + outside TEM monitor antenna (to reject leakage) 2.1 Transmitter Primary: HackRF One in the 2400–2450 MHz part of the 13 cm amateur band, under Dan's license. Output is 13–15 dBm typical (GSC docs; FACT). Add a 2.4 GHz band-pass filter at the output. HackRF output is not band-limited, and §97.307(c) requires spurious emissions to be "reduced to the greatest extent practicable" (FACT, 47 CFR 97.307(c)). Filter part number not chosen (to source). Waveform: coded CW. On-off keying with a pseudo-random sequence, or a slow FM-CW ramp. A coded transmission lets the receiver correlate against a known pattern, so a claimed signal must carry the code. This is a strong defence against noise and interference (ASSUMPTION; standard coherent-radar practice, Skolnik ch. 3 and 11). FM-CW example: triangular modulation at f_m = 100 Hz over Δf = 50 MHz (the whole 2400–2450 MHz segment) gives beats of 67 / 200 / 667 Hz for targets at 1 / 3 / 10 m (Skolnik Eq. 3.11; slw-radar/radar_numbers.json; TEM FACT, not established for SLW). transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis Lower bands. 1296 MHz (Experiment A) and 433.59 MHz (Experiment B) reuse Dan's existing antennas and hub models. TinySA + Zeenko gives about +2 dBm (hub PHYSICS_LOCK.md:39). Doppler shifts at 1 m/s are 8.65 Hz (1296) and 2.89 Hz (433.59), against 16.34 Hz at 2450 (Eq. 3.2a). Optional high power: magnetron, only inside the closed oven cavity. Why it's a poor radar source (FACT): Oven magnetrons are driven by a half-wave doubler. The anode voltage is roughly a 4 kV square wave on one half of each mains cycle, and the anode current is swept from zero to about 1 A and back every cycle. This produces sideband noise and low-frequency noise (UNM Microwave Memo 23, Particle-in-Cell Modeling of Oven Magnetron: A Review, quoting the rectified-drive explanation). Near start-oscillation current the spectrum is "extremely noisy", and ovens repeat that start-up phase 60 times per second (Neculaes, Gilgenbach, Lau et al., Appl. Phys. Lett. 2003, doi:10.1063/1.1609040; journal details from the DOI, page not checked). Oven emission sweeps about 50 MHz and is gated to one half-cycle of 60 Hz (IEEE 802.11-98/240, as cited in REDO_SLW.md). Consequence: no stable reference, so there is no Doppler or FM-CW coherence (TEM FACT). transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis As an SLW source experiment (not a radar), the magnetron's output probe is an open-ended conductor into a closed cavity, which is Hively's monopole geometry (HYP; REDO_SLW.md §3.1). Its 60 Hz on/off gating gives a natural fingerprint for a caged receiver outside the oven (§2.5 control C8). 2.2 Receiver Chain T: HackRF #2 (I/Q, phase-coherent Doppler) or TinySA zero-span (amplitude envelope, enough for on/off and slow Doppler beats). RTL-SDR only for the 433.59 and 1296 MHz variants. Coherence between two separate SDRs needs a shared 10 MHz reference; HackRF has clock in/out (GSC docs; verify). Chain T is in open air, so a reference cable is fine there. Chain S (the SLW discriminator): Receiver inside a sealed Faraday cage. TinySA Ultra on its own battery with a DD dipole, a KB-1820/KB-2016 sphere, or the E5/H10 probe. Data saved to SD and read after opening, or sent out over all-dielectric fibre through a waveguide-below-cutoff tube soldered 360° to the wall. TE11 cutoff f_c = 1.841c/(πd), about 32 dB per diameter of length (Ott, Electromagnetic Compatibility Engineering, Wiley 2009, as used in expt-d/rxchain/REPORT.md; FACT). No reference cable can enter the cage. Coherent processing across the wall therefore needs either an independent disciplined clock on each side (GPS-disciplined oscillator; to source) or a reference sent in on fibre through the WBC tube (question for Dan, §5). Watch the TinySA's own LO leakage in ULTRA mode: it radiates inside a sealed reflective cage. Check with a 50 Ω load in place of the antenna (§2.5 control C5). Outside TEM monitor (mandatory): a second receiver with an ordinary antenna just outside the cage, logging at the same time. A "signal" that tracks the outside monitor is TEM leakage (ASSUMPTION of method; same idea as the reference channel in expt-d/rxchain/SHOPPING_LIST.md §c). transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis 2.3 Antenna and coupling: how the scalar/longitudinal aspect is attempted (all HYP) Hively's charge-accumulation source. The SLW is produced by an irrotational (gradient-driven) current with non-zero divergence, i.e. charge piling up where current must stop (Hively & Loebl 2019 App. B p. 123; Hively & Reed 2020 pp. 10–11; US 9,306,527; HYP). The monopole with a skirt or sleeve balun is the claimed transmitter (US 9,306,527; Paulus & Gentile, NUWC Keyport, US 12,525,711 B1, "Antennas with baluns for transmitting and receiving scalar longitudinal waves"). Keyport claim 30 adds a "resonant spark system" feed. Dan's hub sleeve-balun builds (sleeve-balun.html) already implement this. Closed-loop control: Hively & Loebl App. C say closed return currents give C = 0 (no SLW; HYP). A small loop driven at the same TEM power is the matching "no-SLW" transmitter. transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis Monostatic vs bistatic. Because no SLW echo law exists (§1.3), Chain S is bistatic: transmitter outside, receiver in the sealed cage. The "target" is placed in the path and moved, rotated or swapped. This measures modulation of the received SLW (if any), not an echo. Monstein & Wesley polarizer test (EPL 59(4) 514, 2002; hub monstein.html; HYP). A rod array between transmitter and receiver: δP = −σ A E₀² cos²φ δL (M&W Eq. 7) and transmission T = exp[−κ cos²φ] (M&W Eq. 9), κ_fit = 4.4 for brass λ/2 rods. Rotating the rods through 360° should give two dips per turn (180° periodicity). Material enters only through σ (brass about 3× tungsten W1 by σ; rod-thermal/README.md). Receivers already in Dan's program (HYP as SLW receivers): KB-1820 / KB-2016 spheres (Experiments A and B), the FX-1 driven Faraday sphere, DD-433/1296/2450 dipoles, and the bifilar coil cage. No SW receiver exists: the hub says one would need a loop / E-probe / bifilar triad (expt-d/REPORT.md line 147). SW is not testable with the current kit. 2.4 Signal processing (TEM FACT methods; applied to both chains) transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis Doppler: FFT of the received envelope or I/Q. Expected shifts at 2450 MHz are 1.63 / 8.17 / 16.34 / 81.72 Hz for 0.1 / 0.5 / 1 / 5 m/s (Eq. 3.2a). A slow ceiling fan or a person walking is easy to see in Chain T. FM-CW range: mix the received signal with the transmit reference, FFT the beat (Eq. 3.11). Chain T only, because it needs the reference. Coded-CW correlation (Chain S): record receiver power in time bins synchronised to the known on/off code, then correlate. A true detection must (a) correlate with the code, (b) survive every control in §2.5, and (c) not appear on the outside TEM monitor. Detection statistics come from repeated, blinded runs (ASSUMPTION of method). transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis Rotation analysis (M&W): fit received power vs rod angle φ to M&W Eq. 9 and test for 180° periodicity. See the confound note in §2.5. 2.5 Control plan: separating an SLW claim from ordinary TEM leakage transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis Every run is logged with timestamp, band, drive level, RBW, cage state and antenna. A claimed SLW signal must pass all of these. # Control What it checks Reading C1 Source-off baseline (TX powered but RF off, then TX unplugged) Receiver self-noise, ambient, TinySA spurs Establishes the floor. Required before and after every session. C2 Cage closed vs open Leakage through the wall TEM rises with the lid open by the cage SE (TEM FACT; SE only strips TEM noise). SLW passing the wall is HYP. A signal that appears only with the lid open is TEM. A signal equal in both states and absent on the outside monitor is the candidate. Cage SE is never used to rank SLW. C3 Outside TEM monitor (simultaneous) Is the "signal" just ordinary radio? If the outside monitor tracks it, it is TEM. C4 50 Ω dummy load at the transmitter (antenna replaced by a shielded load, same drive) Leakage from the TX box, cables and power leads Anything still received is leakage, not antenna radiation. C5 50 Ω load at the receiver (antenna replaced, inside the sealed cage) Receiver self-noise, TinySA LO re-radiation in ULTRA mode Anything still seen is internal. C6 Antenna swap: sleeve/skirt-balun monopole vs closed loop at equal TEM power Hively's C = 0 prediction for closed currents (App. C; HYP) HYP predicts a difference; TEM predicts only the ordinary pattern and gain difference, which Chain T measures. C7 M&W rod rotation, 0–360° in 15° steps, repeated T = exp[−κ cos²φ] (M&W Eq. 9); 180° periodicity Required but not sufficient. Confound (transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis): an array of parallel conducting rods is also an ordinary wire-grid polarizer for TEM, which gives two dips per turn too. The rotation test only discriminates with the receiver sealed (C2) and the outside monitor quiet (C3). C8 Fingerprint match Is it really from our source? The received signal must carry the TX code (coded CW), or, for the magnetron-in-cavity source, its 60 Hz half-cycle gating (16.7 ms repeat, about 50 % duty; IEEE 802.11-98/240). C9 Blind and randomised order Experimenter bias A helper sets TX on/off, cage state and rod angle from a random list. The analyst sees only file IDs. C10 Distance scan Near-field vs far-field behaviour Hively claims 1/r² for SLW one way (HL2019 Table I item 11). TEM far-field power is also 1/r², so this alone does not discriminate. Log it anyway to compare with the hub's SleeveBalunSNR HYP curve. C11 Target in/out and moving/still (the radar part) Does a target in the path modulate the caged signal? Chain T gives the TEM expectation. A Chain S modulation present with the lid closed, correlated with target motion and the TX code, and absent on the outside monitor, is the SLW-radar candidate. 2.6 What the TEM baseline should achieve (TEM FACT numbers, Skolnik) transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis From Skolnik Eqs. (1.7) and (1.8) at 2450 MHz (slw-radar/radar_numbers.json, computed in Python; WL compare owed): Assumptions: P_t = 13 dBm (HackRF), σ = 1 m² (ASSUMPTION), TinySA floor as S_min (SNR 0 dB, no losses). Half-wave dipole (2.15 dBi): ideal R_max ≈ 50 m at 30 kHz RBW, 118 m at 1 kHz, 210 m at 100 Hz. 15 dBi can or horn (ASSUMPTION): ≈ 221 / 517 / 920 m. These are ideal upper bounds. The TinySA floor is quoted at 30 MHz and is about 10 dB worse near 2.5 GHz, which cuts range to about 0.56×. With two half-duplex boxes, direct TX-to-RX leakage usually limits a bistatic CW radar long before the noise floor does (ASSUMPTION). Expect metres to a few tens of metres in practice. None of this is established for SLW. 3. Parts list The hobby kit contents are unknown (question for Dan). The table lists Dan's known gear from sim-lab and hub files, the oven parts, and what is missing. Prices are not checked here unless stated. 3.1 Dan's known gear ⚠ Rows/columns in this table that refer to TEM / classical / cage SE: transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis Item Role here Source in sim-lab / hub TinySA Ultra (at least 1; FX-1 mentions up to 3) Caged receiver on battery (Chain S); zero-span envelope receiver (Chain T); low-power generator (−19 dBm max, hub FACT) hub physics-constants.json; INVENTORY.md §6 HackRF One Primary TX (13–15 dBm at 2.17–2.74 GHz); I/Q receiver when not transmitting (half-duplex) sub-sources/VERIFY.md; GSC docs RTL-SDR 433.59 / 1296 MHz receiver or outside monitor (not 2.45 GHz) sub-sources/VERIFY.md Zeenko ZK06-UM amp +21 dB to reach about +2 dBm from the TinySA (433/1296) expt-d/rxchain/SHOPPING_LIST.md; hub PHYSICS_LOCK.md:39 Spheres KB-1820 (0.75 in) and KB-2016 (2.5 in), 3003 Al Experiment A/B antennas; caged receivers (HYP) hub index.html (Experiments A and B); fx1/wolfram/PHYSICS_LOCK.md Bifilar coil cage Existing caged coil receiver (HYP) rod-thermal README (cage-coil observation) Brass dipoles DD-433 / DD-1296 / DD-2450 TEM antennas; caged receivers (HYP) /workspace/sim-lab/rod-thermal/dipole-detector/ Tekbox E5 / H10 near-field probes Near-field probing inside the cage; leak hunting on seams hub probe factors (rod-thermal notes) IR thermometer Temperature logging (rods, magnetron cavity load), through a WBC tube dipole-detector/CAGE_ESTIMATE.md §7 NanoRFE VNA6000-A Antenna SWR, cage-seam S21, filter checks expt-d/rxchain/SHOPPING_LIST.md §c ("Dan already owns one") Sleeve-balun monopoles, RG-405, SMA parts Hively/Keyport-style SLW transmitter (HYP) hub sleeve-balun.html, tools.html Brass λ/2 polarizer rods (Experiment B) M&W rotation test (C7) hub monstein.html; rod-fixtures/README.md 3.2 Oven parts, mapped ⚠ Rows/columns in this table that refer to TEM / classical / cage SE: transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis Oven part Use in this project Recommendation Magnetron (e.g. LG 2M246-class, 2460 MHz, 1 kW class) Optional SLW source experiment inside the closed oven cavity only (C8 fingerprint). Not a radar transmitter. Keep it in the intact, interlocked oven. Never run it out of a cavity. Never break its ceramics. Waveguide launcher Part of the oven's closed microwave path Leave installed. Not an antenna. Cavity (with door and interlocks) The sealed test cavity for any magnetron run Use as-is, only if interlocks and door seals are intact (21 CFR 1030.10(c)(2)). Put a water load inside for any run (service manuals require one). HV transformer (MOT) None Do not use. Lethal. Leave in the oven or retire it. HV capacitor None Do not use. Holds a lethal charge after unplugging (§4). HV diode None Part of the lethal doubler; leave in place. Door choke, mesh window Instructive example of a working TEM choke (TEM FACT) Leave in the door. Turntable motor, fan, lamp Handy slow-motion target (turntable) for Chain T Doppler Low-voltage/mains parts only, used separately. 3.3 Missing or to be sourced (nothing bought) 2.4 GHz band-pass filter for the HackRF output (Part 97 spurious; §2.1). Part number not chosen. Second coherent SDR receiver (e.g. a second HackRF) or an external mixer and splitter for phase-coherent Doppler / FM-CW (Chain T). 10 MHz reference distribution (Chain T), or GPS-disciplined oscillators for the cross-wall timing question (Chain S). Sealed Faraday cage for the receiver: per dipole-detector/CAGE_ESTIMATE.md, about $155–420 in materials and 9–16 h to build. Includes a WBC tube (3/4 in Type L copper, 80 mm, about 128 dB by the Ott rule) and optional fibre-optic data link parts. 50 Ω SMA terminations: several, for C4/C5. A small closed-loop transmit antenna for C6 (easy to make from coax). Rotation stage with angle marks for C7 (the existing Lazy Susan plus a printed protractor). Calibrated microwave leakage survey meter, needed before any magnetron run. Service manuals list one (LG LSMC3089BD service manual lists a "Microwave survey meter – Holaday HI-1500"). Model and price to source. HV discharge probe: an insulated probe with a 10 kΩ series resistor to ground, as the LG service manual specifies. Only if the oven is ever opened. 4. SAFETY (read before touching the oven) Bottom line: for the radar work you do not need to open the microwave oven at all. Everything in Phases 1–3 runs on the HackRF/TinySA at milliwatt levels. The oven parts are optional, and the only acceptable use of the magnetron is inside its own sealed, interlocked cavity. 4.1 Lethal high voltage: transformer, capacitor, diode FACT: "SINCE NEARLY 4000 VOLTS EXISTS IN SOME CIRCUITS OF THIS UNIT REPAIRS SHOULD BE CARRIED OUT WITH GREAT CARE" (LG microwave oven service manual LSMC3089BD, Important Notes). FACT: the magnetron in this class runs at 4.40 kV peak anode, with the filament at about −4 kV (LG/Pactra 2M246 datasheet). The transformer secondary is commonly about 2 kV AC, doubled by the capacitor and diode (ASSUMPTION, typical; read your MOT nameplate). The HV capacitor keeps its charge after unplugging. The LG manual: wait at least one minute after disconnecting, then discharge the capacitor "BY USING INSULATED WIRE - I.E. TEST PROBE CONNECTED TO 10K-OHM RESISTOR IN SERIES TO GROUND" (FACT, LG LSMC3089BD). Rules (ASSUMPTION: standard HV practice, consistent with the manual): Unplug first. Discharge with a proper bleeder probe (10 kΩ, insulated, grounded lead). Discharge again. Assume it is charged until you have measured zero. Work one hand only, with the other hand away from the chassis. Never work on it live. No "quick tests" with the cover off. Don't work alone. Home MOT experiments (arcs, "MOT stacks") are widely reported as a cause of fatal shocks (ASSUMPTION: not sourced here). They are not part of this plan. 4.2 Microwave exposure FACT, 21 CFR 1030.10(c)(1): oven leakage "shall not exceed 1 milliwatt per square centimeter at any point 5 centimeters or more from the external surface of the oven, measured prior to acquisition by a purchaser, and, thereafter, 5 milliwatts per square centimeter at any such point." (The brief quoted "5 mW/cm² at 5 cm"; confirmed as the in-service limit, with 1 mW/cm² for new ovens.) FACT, 21 CFR 1030.10(c)(2): at least two safety interlocks, one concealed. Plus monitoring that disables the oven if an interlock fails. FACT, 47 CFR 1.1310 Table 1: the general-population MPE at 1,500–100,000 MHz is 1.0 mW/cm² averaged over 30 min (occupational/controlled: 5 mW/cm², 6 min). A 1 kW magnetron radiating out of a waveguide exceeds these limits by orders of magnitude close to the opening (ASSUMPTION, order-of-magnitude; not computed). The harm is RF heating: burns, and damage to eyes and deep tissue (ASSUMPTION: general safety knowledge, not sourced here). The hub's own lab page: "never look into an open waveguide" and "Do not cook a sealed cage" (hub-efield-repo/lab.html:240). Rule: the magnetron never radiates outside a shielded cavity. Only run it in an intact oven with a water load. Check leakage with a calibrated survey meter before trusting any setup. Never defeat an interlock. HackRF at 13–15 dBm is milliwatts. Normal RF-exposure evaluation still applies to any amplified station (47 CFR 1.1310). A 2.45 GHz amplifier is not in this plan. 4.3 Beryllium oxide in magnetron ceramics Some magnetron insulators are beryllium oxide (BeO) ceramic. It is inert when intact, but the dust is dangerous. FACT: a BeO ceramic SDS classifies it "Fatal if inhaled" (H330), "May cause cancer by inhalation" (H350i), and damaging to the respiratory system through repeated exposure (H372) (Materion, Beryllium Oxide Ceramic Product SDS). Whether a particular oven magnetron contains BeO usually can't be told by eye (ASSUMPTION), so treat every magnetron as if it does. Rules: Never break, drill, grind or sand the magnetron or its ceramic parts. If one cracks: stop, don't vacuum, wet-wipe fragments into a sealed bag, and take it to hazardous-waste disposal (ASSUMPTION: standard beryllium practice; check your county's rules). 4.4 FCC rules (legality of radiating) FACT, 47 CFR 18.107(c) and (g): microwave ovens are consumer ISM equipment. ISM means equipment that generates and uses RF energy locally for heating etc., "excluding applications in the field of telecommunication". FACT, 47 CFR 18.301: the ISM frequency is 2450 MHz ± 50 MHz. Reading (ASSUMPTION, not legal advice): radiating a magnetron into free space as a radar or signal source is not an ISM heating application, so Part 18 does not authorize it. It would need authority under another rule part. Part 97 (amateur): FACT, 47 CFR 97.301(a): Technician and higher licensees may transmit in the 13 cm band, 2300–2310 and 2390–2450 MHz. FACT, 97.303(e): amateurs receiving at 2400–2450 MHz must accept interference from ISM equipment. FACT, 97.307(a)–(c): emissions must use no more bandwidth than necessary, be "confined to the band", and spurious emissions must be "reduced to the greatest extent practicable". (97.307's numeric spurious limits cover only transmitters below 225 MHz.) An oven magnetron can't meet this: Its matched-load centre frequency is 2460 MHz, above the 2450 MHz band edge (LG/Pactra 2M246 datasheet). It sweeps about 50 MHz and is gated at 60 Hz (IEEE 802.11-98/240). Its sidebands are broad (UNM Memo 23; Neculaes et al. 2003). Verdict: not usable as an amateur transmitter (FACT for the frequency; ASSUMPTION for the overall compliance judgement; verify with ARRL Regulatory Information if Dan ever wants to go further). HackRF at 2400–2450 MHz under Dan's amateur license: legal in principle, with a band-pass filter and good practice (97.307(c)). Keep the FM-CW sweep inside 2400–2450 MHz. Experimental route: non-amateur high-power experiments normally go through an FCC Part 5 experimental license (ASSUMPTION; not researched here). Recommendation: the magnetron stays inside a sealed test cavity only. For a radar, use the HackRF. 5. Phased plan, milestones, open questions Phase 0: Safety and paperwork (1 evening) Decide whether the oven is opened at all. Default: no. Survey-meter plan for any magnetron run. Choose HackRF filter and frequencies (2400–2450 MHz; 1296 MHz; 433.59 MHz). Milestone M0: written run sheet with every §2.5 control, and a safety checklist signed off by Dan. Phase 1: Bench TEM baseline (Chain T; TEM FACT) (1–3 weekends) transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis HackRF TX (coded CW, then FM-CW) → DD-2450 or can antenna; TinySA / SDR receiver in open air. Targets: turntable, ceiling fan, a person walking, a metal plate. Measure Doppler (Eq. 3.2a), FM-CW beats (Eq. 3.11) and received level vs range. Compare with Eq. 1.7. Build the Dipole Detector cage (CAGE_ESTIMATE.md). Measure its TEM leakage at 2.45 GHz with the lid open and closed, known source outside. transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis M1a: Doppler of a walking person detected at ≥ 3 m. M1b: measured TEM cage leakage (lid open vs closed) at 433.59 / 1296 / 2450 MHz. Defines "ordinary leakage" for Phase 2 (used only to strip TEM, never to rank SLW). transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis M1c: C1, C4 and C5 floors recorded. Phase 2: Caged-receiver SLW tests (Chain S; HYP) (2–6 weekends) Transmitter outside: sleeve/skirt-balun monopole (Hively/Keyport), then a closed loop at equal TEM power (C6). Receiver sealed inside on battery. Outside TEM monitor running. transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis Run C1–C9 in blinded, randomised order at 1296 and 433.59 MHz (existing hub models), then 2450 MHz. M&W rod rotation (C7) between TX and the cage. Optional: magnetron in the intact oven with a water load as the source, caged receiver outside, looking for the 60 Hz fingerprint (C8) with the cage closed. Only after a survey-meter check. M2 (null or candidate): either an upper bound on η·(wall transmission) (a null result, still useful), or a candidate signal that passes all of C1–C9 and is reproduced on at least 3 separate days. A candidate is not a discovery. It triggers replication with a second cage and a second receiver, and an invitation to an outside ham to repeat it. Dan decides who; contact no one before then. Phase 3: Range and Doppler, the "radar" step (Chain S + targets; HYP) (only if M2 gives a candidate) Keep the bistatic geometry. Move a target (metal plate, then a person) in the path between the transmitter and the sealed cage. Look for coded-CW modulation correlated with target motion (C11). Compare against Chain T's TEM expectation for the same motion. transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis Distance scan (C10) and FM-CW attempt, if a cross-wall timing reference is solved (question Q4). M3: target-motion modulation seen with the cage closed, the outside monitor quiet, and every control passed. Only then is an "SLW radar" claim even worth writing up. Open questions for Dan Hobby kit contents: what exactly is in it (mixers, filters, amplifiers, Arduino/ADC, a second HackRF, GPSDO)? Oven parts: which oven and magnetron model? Is the oven intact with working interlocks, or already stripped? (If stripped, the magnetron has no safe cavity and should not be powered at all.) Goal: is the aim a real ranging/Doppler SLW radar, or an SLW detection test with radar-style signal processing? This brief recommends the second, because no SLW echo law exists. Cross-wall timing: may a timing reference enter the cage on fibre through a WBC tube (dielectric, no metal crossing)? Or must the cage side be fully free-running with its own clock? Band priority: start at 2450 MHz (the oven's band, best HackRF power) or at 1296 / 433.59 MHz (existing Experiment A/B hardware and hub models)? Magnetron as an SLW source: do you want the "magnetron in its own cavity, caged receiver outside" …

text: Simulation Lab report · SNR / detectors · faithful HTML conversion H 2S tickled-relaxation detector vs Experiment-A sphere at 1057.8 MHz: SNR comparison Desk comparison at 1057.8 MHz: the hydrogen 2S tickled-relaxation detector vs the Experiment A ¾″ sphere with LNA chains. Verdict: the atoms are worse at every field from 1 nV/m to 1 kV/m for every sphere chain with an LNA (55–122 dB gap). MIXED ← Simulation Lab catalogue Provenance /workspace/sim-lab/snr-2s-vs-sphere/NOTE.md (last modified 2026-09-25 20:18 EDT) /workspace/sim-lab/snr-2s-vs-sphere/results_tables.md (last modified 2026-09-25 20:18 EDT) Converted to HTML 2026-09-28 (EDT) as a faithful conversion: text, numbers, equations and labels are the source's own. No new equations were added; only the TEM tags described below and the edits listed here were made. Appendix, 'SNR at reference fields' table: the delimiter row was extended from 8 to 10 columns to match the header and rows (the source has an empty column between 'atom case' and 'sphere case'); no values changed. This side calculation was folded into the (unpublished, held) Experiment G v0.1 model; Experiment G itself is not published here. Status lines inside the source (for example "nothing published", "HELD", "draft") describe the state when it was written. This page is its GitHub Pages twin, published 2026-09-28. No Wolfram Cloud twin planned (analysis/report page, not one of Experiments A–G). Numbers are Python-computed; WL compare OWED where the source says so. Framing rules on this page (Dan). Under the SLW hypothesis no skin-depth, permeability, ferromagnetic or cage shielding-effectiveness argument is used to rank or dismiss SLW/SW. The Faraday cage strips TEM noise (FACT); an SLW passing the cage wall is HYP. Every passage that uses transverse-EM (TEM / classical / cage-SE) reasoning is tagged transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis. FACT / HYP / ASSUMPTION labels are kept exactly as in the source. Downloads results.json (compare.py output) Written Fri 25 Sep 2026 (ET). This is a desk calculation only: nothing was published, sent, bought or pushed. Every number below is recomputed by compare.py, which writes results.json and results_tables.md. The openEMS antenna runs are in openems/. Tags: FACT = published and cited. HYP = the SLW hypothesis. ASSUMPTION = our modelling choice. "Ours" = arithmetic done with a cited formula. Verdict The atoms are worse, by a very large margin, at every field from 1 nV/m to 1 kV/m, for every sphere chain that has an LNA. Field needed for SNR = 1 in 1 s: comparison atoms sphere gap (field dB, 20·log) realistic: atom numbers demonstrated in the lab (N_2S 5×10⁷, ε 2×10⁻⁶), 10 nm filter, demonstrated stray-field level vs the modelled ¾″ sphere into 50 Ω with a ZX60-P33ULN+ LNA 49.6 mV/m 37.2 nV/m 122 dB same atoms vs the same sphere on a TinySA Ultra alone (internal LNA on) 49.6 mV/m 69.2 nV/m 117 dB best physical: N 10¹², ε 0.039, 10 nm filter vs the best sphere (λ²/4π aperture, NF_sys 0.6 dB) 185 µV/m 16.5 nV/m 81 dB the brief's optimistic case: N 10¹², ε 0.3, 10 nm filter vs the best sphere 111 µV/m 16.5 nV/m 77 dB ideal bound: N 10¹², ε 0.3, a filter that passes only the Lyα line, 290 K vs the best sphere 29.2 µV/m 16.5 nV/m 65 dB the same ideal bound in a 4 K radiation shield with no stray field vs the best sphere 9.77 µV/m 16.5 nV/m 55 dB Integration time. When background dominates, the atoms improve as E_th ∝ t^−¼, while the sphere improves as t^−½. So every factor of 10 in averaging time widens the gap by another 5 dB (table in results_tables.md). Crossover. There is none against any sphere chain that has an LNA, with either SNR convention, anywhere up to 1 kV/m. The only crossovers are against the sphere on a TinySA with its LNA off (NF 27.2 dB). They appear only in the σ-convention (defined under "SNR ratio" below), and only for the idealized atom cases A4–A6.
