text: Simulation Lab report · submarine sources · faithful HTML conversion REDO_SLW.md: submarine SLW/SW source survey, redone for SLW/SW propagation only Submarine-borne SLW/SW source survey, redone for SLW/SW propagation only (the earlier TEM-ranked batch is superseded and not published). Joule-loss audit, three readings (Joule-as-assumed, Hively-text-literal, Erratum α=0), rankings, and the 2.45 GHz cage verification steps. MIXED ← Simulation Lab catalogue Provenance /workspace/sim-lab/sub-sources/REDO_SLW.md (last modified 2026-09-26 07:24 EDT) /workspace/sim-lab/sub-sources/redo_slw_numbers.md (last modified 2026-09-26 07:22 EDT) Updated 2026-09-30: author-confirmed note, and the two open items on the exponent marked resolved (no other change). Converted to HTML 2026-09-28 (EDT) as a faithful conversion: text, numbers, equations and labels are the source's own. No new equations were added; only the TEM tags described below and the edits listed here were made. Appendix table A: the vertical bars in the header cells |Z| and |η| were escaped so the Markdown table renders; no values changed. §8: one internal process bullet about an unsent internal summary draft was omitted (outbound/internal drafts are excluded from Pages). Batch-1 files (SOURCES.md, SUMMARY.md, VERIFY.md) are superseded and are not published. Status lines inside the source (for example "nothing published", "HELD", "draft") describe the state when it was written. This page is its GitHub Pages twin, published 2026-09-28. No Wolfram Cloud twin planned (analysis/report page, not one of Experiments A–G). Numbers are Python-computed; WL compare OWED where the source says so. Framing rules on this page (Dan). Under the SLW hypothesis no skin-depth, permeability, ferromagnetic or cage shielding-effectiveness argument is used to rank or dismiss SLW/SW. The Faraday cage strips TEM noise (FACT); an SLW passing the cage wall is HYP. Every passage that uses transverse-EM (TEM / classical / cage-SE) reasoning is tagged transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis. FACT / HYP / ASSUMPTION labels are kept exactly as in the source. FACT, author-confirmed Author-confirmed, 2026-09-30. In a private email from Dr. Hively to Dan (2026-09-30), Dr. Lee Hively confirmed the charge-relaxation exponent: "The form, E = E0 e^(-sigma t/epsilon), is the correct one." So Eq. (A5), p. 122 of Hively & Loebl 2019, and the exponent before EQN. 12 in US 9,306,527 B1 (col. 5), which print e^(−εt/σ), have ε and σ swapped (typos as printed). The correct form is E = E0 exp(−σt/ε) with relaxation time τ = ε/σ, and IARD 2020 slide 60 is correct. See the Corrections log. The two open items below that flag the hub's exponent as a typo are now resolved: the hub page was fixed in PR #58 (2026-09-26), and the author confirmed the form. Downloads redo_slw_numbers.json Simulation Lab · sub-sources · 2026-09-26 (EDT) · literature and reasoning only. Nothing sent, published, pushed or merged. SYNC_LEDGER.md untouched. Labels: FACT: textbook, measured, or peer-reviewed mainstream. HYP: published Hively / Monstein / scalar-wave hypothesis or claim. ASSUMPTION: our modelling choice. SPECULATION: no published backing. No new physics equations. Every equation is either quoted from the source named next to it or is an existing line of the Experiment G code (/workspace/sim-lab/expt-g/sim/expt_g_model.py). Numbers come from redo_slw_numbers.py, saved as redo_slw_numbers.json and redo_slw_numbers.md. 0. What changed and why The error. Batch 1 (SOURCES.md, SUMMARY.md, VERIFY.md) ranked sources partly on TEM losses: TEM seawater skin depth, TEM hull absorption, and TEM cage shielding. It then put the 2.45 GHz magnetron last, citing "~95,000 dB/100 m". transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis Dan's target is SLW and SW only. In Hively's framework these have no eddy-current or skin-effect loss (HYP; Hively & Loebl 2019 p. 117; Erratum 2022; US 9,306,527 cols. 5–7). So TEM figures are irrelevant here and are no longer used to rank or dismiss anything. Eq. 44 is a local energy balance with four kinds of term: storage (B², C², E²); flux (E×B/μ, plus the SLW flux CE/μ); Joule work J·E; a source ρC/(εμ). It contains no attenuation constant and no length scale. Hively's own text says field energy is constant through any sphere (p. 115–116). It says attenuation in conductive media is "future work" (p. 120). The Erratum says the J·E term cancels once the other terms are substituted. Verdict: Eq. 44 alone cannot give a per-metre attenuation without added steps that are not in the source. HYP (source text) + ASSUMPTION (our reading). (b) The added steps our α_J needed (all ASSUMPTION unless marked): The flux. Treat CE/μ as the only energy flux of the SLW. B = 0 removes E×B/μ (HYP, Eq. 27). Impedance, magnitude only. Replace C/μ by E/|Z| using Eq. 37, keeping only the magnitude of Z. This fixes both the E-to-flux relation and the phase convention (see d). E∥ definition. Take J·E = σE∥² with E∥ = E_L, the radial field of the Eq. 37 spherical wave, and J_L = σE_L. The E_L = J_L/σ relation is Hively's (p. 117, HYP). Using σ = σ_H = ε₀ε″ω, which includes dipolar loss, is Hively's definition (HYP). Drop the source term. Discard ρC/(εμ) and the time-averaged storage terms. This is the decisive invented step: the Erratum says ρC/(εμ) cancels J·E exactly. Far field and local plane wave. Set kr → ∞ in Eq. 37 and treat the loss as a local exp(−2αr) on the flux. Spreading is handled separately. Then flux loss per metre = σ_H|Z| (in power), so α_J = σ_H|Z|/2 (in field). This is the existing Expt G code line (water()), and it is our construction, not Hively's. Reading (HYP): the source is an irrotational charging current where current must stop: open ends, gaps, capacitive terminations. The insulator as such plays no role; the patent says the jacket "may make no difference". Strength would scale with the charging current, i = C dv/dt (FACT circuit law). Negative case (HYP): closed return currents give C = 0 (Hively & Loebl App. C; Hively & Reed p. 9). Mainstream counterpoint (FACT): Bray & Britton 2004: the radial current density must vanish at the conductor surface. Retarded potentials satisfy the Lorenz condition under charge conservation. 5. Verification checklist for Dan's 2.45 GHz cage reading (no TEM-based dismissals) transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis Standing rules: No cable crosses the cage wall. The battery is inside. Data leaves by fiber. Nothing modifies or opens an oven. We contact nobody. The Steve Morris comparison is Dan's own. Classical alternative to rule out experimentally, not by a propagation argument: ordinary TEM leakage through seams, apertures or penetrations of the cage. Steps 4–7 test for it directly. transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis 50 Ω swap (TinySA spurs). Replace the sphere with a 50 Ω load at the amp input, then at the TinySA input: same settings, same place, closed cage. Above ~800 MHz the TinySA Ultra generates "various mirrors and spurs" and LO leakage "up to -10dBm" (tinySA wiki; FACT). If the feature stays with the load, it is internal. Also run the amp alone, terminated, to catch ZK06-UM oscillation. Internal emitters. Power the inside instruments one at a time (fiber converter, battery booster, TinySA CPU). Change RBW and span: spurs move with settings, real signals do not. Magnetron fingerprint. Use HackRF or TinySA zero-span/waterfall, time-stamped. Look for: (i) 2.45 GHz present only in one half of each 60 Hz cycle (16.7 ms repeat, ~50 % duty; IEEE 802.11-98/240), or 8.3 ms alternation for dual-magnetron ovens; (ii) a ~50 MHz intra-cycle sweep and warm-up drift; (iii) at reduced power, a 32 s-class on/off envelope (Sharp manuals); (iv) no 60 Hz gating if the local oven is an inverter type (20–50 kHz; Panasonic). Compare with Wi-Fi (20 MHz OFDM, 102.4 ms beacons) and Bluetooth (1 MHz hops). A feature locked to the local mains half-cycle is the oven signature, whatever the path. Router and oven off. Router off, phones in airplane mode, household oven unplugged; log times. Optionally run the unmodified oven normally (a cup of water), with times logged, to see if the feature follows it. Cage SE check at 2.45 GHz. Battery TinySA plus sphere or E5 inside, logging to SD. Known 2.45 GHz source outside (HackRF) at 1–3 m. Measure door open vs closed. Seam-coupon S21 with the NanoRFE VNA outside the cage. transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis Seam bonding. Add continuous conductive-adhesive copper tape or more clamps along the rolled overlap, then repeat steps 5 and 3. If the feature falls as SE rises, it is leakage. transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis Nothing crosses; nothing noisy inside. No USB, chargers or metal-sheathed fiber at the wall. No USB 3 devices running inside. Move and rotate the cage. Room standing waves change with position. Sphere vs dummy vs 50 Ω. Only the connected sphere should show the feature. E5 vs H20 (first HYP-specific test). Same spot, then rotate each through 90°. HYP: an SLW has B = 0, so E5 responds and H20 does not. A TEM leak or cavity mode shows both, orientation-dependent. Near a small internal source E/H ≠ 377 Ω, so a lone E response is not proof by itself. transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis Material test (distinguishes the three readings). A water layer or tank between the source and the cage, varying thickness and salinity: (a1) predicts 953 dB/m at 2.45 GHz; (b)/(c) predict 1/r only; the (a3) sensitivity predicts ~7.9 mm 1/e. Timestamped comparison with Steve Morris (Dan arranges it). Both stations log GPS/NTP-stamped spectra with the same span, RBW and windows. Compare event times, spectral shape and gating period, and whether each station tracks its own local router or oven. No propagation argument is used to pre-judge a common source. Under (b)/(c) distance only adds 1/r. Correlation at matching times with matching instrument models means a shared-artefact check first (same firmware spur, mains-synchronous gating at both sites). Tracking of local sources means local leakage or local SLW. Only a feature that passes steps 1–11 at both sites and is not explained by local sources or instruments is interesting. 6. Open questions Which propagation reading is right? (a1), (a3), (b) and (c) differ by up to ~7 orders of magnitude in 1/e length at ELF. That is a spread in modelling conventions; there are no data to decide between them. Only a controlled material test (step 11; Expt G pool mockup) can separate them. No Hively text supplies a per-metre SLW attenuation. Should the hub's Joule default stay? It is Dan's standing rule. §1.2 shows it is our construction, contradicted by the Erratum's cancellation and convention-sensitive. Dan may want to relabel it "pessimistic bound (ours)" rather than "Hively's Joule term". Decision for Dan; nothing changed here. SLW source-term magnitude: unknown for every device. Hively's EQN. 15 (P ∝ I²) applied to ordinary charging currents would make every power system a kW-class emitter (batch-1 MECHANISM §3). No independent report exists. Charge conservation: Hively's own □²C = 0 (patent EQN. 9) and Rentzber 2026 imply zero scalar sourcing by charge-conserving devices. Unresolved within EED. Interfaces (Eq. 26): no transmission coefficient is given for water→steel→air. Hull and cage transmission under (b)/(c) is assumed ≈ 1 (HYP), not derived. Background: under (c), every oven, drive and grid on Earth, plus lightning, is SLW background. No estimate exists. Hub typo (RESOLVED): experiment-c.html wrote "E ∝ exp(−ε t/σ)" where Hively's slide has e^(−σt/ε). Fixed in PR #58 (2026-09-26); author-confirmed 2026-09-30. 7. description: Plain-English guide to the vector network analyzer (VNA): what Zimmerman, Hively and others measured with one, with page citations, and how to use Dan's NanoRFE VNA6000-A on Experiments A, B and C, with button-by-button steps from the manual.
text: Simulation Lab · VNA guide for Steve · 2026-10-03 · vna-guide-v0.1 Using a VNA on our kit: what others measured, and how to do it with Dan's NanoRFE VNA6000-A A plain-English guide for Steve. Part 1 says what a VNA is. Part 2 tells you where to start. The tabs below hold the details: what other researchers measured with a VNA (with page and figure numbers), Dan's exact VNA and whether it reaches our frequencies, how it maps onto Experiments A, B and C, button-by-button steps from the maker's manual, and the manuals and videos. MIXED ← Simulation Lab catalogue · Kit page: VNA6000-A · Three readings of SLW loss · Equation map How to read the labels. FACT = stated in the named source (page or figure given). HYP = a hypothesis (for example an author's reading of what a signal means). Not established physics. IDEA = our suggestion for the bench; it is not from a source. NOT STATED = the source does not say. We do not guess. Numbers on this page are copied from the sources or from the maker's manual and data sheet; the only arithmetic we add is marked "our arithmetic". 1. What a VNA is, and why we use it A VNA (vector network analyzer) is a test box for radio parts. It sends a small, known radio signal into a part and measures what happens to it. Think of it as a sound-and-echo tester: What bounces back (the echo) tells you how well the part is matched to the 50 Ω cable. That is called S11. What comes out the far end tells you how much signal the part lets through. That is called S21. "Vector" means it measures both the size of the signal (in dB) and its timing (phase), at many frequencies in one sweep. Why we use it. Our experiments hunt very small signals. Before a run it helps to know that each antenna feed (sphere, stub, sleeve balun), cable and filter behaves the way you think at the frequency you care about. IDEA A bad connector or a mismatched feed can add or hide signal, and a VNA shows that in seconds. How it differs from the TinySA Ultra. The TinySA is a spectrum analyzer: it listens to what is in the air or on a cable. The VNA tests a part: it sends its own signal and measures how the part passes or reflects it. The hub's kit page says the same: the TinySA is the on-air listener and generator, the VNA is the characterization tool (kit.html#vna6000). Words you will see (plain meanings) DUT Device under test: the part you are measuring (a sphere feed, a cable, a filter). Port An SMA connector on the VNA. The VNA6000 has two. Port 1 does the echo measurement (S11). Port 2 receives what passes through (S21). The manual calls them CH0 (reflection) and CH1 (through) (manual p.16). 50 Ω The standard "size" of the cable and the ports. A part that is not 50 Ω at the test frequency sends some of the signal back as an echo. dB (decibel) A way to count ratios. Every 10 dB is a factor of 10 in power: −10 dB is one tenth, −20 dB is one hundredth, −3 dB is about half. A minus sign means "less than what went in". S11 (reflection) How much of the test signal comes back from the part, in dB. 0 dB means all of it comes back (nothing absorbed or radiated). The more negative, the better the match. Return loss The same echo measurement quoted as a positive number: a return loss of 20 dB is an S11 of −20 dB. Bigger is better. SWR Standing wave ratio: another way to say how big the echo is. 1.0 is perfect; bigger is worse. Radio people quote it for antennas. S21 (transmission) How much of the signal gets from port 1 through the part to port 2, in dB. 0 dB means all of it. −3 dB means about half. Often called insertion loss when the part is a filter or cable. Smith chart A round chart that plots a part's impedance (resistance plus reactance) as a dot. The centre is a perfect 50 Ω match; the outer edge is total echo. You can ignore it at first: the dB and SWR views are enough to start. Sweep The VNA steps from a start frequency to a stop frequency and plots the result across the whole range. Calibration (open, short, load, thru) Measuring parts whose behaviour is known so the VNA can subtract its own cable and connector errors. The place where you calibrate is the "reference plane", the spot the VNA treats as zero. Echo size in plain numbers Textbook definitions, our arithmetic (SWR = (1+g)/(1−g) with g = 10^(−RL/20)). Use this to turn a return-loss reading into "how much power is coming back". Return loss (dB) S11 (dB) Power reflected Power accepted by the part SWR 6 −6 25.1 % 74.9 % 3.01 10 −10 10.0 % 90.0 % 1.92 15 −15 3.2 % 96.8 % 1.43 20 −20 1.0 % 99.0 % 1.22 25 −25 0.3 % 99.7 % 1.12 30 −30 0.1 % 99.9 % 1.07 Cross-check from a source: Zimmerman's QEX article says a 3 dB pad gives a return loss of 6 dB, "for an SWR of 3" (QEX July/August 2011, p.32). That matches the first row. The hub has no stated pass mark for S11; Dan decides what is good enough. For scale, the sources report: a bias-tee with return loss better than 25 dB (MPLB p.650 footnote), a transmitting monopole at about −16 dB (CEM-R-46 p.23), a folded dipole at −15 dB (CEM-R-46 p.25), and Hively's balun at −22 dB in the patent and a 23 dB null in the paper (see the Hively rows below). 2. Where do I start? Pick the box that matches what you want to do. Each one jumps to the right tab. AI want to use the VNA nowButton-by-button: set the sweep, calibrate, measure S11 or S21, save. BIs this the right VNA, and does it reach our frequencies?Short answer: yes for 433.59 MHz, 1296 MHz and 2450 MHz. No for 8 GHz. CWhat do I measure on Experiment A, B or C?Sphere feed, stub or sleeve balun, cables, the filter, the rod cube, and the cage rule. DWhat did the other researchers do with a VNA?Zimmerman, Hively, Monstein and Wesley, and the rest, with page and figure numbers. First session in six lines (details in tab A) Put the two SMA connector savers on the two ports and leave them on. Open the menu (tap an empty spot on the screen) and set the sweep: STIMULUS → START and STOP. Calibrate at the end of the cable you will measure through: CAL → RESET → CALIBRATE, then OPEN, SHORT, LOAD, DONE. Connect the part. Show S11 as LOGMAG or SWR. Move a marker to the dip (the best match) and write down the frequency and the dB. Save the calibration (CAL → SAVE) and photograph the screen for your log. Three rules before you plug anything in. Limits. Never put more than +10 dBm (10 mW) of RF, or more than 5 V DC, into either port (manual p.3; data sheet p.2). Do not connect a transmitter, an amplifier output or a DC-biased tube straight to a port. IDEA If you are unsure of a source's level, put a fixed attenuator in line first. The Faraday cage. No cable crosses the cage wall (Dan's standing rule). VNA measurements of parts happen outside the cage. Inside, only a battery-powered VNA with the USB cable unplugged, and never during a real listen: the VNA sends its own test signal (typically −10 dBm, data sheet p.3), which is far stronger than the faint signals we hunt. For the framing: the cage strips ordinary transverse-EM (TEM) noise (FACT); whether an SLW passes the cage wall is HYP. A VNA reading of a part does not test that either way. Test signal on an antenna. A VNA sweep sends its test signal across the whole range you set. The hub says on-air work at 23 cm and 70 cm needs a licence. IDEA With an antenna connected, keep the sweep narrow and the level low, or use a dummy load, and check your local rules. This page is not legal advice. What others measured with a VNA Short answer. Dan's hunch is right: the Zimmerman papers are the ones where a VNA is the main instrument, and S11 and S21 are the data. In our library that is three papers: Nikolova & Zimmerman (2007), Zimmerman's Modern Physics Letters B paper (2011) and his Journal of Applied Physics paper (2013). Zimmerman's QEX article is a how-to that talks about return loss and SWR but reports no VNA measurement. Hively's patent names a VNA model and the 2019 Hively & Loebl paper plots S21 and S12, but that paper's text does not name the instrument. Monstein & Wesley (2002) and Butterworth et al. (2013) did not use a VNA (a log detector with a voltmeter, and a USB spectrum analyzer). Summary table Page numbers: "p." is the journal page where the journal's page numbers are printed on the copy we have; "PDF p." counts pages of the file. Figure and equation numbers are the papers' own. Scanned papers were read by text recognition (OCR), so those rows say "none found" rather than "none". Source VNA used? An "E-Field scanner" was used Scanner images of radiation from the balun for two balun positions (Figs. 1B and 2B) PDF p.11 (detailed description) FACT Other papers in the hub library Chiao et al. arXiv 2013: yes (HP 8720C), but at 11.5 GHz. Others: none found Chiao et al. 2013: S21 resonance of a TE112 cavity mode near 11.50 GHz, then a splitting of about 400 MHz with a wire inserted. Chiao 2007 only plans a network-analyzer study. The rest of the library (Tomilin 2021, Chiao 2017 and 2023, the NASA report, Hubler 2023, Hively 2026, Yue 2021, US 12,562,930 and others): none found Chiao 2013 PDF p.9 FACT "None found" for Hively & Land 2021, the Keyport patent and the other library papers means a text search of the copies we hold found no VNA, S11 or S21 measurement. It is not proof the authors did not use one. Details by paper Nikolova & Zimmerman 2007 (CEM-R-46): VNA used, S21 and return loss FACT Setup (Fig. 3, PDF p.19). A transmit folded dipole, a propagation path, a fluorescent U-tube detector, a bias-tee, a current-regulated supply, a 30 dB amplifier in the RF path, and a vector network analyzer. A 50 Ω coax carries both the RF to the VNA port and the DC bias, separated by the bias-tee (PDF p.21). FACT Instrument. "an Advantest VNA R3765CG" (PDF p.21). VNA output power "set at 5 dBm" (PDF p.20). FACT What they did with it. Measured the complex S21 with a positive and then a negative DC bias, and formed the sum and difference: S_A = 0.5 (S21+ − S21−) and S(E,H) = 0.5 (S21+ + S21−) (Eq. 70, PDF p.22). They state that a VNA is "a phase-coherent system" that allows this. FACT Frequencies and results. 1.1 to 1.5 GHz. In a compact anechoic chamber at 1.2 to 1.5 m with no amplifier, the transmitting monopole's "return loss is minimum at 1.22 GHz and is about −16 dB" (PDF p.23). Magnitude and phase of S21 at 1.2 m are in Figs. 7 and 8 (PDF p.23 to 24). The measured S_A at 1.3 GHz and 1.2 m is −59.7 dB against a calculated −56.7 dB (PDF p.24). FACT In the open. A folded dipole fed through a 4:1 balun, "reflection loss is −15 dB at about 1.21 GHz", with an amplifier of 29 to 30 dB gain and data every 25 cm (Fig. 10, PDF pp.25 to 26). FACT Balun remark. Power-type signals "may be picked up by the feed coaxial lines … if the feed baluns are not well tuned" (PDF p.22). That is the reason to check a balun with a VNA. FACT Their estimate for 3 m is an S21 of about −65 dB, "well above the noise level of the system" (PDF p.21). HYP The authors read the bias-dependent part of S21 as a "potential signal" (vector potential). That interpretation is theirs and is not settled physics. Zimmerman 2011 (MPLB): VNA used, S11 and S21 across 1280 to 1380 MHz FACT Setup (Fig. 1, p.650). A 3 m long, 17.78 cm diameter circular copper waveguide excited by a centred coaxial probe at the head. A folded mercury-vapour plasma tube (a compact fluorescent lamp) at the far end is the detector. VNA port 1 feeds the probe. The tube connects through a bias-tee to VNA port 2 (p.650). The DC bias polarity is reversed with a switch. FACT Calibration. "The experimental data are taken with a full 2-port calibration of the VNA and cables with reference loads, shorts, and opens traceable to NIST" (p.653). FACT What was plotted (Fig. 5a, p.654). |S11|² at the top, the calculated (1 − |S11|²) below it, and |S21|² at the bottom for both bias polarities, 1280 to 1380 MHz. When losses are present, (1 − |S11|²) exceeds |S21|². The negative-bias S21 has a mean of −16.5 dB ± 1.0 dB; the positive-bias curve is some 5 dB lower; both S21 curves are anti-correlated with (1 − |S11|²) (p.653). FACT Control. A copper mock-up of the tube was measured instead (Fig. 5b, 5c): its S21 does not split with bias current and tracks (1 − |S11|²) (p.653). This is a good habit: swap in a dummy and see what the VNA shows. FACT Free-space tests. Open-ended waveguides at 1.5, 6 and 25 m with phase data; the VNA output was +10 dBm for the waveguide test and the 1.5 m test, and an external amplifier at +20 dBm was used for 6 and 25 m (pp.655 to 658). The conclusion lists that A and E "may be individually calculated from amplitude/phase data collected with a VNA" (Eqs. 3a, 3b; p.658). FACT A bias-tee used here had "return loss … < −25 dB from 1 GHz to 1.48 GHz" and an RF insertion loss of −0.04 dB (footnote, p.650). HYP The split into Az and Ez components, and the Aharonov-Bohm reading, are the author's interpretation. Copy note. The hub's library copy of this paper carries the publisher's "re-use … strictly not permitted" stamp, so this guide links the publisher's DOI page and not the PDF. Zimmerman 2013 (J. Appl. Phys.): network analyzer used, S21 magnitude and phase at 1300 MHz FACT Setup (Figs. 1 to 3, pp.044907-2 and -3). A transmitting monopole with a quarter-wave-radius reflector at 1300 MHz, aimed at an NE-2 neon bulb 2 m away. DC bias reaches the bulb through a bias-tee with 0.04 dB insertion loss and more than 25 dB isolation. FACT How the VNA was used. "The monopole is driven with 1 mW of RF power (0 dBm). With this power level as a reference, the network analyzer display may be read directly in dBm" (p.044907-3). FACT Fig. 4: S21 for both bias polarities (bias current 8.8 mA). The two traces differ by more than 10 dB at the centre frequency; the mean received power is −52 dBm (p.044907-3). FACT Fig. 5: phase. The RF phase reverses when the bias current is reversed. The plot is 360 degrees per division, centre 1300 MHz, span 50 MHz, with "a port extension of 73 ns" on port 1 to "unwind" the phase (p.044907-3). FACT Fig. 7: the gain antenna. With the bulb a quarter wave in front of a planar reflector, the VNA S21 plot (Fig. 7) shows about a 6 dB improvement (p.044907-4). FACT The paper says signal levels were "confirmed for R = 2, 50, and 100 meters" (p.044907-4). Which instrument was used at 50 and 100 m is NOT STATED. FACT A worked mismatch example (not a VNA reading): a bulb of 8522 Ω on a 50 Ω cable has a voltage reflection coefficient of 0.9885 (Eq. 14, p.044907-2). That is the same idea as S11, taken to the extreme. HYP The paper reads the phase reversal as "a cardinal sign of vector potential detection". That is the author's claim. Copy note. AIP's copyright notice is stamped on each page, so this guide links the publisher's DOI page and not the hub copy. Zimmerman 2011 (QEX): a how-to, no VNA measurement FACT A 3 dB pad on the coax to the waveguide "will provide a return loss of 6 dB for an SWR of 3" (p.32). The text warns that a zero-ohm load "will yield an infinite SWR" on the transmitter's cable, so a pad (or a circulator) protects the transmitter (p.32). FACT The lamp tube carries the received current "similar to a parallel transmission line" out to a coax and on to the receiver (p.31). The MPLB paper puts a number on that line: 125 Ω, against the 50 Ω cable, so the mismatch reflection is (50 − 125)/(50 + 125) = −0.43 (MPLB p.653). FACT A bias-tee design at 1296 MHz built on a 50 Ω quarter-wave stub with two 1000 pF capacitors, one to block DC from the receiver line and one to bypass the stub's cold end (p.34). About −400 V DC is momentarily needed to ignite the tube (p.33). The text says the report is based on the MPLB paper. No S-parameter measurement is reported. Scanned copy; read by OCR. Works & Works 2012 (QEX): no VNA FACT Test range at 1296.1 MHz with antenna mounts 15.2 m apart; a Flex-3000 SDR receiver with S-meter averaging; 21.6 dBm transmit power available; over 500 measurements; EZNEC models (PDF pp.1 to 2). FACT "An isolator at the transmit mount provides low SWR on the transmit feed line" (PDF p.1). No VNA or S11 is reported. Monstein & Wesley 2002 and Butterworth et al. 2013: no VNA FACT M&W 2002: the rod-cube test (Fig. 3) is a measured transmission coefficient T at 433.59 MHz against the angle φ, with the curve T = exp[−κ cos²φ], κ = 4.4 (Eq. 9; pp.516 to 517). The instrument for Fig. 3 is NOT STATED. FACT M&W 2002 Rhine test: a Trio TR-9500 transmitter on a 12 V car battery, triggered by a 1 s oscillator so each cycle includes a quiet reference; receiver = ball antenna + LNA435 low-noise amplifier + AD8307 logarithmic RF detector + digital voltmeter, with a PICO-ADC10 analog-to-digital converter to a PC and GPS positions (p.518). FACT Butterworth et al. 2013: Realistic HTX-404 UHF transceiver at 446 MHz; received signal "analyzed using a Signal Hound USB-SA44B Signal Analyzer" (p.16). They did not see the M&W polarizer null with ball antennas; the arrays did act as polarizers with simple half-wave dipoles (p.17). IDEA Our arithmetic from M&W's own formula: at φ = 0 the model gives T = e^(−4.4) = 0.0123, which is −19.1 dB relative to no loss. That is the size of drop to look for if you repeat the rod-cube test with the VNA (see the Experiments tab). Butterworth's result is a reason to keep a dipole-antenna control. Hively & Loebl 2019 (Appendix D, pp.124 to 125) prefer a network analyzer's phase-locked signal to M&W's custom transmitter and receiver. That is their view of the method (HYP). Hively patent (US 9,306,527 B1) and Hively & Loebl 2019: S-parameters at 8 GHz FACT Patent, col. 7 (PDF p.14). "Some implementations may include an Agilent Technologies E5071C network analyzer (300 kHz to 20 GHz)." Transmitting and receiving antennas "may be identical, because the reciprocity theorem guarantees" the transmitter can also act as a receiver. This VNA is a bench instrument; Dan's VNA6000-A tops out at 6 GHz, below the 8 GHz these tests used. FACT Balun numbers as printed. Patent col. 7: "The measured return loss was −22 dB for a single skirt balun … and −42 dB for a double balun (not shown)", and an antenna-balun impedance of 49.76 − 0.24j Ω against the 50 Ω source. The 2019 paper (p.118 and Fig. 3, p.120) shows the measured balun return-current attenuation with a shallow null of 23 dB at 8.00 GHz, against a simulated null of 49 dB at 7.94 GHz, and gives 42 dB for a double balun (not shown). The two documents state this differently (22 versus 23 dB). HYP They may describe the same measurement; we have not reconciled them. FACT Attenuation versus distance. Patent cols. 9 to 10 and 2019 Fig. 4 (p.120) show two facing antennas at 8.00 GHz, each inside its own copper pipe enclosure, inside an anechoic Faraday chamber ("90 dB isolation", p.119). The patent labels the antennas "port-1" and "port-2"; the paper labels the plots S21 and S12. The instrument is not named in the paper's text. The test layout uses "directional couplers" described as 45 dB isolators (p.118). FACT The paper reports "an attenuation between 115 dB at r = 2 cm separation and 137 dB at r = 30 cm" for that test (p.120). Any comparison with an ordinary skin-depth shielding estimate is transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis, so this guide makes none. HYP Whether the SLW passes the enclosures is the paper's claim, not an established result. What the VNA papers teach us for our bench FACT They measured S11 and S21 together and compared them: (1 − |S11|²) against |S21|² (MPLB Fig. 5). IDEA For each antenna pair, record both. FACT They calibrated with the cables on (MPLB p.653) and used a port extension to straighten out phase (JAP Fig. 5). The VNA6000 manual says a saved calibration also keeps the "electrical delay" setting (manual p.22). FACT They used a dummy (a copper stand-in for the plasma tube) as a control (MPLB Fig. 5b, 5c). FACT Their drive levels were higher than Dan's VNA: +10 dBm (MPLB), 5 dBm (CEM-R-46), 0 dBm (JAP), against a VNA6000 test-port output of about −10 dBm typical (data sheet p.3). Our arithmetic: that is 10 to 20 dB lower. The S21 reading in dB does not depend on the drive level, but the noise floor eats more of a weak signal. The data sheet gives a 95 dB transmission dynamic range for the VNA6000-A at 200 MHz to 5.8 GHz (data sheet p.4, measured with IF bandwidth 0.8 kHz and 10 averages), so S21 values of −45 to −70 dB, as in CEM-R-46, should sit above the floor (our arithmetic, not a test). IDEA Use a narrow IF bandwidth or averaging on weak S21 readings. FACT DC bias needs a bias-tee. All three Zimmerman VNA papers feed the DC bias to the plasma tube or bulb through a bias-tee. The VNA6000 ports take at most 5 V DC (data sheet p.2), and Zimmerman's QEX article says about −400 V DC is momentarily needed to ignite the tube (p.33). Never connect a biased tube straight to a VNA port. Dan's VNA: the NanoRFE VNA6000-A Which one is it? The hub's kit page records it as the NanoRFE VNA6000-A (kit.html#vna6000). The maker (NanoRFE) sells the VNA6000 as a two-port, 6 GHz instrument in two versions, A and B. It is a pocket "NanoVNA family" instrument with a touch screen. It is not a Mini-VNA. FACT from the maker's data sheet and product page; FACT from the hub for "-A". Does it reach our frequencies? Maker's stated range: 50 kHz to 6 GHz (data sheet p.3, "Frequency range"). Where Frequency In range? Comment Experiment B 433.59 MHz YES Comfortably inside. Good for the KB-2016 balls and the 346 mm rods. Experiment A (Dan sometimes says "1.3 GHz") 1296 MHz YES Inside. The Zimmerman papers worked at 1.1 to 1.5 GHz, so you can compare your plots with theirs. Experiment G 1057.8 MHz YES Inside. Magnetron / dipole work 2450 MHz (2.45 GHz) YES Inside. The maker quotes its dynamic range at 2.5 GHz (95 dB for the A version). Accuracy is better with a good calibration kit, and the maker warns that clones are inaccurate above 1 GHz, so check the unit is genuine. Hively's lab tests 8 GHz NO Above the 6 GHz limit. Hively's own bench used a different, much bigger instrument. We cannot repeat his 8 GHz work with this VNA. Chiao's cavity 11.5 GHz NO Above the limit. Our three working frequencies all fall inside the range, so 2.45 GHz does not exceed it. This verdict is from the maker's published range; it has not been checked on Dan's own unit. The numbers worth knowing (from the maker's data sheet, revision dated 2022/08) Ports Two SMA female ports, 50 Ω (data sheet p.3). You need SMA male connectors or adapters on whatever you test. What it measures A "T/R" type: S11 and S21 directly. To get S22 and S12 you turn the part around (data sheet p.3; manual p.3). Test signal About −10 dBm per port, typical (data sheet p.3). That is 0.1 mW. Do-not-exceed +10 dBm RF and 5 V DC at either port (data sheet p.2; manual p.3). Dynamic range (S21) VNA6000-A: 95 dB from 200 MHz to 5.8 GHz, 90 dB at 5 MHz. VNA6000-B: 110 dB (data sheet p.4; measured calibrated, 0.8 kHz IF bandwidth, 10 averages). Anything weaker than the floor shows only noise. The letter on the unit's label tells you which one you have. Sweep points 10 to 4096 on the device; more with a PC (data sheet p.3). IF bandwidth 0.8, 1.7, 3.1, 4.7, 6.2 or 10 kHz. Narrower is slower but quieter (data sheet p.3). Biggest signal it can measure 0 dB. An amplifier with gain needs an attenuator in line that is at least as big as its gain, or the reading is wrong. Dan's low-noise amplifiers (about 21 dB gain) need a 20 dB or bigger pad on the output side when you test them. IDEA (the 0 dB limit is the data sheet's; the pad advice is ours). Power and battery USB 5 V supply, or an internal 18650 lithium cell (flat-top, unprotected only; button-top or protected cells do not fit). It also runs from USB with no battery (manual p.4). Four red LEDs show charge (manual p.6). Software Optional PC program "VNA View" (a NanoVNA-QT variant) over USB; the maker lists NanoVNA-Saver also (see Links). Weight and weather About 300 g; works 0 to 45 °C (data sheet). What should be in the box (the two lists disagree: check yours) Manual p.4 says: the VNA, a USB cable, a stylus, two SMA connector savers, calibration standards (the manual says "5" but names a Short, an Open and 2 Loads, which is four; count what is in yours) and optionally two SS405 / SS402 SMA male-male cables. The maker's product page also lists a Thru and two 30 cm SS405 cables. Check yours against both lists. If there is no Thru in the kit, you can still do the one-port (S11) calibration; the two-port S21 calibration works best with a Thru, and a short SMA female-to-female adapter can stand in for one. IDEA How it complements the TinySA Ultra TinySA Ultra VNA6000-A What it is Spectrum analyzer: it listens, and shows how much signal there is at each frequency Network analyzer: it sends a test signal and shows how a part passes or reflects it Question it answers "What is coming in on this cable or antenna?" "How well does this part pass or reflect, from 50 kHz to 6 GHz?" Use on the bench Watch the real signal during a run Check the parts before the run: match, cable loss, filter shape During a sealed run Used as the hub describes Off. Its test signal would swamp the faint signals we are after To confirm on the unit (not verifiable from our files). The label on the back: does it say VNA6000-A? (The hub says A; the label is the proof.) Firmware: CONFIG → VERSION. The manual is dated 2022/11, and the maker's pages show newer firmware, so a menu on your unit may be named differently from this guide. Calibration kit contents: is there a Thru or a second cable? (see the two lists above) Is a battery installed? The manual shows how to tell from the LEDs (p.6). If any of these differ from what this page says, trust the unit and the maker's manual, and tell Dan. What to measure on Experiments A, B and C Everything in the recipes below is an IDEA of ours: a way to apply the VNA to the hub's kit, patterned on what the sources did. The hub's kit page lists these same uses (S11 of the sphere feed, S21 of the 23 cm filter, a TDR check of cable pigtails, an optional stub S11). Keep the sources' HYP framing: a good S11 only tells you a part is a decent 50 Ω match; it does not test the SLW hypothesis. Experiment Frequency Hardware (hub pages) Sweep to try first Experiment A 1296 MHz K-Mac KB-1820 ¾″ hollow aluminum sphere fed by an Amphenol 901-9875 SMA bulkhead (small coax into the ball, outer conductor as shield); 23 cm band-pass filter in the transmit chain; RG-405 sleeve stub (archived in the setup page); mesh tents; TinySA Ultra 1100 to 1500 MHz (the N&Z band), then 1250 to 1350 MHz Experiment B 433.59 MHz KB-2016 2.50″ balls with the 901-9875 feed, no balun, two SMA male-male RG-316 jumpers, 3×3 array of brass half-wave rods (346 mm) for the polarizer cube 400 to 470 MHz (a video below uses 420 to 455) Experiment C 1296 MHz RF arm, plus the optical arm The RF arm re-uses Experiment A practice (stub, sphere, bifilar); the photomultiplier / optical arm is not a VNA job As Experiment A Recipe 1: S11 of a sphere and its feed (Experiments A and B) What it tells you: how much of the test signal the ball and its feed send back. A dip at your frequency means the ball accepts power there. A ball with a short-circuited or open feed shows almost 0 dB everywhere. IDEA Calibrate at the end of the cable you will use (see the Step-by-step tab), with the sweep window from the table above. Connect the sphere's SMA bulkhead to the cable end. Show S11 as LOGMAG and again as SWR. Touch test: hold the ball by hand and by its stand, and move the cable. A reading that jumps means the outer conductor of the cable is carrying signal. That is the same worry N&Z (2007, PDF p.22) raise about badly tuned feed baluns. IDEA Control: repeat with the ball replaced by a 50 Ω load (a dummy), as Zimmerman did with his copper stand-in (MPLB Fig. 5b, 5c). If the readings look alike, the ball is not telling you anything yet. Log: frequency of the dip, depth in dB, SWR at your operating frequency, the cable, and a photo of the screen. Recipe 2: the sphere with its stub or sleeve balun (Experiment A, C) Measure the sphere alone (Recipe 1), then the sphere with the sleeve stub / sleeve balun fitted, with the same calibration. Overlay the two saved traces. What to look for: whether the match moves and whether the cable-touch jump goes away. A sleeve balun's job is to keep signal off the outside of the coax. IDEA See the hub's sleeve balun page for the geometry. Source analogs: Hively's patent reports a balun return loss of −22 dB (single) and −42 dB (double) at 8 GHz (col. 7; FACT as printed), and N&Z measured a folded dipole with a 4:1 balun at −15 dB at about 1.21 GHz (PDF p.25). Neither number is a target for your hardware; they only show what the others measured. Recipe 3: cables, pigtails and connectors Cable loss (S21): connect the cable between port 1 and port 2 (Thru calibrated). Read S21 at your frequency. A good short jumper reads a small negative number of dB. A sudden worse reading usually means a bad crimp or connector. Cable fault finding (time domain): the manual covers a time-domain (TDR) mode that shows reflections against distance (manual pp.18 to 21). Enter the cable's velocity factor as a whole number such as 67, not 0.67 (manual pp.18 to 21). Use the RG-316 data sheet value for your cable. The hub's kit page lists this as a use of the VNA. Hints: SMA connectors want a snug finger-tight turn, then a gentle nudge with an SMA wrench (do not over-tighten and do not twist the cable). Keep the cable still while the sweep runs, and keep the same cable from calibration to measurement. Use the supplied connector savers on the VNA ports, so wear happens on a cheap adapter. Avoid tight bends in the RG-316. IDEA (manual p.4 introduces the connector savers; the torque and handling hints are our general practice, not from the manual). Recipe 4: the 23 cm band-pass filter (Experiment A) — S21 Calibrate both ports with the Thru, sweep 1000 to 1600 MHz. Connect the filter between port 1 and port 2. Show S21 as LOGMAG. Read the pass band: the loss at 1296 MHz, and how fast it drops each side. The filter's data sheet gives the maker's expected curve; compare. IDEA This is the same kind of measurement as the low-pass filter video in the Links tab. Recipe 5: the rod polarizer cube (Experiment B) — S21 and loading The hub says the polarizer cube is not by itself a two-port part, so the following are our suggestions, not something a source did with a VNA. (Monstein & Wesley did not use a VNA; their measurement instrument for the cube curve is not stated.) Path S21: put the transmit ball on port 1 and the receive ball on port 2, with the cube between them at a fixed spacing. Calibrate with a Thru at the cable ends. Record S21 at 433.59 MHz at each cube rotation angle φ. IDEA What to compare: M&W's formula gives T = exp[−4.4 cos²φ] (Eq. 9, p.516); our arithmetic: that is a 19.1 dB drop at φ = 0. Butterworth et al. (2013) did not see that null with ball antennas but did with half-wave dipoles (p.17). Whatever you see, log it as measured, and say which antennas were used. Loading S11: measure the transmit ball's S11 with the cube removed, then in place at each angle, to see whether the cube pulls the match around. IDEA Keep the room fixed. People moving, metal tables and the cables will change an air path S21 by several dB. Do all angles in one sitting with the cables taped down. Rule: This is a bench job outside the cage, with the VNA at a low sweep rate. The cage itself is not on this list. The cage rule, again No cable crosses the Faraday cage wall (Dan's standing rule). Parts are measured outside. If a measurement must be done inside, it is battery or optical only, with no cable through the wall, and the VNA off during any real listen. Cage framing: it strips ordinary transverse-EM noise (FACT); whether an SLW passes the wall is HYP. The hub's submarine page lists a "seam-coupon S21 with the NanoRFE VNA outside the cage" (tagged transverse-EM reasoning); keep that tag if you do it. Under the SLW hypothesis we do not argue from skin depth or permeability. Any such reasoning carries the tag "transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis". What a VNA in air cannot tell you about the Joule term The hub's loss-modes page (sim-lab/loss-modes) compares three readings of SLW loss: the Joule-literal default, the erratum's "no loss", and a charge-relaxation-only hypothesis. For a path through air all three give the same prediction, so an S21 in air cannot decide between them. They differ only in a conductive medium such as seawater (see that page). The Joule-literal reading remains the hub's default. Parts list for a VNA session Item Qty Note NanoRFE VNA6000-A with USB cable and stylus 1 Charged, or on USB power SMA connector savers (supplied) 2 Leave on the ports Calibration standards: Open, Short, Load (and Thru if supplied) 1 each; 2 Loads in the kit SMA male, per the manual's list SMA male-male cables for test leads 2 Same cables for calibration and measurement; RG-316 jumpers from the hub kit work SMA female-female adapter 1 or 2 For a Thru, and for jumpering cables SMA wrench (small, 5/16″) 1 Gentle torque only Fixed 20 dB SMA attenuator 1 For amplifier tests only; not supplied; do not buy until you need it Dummy 50 Ω load (a spare from the kit) 1 The control for every antenna test Notebook and phone camera 1 Log the settings and photograph the screen SMA wrench size is our general knowledge; it is not from the manual. Button-by-button with the VNA6000-A Where these steps come from. The NanoRFE VNA6000 User Manual, edition 2022/11 (30 pages). Every step below names its manual page. Menu names are written the way the manual writes them, in capitals, with an arrow between menu and item (for example CAL → RESET). Steps tagged IDEA are our advice, not the manual's. Your unit's firmware may be newer than the manual, so a menu name may differ; the "Not verified" list at the bottom says what the manual does not cover. A. Set the frequency range (manual pp.11 to 12) Open the menu. Tap an empty spot on the touch screen (not on a marker), or press the ENTER button (p.7). You see: a menu list with DISPLAY, MARKER, STIMULUS, CAL, RECALL, CONFIG and CLOSE. Tap STIMULUS → START, type the number on the on-screen keypad, then tap the unit key (for example M for MHz). The unit key multiplies your number and ends the entry (p.8). Then STIMULUS → STOP the same way. Or use the middle and width instead: STIMULUS → CENTER and STIMULUS → SPAN (p.12). Suggested windows IDEA: Experiment A: START 1100 MHz, STOP 1500 MHz. Experiment B: START 400 MHz, STOP 470 MHz. Pause the sweep with STIMULUS → PAUSE SWEEP if you want a frozen picture (p.12). Turn it off again to keep measuring. B. Calibrate (manual pp.13 to 14) Always set the frequency range first. If you change the range afterwards, the old calibration is only stretched to fit and the manual says it "may degrade accuracy", so calibrate again (p.13). Choose where the reference plane goes. Calibrate at the VNA ports (p.13) if you will plug the part straight in. Calibrate at the end of your cable (p.14) if a test cable will go between the VNA and the part. For our work you will nearly always want the cable version: keep the same cable on for calibration and measurement. Clear any old calibration: CAL → RESET, then → CALIBRATE (p.14, step 1). Attach your SMA cable to port 1 (p.14, step 2). Skip this step if you are calibrating at the port itself. Put a LOAD on port 2 (p.14, step 3). OPEN: screw the OPEN standard onto the end of the port-1 cable and tap → OPEN. Wait until the menu item lights up (highlights). SHORT: swap in the SHORT standard, tap → SHORT, wait for the highlight. LOAD: swap in the second LOAD standard, tap → LOAD, wait for the highlight. The manual says you need not wait for the plot to redraw before tapping the next item: each tap does one full sweep with extra averaging, and the highlight tells you it is done (p.14). (Only for S21 / through measurements) THRU: connect a second cable to port 2 and join the two cable ends with the THRU standard, then tap → THRU (p.14, steps 7 and 8). Then take the THRU out. Tap → DONE. You see: "Cx" on the left side of the screen, meaning calibration is active (p.13). Save it: CAL → SAVE → SAVE 0 (p.13 and p.22). IDEA Use slot 0; the manual says "0 to 6" in one place (p.13) and gives a different count on p.22, so we do not rely on higher slots. Check it: CAL → CORRECTION shows whether the correction is on (p.22). IDEA With the open standard on the cable end, S11 should read close to 0 dB across the range; with the load on, S11 should be very low. If not, redo the steps. To restore later: CAL → RECALL → RECALL 0 (p.22). Remember it only fits the range that was in use when you saved it. C. Measure S11 (reflection) (manual pp.15 to 17) Connect the part to the port-1 cable end. Leave port 2 on its LOAD. …

description: HYP/illustrative 2D E∥≈√(S·Z0) maps (CoS Mathematica PNGs + optional canvas) around Navy Keyport sleeve + LAB Al spheres KB-2016 / KB-1820. Style nod US 9,306,527 FIG. 2B; geometry ≠ patent skirt+monopole. Educational.
text: HYP / illustrative · efield-maps-v0.2-snr-dual-sim-params-v0.2.1 Sleeve + sphere TX — 2D E∥ color maps Cloud twin pending sync (efield-maps-v0.2-snr-dual-sim-params-v0.2.1). The page, JS and physics-constants.json now use maps ID efield-maps-v0.2-snr-dual-sim-params-v0.2.1, which is the ID the current SleeveBalunEFieldMaps.wl produces. The E∥ numbers are the same (E∥(λ) = 9.197e-2 V/m, E∥(10 m) = 2.127e-3 V/m at −19 dBm). The Cloud and PNGs will be re-exported and republished at the next Wolfram session. CoS Mathematica exports (primary) plus an optional hub canvas using the same locked formulas. Assemblies: Navy Keyport-style λ/4 sleeve (US 12,525,711 — open toward tip) + LAB aluminum spheres KB-2016 2.50″ @ 433.59 MHz and KB-1820 ¾″ @ 1.296 / 2.45 GHz. Drive: TinySA Ultra −19 dBm. Physics: physics-constants.json · SNR sibling: sleeve-balun-snr.html · Cloud: SleeveBalunEFieldMaps. HYP / toy / illustrative — not a measurement. Cartoon E∥ ≈ √(S·Z0) from the Hively & Loebl 2019 Eq. 38/B5 as corrected by the Erratum → S(r) (FACT for the ½; I = peak is an ASSUMPTION; the E∥ cartoon itself stays HYP). Not a full Maxwell near-field solution; SLW is not settled physics. Style nod: US 9,306,527 B1 FIG. 2B / Loebl–Hively 2019 FIG. 2 constant |E| vibe — but that patent figure is PATENT skirt balun + linear monopole (~8 GHz). These panels draw LAB Keyport sleeve + KB spheres — different mechanical layout. Do not equate. Lock @ −19 dBm (JS ↔ WL) E∥(10 m) = 1.504×10−3 V/m (all bands) E∥(λ) = 2.176×10−2 / 6.503×10−2 / 1.229×10−1 V/m · 433.59 MHz / 1.296 GHz / 2.45 GHz Source: img/efield/efield_summary.json · Cloud Manipulate Formula history (2026-09-29). Before this date the page used P_rad = I_peak² Z0/(4π), so S = I_peak² Z0/(4π r)² (patent Eq. 15; the same as Eq. 38/B5 as first printed in 2019, without the ½). The erratum adds the ½, so every E∥ value is 0.7071× (−3.01 dB) and P_rad is halved: E∥(10 m) was 2.127×10−3 V/m; E∥(λ) was 3.077×10−2 / 9.197×10−2 / 1.739×10−1 V/m. The three PNG maps below are Mathematica exports made with the old form; their colour scale is 3.01 dB too high until they are re-exported (owed). The live canvas above uses the erratum form. See P_OUT erratum audit. Units (2026-09-30, label change only; no number changed): P_OUT is the paper's power density in W/m² at range r; total watts (4πr²·P_OUT = I_peak² Z0/(8π), code name P_rad) are a DERIVED / ASSUMPTION quantity; I = peak confirmed by Dan Britton 2026-09-30. Patent optional sphere (radius = λ/4) is a PATENT scale — not Dan’s catalog balls. Drive: TinySA Ultra (ZS406) −115…−19 dBm → I into 50 Ω, or exploratory high-I (external PA). Constants: physics-constants.json. Default in v0.3: Hively's Joule-loss term is on Loading… Symbols. SLW: scalar-longitudinal wave, the untested wave of Hively's extended electrodynamics (HYP). SW: scalar wave, the E = 0 special case (HYP). TEM: ordinary radio (FACT). σ: electrical conductivity of the medium (S/m). α: attenuation. The field falls by a factor e every 1/α metres; 1 Np/m = 8.686 dB/m. dB: decibels of power. Shielding. The receive sphere and its detector sit inside their own Faraday cage (the RadioScreen tent), which strips ordinary radio (TEM) noise (FACT for TEM; see the cage control below). That an SLW passes through the cage wall is a HYPothesis. Why Joule loss is the default, the seawater numbers, and the Erratum toggle (sources) Hub rule (25 Sep 2026): include Hively's Joule-loss (Ohmic) term for SLW in conductive media. Hively & Loebl, Phys. Essays 32, 112 (2019), Eq. (44), has the Joule term J·E in the energy balance, with Ohm's law J = σE (HYP). Experiment C's field dictionary lists SLW as “Eddy / skin: no; Ohmic (Joule): yes (J=σE∥)”, lists SW as “no” for both, and says: “Do not say ‘SLW has no losses.’ Say: no eddy / no classical skin barrier; SLW still has linear Ohmic loss; SW has neither.” Its Ohmic section adds that longitudinal E “still drives J=σE and local Joule density σE∥². Pure SW (E=0) has no σE² term.” How much, in seawater. We use Experiment G's code unchanged (experiment-g.html, hub PR #56, not yet published, so the link may 404 for now; seawater ε′, ε″, σ from Meissner & Wentz 2004, FACT). The Joule-literal attenuation is αJ = σH|Z|/2, with σH = ε0ε″ω and |Z| from Hively's Eq. (37). That is our reading of Eq. (44) (ASSUMPTION), not an equation Hively prints. TEM-equal uses the textbook plane-wave αTEM (FACT). Air conducts almost nothing, so both are ≈ 0 in air (ASSUMPTION σair ≈ 0). Copper and steel walls have no model yet (UNKNOWN), so they add 0. Frequency (seawater 15 °C, salinity 35, σ = 4.29 S/m) SLW with Joule loss default: 1/e length TEM-equal (classical comparison) Erratum α=0 toggle 91.44 m seawater (Submarine preset): Joule / TEM / Erratum 1296 MHz (Exp A) 1.29 cm (671 dB/m) 1.04 cm (832 dB/m) no loss 61,371 dB / 76,090 dB / 0 dB 2450 MHz (ISM) 0.91 cm (953 dB/m) 0.82 cm (1063 dB/m) no loss 87,180 dB / 97,224 dB / 0 dB 433.59 MHz (Exp B) 2.78 cm (313 dB/m) 1.42 cm (614 dB/m) no loss 28,606 dB / 56,114 dB / 0 dB This page's αohm multiplies power density S (S = Sgeom·e−αohmL). Experiment G's α is a field coefficient, so αohm = 2α (a unit conversion, not new physics). Path losses use the page's locked 4.343·αohm·L. Erratum α = 0: a non-default toggle (HYP). Hively & Loebl's 2022 Erratum argues that the Joule term cancels. What it says, in context (Phys. Essays 35, 320, 2022, doi:10.4006/0836-1398-35.3.320): “This Erratum corrects errors in Appendix A of our paper for derivation of the no-skin-effect constraint. The scalar longitudinal wave (SLW) has only irrotational fields and no magnetic field from Eq. (27), B = 0 … Substituting the expressions for E and C from Eqs. (18) and (20) into Eq. (A.5) gives the longitudinal component of the A-wave equation: … (A6). Physically, Eq. (A6) means that the SLW is not subject to resistive loss in conductive media. The same no-loss result occurs from the energy balance equation, Eq. (44), by substituting for (ρ/ε) from Eq. (22) and by substituting for JL from Eq. (21) with B = 0; then cancelling terms. Consequently, the SLW is unconstrained by the skin effect and power loss in resistive media.” With the toggle on, no medium absorbs anything (α = 0). Choose it in “SLW loss in conductive media” below. ⚠ Open conflict, flagged and not resolved here. The Erratum's “not subject to resistive loss” contradicts Experiment C's dictionary and Ohmic section (“SLW still has linear Ohmic loss”, “Do not say ‘SLW has no losses’”). This page follows the hub rule and uses Joule loss by default. It keeps the Erratum only as a labelled toggle. experiment-c.html is left unchanged. Not a measurement. SLW is not settled physics. text: Manufacturing guide · Keyport-style sleeve · A · B · 8 GHz Sleeve balun on RG-405/U — cut, solder, verify New: VNA guide for Steve: how to check a sleeve balun or stub with S11 on the VNA6000-A, and what Hively and Zimmerman measured. Shop page for building a close-fitting λ/4 sleeve balun (Navy Keyport / US 12,525,711 geometry — open end toward the tip/sphere), not Hively US 9,306,527 Fig. 2A’s fat annular skirt. Cut lengths track 1/f for Experiment A (1296 MHz), Experiment B (433.59 MHz), and an optional 8 GHz Hively-class build. Live slider calculator: tools.html. Interactive dual-sphere SNR draft: sleeve-balun-snr.html. E∥ maps: sleeve-balun-efield.html. Educational RF construction only. A sleeve choke is ordinary amateur practice; calling the stub an “SLW launcher” is the disputed physics, not the metalwork. Use a licensed band for on-air work (23 cm for A; 70 cm for B). 8 GHz needs appropriate licensed / lab gear — do not invent an unlicensed radiator. Geometry paraphrased from public patents and Dr. Hively’s published talks / clarifying email (no private dump). Experiment B note. The original Monstein–Wesley 433.59 MHz ball page used no balun. This shop order adds Keyport-style sleeves for A and B (and maybe 8 GHz later). Keep B’s sphere feed philosophy (coax into the ball, outer as shield); the sleeve sits on the coax behind the ball. Experiment A is different (corrected 5 Oct 2026): the shield must not touch the ¾″ ball, and the sleeve’s open end stops short of it (exp-1296.html#feed). Tools: sleeve-balun-snr.html — interactive SNR · sleeve-balun-efield.html — 2D E∥ color maps (HYP √(S·Z0) cartoon). Educational · not a measurement. 1. Sleeve ≠ skirt (geometry that matters when you solder) Both structures are λ/4 conductive tubes around the coax outer. The difference is which end is open and where the tube is bonded to the shield: Sleeve (build this) Open end toward the exposed center-conductor stub. Electrical bond to the outer conductor is λ/4 back from that open end (the “cold” end, away from the tip). Looks like a sleeve pulled over the jacket when the stub points up. Preferred for nulling displacement / common-mode current on the shield (Navy US 12,525,711 style; hub how-to). Skirt (do not build for 1296) Open end away from the stub; bond near the feed / tip end. Looks like a skirt hanging down when the stub points up. US 9,306,527 Fig. 2A is a larger-diameter annular skirt that can also act as a counterpoise and can launch extra TEM. Historical patent geometry — not this shop order. In both cases the gap between coax outer and tube is filled with insulator (two layers of electrical tape is a common bench filler). Silver solder (or ordinary electronics solder with a clean fillet) bonds tube ↔ shield at the shorted end only. Strip any outer jacket so the bond lands on bare outer conductor to within about 1 mm of the tube end. cold end (solder ring) open at feed stub tip | | | v v v ======+==============================| | coax |######## SLEEVE (λ/4) ########| PTFE cut back | outer |######## ##|======= center =======* ======+==============================| ^ bond tube to shield here only; leave feed end unsoldered ASCII is schematic. Real tube is snug on the 0.086″ jacket — not a fat radiating skirt. Interactive lengths: tools.html. Side-view SVG on setup: setup.html#sleeve. 2. Physical sleeve length ≈ (λ/4)×VF when the coax–tube gap has dielectric (tape); start at VF≈1 (air) and trim short if needed. Build steps (cold-end solder, open at feed) Connector end. Cut RG-405 to overall length. Install SMA (or Type N) on the generator end in the ordinary way — no special balun connection at the connector. Choose sleeve stock. Use a tube whose ID clears 0.086″ with only a thin gap (or foil). Cut a little longer than 57.8 mm so you can trim. Deburr inside and out. Insulator in the gap. Two layers of electrical tape (or thin PTFE) over the jacket where the sleeve will sit. This sets VF < 1 if thick — plan to trim the physical length. Strip the tip. Remove outer conductor and dielectric so 23.1 mm of center conductor remains as the first-article stub (or 57.8 mm for the TEM-control stub). Keep the stub straight; photograph against a ruler. Slide and locate. Slide the sleeve on from the stub end until the open end sits at (or a millimetre behind) the dielectric cut-back. The opposite end is the cold end. Solder the cold end only. Bond tube ↔ bare outer conductor all around at the cold end (away from the stub). Leave the feed/tip end of the sleeve open — no solder bridges. Silver solder OK if you have it. Trim for VF. If the gap dielectric is significant, shorten toward electrical λ/4. Log physical length, VF estimate, and photos of fillet + open end. Protect. Optional heat-shrink over the cold-end fillet. Keep the open end clear. Foam around the stub on the TX sled so it cannot bend in the bag. TX chain. Keep the 23 cm BPF inside the Faraday wrap: Ultra SMA-F → filter → stub (setup.html#bpf). No 3λ ground disk. 5. Verify before any on-air claim VNA6000-A — S11 of the sleeve-stub; optional TDR of the pigtail. See kit.html#vna6000. Common-mode check — compare outer-conductor current / near-field probe with sleeve on vs a bare stub (same length). A working λ/4 sleeve should raise common-mode impedance at the design frequency. Dummy load — leftover tone should die when the antenna is replaced by a load (leak hunt). Log — frequency, physical sleeve length, stub length, solder photos, S11 export. Label CSV rows as archived sleeve-control if the primary run is the ¾″ sphere. 6. Historical reference — IARD 2020 (~8 GHz skirt tuning) Hively & Land, “Evidence for Scalar-Longitudinal Photons,” IARD 2020 slides. Slide 18 shows historical skirt balun tuning near 8 GHz. If we build at 8 GHz we still use sleeve geometry (Keyport / open-toward-tip); cut from the table above (~9.4 mm λ/4), not by copying the old skirt hardware photos. Slide 19 is Faraday-tube dims, not the balun tube. Slide 18 — antenna return loss vs balun effectiveness near 8 GHz (historical skirt-balun tuning). Scale lengths ×(8/1.296)≈6.2 for a rough 1296 starting point, then measure. Slide 19 — solid-copper Faraday enclosure tube/cap dims from the 8 GHz dynamic-range test (ID 14.34 mm, length 28.89 mm). That is a cage part, not the RG-405 sleeve OD. Full slide deck stays off this page (large).
