description: Analysis page: classical radar cross-section (RCS) of a 1 m PEC sphere (exact Mie series) and a squat 1 m x 1 m cylinder at 433.59 MHz, what Hively and Loebl do and do not say about scalar-longitudinal-wave (SLW) reflection, and a hypothesis-level submarine reflection stack with Hively's Joule term. Every claim labeled FACT, HYPOTHESIS or ASSUMPTION.
text: Analysis page · radar cross-section · not one of Experiments A–G SLW Radar Cross-Section: squat cylinder, sphere, and the multi-layer reflection stack How strongly does a metal object send a radar signal back? For ordinary radio (transverse EM, “TEM”) textbooks answer this exactly, and we compute it here for a 1 m sphere and a squat 1 m × 1 m cylinder at 433.59 MHz. Then we ask the same question for a scalar-longitudinal wave (SLW). There the honest answer is that no cited source gives a reflection law yet, so the SLW parts are sliders, not predictions. Educational only. Mainstream classical electrodynamics treats free-space radio as transverse (TEM); scalar-longitudinal waves are disputed. Section A is textbook physics. Sections B–D mix textbook TEM facts with SLW hypotheses; the SLW parts are labelled and use no equation that is not in a cited source. FACT textbook physics, published measurement, or arithmetic HYPOTHESIS unproven physics (all SLW behaviour) ASSUMPTION taken as true to make the numbers work; check it FACT No Wolfram Cloud twin planned (analysis page, not Experiments A-G); numbers cross-checked in Python. A · Classical RCS FACT FACT Radar cross-section (RCS, σ) is the area that, if it caught the incoming power and re-radiated it equally in all directions, would give the same echo the real object gives back toward the radar. It is measured in m² (or dBsm, decibels relative to 1 m²). It depends on size compared with the wavelength, shape, and material (Knott, Shaeffer & Tuley, Radar Cross Section). FACT Frequency 433.59 MHz (the Monstein & Wesley frequency), so λ = c/f = 0.6914 m. FACT Material: we treat the targets as perfect electric conductors (PEC). Aluminum (σ ≈ 3.5×10⁷ S/m) is effectively PEC at this frequency. Classically the induced currents stay in a micrometre-thin surface layer, far smaller than the 1 m target (the number, 4.1 µm, is in the TEM box in Section C). Copper or steel hulls give a negligibly different classical RCS for the same reason. (This is classical TEM reasoning, used here only for the classical RCS. It is not applicable under the SLW hypothesis.) FACT The size parameter is ka = 2πa/λ. The conventional regions are Rayleigh (ka ≲ 1: object small, σ ∝ f⁴), resonance / Mie (1 ≲ ka ≲ 10: wiggles from creeping waves), and optical (ka ≳ 10: σ approaches the geometric-optics value). ASSUMPTION The boundaries 1 and 10 are rules of thumb, not sharp lines. A1 · Sphere, radius a = 1 m FACT ka = 9.09. This is the top of the resonance region, at the transition to the optical region. FACT Optical limit: σ → πa² = 3.14 m² (Knott et al.; Ruck Vol. 1 ch. 3). FACT Exact PEC Mie series, monostatic (backscatter), computed on this page: σ = (λ²/4π) · | Σn≥1 (−1)ⁿ (2n+1) (aₙ − bₙ) |² , aₙ = ψₙ′(x)/ξₙ′(x), bₙ = ψₙ(x)/ξₙ(x), x = ka where ψₙ(x) = x·jₙ(x) and ξₙ(x) = x·hₙ⁽¹⁾(x) are Riccati–Bessel functions. These are the Bohren & Huffman (1983, ch. 4, §4.4) scattering coefficients in the perfect-conductor limit (refractive index → ∞), with their backscatter sum (ch. 4; see also Ruck Vol. 1 ch. 3 and Balanis AEE §11.8). Terms are summed to n = x + 4x1/3 + 10. FACT Result at 433.59 MHz: σ = 2.731 m² (4.36 dBsm) = 0.869 × πa², i.e. 0.61 dB below the optical value. The shortfall is the creeping-wave ripple, which is still about ±15 % at ka ≈ 9. FACT The Rayleigh formula σ = 9πa²(ka)⁴ (small-sphere limit, Knott et al.; Ruck Vol. 1 ch. 3) would give 1.9×10⁵ m² here, which is absurd. It is inapplicable at ka = 9; it is only valid for ka ≪ 1. FACT Checks on the series: at ka = 0.009 it agrees with the Rayleigh formula to 2×10⁻⁵. Its maximum is 3.65 πa² at ka ≈ 1.03 (for a = 1 m that is about 50 MHz), which is the familiar textbook peak. A2 · Squat cylinder, a = 1 m, h = 1 m, broadside FACT Optical broadside formula σ = 2πah²/λ (Knott et al., optics-region formula for a cylinder at broadside) = 9.09 m² (9.58 dBsm). FACT There is no closed-form exact solution for a finite cylinder. It needs a numerical solver (method of moments or similar), which this page does not run. ASSUMPTION Labelled approximation: we take the exact 2-D series for an infinite PEC cylinder (Balanis AEE §11.5.1 TMz, E parallel to the axis; §11.5.2 TEz, H parallel to the axis) and convert with the standard long-body relation quoted by Knott et al.: σ2D = (2λ/π) · | Σn≥0 εₙ (−1)ⁿ Jₙ(ka)/Hₙ⁽²⁾(ka) |² (TM; TE uses Jₙ′/Hₙ⁽²⁾′), ε₀ = 1, εₙ = 2; σ3D ≈ 2h²σ2D/λ The conversion assumes h ≫ λ and ignores the end caps and edge currents. Here h/λ = 1.45, so it is only a rough guide. FACT (arithmetic, given that approximation) σ2D = 3.163 m (1.007 πa) for TM, giving σ3D ≈ 9.15 m² (TM) and 9.25 m² (TE), within 1–2 % of the optical 9.09 m². The Rayleigh (low-frequency) limit is inapplicable at ka = 9. FACT The cylinder's broadside echo is larger than the sphere's (9.1 vs 2.7 m²) because its flat-in-one-direction side focuses the reflection back like a line mirror. Tilt it away from broadside and the echo falls quickly (the sinc pattern in Knott's relation). RCS vs frequency FACT ASSUMPTION: cylinder 2-D→3-D Frequency Sphere radius a Cylinder radius a Cylinder height h Cylinder polarization Reset to 433.59 MHz, 1 m sphere, exact Miesphere optical πa²sphere Rayleigh 9πa²(ka)⁴cylinder, 2-D→3-D approxcylinder optical 2πah²/λ Shading uses the sphere radius: dark = Rayleigh (ka < 1), mid = resonance (1–10), light = optical (ka > 10). The vertical line is the frequency slider. Log frequency axis 50 MHz–3 GHz. f (MHz) sphere ka Mie σ (m²) σ/πa² cyl. TM ≈ (m²) cyl. TE ≈ (m²) 2πah²/λ (m²) h/λ 50 1.048 11.46 3.646 1.280 1.066 1.048 0.17 (approx. invalid) 100 2.096 4.485 1.428 2.272 2.345 2.096 0.33 (approx. invalid) 433.59 9.087 2.731 0.869 9.149 9.249 9.087 1.45 (rough) 1000 20.96 3.027 0.964 20.99 20.91 20.96 3.3 3000 62.88 3.153 1.004 62.88 62.85 62.88 10 FACT a = h = 1 m. The table values come from the Python cross-check (scipy special functions). The page's own JavaScript matches them to better than 2×10⁻⁹ relative. A3 · Where the echo comes from (classical) FACT Sphere at ka ≈ 9: the echo is mostly a specular point (the spot facing the radar) plus a smaller creeping wave that travels around the shadow side and returns. Their interference causes the ripple in the plot (Knott et al.; Ruck Vol. 1 ch. 3). FACT Cylinder at broadside: a strong broadside flash from the whole side. It narrows as h/λ grows, with angular width about λ/h. B · SLW reflection off conductors HYPOTHESIS What Hively & Loebl, the Erratum and the Hively patent provide on reflection FACT Hively & Loebl, Phys. Essays 32, 112 (2019) give one interface matching condition for the scalar field C: continuity of the normal component of ∇C/μ across an interface, Eq. (26) (derived with a Gaussian pill box, “for long times”). They list it as item 5 of their Table I. They also state that the energy 4πr²(C²/2μ) is constant through a spherical boundary “in arbitrary media” (text around Eq. (25)). FACT They give no reflection coefficient, no transmission coefficient, no angle dependence and no conductor boundary condition for the SLW. One matching condition alone does not fix a reflection law. FACT The 2022 Erratum (Phys. Essays 35, 320) corrects only Appendix A, the no-skin-effect / no-resistive-loss derivation. It says nothing about reflection. FACT Hively US 9,306,527 B1 says qualitatively that “the above tests showed scattering and reflections of the SLW”, “consistent with classical electrodynamics, which predicts scattering of electric fields from conductors due to image charges and image-currents” (col. 14). It attributes the FIG. 6 variability to “scattering and reflections from nearby conductors” (col. 9–10). It proposes “SLW-RADAR” (col. 16; claim 27). It gives no quantitative reflection law. FACT Keyport US 12,525,711 B1 (Navy sleeve/skirt-balun monopole) covers transmitting and receiving SLW, including through water. It contains nothing on reflection or radar. FACT The only measured SLW reflection number is Monstein & Wesley, EPL 59(4), 514 (2002): Earth-surface reflection coefficient ℜ = B²/A² = 0.482 (their Eq. 24) at 433.59 MHz, from the ground-image interference pattern. That is Earth (σ ≈ 10⁻³ S/m), not metal, at near-grazing incidence, and it is one unreplicated experiment. HYPOTHESIS Conclusion: no cited source gives a reflection law or conductor boundary condition for the longitudinal field. We do not derive one. Every SLW reflection value on this page is a user slider. Searched: sim-lab notes (scalar-wave radar brief, REDO_SLW open item 5, JOULE_LOSS_POSITIONS), local text of H&L 2019, the Erratum, Hively–Land 2021, US 9,306,527, US 12,525,711 (Google Patents full text) and Monstein & Wesley 2002, plus a web search on 2026-09-28. Nothing further turned up. B1 · Specular or diffuse? FACT Classical, ka ≈ 9: the sphere gives a specular point plus creeping waves; the cylinder gives a broadside flash (Section A3). HYPOTHESIS SLW: unknown. Whether an SLW echo is specular, diffuse, or follows image charges as the patent suggests has not been measured on metal. Reflection vs incidence angle at 433.59 MHz SLW reflection coefficient (power) HYP Seawater σ (S/m) Earth relative permittivity εᵣ ASM SLW R = 0SLW R = 0.482 (M&W Earth)SLW R = 1 seawater ⊥ (TE)seawater ∥ (TM)Earth ⊥ (TE)Earth ∥ (TM)PEC = 1SLW slider, no angle dependence known (HYP) FACT (TEM) The coloured curves are the classical Fresnel power reflectances |Γ|² for a plane TEM wave (Jackson 3rd ed. §7.3, Eqs. 7.39 and 7.41, with complex permittivity ε′ − jσ/ωε₀; Balanis AEE ch. 5). Seawater ε′ comes from Meissner & Wentz 2004 at 15 °C, salinity 35 (the Experiment G code) ASSUMPTION; σ is the slider. Earth: σ = 10⁻³ S/m (M&W) and the εᵣ slider ASSUMPTION. A PEC reflects everything (|Γ|² = 1). HYPOTHESIS The dotted SLW line is flat because no angle dependence is known (HYP), not because it is predicted to be flat. Default 0.482 is M&W's Earth value at their near-grazing geometry, not a metal value. C · Submarine reflection stack HYPOTHESIS HYPOTHESIS Picture an SLW transmitter inside a submarine. It sits in an air gap some distance from the hull, then the signal meets the 76 mm steel pressure hull, then seawater with the surface above and the seabed below, then a target. At every interface some unknown fraction would be reflected (SLW coefficients unknown, so they are sliders). Inside materials, the only SLW loss allowed on this hub is Hively's Joule term. HYPOTHESIS Interface coefficients (air→steel R₁, steel→seawater R₂, seawater→air R₃, seawater→seabed R₄): unknown, no cited law. Sliders default to 0; a button sets them to M&W's 0.482 for illustration only. HYPOTHESIS Loss inside materials, Joule term only (default ON): Hively & Loebl 2019 Eq. (44) contains J·E with J = σE, i.e. Joule heating σE∥². We reuse the hub's Experiment G code unchanged (PR #56, branch expt-g-v0.1, head 726c896): αJ = σH|Z|/2 with Hively's far-field SLW impedance |Z| = η₀/(√ε′·√(1+tan²δ)) (Eq. 37) and σH = ε₀ε″ω. The field falls as e−αJd. ASSUMPTION The step from Eq. (44) to a per-metre αJ is the hub's own construction (Experiment G), not a formula Hively wrote. HYPOTHESIS Erratum toggle: Hively & Loebl's 2022 Erratum says the SLW “is not subject to resistive loss in conductive media” (α = 0). This is available as a labelled toggle. It conflicts with the hub's Experiment C Joule rule, and that conflict is flagged, not resolved. ASSUMPTION Material enters the SLW model only through σ (plus ε′ inside Eq. 37's |Z|). No permeability, skin depth or shielding number is used in the SLW path. For steel we take ε′ = 1. In that good-conductor limit the Joule construction gives αJ → (ω/2c)√ε′ = k₀/2 whatever σ is (a property of the construction, not a Hively statement). At 433.59 MHz that is 4.54 Np/m, so the 76 mm hull costs 3.0 dB. FACT (arithmetic in the model) Seawater σ = 4 S/m at 433.59 MHz: αJ = 35.6 Np/m, so the field falls by e every 2.81 cm (310 dB/m). With the model's σ = 4.29 S/m (15 °C, S = 35) this reproduces Experiment G's αJ exactly (checked in Python). ASSUMPTION Air: σ ≈ 0, so no Joule loss in the air gap. Straight rays with no refraction (no SLW refraction law is known either). Spreading 1/r² in power (H&L 2019 Eq. 38, Table I item 11 HYP). Energy not reflected at an interface is transmitted (bookkeeping; no interface absorption term is cited). Stack calculator and power budget HYPOTHESIS Frequency (MHz) Tx air gap to hull Steel hull thickness Steel σ (S/m) ASM Seawater σ (S/m) Target horizontal range Sub depth (m) Target depth (m) Water depth (m) Target projected area (m²) R₁ air→steel HYP R₂ steel→seawater HYP R₃ seawater→air (surface) HYP R₄ seawater→seabed HYP Hively Joule term σE∥² ON (default; H&L 2019 Eq. 44, Experiment G code). Untick = 2022 Erratum α = 0 (no loss anywhere, HYP toggle). Apply the same Joule construction to the steel hull (default). Untick = steel loss 0, as the PR #57 sleeve page does (“metal Joule model UNKNOWN”). All R = 0All R = 0.482 (M&W Earth value, illustration)Reset defaults internal multipath (R₁ + R₂ back into the hull)Joule loss in steelJoule loss in seawater before the targetreaching the target range HYPOTHESIS The whole budget is hypothetical. Fractions are of the power sent toward the target along one ray, before geometric spreading. HYPOTHESIS Even the “reaching target” number is one-way. An echo would also need the target's SLW reflection (unknown), the return trip, and R₂/R₁ again on the way in. So no SLW radar range can be computed. Transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis transverse-EM reasoning, NOT applicable under the SLW hypothesis Classical skin depth, wall-attenuation and cage numbers. These are ordinary radio (TEM) numbers, shown so you can compare. Under the SLW hypothesis they are not used to rank, limit or dismiss the SLW. Steel relative permeability μᵣ ASM FACT (TEM) Skin depth δ = √(2/(ωμσ)) for a good conductor (Jackson 3rd ed. §8.1 and §5.18; Balanis AEE ch. 4). A TEM wave crossing a wall of thickness t falls by about 8.69·t/δ dB. Seawater at 433.59 MHz is only a moderate conductor (tanδ ≈ 2.3), so the exact lossy-medium attenuation is also shown. FACT (TEM) A closed Faraday cage or steel hull strips ordinary TEM noise and signal almost completely. That is exactly why caged receivers are used as TEM controls. HYPOTHESIS An SLW passing through a cage wall or hull is a hypothesis (Hively's 8 GHz copper-box tests, H&L 2019 Fig. 4 and US 9,306,527 FIGs. 3–5, are single-lab results). It is not ruled out or limited by the TEM numbers in this box. D · Images inside a cavity FACT (TEM) A charge near a flat conductor behaves as if an opposite “image” charge sat behind the surface (method of images, Jackson 3rd ed. ch. 2). Between two parallel conducting walls the images repeat without end, an infinite image series, like facing mirrors. FACT (TEM) A closed metal box is a resonant cavity. Only certain field patterns (modes) at certain frequencies fit, and a source inside drives those modes. The energy bounces around until wall losses (finite Q) absorb it (Jackson 3rd ed. §8.7–8.8). A transmitter inside a submarine hull is, classically, inside a large lossy cavity: nearly all TEM power stays inside as internal multipath. HYPOTHESIS For the SLW, image behaviour inside a closed conductor is untested. The Hively patent says SLW scattering is “consistent with … image charges and image-currents” (col. 14), but gives no measurement inside a cavity. Whether an SLW inside a hull builds up cavity-like internal multipath (large R₁ and R₂) or leaks straight out (R ≈ 0) is exactly what the R sliders in Section C leave open. E · Conclusion and decisive experiments FACT Classically (TEM, PEC) at 433.59 MHz: 1 m sphere σ = 2.73 m² (exact Mie; 0.87 × πa² = 3.14 m²); 1 m × 1 m cylinder broadside ≈ 9.1 m² (optical 9.09 m²; 2-D→3-D approximation 9.15 m² TM). Both targets sit at ka ≈ 9, the resonance/optical transition. Rayleigh formulas do not apply. HYPOTHESIS An SLW radar off a submarine cannot be designed yet, because no cited source gives an SLW reflection law or boundary condition at a conductor. Hively & Loebl give only the Eq. (26) matching condition, and the only measured SLW reflection is M&W's 0.482 off Earth. HYPOTHESIS With the Joule term ON (default), seawater at 433.59 MHz costs about 310 dB per metre one way, which alone rules out any useful range. With the Erratum toggle (α = 0) only spreading and the unknown reflection coefficients remain. Which reading holds is itself an open experimental question. Decisive experiments (3–5 that would settle the unknowns) HYPOTHESIS test SLW reflection off an aluminum plate vs Earth. Use Monstein & Wesley ball antennas at 433.59 MHz. Repeat their ground-image null survey (see the ranging page) over bare ground, then over a large aluminum sheet laid on the ground. Null depth gives B/A. Does ℜ change from 0.482? Include TEM dipole controls at the same geometry. HYPOTHESIS test Caged-receiver transmission through a steel plate, with TEM controls. Battery receiver sealed in a Faraday cage; transmitter outside. Insert or remove a steel plate (76 mm if possible, thinner plates first) in the path. Controls: a closed-loop (C = 0) antenna, a TEM dipole, and cage-open vs cage-closed runs. This gives R₁R₂-type transmission directly. HYPOTHESIS test Seawater tank: Joule vs Erratum. Vary salinity and path length in a tank (Experiment G's G2 control e). The Joule reading predicts about 310 dB/m at σ = 4 S/m (433.59 MHz), falling with salinity like σ; the Erratum predicts 1/r only. HYPOTHESIS test Curved-target glint test. Rotate a sphere and a squat cylinder (Section A sizes, or scaled) in an SLW bistatic setup. A broadside flash that narrows with h/λ would mean SLW scattering follows classical optics; a flat angular response would mean something else. HYPOTHESIS test Multipath inside a closed metal box. Transmitter and receiver both inside a sealed box. Sweep the frequency and look for cavity-mode peaks at the TEM-predicted frequencies (FACT for TEM, Jackson §8.7) versus an SLW response that ignores them. This measures internal multipath, the “R₁” question. Sources and citation notes FACT E. F. Knott, J. F. Shaeffer & M. T. Tuley, Radar Cross Section, 2nd ed. (SciTech, 2004): RCS definition, optics-region formulas (sphere πa², cylinder broadside 2πah²/λ), Rayleigh sphere 9πa²(ka)⁴, the long-body relation σ3D = 2L²σ2D/λ (times the sinc² off broadside), specular and creeping-wave mechanisms. FACT G. T. Ruck (ed.), Radar Cross Section Handbook, Vol. 1 (Plenum, 1970): ch. 3 sphere (exact series, Rayleigh and optical limits), ch. 4 cylinders. FACT C. F. Bohren & D. R. Huffman, Absorption and Scattering of Light by Small Particles (Wiley, 1983), ch. 4 (§4.4 scattering coefficients aₙ, bₙ; backscatter series), taken to the perfect-conductor limit. FACT C. A. Balanis, Advanced Engineering Electromagnetics (Wiley): ch. 11 §11.5.1–11.5.2 (conducting circular cylinder, TMz / TEz), §11.8 (sphere); ch. 4–5 (lossy media, oblique incidence). FACT J. D. Jackson, Classical Electrodynamics, 3rd ed. (Wiley, 1999): §7.3 Fresnel (Eqs. 7.39, 7.41); §5.18 and §8.1 skin depth; ch. 2 method of images; §8.7–8.8 resonant cavities and Q. FACT M. Abramowitz & I. A. Stegun, Handbook of Mathematical Functions: 9.1.88 (Neumann series for Y₀) and 9.1.22 (integral for Yₙ), used only as numerical routines. HYPOTHESIS L. M. Hively & A. S. Loebl, “Classical and extended electrodynamics”, Phys. Essays 32, 112 (2019): Eqs. (25), (26), (37), (38), (44); Table I. PDF on this hub. Erratum: Phys. Essays 35, 320 (2022), doi:10.4006/0836-1398-35.3.320. HYPOTHESIS L. M. Hively, US 9,306,527 B1 (2016), cols. 9–10, 14, 16, claim 27. PDF. M. E. Paulus & D. A. Gentile (NUWC Keyport), US 12,525,711 B1 (2026). PDF. FACT (as a published measurement) C. Monstein & J. P. Wesley, “Observation of scalar longitudinal electrodynamic waves”, EPL 59(4), 514 (2002): ℜ = B²/A² = 0.482, Eq. (24). PDF. Related longitudinal-potential work: Zimmerman (QEX 2011; MPLB 2011; JAP 2013; hub library). It is not used for any number here. FACT Hub code reused: Experiment G seawater and Joule-term functions (PR #56, branch expt-g-v0.1, head 726c896; Meissner & Wentz 2004 seawater model), read only. PR #56 and #57 are not modified. ASSUMPTION Citation precision: the textbooks are not on the box. Balanis section numbers match the publisher's 3rd-edition contents. Knott is cited at book level with the topic. Other chapter, section and equation numbers are from standard editions and should be checked against your copy before you quote them. The formulas themselves are cross-checked numerically: Mie small-ka → Rayleigh, Mie large-ka → πa², 2-D cylinder large-ka → πa, and scipy vs page JS. Hively (is the catalog hollow 3003 Aluminum ball + SMA bulkhead an acceptable Fig. 1 substitute?). This sheet is the 433.59 MHz Monstein ball-and-rod polarizer (this page and monstein.html). The other category on the hub is the 1.3 GHz Faraday-cage bench with a ¾″ KB-1820 sphere first article (setup#sphere-a / lab / fields; bifilar optional) — different frequency, different antennas, different shopping list. No balun. Experiment B feed is MW Fig. 1 / 901-9875: coax into the ball, outer as shield. Not a sleeve, not a skirt. Who this sheet is for (in that order) Dan — two paths: buy catalog hollow balls and stock brass/coax, or send Fig. 1 out for a real qty-2 quote. Catalog path is about a $400 class before shipping/tax/cutting. Exact Fig. 1 CNC is almost certainly more; we do not have a firm shop bid. Steve Morris (human tech) — five 36″ × 1/8″ brass sticks, cut to 346 mm (two rods per stick; leftover ~22 cm, do not splice); two SMA-M/M RG-316 jumpers (or the TinySA Ultra kit jumpers); 901-9875 bulkheads already purchased; optional W1 five-pack for the hysteresis follow-on. Hively — electrical question below: hollow 2.50″ 3003 Aluminum + 901-9875 vs machined 60.0 mm ball with 10H7/3H7 bore. The question, stated plainly Is this hollow 2.50″ 3003 Aluminum sphere (K-Mac KB-2016, existing ¼″ hole) plus an Amphenol 901-9875 SMA-F bulkhead through that hole an acceptable substitute for Fig. 1’s machined 60 mm aluminium ball with a 10H7/3H7 coaxial cavity, or does the missing internal shaft/bore / the 3.35 mm wall / the 3003 Aluminum alloy change the feed (outer as shield vs center conductor) enough that you would not treat them as equivalent for a 433.59 MHz ball-antenna polarizer bench? What Fig. 1 actually shows Monstein & Wesley used identical aluminium ball antennas, 6 cm diameter, coax fed to the inside of the sphere with the outer conductor as shield. Fig. 1 of the 2002 letter is a machine-shop sketch (dimensions in millimetres): R30 — 60 mm outside diameter (radius 30 mm). 10H7 / 3H7 coax bore (outer / inner fits on the coaxial cavity). 18 mm shaft into the ball. 34 mm base. Centrally fed; outer of the ball as shield. Two pieces as printed (turned ball + feed/base). Monstein & Wesley EPL 59, 514 (2002) Fig. 1. Sketch of the aluminium ball antennas. All given dimensions are in mm. Educational comparison only. doi:10.1209/epl/i2002-00136-9 Author-hosted copy (filename typo “electroydnamic”): jamespaulwesley.org. Full 433 MHz Monstein briefing: monstein.html. Proposed procurable substitute Instead of machining Fig. 1 from solid aluminium, the catalog path is a hollow 3003 Aluminum ball that already has a ¼″ hole, plus a stock SMA bulkhead through that hole. K-Mac 2.50″ hollow 3003 Aluminum Vendor: k-mac-plastics.com/balls/hollow-metal-balls.htm · KB-2016 2.50″ 3003 Aluminum hollow, wall 0.132″, ¼″ hole, $126.96 each; two (TX+RX) ≈ $253.92 before shipping. Closest catalog OD to MW’s 60 mm. 2.50″ (63.5 mm) OD — 3.5 mm larger than Fig. 1’s 60.0 mm. 3003 Aluminum, hollow, wall 0.132″ (3.35 mm). Existing ¼″ hole — intended for the SMA bulkhead (clearance + nut; not a 1/4-36 tap drill), not a 10H7/3H7 internal coax cavity. See #sma-install. Need two (TX + RX): catalog $126.96 each, ≈ $253.92 before shipping. Same vendor also lists 2.00″ KB-2014 and 3.00″ KB-2015; Butterworth’s reconstruction used ~3″ Al. Catalog cost (K-Mac KB-2016, 2.50″ 3003 Aluminum hollow): $126.96 each; two (TX+RX) ≈ $253.92 before shipping. Source: k-mac-plastics.com/balls/hollow-metal-balls.htm. Optional follow-on rods (same 9 × 34.6 cm geometry as the brass λ/2 polarizer; this is the Hively-question page, so the full rod list stays on monstein.html#parts): 1/8″ W1 water-hardening drill rod, Speedy Metals 1/8 RD W-1, $11.11 per 36″ stick; 36″ = 91.4 cm; 91.4 / 34.6 = 2.64, so two finished 34.6 cm rods per stick (leftover ~22 cm; do not splice). Four sticks yield only eight rods. Buy five 36″ sticks for nine rods (ten cuts, one spare). Five sticks ≈ $55.55 before cutting/shipping. Procurable high-carbon / high B–H-loop stand-in for Hively’s unpublished “high-magnetic-hysteresis rods,” not a claim it is his exact alloy. Brass 1/8″ 360 remains the first polarizer article. Amphenol 901-9875 SMA-F bulkhead Amphenol 901-9875 SMA female bulkhead crimp, RF Parts rfparts.com/901-9875.html. Gold-plated brass body, BeCu gold center, PTFE; cable group B (RG-316 / LMR-100A), 50 Ω. $11.90 each; qty 2 purchased 2 Sep 2026. Gender chain on this bench: TinySA Ultra RF port is SMA-F (hole). Jumper is SMA-M/M (pin both ends). Bulkhead through the ¼″ hole is SMA-F on the outside so the cable pin screws on. Prefer 901-9875 as the “coax into the interior” part (crimp RG-316, center soldered inside the sphere). See monstein.html#bulkhead. Not a claim this is Hively’s exact alloy. $11.11 × 5 = $55.55 Catalog path subtotal (balls + 2 bulkheads + 2 RG-316 jumpers + brass five-pack + W1 five-pack) ≈ $254 + $24 + $34 + $35 + $56 ≈ $403 before shipping/tax/cutting. Call it an about $400 class — not a fake precise total. The 3 ft (91.4 cm) store-bought brass and W1 sticks get cut to 34.6 cm because they are a parasitic λ/2 polarizer, not a driven λ/4 monopole. Leave them uncut only as a named deviation — why: monstein.html#rod-length. Exact Fig. 1 machine-shop path (no vendor bid) We do not have a firm shop quote. Do not treat the band below as a bid from a named shop. Fig. 1 is a turned 60.0 mm Al ball (R30) with 10H7/3H7 coax bore, 18 mm shaft, 34 mm base, two pieces, millimetre dimensions as printed. Qty-2 custom US prototype CNC (spherical turn + H7 ream/inspect) is typically in the $500–$1,500 per pair band because programming/setup dominate; aluminium bar stock itself is only tens of dollars (e.g. 2½″ 6061 round, All Metals ~$13.64 for a short cut — allmetalsinc.com 2½″ 6061 — not the finished antenna). So yes: two exact Fig. 1 spheres are almost certainly more than two hollow KB-2016s (~$254). Material is cheap; the shop hours are not. Request-quote checklist (next step for a real number) Send the Fig. 1 PDF to a local FL/RI shop or Xometry/Protolabs. Ask for a quote; do not invent one here. Quantity: 2 (TX + RX). Material: 6061-T6 aluminium (or shop-equivalent machining alloy; Fig. 1 does not name 3003). Geometry: millimetre dimensions as printed on Fig. 1 — 60.0 mm ball (R30), 10H7/3H7 on the coax bore, 18 mm shaft, 34 mm base, two pieces. Inspect: H7 on the bore. Attach: Fig. 1 page (doi:10.1209/epl/i2002-00136-9 / author PDF linked above). Still electrically small At 433.59 MHz, λ = c/f ≈ 0.692 m. The MW ball has a/λ ≈ 0.043; the 2.50″ ball has a/λ ≈ 0.046. Both are ka ≪ 1 (k = 2π/λ). The open question is not “is it a 6 cm dipole at UHF?” — it is whether dropping the internal coaxial shaft/bore, using a thin 3003 Aluminum wall, and feeding through a stock SMA bulkhead still counts as Fig. 1’s “centrally fed, outer as shield” geometry. Machine-shop / install — mating 901-9875 to the existing ¼″ hole Post-install check: VNA6000-A S11 @ 433.59 MHz — kit.html#vna6000. Printable shop drawing (Exp B) Exp A sheet (¾″) K-Mac KB-2016 already has a ¼″ (0.250″) hole. That hole is not the correct tap drill for the bulkhead thread, and this hub does not recommend tapping the existing ¼″ hole. Thread facts (Amphenol 901-9875 / typical SMA panel bulkheads): thread is 1/4-36 UNEF (¼″-36 Unified Extra Fine), major diameter ≈ 0.250″ (6.35 mm). An existing ¼″ hole is essentially the thread major diameter — little/no material left to cut threads — and is also slightly tight as a clearance for the threaded body. Preferred path — clearance + nut-clamp Clearance hole: recommended panel hole 6.5 mm (≈ 0.256″); acceptable window ~6.3–6.6 mm. If the bulkhead will not slide through the stock ¼″ hole, ream carefully to 6.5 mm / letter F drill (≈ 0.257″). Deburr so the O-ring/flange seats. Mount: nut-clamp with locknut/washer through the wall — not tapping the thin stamped hollow-ball wall. Wall on KB-2016 is ~0.132″ (3.35 mm); that is still thin for a reliable tapped thread. Mate the feed: crimp RG-316 / LMR-100A on 901-9875; feed coax into the interior; bond the bulkhead body / outer conductor to the aluminum shell (MW “centrally fed, outer as shield”). Center to a short interior post or contact as your shop plan allows. No balun on this bench. If the interior nut will not fit Exterior flange / solder fillet + conductive bond to the shell (same idea as Experiment A’s tight ¾″ access notes on setup.html#sma-shop-a). Solder/weld a small boss, then tap 1/4-36 UNEF 2B into the boss only if it is thick enough for ≥2–3 full pitches. Tap drill if needed: #3 (0.2130″) usual ~75% chart; some shops use #2 (0.2210″) for easier tapping in aluminum — confirm against the shop chart and datasheet. Temporary access cut for nutting, then close/bond the access carefully (RF continuity of the shell matters). Do not recommend tapping the existing ¼″ hole as if it were a tap drill. Thin hollow-ball walls usually cannot take a reliable tapped thread without a boss or other thickening. What this page is not Not a Meyl kit. Meyl Demo / Experimental kits are HF Tesla pancakes with spherical electrodes (kHz–low MHz). Do not treat them as a 433 MHz ball feed. See monstein.html#meyl-kit. No balun of any type on this 433.59 MHz ball feed. Coax into the ball, outer conductor as shield (MW Fig. 1 / 901-9875). Sleeve-build steps are Experiment A only: setup.html#sleeve. Different experiment (not this polarizer): 1296 MHz Faraday-cage TEM vs SLW — setup.html / fields.html. Back to the 433 MHz parts list Balls, rods, cables, and bulkhead SKUs for the 433.59 MHz bench live on the Monstein page: monstein.html#parts and #bulkhead. Dollars and the shop-vs-catalog decision are this page’s #cost table. This page asks whether the catalog 2.50″ 3003 Aluminum + 901-9875 pair is electrically close enough to Fig. 1 to buy. Rods for the polarizer (brass 1/8″ 360 first; optional W1 follow-on) are listed on monstein.html#parts. DOI: Monstein & Wesley, EPL 59, 514 (2002), doi:10.1209/epl/i2002-00136-9. title: SW vs SLW · detection gap
headings: Why this bench is adequate for SLW and not for SW
Joule loss: implication for SLW vs SW
Why the same bench is not an SW detector
What would have to be added for an SW claim
description: Why this bench is adequate for Hively SLW and not for SW. Joule loss and Puthoff US 5,845,220 mapping.
text: Lab note · 2026-09-04 · Hively EED Why this bench is adequate for SLW and not for SW Scope: Hively EED split between scalar-longitudinal wave (SLW) and scalar wave (SW). This page does not claim SW has been detected here. Simulator pages stay separate. Public summary (do not strengthen): This repository’s hardware and the published Hively/Loebl cage tests are SLW-class: they launch and receive a gradient-driven channel with suppressed B and a non-zero longitudinal E. That is sufficient to study SLW attenuation, Faraday penetration, and seawater loss. It is not sufficient to claim detection of Hively’s SW (E=B=0, C≠0). No public, replicated, modulated SW-only link through seawater and steel exists. Hull-transparent signalling remains a theoretical SW advantage, not a result of this bench. Core lock-in: this setup couples to (C, EL), so it can stress-test SLW skin-effect claims. SW needs E=B=0 at the receiver. That needs a loop + E-probe + bifilar triad, a conductor that kills the first two, and a tone that remains on the third. This bench does not log that triad. The distinction that matters Hively’s EED promotes the Lorenz leftover to a physical field C ≡ ∇·A + (1/c²) ∂Φ/∂t SLW SW Fields B=0, C≠0, longitudinal E∥∇C B=0, E=0, C≠0 Energy ∼ε E²/2 + C²/2μ ∼ C²/2μ Momentum ∼ −C E/μ none (pressure only) Source irrotational / gradient-driven current J=∇κ charge-fluctuation mismatch on short timescales Ohmic / Joule loss in a conductor J=σE is available no E → no σ E² Joule term Both are claimed to avoid the classical skin effect (no circulating B, so no Faraday eddy currents). Only the SLW still has a longitudinal E that can drive conduction current in seawater or steel. Long-range hull-transparent signalling is a stronger theoretical SW candidate than SLW — the two must not be treated as the same measurement. Joule loss: implication for SLW vs SW In a linear conductor the local ohmic (Joule) power density is pJoule = J·E = σ E² SLW: nonzero EL ⇒ expect ohmic attenuation in seawater or steel even if the classical eddy-current skin effect is suppressed (no circulating B). SW: E=0 ⇒ no σ E² term ⇒ a theoretical hull / seawater transparency advantage relative to SLW. The table row Ohmic / Joule loss in a conductor already encodes that split. Cage and seawater runs on this bench therefore stress-test SLW claims; they do not by themselves demonstrate SW transparency. Monstein & Wesley, Europhys. Lett. 59, 514 (2002), Fig. 5 — received power (dB) vs TX–RX distance x. The authors note that beyond ~100 m the signal falls faster than 1/r² (about a 1/e drop in 145 m), which they attribute to Ohmic losses from the longitudinal E inducing currents in the Earth. On this hub that is an SLW-class Joule (σ E²) implication — residual EL in a conductor — not SW proof (SW would lack that E-driven Ohmic term). doi:10.1209/epl/i2002-00136-9; educational fair-use excerpt. What this bench actually measures The working apparatus is an SLW-class launcher/receiver: balun monopole (1296 MHz build: close-fitting sleeve / bazooka; patent Fig. 2A skirt is historical) and/or bifilar pancake TinySA / conventional RF chain Faraday-cage and seawater-cell attenuation runs PMT / optical side channel as a downstream effect sensor, not a first-principles C meter Those antennas couple to the pair (C, EL). They can support SLW-class statements about gradient-driven channels, Faraday penetration vs TEM skin estimates, and seawater loss on a channel that still has EL. They cannot support “the surviving tone is a pure SW.” Cage penetration and PMT response are not SW proof. Why the same bench is not an SW detector No E-null at the receiver. Bifilar or balun monopole still responds to residual longitudinal E. No independent field inventory. SW needs three simultaneous channels: loop → B; short dipole / E-probe → EL; bifilar / second balun monopole → C + residual EL. SW is only when the first two die in a conductor and the third remains. This bench does not log that triad. No field-free potential sensor (Josephson/SQUID or Puthoff-class A–Φ architecture) in the current RF chain. Naming an architecture is not evidence a test was run. No isolated information channel. Public EED work shows CW/swept tones through cages, not a modulated payload that exists only in C. Zimmerman plasma-tube work is a different ontology. Meyl kits are not used as evidence here. Puthoff potential communication (NASA/CR-2005-213749 §3.4.2.2) The MSE Technology Applications survey for NASA Langley, Advanced Energetics for Aeronautical Applications: Volume II (NASA/CR-2005-213749, Alexander, April 2005), §3.4.2.2, summarizes Harold E. Puthoff’s U.S. Patent US 5,845,220, titled Communication Method and Apparatus with Signals Comprising Scalar and Vector Potentials without Electromagnetic Fields. Transmit framing (as reported): a time-varying signal of scalar and vector potentials without accompanying electromagnetic fields. Receive framing (as reported): an electromagnetically shielded, cryogenic Josephson Junction converts the penetrating scalar/vector potentials into conventional EM that an ordinary radio can detect. MSE reportage of Puthoff’s answers: only potential is transmitted and received; no energy is transferred as shielded E/B; and the system was built and tested “as part of a classified project” (quoted here only as NASA contractor survey reportage). NASA/CR-2005-213749 §3.4.2.2 — Puthoff patent framing: scalar and vector potentials without accompanying electromagnetic fields; electromagnetically shielded cryogenic Josephson Junction receiver. Educational fair-use crop from Alexander, Advanced Energetics for Aeronautical Applications: Volume II (NASA Langley contractor report, April 2005). NASA/CR-2005-213749 §3.4.2.2 (MSE Q&A) — survey reportage of Puthoff’s answers: potential only; no energy transferred as shielded E/B; “as part of a classified project.” Educational fair-use crop from the same NASA contractor report. Treated here as reportage only — not public SW evidence for this bench. Mapping to this page: the patent’s “potentials without EM fields” framing sits closer to Hively’s SW (E=B=0, C≠0) than to SLW (which keeps EL and therefore the σ E² Joule term). That is an ontology map, not a replication claim. Not public SW evidence for this bench: the classified-project remark in the NASA survey is not treated here as a public, replicated, modulated SW-only link through seawater and steel. It does not move the Core lock-in or the Public summary. Do not cite it (or Meyl demos) as SW evidence on these pages. Local copy: NASA/CR-2005-213749 PDF · catalogued on Library. What “fine for SLW” means launcher family: gradient-driven, B suppressed cage and seawater cells: right stress tests for no-classical-skin-effect claims PMT / decay-rate side channels: optional SLW effects, not SW proof label results SLW (or “SLW-like, EL not excluded”) SLW still has EL, so σ E² loss in seawater is expected even if eddy-current skin effect is not. What would have to be added for an SW claim Launch with the existing gradient-driven source. Receive on the three-channel set (loop / E-probe / bifilar). Insert conductivity (seawater cell, then steel plate/can). Require: loop and E-probe die; bifilar tone remains; TEM leakage paths closed. AM or slow FSK on the drive; recover the same spectrum on the surviving channel. Repo stance: SLW-class hardware; SW requires E=B=0 isolation, a three-channel (B / EL / C) conductor test, and a modulated payload on the surviving C channel. Maintainers: Keep SLW simulator / Original Pages SNR tools separate from this page. Do not cite Meyl over-unity / superluminal demos or unclassified “classified test” remarks as SW evidence. Source: SW-vs-SLW-detection-gap.md (2026-09-04); Puthoff mapping from NASA/CR-2005-213749 §3.4.2.2; range figure from Monstein & Wesley 2002 Fig. 5. Learn · Lab · Setup · Library · Monstein.

description: 1.3 GHz bifilar pancake coil calculator, RG-405 stub and sleeve balun.
text: Tools · 1.300 GHz default Bifilar pancake, RG-405 stub, and sleeve balun Merged from the Hively-style coil calculator and the RG-405 sleeve-balun page. Cut-list / BOM photos: sleeve-balun.html. Experiment A build is a close-fitting sleeve, not US 9,306,527 Fig. 2A skirt. All linear dimensions track 1/f. Default is the hub lab frequency, not 2.45 or 8 GHz. Design aid only. A sleeve (bazooka) choke is ordinary RF practice; calling the stub an “SLW launcher” is the disputed part. Do not build the patent skirt. Verify with the on-hand NanoRFE VNA6000-A (S11/S21/TDR) before any on-air use — kit.html#vna6000. 1.30 GHz 1296 MHz 2.45 GHz 8 GHz (IARD ref.) 1. Operating frequency Transmit frequency 1.300 GHz Wavelength λ = c/f — Copper skin depth — c = 299 792 458 m/s. δ = 1/√(π f μ₀ σ), σ_Cu ≈ 5.8×10⁷ S/m. Near / far field (classical) Reactive NF ≈ 0.62 √(D³/λ). Far field (Fraunhofer) r > 2 D²/λ. Electrically small rule of thumb r ≈ λ/(2π). Structure D Reactive NF ends Far field begins λ/(2π) 2. Transmitter: RG-405/U exposed center conductor RG-405/U (0.086″ semi-rigid) fixed data: Center conductor: 0.020 in (0.51 mm) silver-plated copper-clad steel Dielectric (PTFE) OD ≈ 0.066 in (1.68 mm) Outer conductor OD ≈ 0.0865 in (2.20 mm) Exposed stub length 0.25 λ Recommended stub — Hively-style notes often use λ/10–λ/4. Spherical wavefront originates near the tip. Short stub, not a magnetron probe. 3. Sleeve (bazooka choke), not a patent skirt Conductive sleeve over the outer conductor, shorted at the antenna end, open at the far end. At electrical λ/4 the open end is a high common-mode impedance. Zin = j Z₀ tan(βL) → infinite when L = λg/4 Velocity factor (air ~0.95–1.00) 0.95 Electrical λ/4 — Physical sleeve L = (λ/4)×VF — At 1.3 GHz the sleeve is ~6× longer than at 8 GHz. Length must track 1/f. Balun construction (from the original page) Install SMA (or Type N) on the source end of RG-405/U in the ordinary way. No special balun connection at the connector. Strip outer copper and PTFE for the calculated stub length. Leave a clean, straight center conductor. Deburr. Cut thin-wall copper/brass tubing (or foil tube) slightly longer than the physical sleeve. ID must clear 0.086″ with an air gap or thin dielectric. Slide the sleeve to the dielectric cut-back plane. Solder the near end all around to the RG-405 outer. Leave the far end open — no solder bridges. Optional: thin PTFE or tape between coax and sleeve to lower VF (shorter physical length). Confirm choking: S11 and a field probe on the outer conductor at the design frequency. 4. Bifilar pancake coil For a pancake facing a spherical wavefront from a small stub, a partial-wavelength OD (typically 0.1–0.3 λ) is preferred. Full-λ diameters get large and are less matched to near-zone curvature. Outer diameter 0.15 λ Magnet wire gauge Bifilar turns (each turn is a pair) 20 turns Outer diameter — Approx. inner diameter — Wire OD (single-build approx.) — Radial build (two wires / turn) — Length of one leg (fold to free end) — Buy one strand (both legs + ~12%) — Buy one long strand (~2.2 m first article). Fold it in half — the fold is the hub. Do not cut two separate wires and do not parallel the legs. AWG quick reference (approx. single-build film) AWG Bare diam. Typical OD Notes 18 0.0403 in / 1.024 mm ~0.043 in Heavy; original “table-top” notes 20 0.0320 in / 0.812 mm ~0.035 in Robust 22 0.0253 in / 0.643 mm ~0.027–0.029 in Easier to handle (default) 24 0.0201 in / 0.511 mm ~0.022–0.024 in Good compromise 26 0.0159 in / 0.404 mm ~0.017–0.019 in More turns 28 0.0126 in / 0.320 mm ~0.014–0.016 in Fine; handle carefully 5. Winding — fold first, fold is the center Cut one long strand of 22 or 24 AWG, about 2.2 m (not two separate wires). Fold it in half with a gentle U, not a crease. That fold is the center/hub (series-opposing). No hub solder. You never scrape the midpoint. Park the fold at the 6 mm hub on a Cricut / Cricket StandardGrip sticky mat. Wind both legs outward together as a pair to OD 35 mm. Same geometry as setup.html#fold. The two free ends are the RF terminals (TinySA center and ground). Do not cut the fold open. When a longitudinal E drives charge, current goes out one free end and returns on the other, so neighboring turns have opposite current and magnetic fields cancel. Net inductance ≈ 0. Do not cut two wires and solder a hub. Do not parallel the two legs. Keep interconnects short. Bench protocol lives on setup.html#fold.

description: Practical NanoRFE VNA6000-A guide for Experiments A, B and the 2.45 GHz tests: SOLT calibration, S11 of stubs and Dipole Detectors, S21 TX-RX ranging, sleeve balun checks, field power and safety.
text: Test gear · NanoRFE VNA6000-A How to use the VNA in our work Practical bench notes for Experiment A (1296 MHz), Experiment B (433.59 MHz) and the 2.45 GHz Dipole Detector tests. Written by Grok Bot for Dan Britton, 3 Oct 2026. Engineer-to-engineer, not a physics claim: the VNA only tells us what the RF hardware does (match, loss, phase), not whether any scalar or longitudinal wave exists. Status: v0.1 draft. Written from the NanoRFE VNA6000 user manual (2022/11) and specifications sheet (2022/08), the hub kit page, and public sources. Menu paths are quoted from the manual; check them against the firmware on your unit and tell us where they differ. Inferences are labelled INFERENCE. 1. Documents VNA6000-A / VNA6000-B user manual (PDF, 30 pages, 2022/11) (the operator manual; the unit is a NanoRFE VNA6000-A) VNA6000 specifications (PDF, 2022/08) NanoRFE VNA6000 product page VNA View / NanoVNA-QT software downloads (PC control, S-parameter export) Hub kit page, VNA6000-A uses by experiment (A to F) 2. What the instrument is, and its limits Parameter VNA6000-A (manual / spec sheet) Type 2-port transmission/reflection (T/R) VNA, 50 Ω, SMA female ports. Measures S11 and S21 directly. S22 and S12 only by reversing the DUT. Frequency 50 kHz to 6 GHz (covers 433.59 MHz, 1296 MHz and 2450 MHz) Port output power about -10 dBm typical (no adjustment) Max input +10 dBm RF and 5 V DC on either port. Do not exceed. Dynamic range (A) about 95 dB transmission at 200 MHz to 5.8 GHz (calibrated, IFBW 0.8 kHz, 10x averaging) Max measurable |S| 0 dB. To measure an amplifier or LNA, put an attenuator at least equal to its gain in the path. Power USB 4.8 to 5.5 V, or one 18650 cell. Only flat-top, unprotected cells fit (button-top or protected cells will not). Operating temperature 0 to 45 °C Channels CH0 = S11 (reflect), CH1 = S21 (through). Four traces, four markers. Every calibration is only valid for the frequency range it was made in. The manual says changing the sweep range interpolates the old calibration and may degrade accuracy, so recalibrate after any range change. Plan one saved calibration per band (table in section 4). 3. How Zimmerman used a VNA Supported by sources: Robert K. Zimmerman (NP4B) published the 1296 MHz transmit and receive hardware in QEX, July/August 2011, pp. 31 to 35: a 7-inch circular waveguide (about 69 cm) launching TM01, a 3 dB pad on the feed, a choke collar, and a folded fluorescent (plasma) tube receiver with about 200 mA DC bias through a bias-T. See the QEX July/August 2011 table of contents. I could not find a VNA measurement inside the QEX article itself. Haralick's 2022 slide deck, which reproduces Zimmerman's work, has a slide titled "Technical Conclusions from Vector Network Analyzer" (slide 71 of 110): a folded plasma tube receives Ez as a simple folded monopole and detects Az as a differential Aharonov-Bohm detector, and "Az and Ez can be calculated from amplitude/phase data collected with a vector network analyzer." The preceding slide (70) states that reversing the 200 mA bias polarity (floating supply, DPDT switch) shifts the detected Az by 180 degrees and leaves Ez unchanged. Slide 103 shows a Tektronix VNA. Source: haralick.org energy_conference_2022_7_3.pdf. The associated papers are Zimmerman, Macroscopic Aharonov-Bohm Effect at L-Band Microwave Frequencies, Mod. Phys. Lett. B 25(9), 2011, and Reception of longitudinal vector potential radiation with a plasma antenna, J. Appl. Phys. 114, 044907 (2013). I only confirmed the abstract page, not the VNA details in the full text. In plain terms: the VNA was used as a phase-coherent source and receiver. By logging S21 magnitude and phase with the bias polarity flipped, the two contributions (an E-like response that does not flip, and an A-like response that flips by 180 degrees) could be separated. Caveat from other hams: a QEX follow-up by George and Shelley Works, as reported in a LA3ZA blog comment, explained the bias-reversal asymmetry by cathode-position asymmetry in the tube instead. Treat the separation method as Zimmerman's claim, not settled. INFERENCE for us: the transferable idea is not the plasma tube. It is a repeatable S21 magnitude and phase measurement between a fixed TX and RX, with one controlled change at a time (polarity, orientation, wall, shield) and the difference between "before" and "after" as the result. The VNA6000-A can do that with S21 PHASE and LOGMAG traces, with the cal reference plane at the antenna feed. 4. Before every session Wear an ESD strap or touch the chassis first. Discharge cable center pins on the ground shell. Never connect a live transmitter, a bias-T with DC on it, a charged capacitor or a plasma tube bias supply to a VNA port (5 V DC max, +10 dBm max). Fit the two SMA connector savers to the VNA ports (they ship in the box) and leave them on. Finger-tight plus a light torque wrench pass (SMA standard is about 5 in-lb); do not overtighten. Use the same cables, adapters and connector savers for calibration and for the measurement. Moving or flexing a cable after cal changes phase, and S21 phase is exactly what we want. Allow a few minutes of warm-up. Let the unit reach room temperature before calibrating (0 to 45 °C operating range). Make one calibration per band, saved in its own slot, and write the slot number on the log sheet: Use Center Suggested sweep Slot Free-space wavelength Exp B (433.59 MHz balls) 433.59 MHz 380 to 490 MHz 0 69.1 cm Exp A (1296 MHz sphere / mesh) 1296 MHz 1100 to 1500 MHz 1 23.1 cm 2.45 GHz tests (DD-2450) 2450 MHz 2200 to 2700 MHz 2 12.2 cm Survey / harmonics n/a 50 MHz to 3 GHz 3 n/a The manual describes slots as 0 to 4 in one place and 0 to 6 in another; use whichever your firmware offers. 5. Calibration (SOL for S11, SOLT for S21) Use the "SOL/SOLT calibration with cable" procedure from the manual, so the reference plane is the end of the cable that mates with the DUT. If the DUT has a different connector, add the adapter before you calibrate. Set the range: STIMULUS → START and STOP (or CENTER and SPAN). Use as many points as the unit offers; more points means better resolution on narrow dips. CAL → RESET, then CALIBRATE. Attach the SMA test cable to port 1. For SOLT, also attach a second cable to port 2. Attach a LOAD to the port 2 cable end (or port 2 if no cable). Connect OPEN to the port 1 cable end. Tap OPEN. Wait for the menu item to highlight. Connect SHORT. Tap SHORT. Wait for highlight. Connect the second LOAD. Tap LOAD. Wait for highlight. For S21 (SOLT): connect the two cable ends together (or via the same adapter used with the DUT) and tap THRU. The manual says to disconnect the port 1 end of the cable afterward. Tap DONE, then SAVE n (calibration slot). The screen should show a C-number (for example C1) on the left. CAL → CORRECTION shows whether correction is on. Verify: LOAD should read deeply below -30 dB on S11 (the Smith chart trace should be at the center), OPEN and SHORT near 0 dB, and a THRU should read 0 dB with a flat phase on S21. If the load is worse than about -30 dB, redo it. Each standard tap performs its own averaged sweep, so you do not need to wait for the plot to settle. Recall later with CAL → RECALL → RECALL n. Settings saved in a slot include range, trace and marker settings, and electrical delay. 6. S11 of the stub antennas and Dipole Detectors (433.59 MHz, 1296 MHz, 2.45 GHz) Recall the cal for the band (section 4). Confirm a C-number is shown. Traces: DISPLAY → TRACE → TRACE 0, FORMAT → LOGMAG, CHANNEL → CH0 REFLECT (S11 return loss). TRACE 1: FORMAT → SWR (VSWR), CH0. TRACE 2: FORMAT → SMITH, CH0. Connect the DUT at the calibrated plane. Use the stub antenna's own SMA connector, or the bulkhead flange for the sphere feeds. Marker 1 on the lowest S11 dip: MARKER → SELECT MARKER → MARKER 1, then drag it or hold the arrow keys. Record the frequency and return loss. Marker 2 at the target frequency (433.59, 1296 or 2450 MHz). Record return loss, VSWR and the Smith chart R + jX there. That value at the target frequency is the number that matters. Return loss (S11) VSWR Rough meaning -10 dB 1.92 Acceptable for a bench check -15 dB 1.43 Good -20 dB 1.22 Very good -30 dB or lower 1.07 or lower Excellent, or a short/very lossy line: check the Smith chart INFERENCE: an electrically short stub will not be matched at all three bands. Do not tune to chase -10 dB. Log the number as the baseline and compare it after any mechanical change (new stub length, sleeve, sphere closed or open). Per device: DD-433 sweep 380 to 490 MHz, DD-1296 sweep 1100 to 1500 MHz, DD-2450 sweep 2200 to 2700 MHz. Do the 50 MHz to 3 GHz survey once per device to see where it really resonates, and recalibrate for the zoomed sweeps. 7. Sleeve balun checks A sleeve (bazooka) balun is ordinary RF practice. Cut tables for 1296 and 433.59 MHz are on the hub (sleeve-balun.html, tools.html). Use the VNA to test whether it is doing anything. Calibrate at the SMA end of the cable run, same as section 5. Measure S11 of the antenna with the sleeve fitted. Mark the dip frequency and depth. Hold the feed cable with your hand or a clamp-on ferrite about one quarter wavelength behind the sleeve, then slide it along the coax. Quarter wavelengths are about 17 cm at 433.59 MHz, 5.8 cm at 1296 MHz and 3.1 cm at 2450 MHz. If S11 moves by more than about 1 to 2 dB or the dip frequency shifts, the cable shield is still carrying common-mode current, so the sleeve is not isolating the antenna. If the trace barely changes, the balun is working (or the antenna is too mismatched to tell, so also check the Smith chart). Repeat with the sleeve removed as the control. Save screenshots of both. S21 option: put two identical antennas at a fixed spacing, set TRACE 0 to S21 LOGMAG and TRACE 1 to S21 PHASE, and compare with and without the sleeve (INFERENCE: a working sleeve should make S21 less sensitive to cable position). 8. S21 TX to RX transmission and precision ranging Port 1 drives the TX antenna and port 2 listens at the RX antenna. The path loss is real (the ideal free-space figure in the table is a far-field reference only; at these short separations near-field effects dominate, so treat it as a sanity check and not a prediction). Frequency Ideal FSPL at 1 m Ideal FSPL at 2 m Phase change per 1 mm of range 433.59 MHz 25.2 dB 31.2 dB 0.52 degrees 1296 MHz 34.7 dB 40.7 dB 1.56 degrees 2450 MHz 40.2 dB 46.2 dB 2.94 degrees With about 95 dB of dynamic range at -10 dBm, a clean S21 is available in all of these cases even with a cavity or wall in the path of 30 to 50 dB. Do an SOLT calibration at the ends of the two cables (section 5, including THRU). Use rigid or semi-rigid jumpers where you can and tape the cables down; a cable that moves during the run is a phase error. Run the traces: TRACE 0 = CH1 THROUGH, LOGMAG. TRACE 1 = CH1 THROUGH, PHASE. Optionally TRACE 2 = CH1 THROUGH, DELAY. Single-frequency ranging: STIMULUS → CW FREQ for zero span. Stand the RX on a rail, move it in fixed steps (for example 5 mm), and log S21 phase and magnitude at each step. Unwrap the phase in the PC. Phase should step roughly linearly with distance by the values in the table above; deviations are the interesting part (reflections off the case, rail, floor). Swept ranging: sweep 1100 to 1500 MHz (or another band), read the slope of phase vs frequency, or turn on DISPLAY → TRANSFORM for time-domain (enter the velocity factor with DISPLAY → TRANSFORM → VELOCITY FACTOR, 100 for free-space air). The band-limited resolution is only about c divided by the sweep width, so use CW phase for sub-centimetre work. Before-and-after: record the empty-setup S21, then each change (lid on, wall in place, polarizer rods, sphere closed), then the empty-setup S21 again at the end. The drift between the first and last empty runs is your error bar. Note: T/R VNA. The measurement is one-way, port 1 to port 2 only. To look at the opposite direction, swap the cable ends and recalibrate (do not just swap the antennas). 9. Antennas inside the spheres, and shielded boxes Reference plane: calibrate to the outer SMA bulkhead flange of the sphere (or the connector of the stub assembly before it goes in). Everything inside the sphere, including the interior coax and stub, is then part of the DUT. Hub reference parts: Exp A 3/4-inch sphere with KB-1820 and the 901-9875 bulkhead feed; Exp B 2.50-inch ball with KB-2016. See sphere.html and setup.html. Open vs closed: measure S11 with the sphere open (or half assembled) and closed. A closed conductive shell is a cavity. Narrow, deep dips that appear only when closed are cavity modes, not antenna match. Log both and say which is which. S21 through the wall (leakage / shielding check): TX stub inside, probe or antenna outside at fixed distance. Compare with the same geometry without the shell. The difference is a shielding number in dB. Use the thru-cal noise floor to know what the smallest believable number is. VNA outside, cable through the bulkhead: do not run a USB cable into a sealed Faraday run; the hub kit page already notes a USB cable is a leak path. For sealed runs, power the VNA from its internal 18650 and do not connect USB. Do not put the VNA inside the box with the experiment. Its -10 dBm swept source is a stray signal source in exactly the band you are trying to listen on with the TinySA. Use the VNA for characterization before and after, then disconnect it for the listening run. Microwave oven tests (2.45 GHz): the oven's leakage can couple into any connected antenna and put real power into the VNA port (limit +10 dBm). Disconnect the VNA, or keep the oven off, when the oven is running. Use the TinySA with 10 dB or more attenuation for oven-on measurements, as your baseline sheet already does. H10 and E5 near-field probes (Tekbox TBPS01) are passive pickups meant for the TinySA. Do not connect them to a VNA port while a transmitter is active. They can be swept S21 against a known small loop or monopole if you want, at -10 dBm, but that is a separate calibration. 10. Saving data On the unit: CAL → SAVE n stores calibration, range, traces and markers. CONFIG → SAVE stores only touch-screen and colour settings, not calibration. Screenshots: take one of every result with the marker readout visible. A phone photo of the screen is acceptable but include the C-number and the frequency axis. Touchstone files: connect USB to a PC (not near a sealed box), open VNA View (see software downloads), choose the serial port under Device, set the sweep range and calibrate (SOL or SOLT T/R), then export .s1p (S11) or .s2p. A T/R VNA only measures S11 and S21; S12 and S22 columns in a .s2p are not real data. The hub kit page also mentions NanoVNA-Saver; I have not verified it with the VNA6000-A. File names: follow the TinySA portal pattern, for example DD-1296-v1-20261004-103000-1296MHz-S11.s1p (experiment ID, version, date, time, center frequency, parameter). Upload to the data portal. The portal advertises CSV and S2P uploads; if it rejects .s1p, upload a .s2p or a CSV. Add to every log line: cal slot, cables and adapters used, battery or USB power, temperature, and whether the sphere was open or closed. 11. Field power The VNA6000 runs from an 18650 or from USB 5 V. The 4 red LEDs along the bottom-left edge show battery percentage; the screen does not. Use flat-top, unprotected cells only. The Battery Junction order BJ-777166 contains four Molicel P30B INR18650 3000 mAh unprotected flat-top cells and an XTAR VC4SL charger, which matches that requirement. Check polarity before inserting. A USB power bank also works for open-air runs. Carry spares, and keep the cells out of a hot car. The unit is rated 0 to 45 °C. Never leave a lithium cell charging unattended. Use the XTAR charger, not the VNA, to charge loose cells if you want to avoid heat in the case. 12.
